text:
Backpacking in the Ruby Mountains in northeastern Nevada. (Photo: Sydney Martinez/Travel Nevada.)Our public lands are not just wasted acres, they are economic and ecological powerhouses. While some argue that these lands would be better utilized by private owners, and look to sell off public lands for the potential payoff and tax revenue, they miss seeing the boon these lands are to Nevada as public resources.
Rural lands in the American West are famous for their recreational opportunities. And public lands are the mainstay of western outdoor recreation. Nevada’s public lands are a significant asset to the state.
Outdoor recreation is an economic powerhouse, bringing in jobs and money. In Nevada alone, outdoor recreation generates $13.7 billion in economic output and provides 75,000 jobs. These jobs include outdoor outfitters, guides, restaurants, hotels, retail, and even businesses like local grocery stores. And 40% of these economic benefits accrue to rural counties. Additionally, state and local revenue comes in through hotel, sales, gas, and rental car taxes.
Outdoor recreation on public lands is more profitable than other land uses. In Nevada, outdoor recreation contributes more money to the state’s GDP than mining. Nationwide, more jobs are provided by recreation on U.S. Forest Service lands than all the jobs provided by forest products, livestock grazing, mineral extraction, and energy production on those lands combined.
And the incredible thing about income that comes from recreation is that it’s almost inexhaustible. While mining or logging can bring income and jobs for a period of time, eventually the resources are used up, along with the money that comes with it. Recreation dollars keep coming indefinitely, especially when lands are well-maintained.
Public lands are vital to outdoor recreation. Throughout the United States, one in five jobs in outdoor recreation depend on federal public land. And rural counties with the highest percentage of federal land show increased population growth, employment growth, and personal income growth. 
And while jobs and economic growth are extremely important, protected public lands provide more benefits than just the money. Locals enjoy year-round outdoor recreation even more than do tourists, whether it be fishing, hiking, boating, or camping. Generations of local families pass on their love of the outdoors to their children and grandchildren. Locals also get the benefit of pure water, clean air, dark skies, and biodiversity that comes from protected lands. What is lost when these lands are sold off to the highest bidder is far more than the purchase price.
Federal funding to local governments is supposed to be another benefit of public lands, although recently it has been inconsistent. Nevada usually receives Payment in Lieu of Taxes (PILT) and Secure Rural Schools (SRS) funding from the federal government. PILT and SRS funds compensate local governments for non-taxable federal lands. With federal funding cuts widespread, the future of PILT and SRS payments is uncertain. In 2026, Nevada did secure $35.6 million in PILT funds and $4 million in SRS funds for local counties, and Nevada lawmakers have vowed to continue to fight for Nevada’s compensation.
With or without federal funding, Nevada’s public lands are worth protecting. Nevada’s public lands bring wealth to her communities: in revenue, in business opportunities, in jobs, in state and local tax revenue, in fishing, hunting, boating, camping, and hiking, in starry nights and pure water and fresh air. Selling off Nevada’s lands to corporations for a quick buck is like cutting down your house to use as firewood. The warmth of the money will come and then the warmth of the money will go, while our public lands are a resource that will continue to give without end so long as we keep them protected.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: $15B spending plan approved with no legislator-requested projects
description: A compromise creating a panel to review projects fell apart at the last minute, creating frustration in both chambers.
text:
Sen. Davis, R-Beaufort, pictured on the Senate floor on Wednesday, May 7, 2025, was a member of the negotiating committee that came up with the final state budget. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — The $15.7 billion spending plan legislators passed Tuesday, six weeks after the fiscal year began, included no legislator-requested earmarks but did increase tax breaks for older homeowners.
Budget negotiators in the House and Senate pointed fingers at each other over a process that lasted months longer than usual. Since July 1, the state has operated under a stopgap plan that kept spending at the same levels as last year.
SC budget deal gives homeowners smaller break, postpones decisions on local projects

Tuesday’s votes sent the spending plan to Gov. Henry McMaster’s desk. The governor has until Monday to issue his vetoes. The budget will take effect with his veto message.
Members of both chambers said they believe what ultimately passed is a good spending plan.
The budget includes money to increase teachers’ starting pay from $48,500 to $50,500, upping the entire salary schedule by $2,000. That doesn’t mean every teacher will get a $2,000 raise. Many districts pay above the state minimums by supplementing state aid with local property taxes. In districts already paying more than the new minimums, salary decisions are up to local school boards.
Also included are 2% raises for state employees, extra funding to keep operating the state’s grocery assistance program and money to settle a years-long lawsuit over a barrier island called Captain Sams Spit.
The final spending plan also includes a reduction in property taxes for homeowners 65 and older. That piece was a priority for senators, who passed a bill with a larger tax break earlier this year, but expanding the Homestead Exemption as part of the state budget proved to be a sticking point for the House.
Another part of the compromise plan, which would have created a panel of legislators to review earmarks and decide what to fund, fell apart Tuesday. The two chambers blamed each other for the idea disintegrating ahead of voting.
The panel would have had until the end of September to decide how to spend about $380 million on projects legislators requested for their districts, as well as how much to put toward the state’s cost overruns at the Scout Motors site in Blythewood. That would have meant significant cuts to the proposed projects, which exceeded a combined $430 million.
But Republicans in the House said they didn’t want to come back ahead of the November election to vote on a second spending package, said House Ways and Means Chairman Bruce Bannister.
“We’re better to just punt it to next year if we couldn’t reach some kind of resolution on the projects,” the Greenville Republican told reporters.
Senators were frustrated with the change Tuesday morning, since the earmark-review committee was part of the compromise they agreed to last month. Earmarks refer to state spending sponsored by legislators rather than requested by the agency the money flows through.
“I thought we had an understanding,” said Sen. Tom Davis, a Beaufort Republican on the negotiating committee.
Pointing fingers
Bannister said senators weren’t “negotiating in good faith.”
The House proposed more than $300 million for earmarks — what legislators prefer to call community investments — compared to the Senate’s roughly $130 million.
Bannister said the House spent more because the chamber has more members — 124 compared to 46 — and called the Senate’s requested cuts arbitrary. Senators, who represent more people in bigger districts, contend that doesn’t mean the House’s spending should be more than double.
“Their senators had their feelings hurt, or their egos cringed, as a result of the things that we did for our constituents being more than what they did for their constituents,” Bannister said on the floor.
A bridge, a stadium, a leadership center: How the SC House spends more than $300M locally

 
Senators called the House’s negotiators uncooperative, saying they refused to reduce the amount of spending despite senators being flexible.
After initially asking for the House to match the Senate’s proposal, senators asked for a reduction to $175 million, or something around that number, said Senate Minority Leader Brad Hutto.
“We were flexible in that regard,” the Orangeburg Democrat said. “They weren’t moving at all.”
What’s lost
Legislators in both chambers lamented what people will lose without earmarks in the budget.
The money goes toward local government projects and nonprofits. That includes small, rural areas without the tax base necessary to pay for necessities, such as improvements to water and sewer systems, legislators said.
Senators weren’t opposed to legislator-directed spending entirely. A lot of the money went toward worthy causes, Hutto said.
SC Senate budget includes $130M for local projects, but zero earmarks for nonprofits

Rather, the problem was that senators felt the House spent too much without enough oversight to ensure the money was going toward good causes, he said.
“These are real needs of real South Carolinians,” Hutto said. “We want to take care of as many of those as we can.”
Major projects included help on Columbia’s Congaree riverfront development and improvements to a historic swing bridge in Horry County, each of which were slated for $10 million.
Bannister asked for funding for several projects the Department of Commerce wanted but didn’t ask for in its official budget request, he said, including $7.5 million to prepare a site for a proposed undersea location for fiber optic cables in Myrtle Beach.
Davis had $3 million in the Senate’s spending plan for a transportation system connecting some of the islands off the coast of Beaufort and Jasper counties.
“I’m not saying earmarks are inherently bad,” the Beaufort Republican said. “Hell, I had an earmark in there that I wanted.”
Future earmarks
Whether future budgets will involve similar disagreements is unclear.
Bannister said he felt the relationship between the two chambers was strained, bringing into question what sort of spending might fly next year. Senators said they want more oversight in choosing projects to fund and awarding money, with more time for senators to review the House’s spending.
The process of allocating earmarks is much more transparent than it used to be. For years, legislators snuck spending into agency budgets. In recent years, McMaster vowed to veto any spending without at least some documentation.
The earmark debacle left nearly $380 million unspent in this budget, which senators said they could spend in a separate bill next session, which begins in January. Bannister said he didn’t expect legislators to spend it this fiscal year.
“The money hasn’t gone anywhere,” Hutto said.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: What happens to Utah taxpayers when a new data center comes to town? It depends on timing
description: When a data center’s walls are first raised on Utah land, neighboring property owners will likely get some tax relief. That break, however, is likely to be temporary. The enormous property values of data centers often carry complex tax questions for the municipalities that host them, a Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute brief says. What […]
text:
Construction continues on the new QTS data center in Eagle Mountain on Friday, April 17, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)When a data center’s walls are first raised on Utah land, neighboring property owners will likely get some tax relief. That break, however, is likely to be temporary.
The enormous property values of data centers often carry complex tax questions for the municipalities that host them, a Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute brief says. What initially starts with tax relief for property owners may be followed by tax volatility in the future as the state’s truth in taxation policies take effect.
“Understanding how Utah’s Truth in Taxation system treats real and personal property is essential for evaluating the long-term fiscal impacts of individual projects,” Maddy Oritt, director of public finance research at the Gardner Institute said in a statement. “Careful, project-specific analysis can help communities maximize the benefits of data center investment while minimizing unintended tax shifts for existing taxpayers.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
During its first year, a hypothetical $2 billion data center with $1.5 billion worth of personal property, like computers and other equipment, can substantially reduce the tax rate of counties — especially smaller ones, where it may represent a large portion of total tax base.
But, that equipment will rapidly depreciate. And as data center managers seek to replace it, Utah’s truth in taxation system can create a boomerang effect, shifting the tax responsibility back to homeowners and other taxpayers, the Gardner Institute said in a news release. 
That’s because of the state’s definition of “new growth.” A new building is considered to be new growth under Utah’s tax system. Servers and equipment are not.
Buildings like data centers are changing the status quo of how commercial property value works. Usually, real estate valuation far exceeds a site’s personal property valuation. But in data centers, the tables are turned.



Let us know what you think...


 


“A data center’s personal property value (primarily high-value computer equipment) can amount to three to four times the value of its real property value (large warehouse-type facilities), assuming continued investment in personal property over time,” the report says.
Taxing entities may only collect the same dollar amount of tax revenue each year unless it experiences new growth, or if it follows a prescriptive and highly-advertised process to raise taxes. So, a big, new data center coming to town and generating more revenue for the taxing entity will help other property owners to pay less in taxes during the center’s first year.
However, the quick depreciation of the centers’ equipment “may increase the certified tax rate in future years to maintain revenue neutrality,” analysts from the institute said. 
“These certified tax rate fluctuations affect all property owners within the taxing entity. Property owners, particularly in rural counties with smaller tax bases, will likely experience higher property tax volatility,” the brief says. 
That impact may be mitigated by replacing equipment in phases, the institute said. Replacing, say, 20% of it annually would substantially reduce the boomerang effect on neighboring taxpayers. An “all-at-once replacement amplifies it.”
“Policy treatment of data centers’ real and personal property, combined with how quickly data centers materialize, will shape the magnitude of these effects,” the analysts recommended.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Seismic worries fuel exodus from WA transportation agency’s headquarters
description: The Washington State Department of Transportation is relocating employees and scaling back access to its aging headquarters on the Capitol Campus in Olympia amid continuing concerns about the building’s structural integrity. On average, fewer than 50 people a day work in the four-story edifice on the east side of the campus, across the street from […]
text:
The headquarters of the Washington State Department of Transportation on July 30, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)
The Washington State Department of Transportation is relocating employees and scaling back access to its aging headquarters on the Capitol Campus in Olympia amid continuing concerns about the building’s structural integrity.
On average, fewer than 50 people a day work in the four-story edifice on the east side of the campus, across the street from the Capitol. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, daily occupancy averaged about 840 employees.
“Over the years, the building has experienced ongoing maintenance issues and has documented seismic safety concerns. To prioritize employee safety, WSDOT is reassigning most employees who work in the building to other agency facilities throughout Thurston County,” Ryan Overton, agency communications director, said in an email.   
Agency leaders began asking employees last fall to limit in-office work because of issues identified in a structural assessment by the Department of Enterprise Services, which owns the building, he said.
On Nov. 24, 2025, employees reported cracks in a lower-level office. A structural consultant hired by the Department of Enterprise Services carried out an emergency inspection. They examined the reported cracks, as well as horizontal cracking in the parking garage and found no buckling, concrete spalling or damage to the building’s structural columns, Overton said.
Though it remains open, employees “have been directed to minimize their time working in the building by using alternative meeting locations and maximizing flexible work options like telework,” he said. There is no immediate deadline for vacating the site.
Constructed between 1969 and 1970 for $8 million, the 183,000-square-foot building is designed in the shape of the letter H. It originally housed the state’s highway department before it became the Department of Transportation in 1977. 
The agency, which rents the building from the Department of Enterprise Services, has apportioned roughly three-quarters of the space for offices and the remainder for uses like storage, a resource library, laboratories and a cafeteria.
Over the years, the transportation agency’s top leaders worked there and the Washington State Transportation Commission held public meetings in a conference room a few strides down a hall from the main public entrance. Today, those doors are locked and only employees with access cards can enter.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The headquarters isn’t the only aging structure in the Department of Transportation’s portfolio of facilities.
Of 286 primary buildings — those with more than 2,000 square feet of space — 129 were over 50 years old as of June 2022, according to the agency.
Every two years, buildings are examined and catalogued in good, fair, or poor condition. This information is used to prioritize what to repair and replace.
As of Sept. 2021, only 28 of those 286 buildings were deemed in good shape, with 132 listed as fair and 126 as poor, according to the most recent capital programs overview.
Meanwhile, the current state transportation budget required the agency to end its lease at the Edna Lucille Goodrich Building in Tumwater. Approximately 478 employees worked in that building and needed to be relocated by June 30.
That’s forced the transportation department to figure out where those employees and those in the headquarters could work.
In July, the department released an update on its efforts to consolidate operations into fewer locations. It notes that some of those workers are now fully remote while others have been dispersed to the State Materials Lab and Mottman Environmental Office, both located in Tumwater, and the Olympic Region Maintenance and Administration Facility in Lacey, according to the report.
Those sites are at capacity and lack space for services, emergency operations, and parking. They also are miles apart and prevent productive employee collaborations, the report notes.
“The need for a physical headquarters building remains essential to support critical operations, coordination and public service,” it reads.
Overton said the department is working with the governor’s office, Department of Enterprise Services and the Office of Financial Management on a long-term plan that could lead to reestablishing a headquarters in a different location.
The department “takes employee safety seriously. We are also complying with budget directives and facility constraints,” he said. “These changes reflect a broader statewide effort to reduce office space while making the best use of available state resources.”
Last week, the Department of Enterprise Services announced it was selling two 1950s-era office buildings that occupy a half-block in Olympia. The state acquired the buildings in the 1980s. 
“These properties have outlived their usefulness,” Jo Aiken, the department’s chief operations officer, said in a statement.
This summer, the state is demolishing the 283,865-square-foot General Administration Building, which had been sitting vacant. Construction of that building was completed in 1956. Officials determined that renovating it would be costlier than a full replacement.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Democratic AG candidate Nate Willems proposes wage theft recovery unit
description: Nate Willems, the Democrat running for Iowa Attorney General, said he plans to create an enforcement unit dedicated to wage theft recovery if elected in 2026. Willems, a labor lawyer and former state representative, released a “Protecting Your Paycheck” policy platform Wednesday as part of his campaign for Iowa attorney general in 2026, focused on […]
text:
Democrat Nate Willems is running for Iowa attorney general. (Photo courtesy of the Nate Willems campaign)Nate Willems, the Democrat running for Iowa Attorney General, said he plans to create an enforcement unit dedicated to wage theft recovery if elected in 2026.
Willems, a labor lawyer and former state representative, released a “Protecting Your Paycheck” policy platform Wednesday as part of his campaign for Iowa attorney general in 2026, focused on combatting wage theft in Iowa — an issue he said costs Iowa workers $900 million through unpaid overtime, stolen tips, time worked off the clock and being misclassified as independent contractors rather than employees. In an interview, Willems said wage theft represents “ten times the amount of all other types of theft in the state of Iowa combined,” and said the Iowa attorney general, as the state’s top legal officer, should be focused on this problem.
“The AG’s office just has never taken that on,” Willems said. “And I think it’s past time that the AG’s office have a wage enforcement unit dedicated, not just to ensuring that the payment of wages, but also related items — whether there be falsification of time cards, whether it be failure to maintain workers’ compensation insurance, other … long-existing laws in the state, that have just never really been enforced in a systematic manner.”
The candidate proposed establishing the “first-of-its-kind” wage theft recovery unit within the attorney general’s office, a team that would have staff dedicated solely to investigating employers that violate or ignore labor laws.
Currently, there are staff within the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing (DIAL) who handle enforcement of wage and labor laws that seek to recoup unpaid wages. However, Willems said, these staff do not seek liquidated damages or attorney fees in these cases.
“Under the existing enforcement mechanism in state government, the worst case scenario for an employer that steals from their workers’ paychecks is that they essentially got an involuntary zero-interest loan, so there’s no real disincentive,” he said.
The new unit, he said, would be focused on bringing litigation against employers who violate existing labor laws — and pursuing enforcement of the laws that would discourage violations. The platform says “corporations who intentionally break the rules or chronic offenders who ignore repeated warnings” would be the focus for the unit, and that employers found intentionally or chronically committing wage theft would be subject to further investigation.
This work would involve collaboration with other entities, including local county attorney’s offices and private attorneys “when appropriate,” he said — as well as other agencies within the state government. He said he plans to work with prosecutors to pursue criminal charges instead of simply civil penalties for entities found in violation of labor laws.
The platform also proposes giving Iowa workers a “direct line” for reporting wage theft to the AG’s office. Though the wage theft recovery unit would not “have the capacity to take on each and every claim across the state of Iowa,” he said the line would provide ways to both connect workers with AG office staff when appropriate, or provide individuals more guidance on how to move forward.
“A large piece of this, of course, is education, and along with education, it’s an intake process of being able to hear Iowans’ stories from across the state,” Willems said. “… I mean, there are a lot of different ways in which this unit can positively impact this $900 million a year problem that we have.”
Willems is running against incumbent Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird, a Republican, in the upcoming election. She launched a cold case unit in the attorney general’s office in 2024, and on the 2026 campaign trail has highlighted work done during her time in office to support crime victims and law enforcement.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Blues enthusiast Morgan Freeman’s album covers 100 years of the genre
description: Morgan Freeman appears at the world premiere of "Now You See Me: Now You Don't" in New York on Nov. 10, 2025.
text:
NEW YORK — It happened out of necessity. Academy Award-winner Morgan Freeman was in Clarksdale, Mississippi, 25 years ago when some out-of-towners asked where they could hear blues music. Musicians were abundant; venues were not.
“There was no place where we could guarantee that you could go in and hear it,” he told The Associated Press. “So, we had to establish that.”
Actor Morgan Freeman, right, and his business partner Bill Luckett are shown during an interview at Ground Zero Blues Club in Clarksdale on Oct. 11, 2009. Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
Freeman and his business partners, then-Mayor Bill Luckett and Howard Stovall, were inspired to open a juke joint in Clarksdale called Ground Zero Blues Club. Then, much more recently, a team created “Morgan Freeman’s Symphonic Blues Experience,” a touring ensemble of blues musicians who marry the beloved Southern genre with classical, symphonic compositions. On Friday, they’ll release an album under the same name. (Luckett, who unsuccessfully sought the Democratic nomination for Mississippi governor in 2011, died in 2021.)
The legendary actor is a producer and narrator on the release, not a performer. That’s left up to the professionals: all-star acts like Taj Mahal, Keb’ Mo’, Shemekia Copeland, Tiernii Jackson, the Stax Music Academy Choir, the Chineke! Orchestra out of London, and many more.
“I like the blues. I like music. I cannot claim to be an aficionado. That’s not my place,” says Freeman. “I’m an enthusiast, but that’s a necessity.”
From live performances to a full-length record
Before the album, the “Morgan Freeman’s Symphonic Blues Experience” traveling performances were born out of a simple idea: How could Freeman and his team bring this music to the world?
Morgan Freeman smiles as Jackson Mayor John Horhn proclaims March 27 as Morgan Freeman Day during Morgan Freeman’s Symphonic Blues Experience at Thalia Mara Hall in Jackson on Friday, March 27, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“Blues is an important American story birthed in the Mississippi Delta out of hardship but obviously resonates with people and cultures on a global basis, both for how good it sounds, but also the message underneath it,” said Eric Meier, Freeman’s partner and co-producer on the project who joined the actor’s blues club in 2018. “We conceived of this concept to really take this music to new geographies and new audiences.”
Turning the live performance into an album meant cutting down a nearly two-hour show to around 45 minutes across 12 tracks, while still honoring the format. It includes video vignettes as well as “cinematic narration,” courtesy of Freeman, recorded at the club in Clarksdale.
“We offer a musical story, a 100-year arc from the 1930s to modern day, so the evolution of blues music,” says Meier.
Freeman’s idiosyncratic voice opens the record, describing the genre with a real poetry, delivered atop a haunting rendition of Blind Willie Johnson’s 1927 gospel blues classic, “Dark Was the Night, Cold Was the Ground.”
“This is music that gave voice to a people, to their pain, their hope and their resilience,” Freeman recites. “Music isn’t just melody, you know. It’s memory, it’s history wrapped in ribbon, the echoes of lives lived and lost, heartache and hope all tangled together. And nowhere is that truer than in the blues.”
Freeman wants to keep the blues alive
The last song on “Morgan Freeman’s Symphonic Blues Experience” sees singer-songwriter Muddy Waters’ great-nephew Keith Johnson covering Raphael Saadiq and Ludwig Göransson’s “I Lied to You” from the Oscar-winning 2025 film “Sinners.” It brings the 100-year story of blues to its coda, but it also serves as a reminder of the film’s ability to bring the genre into mainstream conversation.
That’s something Freeman hopes to accomplish, too. He wants to make sure blues is not forgotten.
“It is a responsibility that we’ve taken on. And the hope is that it, like everything else that catches on, takes root, as it were. You know, the blues is actually America’s music,” he says. “So, it’s incumbent upon us to water it, nurture it, keep it alive, keep it going.”
Meier adds that their album project predates “Sinners” — he says director Ryan Coogler told him the film’s juke joint was partially inspired by Ground Zero Blues Club; the film is set in Clarksdale after all — but it has been “a wonderful coincidence” that both works have the power to bring the blues to the masses.
And maybe one day, “Morgan Freeman’s Symphonic Blues Experience” will receive the same kind of critical praise given to “Sinners.” The album is eligible for the 2027 Grammy Awards.
“We will be submitting in multiple categories,” says Meier. “You got room on your trophy shelf, Morgan?”
“Yeah, yeah. I want it,” Freeman smiles.
Adding Grammy Award-winner to his Academy Award-winner title? “Sounds pretty good to me.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Kansas City ignored its own study — until it got sued
description: On May 14, Kansas City was told in no uncertain terms by its own consultants that its practice of racial and sex-based preferences in city contracting faced serious legal problems. The Council chose not to end the program. There was no coverage of the report in local media until my column in The Kansas City Star […]
text:
Kansas City Mayor Quinton Lucas delivers his State of the City address in February 2024 (photo courtesy of the City of Kansas City). 
On May 14, Kansas City was told in no uncertain terms by its own consultants that its practice of racial and sex-based preferences in city contracting faced serious legal problems.


The Council chose not to end the program.


There was no coverage of the report in local media until my column in The Kansas City Star a month later.


Then, on July 22, Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway filed a lawsuit against the city. That got people’s attention.


The Star finally published a few stories and at least one opinion column from an editorial writer. Others blogged about it. But much of that coverage focused on racial wealth gaps, Hanaway’s politics or the effect of the program on white male contractors.


Those are legitimate subjects for debate. But they largely sidestepped a more immediate question: What did Kansas City do after its own consultants warned that the existing program was legally vulnerable?


Mayor Quinton Lucas did more of the same when we spoke on a local radio program on July 30. While he dismissed the study’s findings, he offered no criticism of the study itself and no competing analysis or data that would challenge its findings. He could not even identify what it would take for him to change his mind on the city’s existing contracting policy.


Later that same day, Councilwoman Melissa Patterson Hazley posted a statement on social media announcing the introduction of several new ordinances, “to begin the process of reimagining Kansas City’s business enterprise programs.” FOX4KC reported on the 31st that Lucas said, “the city had already begun reviewing and revising the program months before the lawsuit was filed.”


Maybe so. But the public record raises questions about how far that work had progressed before Hanaway sued.


While the city did open a 45-day public-comment period on its Minority and Women Business Enterprise (MWBE) program after receiving the consultant’s report, it continued operating under same contracting preferences its consultants had warned could face legal challenges.


The ordinances that Lucas claims were the product of months of deliberation were introduced eight days after the lawsuit. Hazley’s own press release indicates the ordinances were meant “to begin the process” and were the result of the consultant’s report, “and the lawsuit subsequently filed by our own state attorney general’s office.”


Four of the five ordinances are largely overlapping alternatives. Ordinances 260688 and 260689 would suspend different combinations of the city’s MWBE and construction-workforce programs. Ordinances 260690 and 260691 would repeal different combinations of those same programs. These are not five complementary parts of a carefully assembled package; they are competing options for what the council might do.


The fifth, Ordinance 260692, attempts to establish the replacement small-business program. It runs 49 pages — it looks unfinished.


It contains unresolved drafting choices such as “three / five consecutive years.” It refers to “Emergency contracts as defined in Code Section XXXX Chp 2.” It is inconsistent with capitalization and formatting, uses “13cfr” instead of “13 CFR” and includes obvious grammatical mistakes. One provision refers to work performed with a firm’s own “focus,” apparently where “forces” was intended. Another uses the plural “cities” where it presumably means the possessive “city’s.”


Councilman Johnathan Duncan’s name is misspelled as “Dunca” in the ordinance’s sponsor line.


None of the five measures was accompanied by a substantive docket memorandum explaining its legal, administrative or financial consequences.


Perhaps city officials began discussing changes soon after the May 14 consultant presentation; the public record does not establish when drafting began. And perhaps early versions of city ordinances routinely contain placeholders and typographical errors.


But the known timeline is hard to ignore. The council had the consultant’s findings for more than two months without suspending, repealing or materially changing the program. It then produced five overlapping ordinances eight days after the attorney general filed suit.


The councilwoman promoting the package expressly connected it to that lawsuit. The replacement ordinance contains the sort of placeholders, alternatives and mistakes ordinarily found in an internal working draft — not legislation that appears ready for public consideration.


The urgency became explicit at the council’s Aug. 11 Finance Committee meeting. Without objection, the committee recommended passage of Ordinance 260690, which would repeal the city’s existing MWBE program, and Ordinance 260692, which councilmembers described as a temporary small-business substitute while the city reimagines the program. The committee held the other three alternatives—260688, 260689 and 260691.


Councilmembers and Mayor Lucas repeatedly connected the need to act quickly to Hanaway’s lawsuit and an upcoming court hearing. Whatever work may have begun before the lawsuit, it was plainly the lawsuit—and its immediate legal timetable—that forced the council to choose among its unfinished alternatives.


The city’s own May presentation laid out a sensible process: conduct a gap analysis, identify necessary legislation, develop an implementation plan, determine staffing and budget needs, and train employees. If that work occurred before July 30, the city should show it.


For now, the available evidence supports a much less flattering conclusion: Kansas City paid for a study, received a warning about its program’s legal vulnerability, left that program in place for more than two months and moved publicly toward major changes only after Hanaway sued.


Mayor Lucas has repeatedly complained about the waste of city and state tax dollars on the lawsuit. The Finance Committee has now recommended ending the existing MWBE program and temporarily replacing it with a small-business program. But it should not have taken a lawsuit—and the pressure of an approaching court hearing—to produce that decision.


The council had its consultant’s warning in May. It could have acted before Hanaway sued. Any avoidable cost to state taxpayers for bringing the lawsuit or local taxpayers for defending it rests with a council that waited until litigation forced its hand.


If you don’t want to be sued, don’t wait until after the lawsuit to stop breaking the law.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Food insecurity in NJ nearly doubled over four years, new report says
description: Food insecurity nearly doubled in New Jersey between 2020 and 2024, according to a new analysis of federal data by the nonprofit Feeding America.
text:
Nonprofit advoacy group Feeding America has surveyed food insecurity since 2011 and produces an annual study to help illustrate the scope of the problem. (Photo by U.S. Department of Agriculture)Food insecurity nearly doubled in New Jersey since 2020, with some 1.2 million people struggling to regularly afford food here, according to a nonprofit analysis of federal data.
Statewide, 13% of Garden State residents could not always count on three meals a day in 2024, the latest federal figures available, up from 7.4% in 2020, according to a new analysis of U.S. Department of Agriculture figures released by the nonprofit advocacy group Feeding America. That included nearly 330,000 children, the analysis found.
Hunterdon County had the least food insecurity in 2024, with just 7.2% of its residents struggling to put food on the table, while Hudson had the highest rate, with 19.1%, Feeding America found.
Feeding America has surveyed food insecurity since 2011 and produces the annual “Map the Meal Gap” study to help illustrate the scope of the problem. Nationwide, nearly 48 million people — 14.4% of Americans — meet the federal definition of food insecure, meaning the household did not earn enough to always afford food.
The latest report notes that the U.S. Department of Agriculture has since canceled its collection of food-security data.
“Feeding America is collaborating with the nationwide network and partners to explore alternative data sources to ensure local updates can continue in 2027 and beyond,” the organization said.
In New Jersey, close to 900,000 people benefit from federally funded food stamps, which provide cash payments based on their income level to help them afford groceries. These payments, which average $194 a month, have been shown to reduce stress and boost the local economy, prompting some $33 million in direct spending between 2023 and 2025, according to a report commissioned by the state Department of Human Services, which oversees the food stamp program, formally known as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP.
“SNAP remains a critical lifeline that helps ensure families can meet their basic needs and maintain food security,” Human Services Commissioner Stephen Cha said when the office released that data in June.
New Jersey’s food stamp program costs $1.9 billion annually, most of it traditionally covered by federal funding. Feeding America said it would have cost another $920 million to eliminate food security in New Jersey in 2024.
Changes enacted by the Trump administration recently shifted some of the cost of the food stamp program to state governments. Other changes, including new rules requiring certain recipients to prove they are working, in school, or caring for a loved one at least 20 hours a week, could reduce benefits for some people and force at least 47,000 people from the food stamp program entirely, experts warn.
In 2022, the state launched the New Jersey Office of Food Insecurity, as part of the Department of Agriculture, to help more families access nutrition. New Jersey had the fifth-lowest prevalence of food insecurity nationwide in 2024, according to the office.

title: ‘Extreme drought,’ record-breaking heat confront Wyoming ranchers with difficult choices
description:
About 80% of the Cowboy State is in severe drought or worse as water restrictions take a toll.
The post ‘Extreme drought,’ record-breaking heat confront Wyoming ranchers with difficult choices appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Last winter’s low snowpack spurred many Wyoming ranchers and farmers to get ready for a particularly dry summer. To make matters worse, there’s been unrelenting heat and very little rain.
“We could see it coming all winter,” Upper North Platte Water Users Association board member Jeb Steward told WyoFile this week. 
Stock growers in Carbon County, where Steward lives, began culling cow-calf pairs as it became evident that spring runoff had peaked early (March, in many cases) and as first-in-time-first-in-right irrigation restrictions came early, prompting many to spend their limited, legally available water on hay pastures to graze instead of growing feed, he explained.

Jeb Steward of Encampment is pictured at a public meeting in Saratoga Jan. 12, 2023. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)

“I know of a few — they’re going to move their [remaining] cattle to Nebraska in the fall and put them on corn stalks,” Steward, a former Wyoming legislator, said. “They’re just trying to figure out ways to stay in business.” 
Mountain-fed waterways that typically help wet crop and pasture lands in Steward’s neck of the woods are parched. One tributary feeding the Encampment River at Riverside is “damn near down to a piss-trickle,” Steward added. 
About 80% of the Cowboy State is in severe drought or worse — 45% is suffering extreme drought, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. Wyoming State Engineer Brandon Gebhart delivered a dire water report to the Legislature’s Select Water Committee last week detailing water- and drought-related hardships throughout the state.
In January, his agency began juggling dozens of legally enforced water restrictions throughout the state, including some that limited water use for those who have primary access to water based on first-in-time-first-in-right ownership dating back to the 1800s, Gebhart said. Many small reservoirs are approaching, or have already reached, “deadpool,” meaning no water can flow downstream. Some irrigators were forced to shut their spigots after just 10 days or less, he added. If the next water season is a repeat of this season, water users reliant on the North Platte River could see restrictions imposed on them from downstream Nebraska for the first time in decades. 
Most of Wyoming is experiencing severe drought in August 2026. (U.S. Drought Monitor)
“Some of the drainages in our state continue to be on pace to be the lowest on record,” Gebhard told the legislative panel, noting that this year rivals 2002 as among the driest in recent history. “It looks like we’re on pace, in some of our portions of the state, to track that or even be worse than 2002.”
The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s “pasture and range condition” index rated half of Wyoming as “very poor” earlier this month. Averaging 76.9 degrees Fahrenheit, July was the “warmest on record” since 1895 throughout the contiguous United States, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
“Wyoming recorded its warmest July and warmest month on record, with temperatures 5.1 [degrees Fahrenheit] above average and 0.9 [degrees Fahrenheit] warmer than its previous July record set in 2007,” NOAA said.
High-n-dry
Perennial streams are a rare commodity in northeast Wyoming, forcing ag producers to be adept at making the best of ephemeral flows from spring runoff. But many ponds and springs have already dried up. 
“It’s pretty serious,” Niobrara County rancher Jeb Hanson told WyoFile. It’s so dry that when a heavy rain came through a few days ago, it petered out in five minutes, and within an hour the wind kicked up a dust storm in the same spot.
“It’s getting where the grass fires aren’t moving real fast because a lot of places don’t have a lot of grass [to burn] anymore,” Hanson said.
Water wells are expensive to drill here, Hanson said, but the investment — for those who can afford it — is key to surviving a dry year like this one. “It’s normally a profitable way to ranch here. But years like this, it’s probably not the best situation. We’re not as drought-proof as someone that’s close to a big river.”
Crook County rancher Thayne Gray on the family’s Warbonnet Ranch outside Moorcroft on Sept. 23, 2021. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
About 100 miles north, outside Moorcroft, Thayne Gray is wrestling with a choice common to cattle ranchers across the state. You can significantly trim your herd — after all, cattle are fetching strong prices, and ranch operations need the extra cash for supplemental hay to get the rest of the herd through the winter. But it’s a gamble, Gray says. Cows might be more expensive next year, and it takes time to replenish a culled cow-calf herd.
“Our thought is to keep as many cows as possible because of the low national herd inventory,” Gray said. He figures the ranch will have to spend 30% more on hay this year, which is approaching $300 per ton. 
“Hopefully, the banks will carry us through with theories of better times to come,” Gray said. “So, yeah, we’re enjoying high [beef and cattle market] prices right now, but high inputs are keeping us from just really raking in the dough.”

title: Rural health panel divvies $205M in federal funds for Wyoming healthcare
description:
Panel assigned money to hospitals, EMS services and maternal care in attempt to shore up medical access. 
The post Rural health panel divvies $205M in federal funds for Wyoming healthcare appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
In its marathon meeting Tuesday, Wyoming’s new rural health advisory panel earmarked roughly $200 million in President Trump’s Rural Health Transformation funds to a range of applicants hoping to bolster the state’s fragile healthcare system. 
Recipients ranged from hospitals to EMS providers, as well as maternal healthcare and workforce development organizations. 
It was a big push, but alacrity has been a theme running through the process since the federal government launched the program in September. A tight schedule of deadlines has necessitated haste. 
“We know that this has been a rapid process,” Wyoming Department of Health Deputy Director Franz Fuchs told the committee. But, he stressed, it’s important. “We want to use this as an opportunity to make the best decisions with these funds for the state of Wyoming.” 
Entities seeking federal money had a month to submit applications to the state. They were due by Aug. 3. 
That means the advisory committee — which consists of state lawmakers, local elected officials, doctors and health officers — had just over a week to sift through proposals. 
Health department staff eased the process with a series of funding recommendations based on application scores. The committee also approved several awards conditionally as long as applicants meet criteria such as program sustainability. 
The state is required to finalize which entities to fund by the end of October.  
Gov. Mark Gordon encouraged the committee to stick to initiatives tailored to the practical circumstances of life in Wyoming — which may not match up to “the sort of nice talking points on a federal level.”
The plan Wyoming has put together to secure the funds, Gordon said, “is probably one of the most remarkable opportunities to kind of set the course correctly for Wyoming.” 
Thinking big 
The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by President Donald Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The program is designed to funnel $50 billion to states over five years to stabilize and strengthen rural hospitals and providers. It aims to offset some of the federal healthcare dollars cut by the same legislation.
The application process for states unfolded in about two months last fall. Wyoming Department of Health gathered input via stakeholder conferences, public meetings and an online survey. Using that input, department staff drew up a state application. 
The document identified four main areas for Wyoming improvements: access to emergency medical care, rural workforce supply, health technology transformation and “Make Wyoming Healthy Again.”
Specific initiatives it proposed include forging cooperative agreements for EMS agencies to work on a regional basis and funding educational awards related to clinical tracks for healthcare providers. 
Large swaths of Wyoming have 911 response times that exceed 30 minutes. (Wyoming Department of Health) 
When federal administrators with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services approved Wyoming’s application in December, Wyoming received $5 million more than it requested — the second-largest award per capita, behind Alaska.
However, the state ultimately removed two core proposals from its original application. One was a so-called perpetuity. The system of investments that could generate revenue for Wyoming healthcare programs indefinitely did not pass muster with federal administrators. The state also ditched a state-operated public catastrophic insurance plan after legislators frowned on the idea.
Despite that, healthcare providers and advocates celebrated the opportunity to inject millions into programs that could bolster rural hospitals, workforce and preventative health measures.
Wyoming opened applications in July to entities including hospitals, clinics, telehealth platforms, transportation coordinators and fiscal agents.
The specifics
Wyoming passed a law this spring outlining how to spend the Rural Health Transformation Program money. Among other things, it created an advisory committee. 
That committee met Tuesday. Members represent various facets of Wyoming’s healthcare landscape, from Cheyenne Healthworks CEO Tracy Brosius to Carbon County Commissioner Sue Jones, Teton County Health Department Director Travis Riddell and Wyoming Hospital Association President Eric Boley. Several state lawmakers also sit on the panel. 
The committee had an “aggressive” agenda to keep up with the “aggressive” timeline, Wyoming Department of Health Director Stefan Johansson said. 
“We owe the federal government a report, basically a progress report, by the end of August,” he said, “which indicates to them where we are on these initiatives in terms of going from inception to implementation.”
The committee reviewed the applications by category. 
Much of the funding it approved was for a critical access hospitals initiative. Because hospitals under this designation are reimbursed by Medicare based on actual costs, it helps them remain financially viable. 
A man leaves the patient entrance of Ivinson Memorial Hospital in Laramie in March 2020 (Andrew Graham/WyoFile)
The committee approved more than $41 million in funding under this category. This represents a significant infusion of money for Wyoming facilities, including $3 million for Memorial Hospital of Converse County, $3.75 million for Sheridan Memorial Hospital and $1.75 million for Hot Springs County Hospital District. 
“We want to make sure that when we make these investments, that the hospital is building a business model that is sustainable for the future,” Fuchs said. 
Three hospitals were denied funding under this initiative because, among other reasons, they applied late. They were Platte County Hospital, Washakie Medical Center and Torrington Community Hospital, which are all owned by Banner Health. 
Under the initiative, the committee also approved funding to allow hospitals to maintain what are known as “swing beds.” The beds allow facilities to keep long-term patients, alleviating local nursing facility shortages and travel barriers. 
For the EMS regionalization initiative, the panel approved $2.2 million for Laramie Fire Department and city of Laramie, $2.2 million for Crook County Medical Services District and $1.7 million for Campbell County Health Emergency Medical Service, among other awards. 
The committee approved $18 million for graduate medical education programs, with money going to facilities like the University of Utah and University of Wyoming, with the latter contingent on a five-year service commitment. 
The committee also approved more than $30 million for to pay an entity to administer workforce education support to individuals. 
After members had gone through each category and assigned spending — including several conditional approvals — $17 million remained. Committee members agreed to split the funds, directing the health department to contract with one or more fiscal agents to develop grants to promote EMS sustainability and labor and delivery.
“There’s a lot of critical issues facing Wyoming, but I don’t know that there’s a larger one than standing up our EMS when we have the opportunity to do it,” said committee chairman Heath Steel, executive vice-president of Volunteers of America of the Northern Rockies. 
Sonographer Tommi Taylor performs an ultrasound on a patient at Casper Obstetrical & Gynecological Associates in July 2026. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile) 
Boley with the Hospital Association added that maternity deserts “are a huge issue in our state.”
He also said Wyoming hospitals and healthcare facilities are “in desperate need” of capital construction, which the federal agency restricts under the program. 
“I think we need [Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services] to get realistic with their definition of how the funding can be used,” Boley said. “We have a lot of 70-year-old buildings in our state that are falling apart around the patient’s ears, and if we want to transform healthcare, if we want to be prepared for the future, we need to bring those facilities up” to date.

title: Think your dog makes you safer in bear country? The data say otherwise.
description:
New analysis of more than 300 bear encounters suggests canine companions often increase odds of conflict and rarely serve as the early warning systems many recreationists assume.
The post Think your dog makes you safer in bear country? The data say otherwise. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Earlier this summer, I was jogging on a local trail with my 7-year-old black lab mutt, Camas, when she suddenly froze. The fur along her spine bristled. Then she let out a single, sharp bark — a timbre I’d never before heard. 
I caught the unmistakable musk of an animal and my hand shot to the bear spray on my chest. Halfway up a tree less than 20 yards away, a beautiful, small cinnamon black bear stared back at us.

The author’s companion, Camas, in bear country. (Nick Mott)

The bear scampered off as Camas growled, standing her ground in front of me on the trail. “Good girl,” I told her, my heart rate slowing to a normal pace. My dog, I assumed, warned me early of a potential threat. I was proud. 
In bear country, common wisdom holds that dogs serve as early bear alarms, or even deterrents. That belief, however, has long rested mostly on anecdote. Until recently, almost no one had tested whether it was actually true.
A new study in the Journal of Wildlife Management analyzed bear-dog conflicts involving black, polar and brown bears from Alaska to Florida. The results challenge the idea that dogs make people safer in bear country and they have me rethinking my relationship with Camas in the woods.

(Journal of Wildlife Management)

“If you think a house pet is likely going to be your bear, not only detector but deterrent, you might want to think twice about that,” lead author of the paper Tom Smith told me over Zoom, one of his dogs begging for attention in the background while mine snoozed next to me. 
Smith, a research wildlife biologist at Brigham Young University in Utah, analyzed 326 bear-dog encounters spanning more than a century, drawing from newspaper articles, federal and state government reports, books, records compiled by other bear specialists, and internet searches. 
Smith began working with bears more than 30 years ago in Alaska’s Katmai National Park. He’s published influential research on bear spray and guns as bear deterrents, and has become one of the world’s leading experts on human-bear interaction. “As soon as you become the bear guy, then everybody comes running to you for advice on how to be safe,” he said. “So I thought, ‘I’m going to have to get to the heart of this.’”
Smith has long been interested in the way dogs impact humans’ odds of an encounter in bear country. But the issue became urgent and tangible to him following a 2023 attack that left two people and their dog dead in a tent in Canada’s Banff National Park. The issue hasn’t gone away. This summer alone, a jogger and his dog were mauled near Island Park, Idaho, while recordings of separate encounters involving dogs in Banff and Alberta went viral online. 
The findings
The data show people are largely unprepared for bear encounters and naive to their possible consequences. Dogs ran away, fought with bears, provoked confrontations, drew owners in to fight off bears barehanded, and even boomeranged bears back to people. 
The first surprise in the data was how few people carried any deterrent at all. That might be because people thought, erroneously, Smith says, that dogs would be sufficient to keep bears away. Recreators wielded bear spray in only about a tenth of cases and a firearm in roughly a third. All told, five people and 56 dogs died in the encounters Smith analyzed.
Contrary to some common wisdom, dogs also weren’t effective warning systems for bears. In fact, they alerted their owners early of a bear in only 1 in 11 of the encounters the study analyzed. Dogs provoked the bear, instigating the encounter, in more than half the cases. After the bear conflict began, things didn’t look much better: Dogs tangled with bears about 40% of the time, ran away in 20% of encounters, and didn’t engage at all in about 17% of cases. So much for dogs being excellent protectors.

(Journal of Wildlife Management)

Other findings were less surprising. Leashes were a major decider in the severity of the interaction. Unleashed dogs were involved in six times as many incidents as leashed pets. Smith said dogs without a leash can dart ahead of owners or crash through brush and spook a bear. Canines can also act as bear boomerangs. In 27 of the encounters, dogs brought a bear back to their owners. In 70% of these instances, the dog owner was injured. Worse yet, many owners in the data came to rescue their pet when it got in a scuffle with a bear, often with no deterrent. The result: 85% of the time, those owners were injured. 
Additionally, the data reinforced something bear experts have known for years: the larger the group of people, the less likely the encounter. However, the presence of a dog dramatically shifts that risk. Dogs roughly doubled the odds of a conflict compared to the same-sized groups with no canine companions. 
Taken as a whole, the data paint a portrait in which bears and domestic dogs don’t get along. Smith suspects it’s part of the long evolutionary relationship between bears and wolves. For thousands of years, wolves competed with bears for food, killed cubs and even kicked bruins off carcasses. Some of this behavior is on public display in places like Yellowstone National Park, where populations of both species flourish. Modern dogs may still trigger those ancient instincts. 
Smith recognizes limitations and nuance in his data, too. For one, it’s important to note that the dogs in the analysis were domestic companions, not highly-trained guardian dogs meant to fend off predators — which data show can reduce bear presence at ranches and farms. Also, data on human-bear conflict inherently shows a bias, depicting only the encounters that went majorly wrong rather than the majority of experiences when people venture into the places bruins live and the species coexist without incident. “For the most part, people and their dogs pass through bear country without incident,” Smith wrote in the paper.
Should your pup join the hike?
“The takeaway isn’t to keep dogs out of bear country,” Smith said. “The takeaway is there are things you can do that greatly improve your odds.”
Best practices, backed by Smith’s data, say to travel in groups, eliminate smells if you’re camping and make noise. Bear bells, he says, don’t work. Above almost all else? “You have no business being in bear country without a deterrent,” Smith said. 
Dogs just don’t cut it on that front. According to Smith, bear spray has the highest likelihood of fending off an aggressive bear for the vast majority of recreationists in bear country. But firearms can work too for experienced users. Carry your spray (or gun) where you can reach it in a split second. No matter what deterrent you choose, practice with it. Bear encounters can happen in seconds. 
Sota the pudelpointer follows a ridge in the northern Wyoming Range in 2023. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
If you do take your dog, consider a leash. “It’s not just dogs and bears,” Smith said. “It’s also dogs and everything else.” Smith’s own dog had been sprayed by a skunk twice in the last month. Mine finds few greater joys in life than chasing ground squirrels, marmots and grouse. So, we’re both faced with navigating how to behave in wild places with these family members that, if they see a deer or elk or bear, may not be able to hold themselves back.
Since talking with Smith, I’ve thought about the role Camas plays in bear country in a more nuanced way. She’s warned me about bears — even since that encounter on my jog. But she’s also ignored bears less than 30 yards away, chased wildlife she shouldn’t and, even in her younger days, treed a black bear.
The lesson isn’t that dogs don’t belong in bear country writ large. It’s that they’re dogs. If recreating in bear country is an odds game, they’re not doing you any favors. As much as we love and trust them, they’re unpredictable. And they can make things worse as often as they make things better. 
“It’s a personal thing, it really is,” Smith said. “We work in statistics with a pool of instances. But you are not a pool of instances. You’re you.”
The post Think your dog makes you safer in bear country? The data say otherwise. appeared first on WyoFile .

title: State management of grizzlies would be a disaster
description:
Grizzlies make the landscapes we share feel larger, wilder and more alive. They deserve more than bare-minimum population objectives, write guest columnists Chris Kassar and Ryan Kempfer.
The post State management of grizzlies would be a disaster appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
We moved to Jackson because few places still feel as whole as this region does, with Grand Teton and Yellowstone national parks, abundant public lands and waters and a quality of life shaped by wildness.

Opinion

Most of all, we moved here for the incredible wildlife. That includes elk, moose, mule deer, wolves and pronghorn. And also, the iconic grizzly bear, a true symbol of Northern Rockies wildness and the vast, connected landscapes that sustain it.
Our business also benefits from having these magnificent animals in the landscape. Every year, people come from around the world to watch and photograph wildlife. They are in awe of the abundance and diversity here — the sight of a moose coming out of the willows on a misty morning or an elk herd during the rut in fall.
But nothing moves people more than seeing a grizzly bear.
As wildlife guides, we see this again and again. Each time we meet a new group, we ask what they hope to see most. Without fail, the answer is “a grizzly.” Visitors know there are only a handful of places in the Lower 48 where seeing one is even possible. They understand, instinctively, that grizzlies mean something larger: intact habitat, protected public lands, and a landscape still wild enough to hold them.
Yet at the same time, grizzlies are fragile. By that, we mean they are a conservation-reliant species with slow reproduction, large habitat needs and little margin for unnecessary mortality.
They need habitat to roam and survive; wild places where they can gather and scavenge natural foods and rear young free from disturbance. They’re among the slowest-reproducing mammals in North America, and that fragility is why grizzlies were nearly wiped out during the western expansion of our country.
We treated them like vermin to clear the land for livestock, and it showed. By the early 1970s, only an estimated 136 grizzlies remained in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. The population was dangerously close to disappearing. In total, fewer than 600 grizzlies remained in the Lower 48 states, with the largest population living in Glacier National Park and the surrounding wildlands.
Today, there are roughly 1,900 grizzlies in the Lower 48, clearly a conservation improvement. But that didn’t just happen. It took tremendous work over decades by federal and state wildlife officials, conservationists, landowners and communities.
Now the Trump administration is ready to pull the rug out from the progress we’ve made recovering grizzlies and hand management to the states of Montana, Idaho and Wyoming. Their argument is simple: Grizzlies have met the population targets in existing recovery plans, so the job is done and the states should take over management. They’re proposing to do this under a provision of the Endangered Species Act that allows some take of animals under specific conditions, known as “4(d)” rules.
But meeting minimum numbers in isolated recovery zones is not the same as lasting recovery. Those targets were created when grizzlies were on the brink, and we have learned far more since then about what they need to survive over the long term. In 2025, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service laid out a broader vision for recovery — one that recognized the importance of connected habitat and connected grizzly populations across the region. Wyoming, Montana and Idaho rejected that vision and challenged the decision.
That response says a lot. Rather than managing for true recovery, the states appear intent on managing for the fewest grizzlies they can get away with, in populations kept isolated from one another. Montana has pushed to make it easier to kill grizzlies linked to livestock conflicts on public lands. Wyoming even floated the idea of giving elk hunters “kill coupons” for grizzlies. That is not modern wildlife management. It is a throwback to the same 1800s mindset that nearly wiped grizzlies off the map in the first place.
At the same time, the Trump administration is working to industrialize our public lands through a range of policies that protect wildlands. These include undoing the Roadless Area Conservation Rule on national forests, a major push for industrial logging, and moves to dramatically increase motorized use across public lands. All of these are major threats to grizzlies because they rely on secure habitat, as do many wildlife species.
Long-term recovery depends on more than counting bears. It depends on limiting unnecessary killing, protecting movement between populations and allowing grizzlies enough connected habitat to remain genetically healthy and secure for generations to come.
We don’t value grizzlies only because our business depends on people coming here to see them. We value them because they change how this place feels. Their presence makes the landscape feel larger, wilder and more alive. It reminds us that we are lucky to share these public lands with animals that still embody true wildness.
Grizzly bears still need federal safeguards and robust habitat protections because the states have made their management intentions clear. These bears are not just management units or population targets. They are national treasures, and their presence is part of what makes this region whole, wild, and unlike anywhere else in the Lower 48.
Public comments on the proposed changes to protective grizzly bear regulations are due by Aug. 17.

title: Legislators, anti-abortion group promote data that says ID hasn’t lost OB-GYNs. Doctors push back.
description: Dr. Kylie Cooper, a maternal-fetal medicine physician, practices in Minnesota after she left Idaho in the spring of 2023, shortly after Idaho’s criminal abortion ban went into effect.  Although it has been nearly three years since she left, Cooper retained her Idaho medical license, she said.   “I have a sliver of hope that maybe things […]
text:
As campaigns for and against a proposed voter initiative that would repeal Idaho's abortion ban ramp up, an anti-abortion advocacy group has begun to question whether Idaho OB-GYNs have left the state since it went into effect. The state says it's hard to track, and doctors say the effect has been real. (Thanasis Zovoilis/Getty Images)Dr. Kylie Cooper, a maternal-fetal medicine physician, practices in Minnesota after she left Idaho in the spring of 2023, shortly after Idaho’s criminal abortion ban went into effect. 
Dr. Kylie Cooper, a maternal fetal medicine specialist .(Photo courtesy of Kylie Cooper)
Although it has been nearly three years since she left, Cooper retained her Idaho medical license, she said.  
“I have a sliver of hope that maybe things will get better in the future,” Cooper said. 
Cooper’s license, as well as every other active medical OB-GYN license in the state, would have shown up in data recently shared by the Idaho Family Policy Center — a Christian advocacy group that lobbied for Idaho’s criminal abortion ban and helped author a 2022 law allowing family members of a fetus aborted after six weeks to the sue the abortion provider for a minimum of $20,000. 
As campaigns for and against Proposition 1 — a citizen-led ballot initiative that would repeal the state’s strict abortion ban and provide protections for contraception and in vitro fertilization, ramp up for the Nov. 3 general election — the abortion law’s effect on the number of practicing OB-GYNs in Idaho has become a talking point. But determining the true number of doctors providing obstetrician-gynecologist care in the state isn’t easy. 
The state has said the number of active licenses do not reliably reflect how many OB-GYNs are currently practicing in Idaho. 
The Idaho Family Policy Center has underscored the licensing data to question, and file a lawsuit over, a 2025 Boise State University study that found Idaho had lost 35% of its OB-GYNs since 2022, when the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade and Idaho’s criminal abortion law went into effect.
The Idaho Family Policy Center posted this graph on Facebook Aug. 3. (Screenshot)
The policy center on Aug. 3 posted a graph on Facebook showing the number of active licenses increasing from 2022 to 2025, writing “Pro-abortion advocates are lying to you.” 
“The number of actively licensed OB/GYNs in Idaho has actually increased since our pro-life laws went into effect, according to data from the Idaho Board of Medicine,” the post said. 
The center’s posts about the licensure numbers have been shared by Idaho state legislators, such as Twin Falls Republican Rep. Clint Hostetler and Middleton Republican Rep. Tammy Nichols. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Idaho medical board says it has no ‘reliable way’ to count active physicians 

The Idaho Board of Medicine, which is under the state Division of Occupational and Professional Licenses, shows the number of active OB-GYN licenses in Idaho going from around 280 in 2022 to just under 340 in 2024, according to the policy center’s graph. 
Bob McLaughlin, spokesperson at the Division of Occupational and Professional Licenses, known as DOPL, told the Idaho Capital Sun that there are limitations to the state’s data to try and determine how many doctors are practicing in the state. 
“1. It’s a two year license,” McLaughlin said in an email. “The number of licenses could fluctuate since the licensee is required to renew on their birthdate every two years and not annually. 2. Physician specialty information is self-reported and is not required as part of licensure. DOPL does not have a reliable way to determine how many licensed physicians are actively practicing in Idaho. 3. Our records reflect licensure status, and an active license does not necessarily mean an individual is currently practicing.”
Doctors left Idaho after abortion ban, study confirms

The 2025 study, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association, found that Idaho experienced a net loss of 94 out of 264 OB-GYN physicians between August 2022 and December 2024. 
Those numbers were compiled from “from publicly available credentialing files and sources, licensing boards, physician websites, Idaho’s American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists registry, Idaho Medical Association database, local knowledge of the practices, and direct physician confirmation,” the study’s abstract said. 
The researchers tracked relocations, those who stopped practicing obstetrics, died or retired, and counted newly credentialed doctors, the study said. It did not include temporary physicians  or family medicine doctors who also practice obstetrics. 
Idaho Medical Association CEO Susie Keller (Photo courtesy of Susie Keller)
“The unique thing about that JAMA Open study was that it was an actual count of actual individuals in Idaho,” said Susie Keller, CEO of the Idaho Medical Association. “It wasn’t an extrapolation. It wasn’t based on estimates. So it was very unique and went through many, many layers of scrutiny before being published.” 
Keller said physicians left in that time period for a variety of reasons, some of which included Idaho’s abortion laws but others were personal, such as to be closer to family. 
“There are a lot of factors that play into our physician shortage,” Keller said. “And for this particular subset, I think the study did a good job of explaining those different reasons.” 
A spokesperson from St. Luke’s, which has hospital clinic locations across southwest Idaho and Twin Falls, told the Idaho Capital Sun there were limitations to using licensing data to try and quantify how many doctors there are practicing. 
“While we cannot speak for statewide physician licensing trends, our experience is that licensing figures alone do not necessarily reflect the number of physicians actively providing obstetrical care to Idaho patients or available for long-term practice in Idaho,” spokesperson Joy Prudek said in an email.
She said that licenses may include those who “practice intermittently,” or temporary physicians who fill in gaps, or those who retain licenses from multiple states, 
 What are Idaho doctors saying? 

Cooper, the material-fetal medicine specialist, said she left Idaho because of the threat of prison time under Idaho’s criminal abortion ban and her fear she wouldn’t be able to provide the care she normally would. 
As a doctor focused on high-risk pregnancies, she said there were too many potential complications that could warrant an abortion that wouldn’t fall into the law’s exception to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest within the first trimester, if there’s a police report filed. 
“It was a very difficult decision that we made,” Cooper said. “Thinking through a lot of scenarios, thinking through if I went to prison, what would happen to my husband and children? I mean, it’s just very insane conversations that I never anticipated ever having to have.”
Idaho has had a shortage of doctors for years, said Keller of the Idaho Medical Association. The association has been part of an effort to try and increase physician training opportunities for more than 10 years. 
Keller said OB-GYNs have been the focus of tracking because the abortion ban very directly impacted that speciality. 
“This particular law that all of a sudden, made evidence-based practice that many of those OB-GYNs had been providing for their patients for many, many years … one day in 2022, it became illegal,” Keller said. “And it very much changed their ability to practice in Idaho.” 
Idaho needs 1,400 more medical professionals just to catch up to national average

Dr. Brenna McCrummen is practicing as an OB-GYN in Coeur d‘Alene, and told the Sun on Monday she feels the pressure from the loss of other specialists in North Idaho. In 2023, Sandpoint’s Bonner General Health closed its labor and delivery unit, citing the political climate and staffing issues.
Many women in the area now must travel for hours to seek care in Coeur d’Alene, McCrummen said. She said this can be especially problematic if a pregnant mom experiences unexpected complications. 
“Those problems can get much, much worse the farther out you are,” she said. “Those outcomes for baby and for mom are much worse, and I have definitely seen people arrive to our hospital much sicker than they should be, and that’s all due to the time that they have to travel.” 
Prudek, of St. Luke’s, said the health system has made progress in attracting obstetricians and gynecologists, but challenges remain. 
“From St. Luke’s perspective, recruiting and retaining OB-GYN physicians remains a priority,” Prudek said. “We have had some success recruiting OB-GYN physicians, particularly by attracting physicians with ties to Idaho and graduates of regional medical education programs. At the same time, our need for OB-GYN physicians continues to exceed the available workforce, and we have experienced limited success recruiting OB hospitalists.”
 Why is the family policy center suing BSU over the study? 

The policy center filed its lawsuit against Boise State University in Ada County District Court on July 24, Idaho EdNews reported. 
The advocacy group had sought records related to the 2025 study and its data. Its request returned only a two-page document with the raw data, showing a decline in OB-GYNs. 
The complaint alleges the university is withholding records, and that it should not have charged the policy center $257.02 for legal review of the two-page document it received. 
Stephany Galbreaith, director of media relations at Boise State, told Idaho EdNews, “We do not comment on pending litigation.”
