name: Georgia Recorder
title: GOP candidates outraise Democrats so far in most — but not all — of Georgia’s statewide contests
description: With less than three months until the November election, Republican candidates are outraising Democrats in most of Georgia’s statewide races, according to the latest round of campaign filings. However, the most recent data comes with a silver lining for Democrats. Candidates outraised Republicans in three statewide races: attorney general, secretary of state[...]
text:
The first campaign finance disclosures of the general election were due Friday,  offering an initial look at how the Democratic and Republican nominees for some of the most high-profile races are doing. Photo via Getty Images.With less than three months until the November election, Republican candidates are outraising Democrats in most of Georgia’s statewide races, according to the latest round of campaign filings.
However, the most recent data comes with a silver lining for Democrats. Candidates outraised Republicans in three statewide races: attorney general, secretary of state and one of the two Public Service Commission seats up for election this year.
Many of Georgia’s top offices won’t have an incumbent candidate on the ballot in November, leaving candidates competing for an open seat. 
The first campaign finance disclosures of the general election were due Friday, offering an initial glimpse into how the Democratic and Republican nominees for some of the most high-profile races are doing as they hurtle toward the general election.
Here’s what the numbers say.


Governor
Both candidates for governors continued to raise millions in campaign contributions, although Republican Rick Jackson has pledged to super charge his campaign again with his own wealth. 
And now both Jackson and Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms have jumped on the opportunity to raise money through a leadership committee, which is a type of political organization that was authorized under a 2021 state law that allows certain high-level officials and candidates to raise unlimited campaign contributions.
Jackson, who secured the Republican nomination after spending over $100 million of his own money during the primary, raised over $13 million during the reporting that ended in July. Most of those funds came from a $10 million donation the Republican Governors’ Association made to For All Georgians, Jackson’s new leadership committee. 
Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson speaks at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens, Aug. 5, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Jackson so far, unlike in his primary election, has limited the deployment of his own wealth since winning the party nomination, aside from paying for some of the campaign expenses like over $50,000 combined in helicopter and plane transportation and nearly $35,000 in legal fees. While Jackson has not contributed to his own campaign since winning the party nomination in June, he has vowed in public speeches that he’s willing to spend his fortune in order to win Georgia’s top office.
Bottoms trailed Jackson with about $5.6 million in total contributions. That includes about $1.8 million from the Democratic Governors Association that went to Project Battleground Georgia, the leadership committee Bottoms created once she became the official Democratic nominee.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens, Aug. 5, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
The campaign finance filings from Bottoms came a day after the grace period for submitting the forms had passed, which the campaign said was caused by a technical error. That led to Jackson pouncing at the opportunity to remind voters about a $37,000 fine Bottoms received during the 2017 Atlanta mayor’s race. Garrison Douglas, spokesperson for Jackson’s campaign, painted Bottoms as “a candidate with a history of campaign finance violations.” According to the Georgia Ethics Commission, Bottoms will be fined $125 for submitting the form a day late.
Bottoms’ spokesperson TaNisha Cameron did not address comments from the Jackson campaign but said in a statement that there’s enthusiasm behind Bottoms’ proposals “while billionaire insider Rick Jackson continues to pledge his loyalty to Trump as his policies hurt Georgians.”
“Keisha will continue to share her plans to lower costs, expand Medicaid and protect Georgia’s hospitals, and invest in education by guaranteeing pre-k and raising teacher pay,” Cameron said.
Lieutenant governor
Democratic nominee Josh McLaurin raised more than $67,000 during the most recent quarter. An attorney and state senator from Sandy Springs, McLaurin has campaigned on expanding Medicaid, lowering the cost of living and protecting Georgians’ civil rights. 
State Sen. Josh McLaurin, the Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
But unlike the top-ticket Democrats this year, he first had to compete in a runoff election in order to secure the nomination for lieutenant governor, and ended up spending over $157,000 over the course of the quarter.
That leaves him with a little under $36,000 to face off against Republican state Sen. Greg Dolezal of Cumming.
“My campaign will have the resources necessary to inform voters that Greg Dolezal’s record is too toxic for Republican voters — and even some of his elected Republican colleagues — to accept,” McLaurin said in a statement.
Sen. Greg Dolezal, the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Dolezal, who has made issues like election integrity, immigration enforcement and opposition to sharia law central to his campaign, raised more than $291,000 this quarter. His leadership committee, Georgia Liberty PAC, reported an additional $189,800 this quarter. (McLaurin does not currently have his own leadership committee.)
Dolezal also competed in a runoff before clinching the GOP nomination, and is sitting on a war chest of over $377,000 heading into the general election. 
He did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday. 
Attorney general
Rep. Tanya Miller, the Democratic nominee for attorney general. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Republicans dominated the fundraising numbers for the governor and lieutenant governor races. But in the race to become Georgia’s next top lawyer, Democrat Tanya Miller has pulled ahead.
Miller, a state representative who currently serves as chair of the House Minority Caucus, reported raising over $446,000 during the most recent quarter. Campaign Manager Joey Wozniak celebrated the achievement, noting that Miller is the only candidate with experience as a prosecutor.
“This fundraising haul is another clear sign that Georgians are ready for an Attorney General who puts the people first,” Wozniak said.
Sen. Bill Strickland, the Republican nominee for attorney general. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Brian Strickland, the Republican nominee and a state senator from McDonough, raised nearly $324,000 during the most recent quarter. Though he fell short of Miller’s fundraising numbers from over the summer, he still maintained an overall edge, ending the quarter with $448,000 on hand compared to Miller’s $329,000.
“The growing support behind our campaign demonstrates what families across Georgia want in their chief law enforcement officer: steady leadership focused on public safety,” Strickland’s campaign manager Jantz Womack said in a statement.
Secretary of state
Democratic secretary of state candidate Penny Brown Reynolds. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
The battle to be Georgia’s next top elections official is heating up, becoming the second statewide race in which a Democrat has outraised a Republican candidate.
Democratic nominee Penny Brown Reynolds raised nearly four times as much as Republican state Rep. Tim Fleming of Covington during the most recent quarter and ended with a war chest over three times larger.
Republican secretary of state candidate Tim Fleming at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens, Aug. 5, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Brown Reynolds, a former judge, reality TV show star and member of the Biden administration, raised over $133,000 since April, and ended the quarter with nearly $68,000 on hand.
Fleming, who was deputy secretary of state under then-Secretary of State Brian Kemp and is currently serving on a committee dedicated to helping replace Georgia’s election system, only raised about $34,000, and ended the quarter with a little over $20,000 on hand.
Other downballot races
In the race for commissioner of agriculture, two-term GOP incumbent Commissioner Tyler Harper raised over $244,000. That dwarfed the $3,000 raised by his Democratic opponent, Katherine Juhan-Arnold, who ended the quarter with over $500 on hand. Harper ended the quarter with over $541,000.
Insurance Commissioner John King, who is a Republican, raised nearly $72,000 during the most recent quarter and ended with over $545,000 on hand. The Democratic nominee, Keisha Waites, claimed she had no contributions or expenses on her campaign finance disclosure. 
Incumbent Labor Commissioner Bárbara Rivera Holmes, a Republican who was appointed by Gov. Brian Kemp last year, raised nearly $11,000 during the most recent quarter, and is ending with over $174,000 on hand. 
Nikki Porcher, the Democratic nominee for labor commissioner, raised about $4,500 during the most recent quarter. An Air Force veteran, former teacher and nonprofit founder, Porcher’s ending cash balance sits at over $15,000. 
In the race for state school superintendent, Republican incumbent Richard Woods added $4,800 to the bank and is sitting on a total of $30,000. His opponent, Democrat Lydia Powell, raised over $4,000 since April and ended the quarter with over $5,400 on hand. 
For the District 3 Public Service Commission seat, incumbent Peter Hubbard, a Democrat, raised over $105,000 and ended with $82,000 on hand. His Republican opponent, former Commissioner Fitz Johnson, raised more than $60,000 and ended with about $86,000. 
In the open District 5 Public Service Commission contest, Republican Josh Tolbert raised $2,000 and ended the quarter with over $25,000 on hand. Democrat Shelia Edwards raised more than $7,700 but her ending cash balance leaves her nearly $13,000 in debt.
The next round of fundraising reports will be due in October.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Candidates highlight data center plans. Next Ohio governor will select regulators.
description: Ohio’s two candidates for governor have conflicting ideas of what they would like to see happen to future data centers, which have become a political lightning rod in this year’s November election.  Ohio’s next governor will appoint the five members of the Public Utilities Commission, which sets utility rates and set the parameters for data […]
text:
Vivek Ramaswamy and Amy Acton. (Photo by WEWS.)Ohio’s two candidates for governor have conflicting ideas of what they would like to see happen to future data centers, which have become a political lightning rod in this year’s November election. 
Ohio’s next governor will appoint the five members of the Public Utilities Commission, which sets utility rates and set the parameters for data centers opening in cities across the state. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ohio Democratic candidate for governor Dr. Amy Acton announced on July 27 she supports a conditional moratorium on data centers “if requirements on costs, union labor, transparency, environmental standards, community benefit agreements, and development are not met,” she said in a statement.
Innovation Ohio, a progressive policy advocacy organization, said Acton has a strong data center proposal. 
“Requiring data centers to really pay their own money in terms of electricity, electricity in terms of really protecting the environment, protecting water, making sure workers are getting a fair shake out of these fields, that to us is really leveling the playing field and ensuring that going forward,” said Innovation Ohio President Michael McGovern. 
Ohio Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy announced his three-fold data center plan on Aug. 6.
“If a data center is built in your community, then (1) you will no longer have to pay for your home’s electricity, (2) you will pay lower property taxes, and (3) the data center will be required to abide by all air and water quality standards without exception, and we will take the necessary steps to protect Ohio’s fertile farmland,” he said in a post on X.
“If any one of these three conditions is not met, the data center won’t be built. Period,” Ramaswamy said in his statement.
McGovern called Ramaswamy’s idea for data centers to pay for citizen’s electric bills “utter nonsense.”
An Amazon Web Services data center is shown situated near single-family homes on July 17, 2024 in Stone Ridge, Virginia. Opponents of data center construction have pointed to the energy and water resources needed to run them, and the strain that puts on communities. (Photo by Nathan Howard/Getty Images)
“We see Vivek Ramaswamy’s plan that’s just like absolute nonsense in coming up with these wild ideas that don’t make any sense and aren’t based in any actual policy research, and instead are sort of just these silly promises,” McGovern said.
Ramaswamy’s plan does not specify how many miles away from a data center someone must be living to get their electricity for free. 
“There’s no detail, there’s no substance,” McGovern said. 
Ramaswamy said last year it’s a “good thing” AI data centers moving to Ohio. 
“I want the sectors of the future to come here, but that will make a level of demand on our electric grid of a kind that we have not seen in the history of our state … right at a time when we’ve also cut off and reduced the supply of base load power generation, shutting down coal plants that, on my watch, would have remained open,” Ramaswamy said in a video posted to X in March 2025. 
Ramaswamy has a financial stake in data centers by having financial positions in the chips that power AI to the companies that run the data centers, according to a report released earlier this year from Innovation Ohio. 
“He has rolled out a plan that is unserious and does not really tackle this vital issue for Ohioans, and he is personally getting richer off of data centers,” McGovern said. 
“He’s making money here, and all of a sudden that’s a political problem, so he’s walking that back.”
Ohio has more than 200 data centers, the sixth-highest state in the country, according to Pew Research Center. Most of the data centers are in central Ohio. Cincinnati has 26 and Cleveland has 22, according to the Data Center Map. 
Ohioans are seeing increased electric bills. The average Ohio residential utility bills are projected to be about $800 for the summer — a 17% increase compared to last summer, according to a report by Third Way. 
Lawmakers at the Ohio Statehouse have yet to pass any data center legislation. 
Conserve Ohio, the grassroots organization behind a proposed constitutional amendment to ban new data centers, is collecting signatures to make the 2027 ballot.
Follow Ohio Capital Journal Reporter Megan Henry on X or on Bluesky.

title: Pa. poised to lead in quantum computing field, state lawmakers hear
description: The commonwealth’s seven top-level research universities have formed the Keystone AI + Quantum Factory to collaborate and share resources to speed innovation in the field.
text:
The Pennsylvania State Capitol building seen through trees in Harrisburg, Pa. on December 17, 2024. A lawsuit from a Potter County commissioner is challenging the Department of State's interpretation of voter registration law. (Photo by Kriston Jae Bethel for Votebeat)
Pennsylvania is well positioned to be a leader in the development of the next major breakthrough in computing, state lawmakers heard Tuesday in an informational hearing on quantum technology.
“Quantum computing has the potential to transform industries that we care about: life sciences, advanced manufacturing, energy, ag, logistics, and national security,” Jen Gilberg, deputy secretary of technology for entrepreneurship at the state Department of Community and Economic Development, told members of the House Committee on Communications and Technology.
The commonwealth’s seven top-level research universities have formed the Keystone AI + Quantum Factory to collaborate and share resources to speed innovation in the field, she said. They’re working to build a statewide “ecosystem” that brings together research infrastructure, workforce development and commercial applications.
The collaboration includes the University of Pennsylvania and the University of Pittsburgh, as well Carnegie Mellon, Drexel, Penn State, Temple and Lehigh universities.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“Very few states can bring together this depth of research capability in one coordinated effort,” Gilberg said. “So it really is a big deal, and it gives us this great opportunity to compete for federal dollars and also industry dollars.”
Quantum computers employ the rules of quantum physics – the branch of science used to describe the properties of atoms and subatomic particles – which is distinct from classical physics.
Rep. Joe D’Orsie (R-York) noted he and his son had watched a video about “Schroedinger’s Cat,” the famous thought experiment named after physicist Erwin Schroedinger. It involves a theoretical cat sealed in a box with a poison device triggered by a random atomic event. If it occurs, the cat dies, but the cat must be considered to be alive and dead simultaneously until someone opens the box to check.
Matt Brandsema, head of the quantum and multi-physics department at Penn State’s Applied Research Laboratory, said quantum computing employs that concept, called superposition, in which a system can exist in multiple states until it is measured.
Classical computers use units of information called bits to represent information. A bit can either be a one or a zero, but quantum computers use quantum bits, or quibits, that can represent ones and zeroes simultaneously. That allows them to test many solutions to a problem very quickly, Brandsema said.
The likely result, he said, is that quantum computers will eventually be powerful enough to break the encryption now used to secure information transmitted on the internet. Brandsema said that’s unlikely for a decade or more, he added.
“How do we defend ourselves when that happens?” Brandsema said “Because when that happens, basically the whole internet’s trust system goes out the window, and you have to migrate to something else.”
The solution is to make the encryption more complicated to solve, he said, adding that’s a major area of research in the quantum computing field.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Gilberg said the commonwealth and research institutions are also working on workforce development. 
“We want to make sure that Pennsylvanians are prepared for these new quantum age jobs, and the quantum workforce is going to span the whole spectrum from PhDs down through technicians,” she said.
The Keystone AI + Quantum Factory is collaborating with the state departments of Education and Labor and Industry to develop road maps for training a quantum computing workforce, Gilberg said.
“There is a great opportunity to uplift on all ends of the spectrum and make sure we have precision machinists, skilled tradespeople, people who can service the quantum computers,” she said.
Mihir Bhaskar, senior vice president for research and development at quantum computing company IonQ, said quantum tech also has the potential to change the nature of data centers, which Rep. Robert Ledbetter (R-Columbia) noted has become an “incendiary” topic across the commonwealth.
Technologists are motivated to build quantum computers for many of the reasons people oppose data centers so strongly. They require massive amounts of energy and resources.
“What we’re trying to build are … machines that are much more efficient at solving the problems we’re seeking out to solve,” Bhaskar said. “Not using an entire data center to do a chemical simulation that consumes megawatts of power, but to use a quantum computer that will be much, much more efficient and it’s designed to solve those very important tasks.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: America’s sunk so low, dishonor and disgrace don’t end political careers. Ohio politicians prove it.
description: Dishonor should be disqualifying in politics. It is not. Scandalous behavior or public corruption should end political careers. They do not. Ohio politicians proved the point last week. U.S. Rep. Max Miller was a political appointee in the first Trump administration who promoted Trump’s false claims of a “rigged” 2020 election before being elected to […]
text:
Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, leaves a House Republican Conference meeting on Capitol Hill on Nov. 19, 2024 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)Dishonor should be disqualifying in politics. It is not. Scandalous behavior or public corruption should end political careers. They do not. Ohio politicians proved the point last week. 
U.S. Rep. Max Miller was a political appointee in the first Trump administration who promoted Trump’s false claims of a “rigged” 2020 election before being elected to Congress in 2022. 
The 37-year-old has a history of alleged physical assaults against women dating back to high school. Recently, shocking new allegations of domestic violence surfaced. 
His ex-wife, Emily Moreno, accused him of throwing burning water on her, holding a gun to her head, and possibly fracturing the collarbone of their two-year-old daughter. 
Miller denied the accusations, rebuffed belated calls to resign, and vowed to stay in his 2026 reelection race.
In a damage control media tour (that backfired), Miller dismissed the wife-beating and child abuse claims raised in a contentious custody dispute as “politically motivated” allegations cooked up by his lying ex-wife and her father, Ohio U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno. 
The embattled congressman compared his bad press and party badgering to quit with Trump’s bad press in the 2016 presidential campaign for bragging (on the infamous Access Hollywood video) about grabbing women sexually without asking permission and party badgering for him to drop out. 
Miller said the (cringe) comparison bolstered his decision to remain the GOP nominee in Ohio’s 7th District. 
If Trump could beat scandalous recordings of him laughing off predatory sexual assault, “When you’re a star, they let you do it,” his volatile former aide could be equally resilient with serious accusations of physical abuse, threats, and protective restraining orders. 
Trump reacted to those accusations the way a person found liable by a jury for sexual abuse and defamation might — with defensive praise of the former White House staffer. 
“I know Max. He’s a good person. It’s a very sad thing to be going through that,” said Trump. “But it’s accusations.” 
The convicted felon endorsed Miller in May and has not withdrawn support. He warned his one-time aide that he faced a tough reelection cycle with severe domestic and child abuse allegations hanging over his head but stopped short of asking the Ohio Republican to step aside. 
Trump’s political hand puppet in the U.S. House, Speaker Mike Johnson, likewise dodged questions about Miller being allegedly violent toward his ex-wife and daughter — “There’s all sorts of domestic events going on with 435 members of Congress all the time, it’s not my business to get engaged in it,” — and suggested Miller’s request for a House Ethics Committee investigation into the allegations be allowed to play out. Well beyond the November election. 
That gives other House Republicans, desperate to retain their slim majority, an excuse to ignore the elephant in the caucus and pretend an alleged abuser of women and a toddler isn’t their problem. 
The deer-in-the-headlights approach to the Miller scandal is a political calculation to minimize the GOP fallout in the midterms. It is far from a principled stand against indefensible conduct. 
Republicans are simply terrified of losing a solid red seat. 
A smattering of Capitol Hill Republicans urged Miller to withdraw from the race while there was still time to replace him with a less flawed candidate. But otherwise, the response of Ohio Republicans, the state party, and local GOP chairs has been underwhelming. 
No emphatic zero-tolerance messaging about abusive behavior with candidates. The GOP has to keep the R+5 district in its column. Alleged victims of an incumbent with a bad temper are not part of the calculus.
Ohio U.S. Sen. Jon Husted stayed mum on the matter until last Thursday when he posted that Miller should resign in the best interest of his daughter. Initially, Husted had been satisfied to let Miller and his ex-wife “sort through this at a family level.”  
Sen. Moreno said nothing about his former son-in-law’s alleged violence against his daughter and granddaughter for years until publicly denouncing him a week ago. 
Senate Majority Leader John Thune stuck to his “it’s a family matter” refrain about the searing accusations of domestic abuse leveled at Miller. But Thune could downplay the issue of a Republican congressman accused of violently abusing his ex-wife and child because it is no longer a disqualification for elected office. 
According to a recent Politico poll, most of Trump’s MAGA base would vote for a GOP candidate confronted with an array of scandals from grift to sexual assault. A whopping 72% of those voters said they would support a GOP candidate accused of domestic violence.
Maybe that’s why Thune and his Ohio colleagues, Sens. Moreno and Husted, felt invincible confirming Trump’s openly corrupt henchman to head the Department of Justice. 
When Moreno and Husted made Todd Blanche U.S. Attorney General, they surrendered the rule of law in America. But will it matter at the polls? 
They endorsed the most reprehensible candidate ever for the job, a man facing multiple ethics complaints who had already used the DOJ (as deputy and acting AG) to shamelessly advance Trump’s breathtaking corruption. 
Blanche is still ignoring the law on the Epstein files, still likely to fleece taxpayers of $2 billion in a slush fund (to reward Jan. 6 insurrectionists), still insulating the president, his family and businesses from IRS audits. So what? 
Political tribalism absolves all; the moral rot destroying impartial justice, the domestic abuse allegations destroying a family. 
What should be disqualifying for positions of power is not. And here we are.

title: Why is the Green Party trying to kick a Green Party candidate off the ballot in the Pa.?
description: The state Green Party is warning voters that Andrew Tupone's bid may be a ploy to trick voters in a race the Cook Political Report rates as a “toss up.”
text:
Andrew Tupone in front of the Pennsylvania Capitol in Harrisburg. The selfie was posted on his campaign Facebook pageIn one of the most competitive congressional districts in the country, a strange fight is brewing between the Pennsylvania Green Party and a candidate who is petitioning to appear on the ballot under their label.
Andrew Tupone submitted his nomination papers with thousands of signatures to the Department of State last month, seeking a spot on the ballot in Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District. He then released a statement appealing to the Green Party’s progressive voter base.
“[Incumbent] Congressman [Ryan] Mackenzie has been in lock step with Trump and he must be stopped,” it read. “After the Democratic National Party put their thumbs on the scale in the primary for Bob Brooks as the nominee, I believe local grassroots voters deserve another choice and that’s why so many are backing my candidacy.”
Bob Brooks won the Democratic nomination for the 7th Congressional District on Tuesday, May 19, 2026 (Photo via Bob Brooks for Congress)
But the state Green Party is warning voters that the bid may be a ploy to trick voters in a race the Cook Political Report rates as a “toss up.”
On Monday, the party filed an objection to Tupone’s attempt to get on the ballot in Commonwealth Court.
“Tupone and his agents or affiliates … misled voters into signing the Nomination Papers on the mistaken belief that they were helping to place a candidate supported by the Green Party onto the ballot,” the objection reads. “Many of the voters who signed Candidate Tupone’s Nomination Papers would not have done so had they been aware that Candidate Tupone was not actually affiliated with or endorsed by the GPPA.”
The objection notes that Tupone was a registered Republican until mid-February 2026, when he changed his registration to Democrat. He changed it again to Green in April.
“My political beliefs always remained the same. It doesn’t matter what party I was registered to,” Tupone told the Capital-Star. “I am trying to buck the establishment of both parties … I’m running for universal healthcare, ending the genocide in Gaza and standing up to the establishment parties.”

A separate objection to Tupone’s petition to appear on the PA-07 ballot was filed by Democratic voters with ties to the party. They’re alleging issues with many of the 9,460 signatures Tupone collected and, like the Green Party, accusing him of paying out-of-state people to help collect them.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Tupone told the Capital-Star, “I am not aware of any paid operation and just thankful for the volunteers that want change this November and tired of the two party establishment.”
Chris Robinson, a spokesperson for the Pennsylvania Green Party said the group learned about Tupone from the media after he submitted his nomination papers.
“We had no idea who he was,” Robinson said. “There were records of him running for office in the past as a Republican, and you can look up his voter registration — anybody can do that  — and it said he was a Republican up until [February] of this year.”
Robinson also learned Tupone had previously run for election to a Magisterial Judge seat in Northampton County, appearing on the general election ballot as a Republican in 2021. Though Tupone had cross-filed and ran in the Democratic primary as well both times.
Tupone told the Capital-Star that any accusation that he is a Republican acting as a spoiler is “simply not true and a false accusation by political operatives.”
It’s unclear if the Green Party has grounds to challenge Tupone’s place on the ballot. As a minor political party, it is not able to hold primaries the same way Democrats and Republicans can in the state. Instead, hopeful candidates must collect signatures and turn them into the Pennsylvania Department of State to appear on the general election ballot.
U.S. Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-7th District) speaks during a rally with Vice President J.D. Vance at the Uline shipping materials warehouse in Lower Macungie Township on Tuesday, Dec. 16, 2025. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)
“That’s the way the Pennsylvania regulations are written,” Robinson said.
He added that it would take reforms agreed to by Republicans and Democrats in the state House to fix the problem, such as allowing minor parties to hold primaries or implementing what’s called “fusion voting,” which would allow candidates to represent multiple parties.
“There’s a whole bunch of things like that, and every voter you talk to probably has different things they’d like to see,” he said. “But nobody cares about that in Harrisburg. The people who are legislators in Harrisburg would like to keep things the same. It worked for them. Why change it?”
The 7th Congressional District election is expected to be one of the decisive races when it comes to which party controls the U.S. House in 2027.
The contest has been attracting national interest for much of the year.
According to OpenSecrets, a nonprofit that tracks spending in American politics, the race has already drawn over $9.5 million in contributions. Just over 75% of that has come from out of state.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Democratic gubernatorial primary too close to call
description: Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley maintained a slight lead over state Rep. Francesca Hong late Tuesday evening in the Democratic contest for the nomination for governor, prolonging the uncertainty of a primary characterized by unprecedented chaos over the last two months.  An error in uploading absentee ballot data in Milwaukee caused a delay in repor[...]
text:
Supporters of David Crowley at the primary election watch party. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley maintained a slight lead over state Rep. Francesca Hong late Tuesday evening in the Democratic contest for the nomination for governor, prolonging the uncertainty of a primary characterized by unprecedented chaos over the last two months. 
An error in uploading absentee ballot data in Milwaukee caused a delay in reporting that pushed the final results off and both Hong and Crowley ended their election watch parties after midnight with no winner declared.
The winner of the race will face U.S. Rep Tom Tiffany, the GOP nominee for governor, who easily defeated his Republican challenger, and his running mate David Varnam. Varnam defeated Will Martin, who had the endorsement of the state GOP and had been campaigning with Tiffany.
The Democratic primary, which started with seven candidates, all of whose names appeared on the ballot even after three dropped out, dwindled to four candidates competing for the nomination. At 12:25 p.m. Crowley had 39.9% of the vote and Hong had 39.6% with 94% of the vote counted. State Sen. Kelda Roys and former Department of Administration Secretary Joel Brennan trailed the two leaders with 7.6% and 4.7% of the vote respectively.
Crowley launched his campaign in September 2025, dropped out in July and endorsed Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, then reentered the race when Rodriguez dropped out. Gov. Tony Evers, who had declined to express a preference in the race before the final days, encouraged Crowley to rejoin the field and campaigned for him up until Election Day.
Worried that Hong, a democratic socialist, state lawmaker and chef, could not win the general election, undecided Democratic primary voters flocked to Crowley’s resurrected campaign. Hong ran a campaign based on a cadre of grassroots volunteers and a strong  social media strategy. Polls showed her dominating the field with a double-digit lead toward the end of the campaign, a result that was not matched by vote tallies on Election Night.
Victory parties but no result
The crowd gathered at Atwood Music Hall in Madison for Hong’s victory party started the night in a hopeful mood, singing to Pink Pony Girl by Chappell Roan, Stateside by PinkPantheress and Wannabe by the Spice Girls. Supporters made signs at a table and took photos together. Loud boos rang out when President Donald Trump and Republican gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany appeared on the large screens showing CNN’s election night coverage.
The crowd gathered at Atwood Music Hall in Madison for Hong’s victory party started the night in a hopeful mood, singing to Pink Pony Girl by Chappell Roan, Stateside by PinkPantheress and Wannabe by the Spice Girls. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
In the two weeks leading up to the election, Crowley and Evers raced across the state to reintroduce Crowley to voters with Evers telling people he thought Hong would not be able to beat Tiffany. 
April Brown, a Madison resident, said the issues she is most concerned about this election year are affordability, data centers and queer and trans issues. She and her wife, who came out as trans three years ago, moved to Dane County about a year ago from Georgia. 
“The South was increasingly becoming hostile towards people like us, like her,” Brown said. “When I found out about Fran being, not only my district representative in the state Assembly, but also she was running for governor and found how passionate she was about LGBTQ rights, I knew I had to throw my support behind her.” 
Brown said she would get behind Crowley if he won, but she felt hope voting for Hong. 
“I think she really resonates with people because she gets people and she wants to help people,” Brown said. 
Crowley’s supporters gathered at the Regency Ballroom in the Hyatt Regency hotel in downtown Milwaukee Tuesday night.
Darryl Morin, national president and board chairman of Forward Latino, Milwaukee Mayor Cavalier Johnson, and other local elected officials joined the crowd.
Throughout the evening, Crowley maintained a slight lead over Hong as vote totals were reported across the state. Updates on the large TV screens in the ballroom were greeted with cheering from the crowd. 
Talk of a possible recount began as Crowley maintained his razor-thin advantage. 
Calls for unity
“In 11 weeks, no matter who’s on this ballot, we are going to fight to win for one another,” Hong said. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
Just before 11:30 p.m., Hong addressed her supporters, thanking them and telling them that they have “built something that will change politics forever.”
“In 11 weeks, no matter who’s on this ballot, we are going to fight to win for one another,” Hong said. “We will win together, united. Because everyone who’s running in this race, they know that we can make better possible and we must make better possible.”
After Hong left the stage her campaign staff wished everyone a good night and the lights in Atwood Music Hall were turned up. 
Hannah Ecay, a 25-year-old who wore a Madison Area DSA shirt, said she doesn’t have kids, but wants to one day and that’s part of why she supports Hong and her affordability agenda. 
“I don’t have kids yet, but when I do childcare and public education are very important to me, and I’d like to see those things be set up now, before I have children,” Ecay said. 
Ecay said she would vote for Crowley in the general election if he wins.
“Anyone’s better than Tom Tiffany, but I won’t be as excited about it as I would be for Francesca,” she said. 
As votes were being tallied in Milwaukee, election workers announced that a mistake had been made where some of the flash drives used to record the election results were downloaded with audit data instead of information from 15,000 absentee ballots. The mistake was expected to take over an hour to fix. Congresswoman Gwen Moore addressed Crowley’s supporters, saying that she believes that “the red bird will fly,” referring to a story from Crowley’s wife of having seen a red cardinal — a significant religious symbol to her — which she interpreted as a sign that Crowley should re-enter the race. 
By the end of the night Crowley maintained a miniscule lead of 39.5% to Hong’s 39.6% of the vote. Crowley did not appear at his watch party to address supporters before it ended with no official result. 
Congresswoman Gwen Moore addresses David Crowley’s watch party audience after a election workers report a mistake in the flash drive downloads. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Jarrett English, a community organizer in Milwaukee, said that he respects both Hong and Crowley. “I’ve known David since he was an organizer, and so I know that he works hard,” English told the Examiner. “He was always going to do well in Milwaukee because he’s been an incredible county executive, arguably the most successful county executive in a generation, at least in terms of the amount of things that have gotten accomplished with housing, with mental health, with not necessarily shared revenue but getting more revenue for the metro area. All those things show that he is more than ready to be at a higher level.” 
English feels that both Hong or Crowley would make for fantastic governors. “I personally will be happy with whoever wins,” said English, saying that while he doesn’t always agree with Crowley that he’s “a bridgebuilder” and that Hong “is the same.”
Donna Davis, managing partner for Vox Pop Solutions and a Crowley supporter who traveled from Florida, said that “Crowley’s candidacy, who Crowley is and what he believes in, is an idea and a moment whose time has come.” Observing Crowley’s  unexpected surge which kept him in the lead most of the night, Davis said, “I think people want something different. I think they’re unsure about the unknown. I mean this is the Midwest, and people like what they know. And he fits Wisconsin.” 
Davis said that Crowley’s performance Tuesday night is a sign that “Milwaukee is ready to move into the 21st century, Wisconsin is ready for the 21st century.” If she were asked  just three years ago whether his success would have been possible, “I would’ve told you ‘absolutely not.’ I wasn’t even really sure that this was the moment because we’re in the middle of a very divisive era in American history. But this is a democracy, and the voters have the final say.”
Moving into the general election
The Democratic nominee for governor will be joined on the ticket by Secretary of State Sarah Godlewski, who is running in November for lieutenant governor and faced no primary opponent. She previously served as state treasurer from January 2019 to January 2023. Evers appointed her to her current position. 
Democrats have their work cut out for them as they seek to beat Tiffany, a three-term congressman who currently represents the state’s largest congressional district in the northern half of the state. Wisconsin’s statewide races are typically decided by close margins, including in 2018 when Evers defeated Gov. Scott Walker by about 30,000 votes. 
Ahead of Election Day, Democratic candidates had been discussing uniting following the primary to defeat Tiffany.
Godlewski, U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin, U.S. Rep. Mark Pocan and the Democratic nominee for governor planned to meet for a unity breakfast Wednesday morning in the Madison area, seeking to move past the divisiveness of the primary with less than three months until the general election.

title: Republican U.S. Rep. Weid will face Democrat Rick Crosson in 8th CD
description: Rick Crosson, a retired U.S. Army officer and former Green Bay school board member, won the Democratic Party nomination Tuesday to challenge Republican U.S. Rep. Tony Weid in Wisconsin’s 8th Congressional District. Counting ballots for the Democratic primary in the district stretched past midnight. At 12:08 a.m. Wednesday, the Associated Press called the rac[...]
text:
The U.S. Capitol on the evening of Sept. 30, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Rick Crosson (Campaign Facebook page photo)
Rick Crosson, a retired U.S. Army officer and former Green Bay school board member, won the Democratic Party nomination Tuesday to challenge Republican U.S. Rep. Tony Weid in Wisconsin’s 8th Congressional District.
Counting ballots for the Democratic primary in the district stretched past midnight. At 12:08 a.m. Wednesday, the Associated Press called the race for Crosson. With 99% of ballots counted, Crosson had 35% of the vote. 
Former public school teacher turned financial manager Mark Scheffler of Appleton finished a close second, with 33% of the vote, and Katrina deVille, a bartender and musician whose campaign highlighted that she is transgender and a democratic socialist, finished third with just under 32%.
The 8th CD covers Brown, Calumet, Door, Kewaunee, Marinette, Menominee, Oconto, Outagamie, and Waupaca counties and parts of Winnebago County.
Scheffler was endorsed by former U.S. Rep. Steve Kagan, who was the last Democrat to represent the district after he was elected in 2006 and served two terms.
Crosson garnered endorsements from a number of sitting office holders in the state Assembly and in local governments around the district, along with Dr. Kristin Lyerly, a high-profile 8th CD activist who lost to Weid in 2024.
Scheffler outraised his two Democratic opponents with $136,755 in receipts as of July 22. He was helped by a $15,000 personal donation along with a $25,000 loan he made to his campaign.
Crossan raised $75,430 as of that date — 60% of what Scheffler reported — and deVille raised $22,219, according to FEC data.
The 8th District has been viewed as a safe GOP seat this election cycle. Weid won by a 20-point margin in 2024, when it was an open seat and despite Lyerly’s campaign messaging that focused heavily on abortion rights and the U.S. Supreme Court ruling less than two years earlier that threw out a nationwide right to abortion.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Federal judge says proposed immigration facility in Howard County can move forward, for now
description: Howard County residents vowed to fight a federal immigration facility planned for an Elkridge office building, one day after a federal judge ordered the county could no longer block work on the project.
text:
A protester holds a sign voicing their opposition of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Maryland. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Howard County residents vowed to fight a federal immigration facility planned for an Elkridge office building, one day after a federal judge ordered the county could no longer block work on the project.
“The residents of Howard County have made it clear that we do not want this facility in our community,” Liz Kato with IndivisibleHoCoMD said in a written statement Tuesday. “We will continue to work with our elected officials and other local community organizations to make sure that the Elkridge detention center does not become another base for lawlessness and violence.”
Monday’s order by U.S. District Judge Adam Abelson ruled that the project developer, Genesis Strategic One LLC, faced irreparable harm if the county was allowed to continued blocking the project, which has pushed the company toward bankruptcy. He ordered the county to let work continue on the project while the case proceeds.
The ruling comes months after county officials revoked permits that had been granted to Genesis to convert an office building in Elkridge into a facility for federal immigration enforcement. The county approved the project in 2025, but reversed that decision in February.
At the time, County Executive Calvin Ball and others said the permit was approved in error and did not give adequate time for public comment. County officials said the project — to convert the building into offices for Department of Homeland Security employees that would include temporary holding cells and a shower for detainees — failed to give notice and was impermissibly close to schools, parks and shopping centers.
Chorus of voices grows against possible ICE detention centers in Maryland

The Howard County Council rushed through emergency legislation in less than a week in February that specified that only “a government agency is eligible to make application, obtain, or hold a permit” to build a facility with holding cells, not a private contractor.
Genesis sued in March, arguing that the county had interfered with federal authority and that the county law banning privately-owned detention facilities was unconstitutional.
Abelson on Monday enjoined the county’s revocation of the permit for the property, ruling that Genesis’s argument had a likelihood of success and that the company would face irreparable harm without an injunction.
“Genesis alleges that the construction on the Elkridge Property required a significant upfront investment, with over $21 million spent to date,” Abelson wrote. “With construction suspended following the County’s revocation of the permits, Genesis is currently accruing interest of approximately $5,000 each day … and is unable to collect the monthly rent of approximately $132,000 it would be receiving from the federal government had it been able to turn over the building in March as planned.
“These damages are linked to the need for a preliminary injunction as the lack of a permit is the only impediment to Genesis finishing construction and turning the property over to the federal government, which would then start paying rent for its use,” he continues. “Genesis also contends that its bankers have refused to lend funds to Genesis for any other properties until the Elkridge Property is turned over to the federal government and that bankruptcy is now a possibility for them.”
County officials said the reaction from constituents was immediate.
“We’ve heard from residents over the last 24 hours about this,” Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Anne Arundel and Howard) said Tuesday. “Lots of residents in Howard County are angry at this development and wondering what can be done with this.”
Lam said called the ruling a disappointing development that “runs counter to what the community wants.” He expects that county officials are looking at any available legal option to continue to push back against the construction of the immigration facility.
A county spokesperson said in an email Tuesday that the county “does not comment on pending litigation.”
Federal officials did not comment on Abelson’s ruling in their response.
“Is it really news that when a federal agency hires more personnel that they need more space?” a DHS spokesperson said in an email Tuesday. “Thanks to the Big Beautiful Bill, we have an additional 12,000 ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] officers and agents on the ground across the country. That’s a 120% increase in our workforce.”
Lam argues that community input should matter to federal officials and that the proposed facility “makes it more difficult for residents to feel more comfortable in their communities.”
“Unfortunately, it’s kind of where we’re stuck at right now,” he said.

title: Democrats choose Marathon County Hmong leader to run for state treasurer
description: Yee Leng Xiong, a Marathon County school board treasurer and county board member, will face Republican State Treasurer John Leiber in November in the only race for a statewide office held by a member of the Republican party. With 90% of ballots counted, Xiong had 57% of the votes cast in the Democratic primary for […]
text:
The Wisconsin State Capitol reflected in the glass windows of Park Bank on the Capitol Square in Madison. (Wisconsin Examiner photo)Yee Leng Xiong. (Campaign photo)
Yee Leng Xiong, a Marathon County school board treasurer and county board member, will face Republican State Treasurer John Leiber in November in the only race for a statewide office held by a member of the Republican party.
With 90% of ballots counted, Xiong had 57% of the votes cast in the Democratic primary for the office Tuesday. Dylan Ray Helmenstein, of Black Earth in western Dane County, had just under 43%. The Associated Press called the race for Xiong at 9:18 p.m.
Xiong is the treasurer of the DC Everest School District board in Marathon County and a member of the Marathon County Board. He is the former executive director of the Hmong American Center.
Xiong was endorsed by Sen. Tammy Baldwin and several other Wisconsin Democrats, including former Lt. Governor Barbara Lawton and state Reps. Christine Sinicki, Jodi Emerson, Lori Palmeri, Andrew Hysell, Tara Johnson and Brienne Brown. 
Helmenstein is a former Medicaid health care rate analyst in the Wisconsin Department of Health Services and a member of several local boards and commissions in Black Earth, including the village board and the Wisconsin Heights School District board.
The Legislature has moved much of the state treasurer’s duties to other agencies that are under the control of the governor. In 2018, voters rejected an amendment that would have removed the office as an elected position under the Wisconsin Constitution.
The state treasurer is the state’s chief financial officer and signs state checks. The officeholder is a statutory member of the Public Employee Trust Fund, which oversees the state’s public pension and benefit programs, and serves on the state Board of Commissioners of Public Lands, along with the secretary of state and the attorney general. 
The commissioners manage revenues from the sale of state-owned timber. The board distributes the proceeds to the Common School Fund, which purchases books and media for public school libraries and funds certain public works projects.
Leiber was the only statewide Republican candidate to win in the 2022 November election, when Gov. Tony Evers and other Democratic state office holders won reelection.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Fred Clark wins the Democratic nomination in the 7th CD
description: Fred Clark, former Democratic state legislator, former executive director of Wisconsin’s Green Fire and owner of Clark Forestry, Inc., won a three-way race for the Democratic nomination in Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District Tuesday night, with 37.3% of the vote. AP called the race at 11:37 p.m.  Ginger Murray, a small business owner and lawyer from […]
text:
Fred Clark (standing) Democrat from Bayfield County, talking to John Kotar, retired UW-Madision Forestry, Ecology and Management Proffesor in Cable, Wisconsin, Oct. 22. | Photo by Frank Zufall/Wisconsin ExaminerFred Clark, former Democratic state legislator, former executive director of Wisconsin’s Green Fire and owner of Clark Forestry, Inc., won a three-way race for the Democratic nomination in Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District Tuesday night, with 37.3% of the vote. AP called the race at 11:37 p.m.
 Ginger Murray, a small business owner and lawyer from the Northwoods received 31.8% of the vote and Chris Armstrong, a New Richmond resident and IT small business owner got 30.2%. 
Clark will face Republican candidate Michael Alfonso, who received President Donald Trump’s endorsement, in the general election. Alfonso is the son-in-law of Sean Duffy, Trump’s transportation secretary, who previously held the 7th CD seat. The seat is open because current Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany is running for governor. The general election will be an uphill battle for the Democratic nominee in a district that has been represented by Republicans since 2011. Prior to Tiffany and Duffy, Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District was represented by Democrat Dave Obey, the longest serving U.S. House member in Wisconsin history, from 1969 until 2011.
In 2021 Clark, who represented Baraboo as a Democratic representative in the state Assembly from 2009 to 2014, moved north to Bayfield County to retire, but over the last year, he told the Examiner, he has become concerned about what he sees as an assault on the U.S. Constitution and the future of America, so he decided to re-enter politics.
Clark sees an opportunity to mount a strong campaign as he tries to flip the large, Republican-leaning district, which covers much of the top half of Wisconsin, from red to blue.
“I think this is the first time in 15 years to have a truly competitive election in the 7th Congressional District,” he said. 
Clark’s  background in logging, as the owner of Clark Forestry, Inc., could appeal to voters in the northwestern district, where forestry products are a critical part of the economy. He has also worked as a forestry consultant with the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources and as a forest ecologist for The Nature Conservancy, and was the executive director and a founding board member of Wisconsin’s Green Fire, a conservation group. 
He also has a history of building relationships with Republicans and independents, which is critical in a  district that has voted by wide margins for Republicans since 2010, starting with former U.S. Rep. Sean Duffy (R-Hayward), now Secretary of Transportation. Duffy who won the district before it was redrawn following the last Census, and then increased his winning margins in the redistricted boundaries for four more elections. Tiffany also won by wide margins.
Clark celebrated his primary victory in Washburn, Wisconsin. In a statement after he was declared the winner, he said: “This election isn’t about left and right — it’s about right and wrong. And we all know that what we’re seeing is wrong.
“It’s wrong to make healthcare more expensive for millions of Americans. 
“It’s wrong to slash a trillion dollars from Medicaid.
“It’s wrong to do those things so you can call another round of tax giveaways to billionaires and trillionaires “paid for.”
“It’s wrong to turn a blind eye to the staggering corruption going on in DC right now.
“It’s just plain wrong.
“And northern Wisconsin deserves a Congressman willing to say so.
“Tom Tiffany hasn’t. Michael Alfonso won’t.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Byron Donalds says he’ll remove local officials who indulge in ‘sanctuary’ policies
description: One of the hallmarks of the Ron DeSantis administration compared to its GOP predecessors has been removal of locally elected officials from office — or threats to do so — for actions they claim are unlawful. Now Byron Donalds, positioned to succeed Ron DeSantis in the governor’s mansion next year, is promising more of the […]
text:
Protesters gathered in front of the Florida Capitol building on May 30, 2025, a day after ICE raided a Tallahassee construction site, detaining more than 100 workers. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)One of the hallmarks of the Ron DeSantis administration compared to its GOP predecessors has been removal of locally elected officials from office — or threats to do so — for actions they claim are unlawful.
Now Byron Donalds, positioned to succeed Ron DeSantis in the governor’s mansion next year, is promising more of the same.
The impulse extends to DeSantis’ allies. Over the past year and a half, Florida Attorney General (and former DeSantis chief of staff) James Uthmeier, placed in the job by the governor, has threatened to remove elected municipal officials because they balked at fully supporting Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) efforts in removing undocumented immigrants.
Under a state law passed in 2025, “the sheriff or the chief correctional officer” operating a county detention facility must enter into 287(g) cooperation agreements with ICE. It does not require municipal officials to do so, and several Florida cities have opted not to.
Yet Uthmeier threatened city officials in Fort Myers, Key West, Tampa, and Orlando with removal over the past 18 months because they acted or spoke about loosening their 287(g) agreements.
Donalds told the Phoenix over the weekend that Florida is not now and will never be a sanctuary state.
“If we have local officials decide that they want to ignore federal immigration law and the laws of the state of Florida and create sanctuaries, they’ll be removed from office, as well,” he said following a campaign rally in Tampa.
In Miami, Mayor Eileen Higgins campaigned last year on a promise to revisit the city’s 287(g) agreement. In a statement issued last week, she said she intends to fulfill that promise.
“Since my campaign and since taking office, I have made clear to the community that we must all treat all residents humanely and with dignity, which is why I said the City should revisit the 287(g) agreement,” Higgins said as reported by NBC 6 South Florida. “Since then, the Commission held a discussion at the end of June, and I look forward to a legislative item reaching my desk so I can sign it quickly.”
Meanwhile, Charlie Crist, running for St. Petersburg mayor next week against incumbent Ken Welch and four other candidates, told WMNF radio Friday that ICE was “an interesting animal” and that he would consider rescinding the city’s agreement with the agency.
“I’m not a fan of ICE. I’m a fan of enforcing the law but not murdering fellow Americans. That’s unconscionable,” he said, referring to the deaths of two U.S. citizens by ICE agents in Minneapolis in January.
Crist was asked in the interview if he would sign a 287(g) agreement.
“With ICE? Why would you?” he replied. He did not return a message Monday seeking clarification about his position.
St. Petersburg’s police department did sign a 287(g) agreement last year. Welch noted last month that the city had not been trained in the 287(g) program and had no officers “who are active in it now.”
‘Soros prosecutors’
Florida did pass legislation in 2019 that bans state and local governments from enforcing sanctuary policies, defined as any “law, policy, practice, procedure, or custom adopted or allowed by a state entity or local governmental entity which prohibits or impedes a law enforcement agency from complying with federal immigration laws or which prohibits or impedes a law enforcement agency from communicating or cooperating with a federal immigration agency.”
The confusion over whether municipalities need formal agreements with ICE led the city of South Miami to go to court a year ago. During testimony, attorneys representing the state told the judge municipalities are not required by law to enter into 287(g) agreements, WLRN reported.
Donalds also told the Phoenix that he wouldn’t hesitate to suspend state attorneys who he says are not enforcing the law.
DeSantis suspended two elected Florida state attorneys for what he called “incompetence” and “neglect of duty” and replaced them with former prosecutors he had initially appointed to be judges.
“Let me be very clear. You have a responsibility to follow the Constitution and follow the law in our state. If you have a state attorney that is not prosecuting the law and enforcing the law, they’re going to be removed from office, because it destabilizes law and order in safe communities in our state,” Donalds said.
“We’re not going to tolerate that the way that they’ve done in these blue states,” he added. “That’s one of the reasons why people are coming into our state. Because they want to be safe. So, we’re not going to ask some state attorney who’s going to go rogue and follow [George] Soros and the DSA thinking that they’re not going to uphold Florida law.”
Republicans have attacked “Soros prosecutors” over the years, referring to the millions of dollars that Hungarian-American philanthropist George Soros has contributed to the campaigns of reform-oriented prosecutors around the nation. Soros has been a general bogeyman for conservatives because of his financial support of progressive causes.
DeSantis suspended Hillsborough County Democratic State Attorney Andrew Warren in 2022 and Orange/Osceola County Democratic State Attorney Monique Worrel in 2023. Both went to court to win their jobs back. Worrell ultimately returned to office in 2024, winning re-election by more than 15 points.
Worrell’s predecessor, Aramis Ayala, was removed from murder cases on two separate occasions by Florida governors (first by Rick Scott in 2017 and by DeSantis in 2020) because of her public objection to the death penalty, but was never removed from her position.
DeSantis suspended Warren because he pledged not to prosecute people seeking abortions or gender-affirming care for minors. After Warren filed a lawsuit in federal court challenging his suspension, a judge ruled in January 2023 that the governor had violated the First Amendment in removing him because of political differences and anticipated “political benefit” to the governor.
That judge added, however, that he lacked power to reinstate Warren. A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit ruled in January 2024 that the judge should reconsider that decision, but the DeSantis administration appealed. Two months after Warren lost his bid for re-election in November 2024, the same 11th Circuit panel ruled that Warren’s challenge was moot, since his four-year term in office had expired.

title: ‘MAGA activist’ who wants to eliminate elections commission wins GOP nod for secretary of state
description: A self-described “authentic MAGA activist” who vows to bring election administration under control of the secretary of state won the Republican nomination for the office Tuesday. The Associated Press called the secretary of state primary election for Jay Schroeder at 8:42 p.m. With 90% of the ballots counted by 10:30 p.m., Schroeder had 47% of […]
text:
Wisconsin State Capitol (Wisconsin Examiner photo)A self-described “authentic MAGA activist” who vows to bring election administration under control of the secretary of state won the Republican nomination for the office Tuesday.
Jay Schroeder, Republican nominee for Wisconsin secretary of state. (Campaign photo)
The Associated Press called the secretary of state primary election for Jay Schroeder at 8:42 p.m. With 90% of the ballots counted by 10:30 p.m., Schroeder had 47% of the votes — far outpacing the candidate endorsed by the Republican Party.
Schroeder declared himself to be an “authentic MAGA activist” and a “MAGA aligned candidate on election integrity.” He focused his campaign message heavily on election administration, including eliminating the bipartisan Wisconsin Elections Commission.
The Democratic candidate for the post is JoCasta Zamarripa, a second-term Milwaukee alder and former five-term member of the state Assembly. Zamarripa was unopposed in the Democratic primary for secretary of state.
The secretary of state’s duties have been narrowed over the last several decades, but the office remains an elected position under the Wisconsin Constitution and cannot be eliminated without a constitutional amendment.
The remaining duties of the office include haveing responsibility for the official state seal and validating the certificate of Wisconsin’s electoral votes in presidential elections. But the office is otherwise unrelated to election administration.
The secretary of state also sits on the Board of Commissioners of Public Lands, which distributes revenues from timber sales on former federal land that now belongs to the state, donating proceeds to public school libraries and making loans to public projects.
Schroeder’s campaign has focused on moving Wisconsin elections from the bipartisan elections commission, established in 2016 by the Republican majority in the Legislature, to place them under the control of the secretary of state’s office. That would require the passage of new legislation.
Schroeder has run for the office previously. He was the Republican nominee in 2018, losing to incumbent Democrat Doug La Follette, and ran for the party’s nomination in 2022, coming in second to Amy Loudenbeck in the primary, who lost to La Follette that November.
At a 2022 Republican rally, Schroeder told a crowd that he would not have signed “a sheet of paper for the election,” apparently a reference to the certification of electoral votes in the 2020 Wisconsin presidential election, Bill Lueders reported in a commentary for the Wisconsin Examiner.
On his website Schroeder calls the elections commission “corrupt” and “a disaster.”
Nathan Pollnow, a beef farmer endorsed by the state Republican Party, came in a distant second in the primary, with just under 26% of the vote.
Pollnow ran on a platform of promoting government transparency, vowing to create a publicly accessible guide to laws, administrative rules and other actions of government.
Two other Republicans finished in the low double-digits: Cindy Werner, with 14% of the vote and Brayden Myer with just under 13%.
The 2026 election will be the first in more than 40 years without an incumbent running for reelection. The incumbent, Democrat Sarah Godlewski, opted to run instead for lieutenant governor. Godlewski also had no primary opposition Tuesday.
Godlewski was appointed in 2023 after La Follette, a long-time incumbent, resigned only a few months after winning reelection in November 2022.
