title: Arkansas lawmakers, NAACP seek accountability over state trooper punching 18-year-old
description: The Arkansas Legislative Black Caucus and NAACP Arkansas State Conference are calling for answers about a traffic stop involving a state trooper punching an 18-year-old that has gained national attention.  Rep. Jay Richardson, a Fort Smith Democrat and caucus chairman, told the Advocate Tuesday that the incident prompted lawmakers to schedule a meeting Thurs[...]
text:
(Courtesy of Arkansas State Police)The Arkansas Legislative Black Caucus and NAACP Arkansas State Conference are calling for answers about a traffic stop involving a state trooper punching an 18-year-old that has gained national attention. 
Rep. Jay Richardson, a Fort Smith Democrat and caucus chairman, told the Advocate Tuesday that the incident prompted lawmakers to schedule a meeting Thursday with Col. Mike Hagar, Arkansas State Police director and the state’s public safety secretary.
“I think anybody who’s seen the video understands that putting a fist to a young person, a young lady’s face is never acceptable,” Richardson said.
According to a federal lawsuit filed Monday, Alisa Hackett of Osceola was stopped near Manila on Aug. 1 for speeding by Moisses Arellano, an Arkansas State Police officer. 
Dash camera footage obtained by NEA report shows Arellano throwing Hackett, who is Black, to the ground while trying to handcuff her and then punching her in the face. 
Cindy Murphy, a spokesperson for Arkansas State Police, confirmed Tuesday that Arellano is still on active duty, and that “all uses of force are reviewed internally.”
The NAACP Arkansas State Conference is calling for an independent investigation, release of all recordings and review of the charges stemming from the traffic stop. 
In a statement, the organization said it was “deeply concerned” that a traffic stop involving nonviolent offenses escalated into an arrest where Hackett was taken to the pavement and struck in the face by a state trooper. 
“Accountability is not an attack on law enforcement; it is essential to public trust,” the NAACP said. “Officers who serve Arkansas honorably are best served by a system that investigates serious allegations fairly and transparently.”


Let us know what you think...


 

National civil rights attorney Ben Crump announced Monday that he was retained by Hackett in her lawsuit, which was originally filed by Little Rock attorney Luther Sutter. 
In a statement, Crump called on Arkansas State Police to open a use-of-force investigation through its Office of Professional Standards and make the findings public, and release any of Arellano’s prior use-of-force reports.
“Arkansas State Police have to explain to the public how that is a reasonable response to a teenager at a traffic stop,” Crump said. “If you cannot handle a teenage girl without taking her to the ground, cursing at her, and punching her in the face, you should not be wearing a badge.
Crump’s clients have included the family of George Floyd, the Black man killed by a white Minneapolis police officer in 2020. Floyd’s death sparked nationwide protests over policing and racial justice.
The lawsuit against Arellano argues Hackett’s constitutional rights to free speech and to be free from the use of excessive force during an investigatory stop, detention, or arrest were violated during the traffic stop. 
The lawsuit said Hackett continues to “suffer physical pain, humiliation, fear of law enforcement, anxiety, sleep disturbance, and emotional distress” from the arrest.
The suit seeks compensatory and punitive damages, attorney’s fees and a trial by jury.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Judge again bars Trump administration order that sought to limit mail voting
description: A federal judge ruled against the president's executive order to create a federal voter list and involve US Postal Service in limiting mail voting.
text:
BOSTON (AP) — A federal judge on Tuesday ruled against President Donald Trump’s executive order that sought to create a federal voter list and directly involve the U.S. Postal Service in election operations in a way that would limit mail voting.
U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani had already halted the order Trump signed in March, his second one attempting to set national election rules. On June 25, she sided with Democratic state attorneys general in granting summary judgment, preventing the core parts of Trump’s order from taking effect.
Tuesday’s ruling creates another legal hurdle for the Trump administration to overcome should it get the initial injunction lifted by the U.S. Supreme Court.
“That it is now less than 90 days before the November 3, 2026 midterm elections underscores the critical need for an injunction to prevent Defendants from changing election rules on the eve of the election,” she wrote.
The Trump administration in late July requested that the Supreme Court halt lower court decisions that have blocked the sweeping changes in nearly half the country.
In the latest lawsuit, Talwani, who was nominated by Democratic President Barack Obama, sided with the League of Women Voters and other voting rights groups.
[RELATED: CT, other Democratic states sue Trump over mail-in ballot order]
Her ruling granting a preliminary injunction barred the Postal Service from taking any steps to implement the order for this year’s midterm elections. She said the administration has so far declined to defend the constitutionality of the executive order.
“The executive branch has no authority to regulate elections,” she wrote.
Plaintiffs argued in two lawsuits, both filed in federal court in Boston, that the Republican president’s order should be found unconstitutional because the states and Congress, not the president, have the power to set election rules. The League of Women Voters also argued that Trump lacked the authority to issue his order and the U.S. Postal Service and other defendants lack the authority to carry it out.
Trump’s Republican administration, in its motions to dismiss the lawsuits, argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing to bring their claims. They also argued that the motions are premature and that plaintiffs lack the legal basis to bring their claim based on the Administrative Procedure Act, which governs how federal agencies develop and issue regulations.
Stephen Pezzi, a lawyer for the Trump administration, said the harms the plaintiffs referenced were subjective, because much can change with the voting list before it is made final. He also said no one would be prosecuted for violating the order.
Trump’s executive order, the second one aimed at elections during his second term, comes as he continues to suggest that there is widespread voting by noncitizens. Along with his executive orders, Trump is pushing legislation in the Republican-controlled Congress to create a proof-of-citizenship mandate. The SAVE America Act has passed the House but has stalled in the Senate.
States already have detailed processes aimed at keeping their voter rolls accurate, and voting by noncitizens has been shown to be rare. It also is a felony that can be punishable by deportation.
Trump issued the order in March after a bill he supported to overhaul voting stalled in Congress. The order would have had the federal government create a list of eligible voters and then directed the U.S. Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to those on the list. Election officials argued that it was ripe for abuse and could cause chaos, and the postal union has objected to the idea of mail carriers policing ballots.
The Postal Service had published a proposed rule required by Trump’s executive order in the Federal Register, but it was put on hold by Talwani’s first ruling.
In a separate lawsuit filed against the executive order, a federal judge in Washington in May agreed with the Trump administration that it was too early to block the order because it had yet to be implemented. That lawsuit was brought by Democratic and civil rights groups. In July, a three judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia upheld the May ruling by U.S. District Court Judge Carl J. Nichols that said an injunction against the order was premature.
Other rulings have gone against the Trump administration’s first executive order on elections, signed just months after he took office in his second term. That order would have required people to show documents proving their citizenship when registering to vote, among other changes.
Since his 2020 presidential election loss to Democrat Joe Biden, Trump has groundlessly claimed mail voting is rife with fraud and has launched a federal investigation into that year’s vote, even though repeated audits and investigations, including ones run by Republicans, found it was free of widespread fraud. Trump also has said he wants to “take over” election administration in Democratic areas.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Democratic lawmakers discuss possibilities for proposed statewide data center moratorium
description: Two Democratic New Mexico state lawmakers pitched a panel of their colleagues on taking up a data center moratorium in the 2027 legislative session.
text:
Aerial photos taken on June 26, 2026, show the construction site for Project Jupiter, the Oracle and OpenAI data center project planned for southern New Mexico. (Courtesy of Alexa Reynaud, Food & Water Watch, with aerial support provided by LightHawk)Two Democratic New Mexico state lawmakers pitched a panel of their colleagues on taking up a data center moratorium in the 2027 legislative session.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Reps. Micaela Lara Cadena (D-Mesilla) and Angelica Rubio (D-Las Cruces) spoke before the interim Science, Technology and Telecommunications Committee in Socorro on Tuesday about what they envision for the proposed moratorium, which they first announced alongside fellow Democrats in July.
The pair said there are key questions to answer in the months leading up to formally sponsoring legislation for a moratorium, such as what types of data centers should this apply to, and how long should a moratorium last?
Rubio, who along with Lara Cadena has been a vocal critic of the Project Jupiter data center campus under construction in southern New Mexico, compared it to other extractive industries the state has long relied on, such as oil and gas.
The two said that the state needs guardrails around data center development, and cited multiple ongoing lawsuits that accuse Doña Ana County officials of violating the state Open Meetings Act and voting on draft versions of documents when they approved Project Jupiter and issued $165 billion in industrial revenue bonds for it last year.
“Extractive industries and false promises from corporations have been part of New Mexico’s legacy for generations. Our communities have been told time and time again that the jobs will come, that they will be sustainable and that this time, things will be very different,” Rubio said. “Constituents in Doña Ana County are being handed the same promise, just with a fancy new label: artificial intelligence and data centers.”
Republican lawmakers on the committee told Lara Cadena and Rubio that they should conduct a study on how a moratorium would affect the state’s economy and job growth. Rep. Joshua Hernandez (R-Rio Rancho), in particular, questioned the wisdom of a moratorium.
“All of the cat pictures, pictures of our kids, everything we post on Facebook — it’s still going to live somewhere,” he said. “The reality is everybody’s not going to stop posting to social media or consuming that content.”
Lara Cadena and Rubio clarified that there can often be a significant difference between the energy needs of cloud storage data centers and hyperscale AI data centers that often propose to construct their own electric grid for power.
“We need to figure out how to define data centers. That’s going to be really important,” Lara Cadena responded.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: The Pa. budget included additional funding for a handful of school districts for third year in a row
description: For the third year in a row, the annual state budget included provisions that sent additional dollars to a handful of school districts, outside of the typical funding formulas that govern state support for the 500 public school districts.
text:
The state Capitol building in Harrisburg. (Photo by Tim Lambert/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)For the third year in a row, the annual state budget included provisions that sent additional dollars to a handful of school districts, outside of the typical funding formulas that govern state support for the 500 public school districts. 
And for the third year in a row, all of those districts are represented by Democrats in the state House.
Collectively, four school districts are set to receive $8 million in the 2026-2027 school year, on top of what they receive through the commonwealth’s basic education formula and newer adequacy formula. 
That’s on top of $5 million that went to a school district represented by House Speaker Joanna McClinton (D-Philadelphia) last year, and a tweak to the adequacy formula that sent $14 million to 11 school districts in the 2024-2025 budget.
But the four districts all faced unique financial challenges. Democratic lawmakers who sought the funding bumps in the latest budget say it was a product of those needs and their advocacy, not partisan favoritism.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
A spokesperson for House Democrats did not respond to requests for comment.
When asked whether he advocated for similar funding bumps for struggling school districts represented by Republicans, House Minority Leader Jesse Topper (R-Bedford) told the Capital-Star “that’s not something that we normally look at.”
“There are always those kind of provisions that are inserted [in the budget],” he continued. “That’s not something I want to see. I want to redo the entire way we fund education and the adequacy formula. I’m not thrilled with any of them.”
The repeated inclusion of additional funds for certain districts raises questions about the effectiveness of Pennsylvania’s formulas for funding its public schools, and about whether all parts of the state are able to access additional funds when necessary.
“I don’t think that there is a perfect formula out there that fits all,” said Edward Albert, the executive director of the Pennsylvania Association of Rural and Small School Districts. 
While he praised the additional funding some schools have received through the new adequacy formula — the result of a 2023 court decision that found Pennsylvania’s school funding formula was unconstitutionally inequitable — he acknowledged that there are some district leaders who have felt left behind by it.
School bus parked in Upper Burrell Township, Westmoreland County on Jan. 16, 2026. (Photo by John Beale for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“We’re rejoicing this year with what we got in the budget, but I have superintendents emailing me saying, ‘I didn’t get anything,’” he said.
But Albert doesn’t see the apparent partisan divide over which school districts are receiving supplemental funding as necessarily a show of favoritism, even if the rural school districts he works with are more likely to be represented by Republicans.
“If you’re just looking at the bigger picture from 30,000 feet up, Democrats are obviously gonna want more money, and obviously Republicans are a little more conservative,” he said. “The whole thing is not black and white.”
Difficult decisions
The Muhlenberg School District in Berks County faced a $2 million budget shortfall in the 2025-2026 school year, leading officials to mull staff cuts and a property tax hike.
In this year’s state budget, the district represented by Rep. Jacklyn Rusnock (D-Berks) received $2.5 million in additional funds, on top of what it was set to receive from the basic education funding formula and the newer adequacy formula.
“Muhlenberg is the fastest growing school district in Berks County, “Rusnock said. “It’s growing exponentially faster than every other district.”
According to Rusnock, that’s caused a unique financial strain that the school funding formula is not adept at keeping up with. So she went to legislative leaders and asked for help.
“The way I look at it, we’re bringing in additional funding that focuses on the district’s needs, and it’s also not placing an additional burden on the local taxpayers,” she said. “This is something that I’ve been working with leadership on since December.”
Asked about why she thinks only school districts represented by House Democrats have received additional funding outside the formulas in recent years, she said it wasn’t something she’d considered.
“I didn’t realize that had happened,” she said. “I can only speak for myself. I am an advocate of public education. I’m a product of education. I taught in the public education system. I just think it’s really important our school districts are getting what they need … I really can’t speak to why it would be a Democrat or Republican issue.”
The Steelton-Highspire School District in the Harrisburg area in Dauphin County faced a $4.5 million budget shortfall, leading to discussions about cutting dozens of staff. Along with basic education and adequacy funding, Steelton-Highspire will receive $1 million in additional funding after lawmakers pushed for more help.
According to Rep. Dave Madsen (D-Dauphin), who represents the district, the idling of the Cleveland Cliffs steel mill in Steelton, which employed roughly 500 people, strained the community’s tax base. As it stands, it’s not clear what can replace the hundred of lost jobs or the business itself.
“It is a very unique situation when you have such a small population that has the conditions they have in terms of their tax base,” he said. “I don’t see how they could overcome it without some sort of additional help, and that was the case I made to leadership.”
Asked if he thought partisanship played into Steelton-Highspire being awarded money outside the typical school funding formulas, Madsen couldn’t say.
“I advocate for my district, and I know other colleagues, both Republican and Democrat, have similar circumstances. What their conversations with leadership look like, I’m not privy to. I just know with the ones that I had, working with my school district, we just laid out a case for why we would need additional help.”
The Morrisville-Borough School District in Bucks County is set to get $3.5 million in the 2026-2027 school year outside the typical funding formulas.
Rep. Jim Prokopiak (D-Bucks) described issues not entirely dissimilar from those Steelton-Highspire faced.
“Fifty years ago, there was a lot of industry that was attached to the school district. As industries eroded, the tax bases eroded,” he said. “The money for Morrisville this year was correcting a problem that had been decades in the making.”
Years of funding struggles led the school district to take on debt.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Asked about the political tilt of the awards, Prokopiak pointed to issues that have primarily affected suburban and urban school districts, which are more likely to be represented by Democrats.
Pennsylvania has a school funding policy known as hold harmless, which ensures that, even if student population declines, schools continue to receive the same amount of money from the state that they did the year before.
“I don’t think it’s a party situation. I think it’s more demographic changes,” Prokopiak said. “Rural school districts have traditionally, because of the population decreases in those areas, actually gotten more funding than they necessarily would under a new formula. Many counties in Pennsylvania are shrinking, but they still maintain their same funding formula. Areas that are growing tend to be more in the suburban areas, which recently have tended to be more represented by Democrats than Republicans.”
The Whitehall-Coplay School District in Lehigh County is also set to receive $1 million, but Rep. Jeanne McNeill (D-Lehigh), who represents it, did not respond to a request for comment from the Capital-Star.
Like the other school districts, it faced a multimillion dollar budget deficit and officials mulled difficult decisions like whether to cut staff.
How it’s played out in recent years
Last year only one district, the William Penn school fistrict in Delaware County, received an additional funding bump. It had struggled financially for years and was one of six named plaintiffs in the adequacy funding lawsuit – which led to a new formula being created in 2024. 
William Penn is in House Speaker McClinton’s district. 
State budget sent $5 million to a struggling school district represented by the Pa. House speaker

At the time, a spokesperson for House Democrats told the Capital-Star, “the guiding principle for the House Democratic caucus has always been and always will be to help the least advantaged. There is an overlap to the extent that our leaders represent some of the poorest areas. Maybe that is a good thing.”
During negotiations over the 2024-2025 state budget, 11 school districts were singled out to receive annual budget bumps of $14 million collectively, including William Penn and Steelton-Highspire.
Like all the five school districts that received supplemental funding in the 2025-2026 and 2026-2027 budget, all 11 were all represented by Democrats in the state House.
But lawmakers and experts told the Capital-Star that year that the selection of schools in Democratic lawmakers’ districts was the result of tense negotiations over the creation of the adequacy formula.
When creating the new adequacy formula to address the school funding lawsuit, lawmakers in both parties knew that it needed to increase funding for school districts in impoverished areas. But there was disagreement over how that should be measured.

Eleven Pennsylvania school districts got $14 million in extra funding in the latest budget


Democrats advocated for a formula that would measure local poverty based on figures collected by school districts themselves. They argued those numbers were the most accurate available since the district staff  collecting them regularly interacted with, and were likely to be trusted by, impacted families. 
Republicans preferred data collected in annual surveys by the U.S. Census Bureau, arguing that school districts may be incentivized to meddle with data that would affect their own funding.
It was a fight that Republicans ultimately won. But that meant dozens of school districts receiving less funding than they would have under the Democrat-backed plan. 
The additional funding for 11 school districts was a way to bridge that gap for some of those most affected by the change. They were also represented by Democratic lawmakers who plead for additional help ahead of an expectedly close vote over the implementation of the adequacy formula.
Albert, the executive director of the Pennsylvania Association of Rural and Small School Districts, suggests one way lawmakers could help districts that fall under unique strain would be to build funding for them into the budget.
“Maybe there’s a pool of money put off to the side to kind of offset those to make it right,” he said. 
The hope is that the funding being readily available would make lawmakers of both parties more willing to advocate for it reaching school districts they represent.
Albert also advocated for increased transparency and accountability measures to ensure that school districts are using state funding to boost educational outcomes. He hopes that would make lawmakers less reticent to provide additional funding for struggling school districts.
“I’m a firm believer in accountability. I think when we’re asking for money, I think it’s very important for us to say, ‘here’s what we’re using the money for.’ … But that’s a two way street. I think legislators should want to come to schools.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Marshand Crisler, former interim Hinds County sheriff, is released from prison and put on house arrest
description: Former Interim Hinds County Sheriff Marshand Crisler, center, enters the federal courthouse with his wife Eva and attorney John Collette on Wednesday, Nov. 6, 2024, in Jackson.
text:
Former interim Hinds County sheriff Marshand Crisler, who was convicted on bribery charges in 2024, is out of federal prison and under house arrest.
Crisler was originally sentenced to two and a half years in prison, three years of supervision and a $15,000 fine.
The U.S. Bureau of Prisons confirmed Tuesday that he was transferred to community confinement on Aug. 3 and will serve the rest of his sentence on house arrest in Hinds County.
In November 2024, Crisler was convicted of soliciting and accepting $9,500 in bribes from Tonarri Moore, a convicted felon who according to federal officials was acting as an FBI informant. Crisler, who served as a Jackson City Council member from 2001 to 2009, was found guilty by a jury after a three-day trial in Jackson.
While serving as interim sheriff for part of 2021, Crisler was accused of telling Moore about investigations involving him, moving Moore’s cousin to a safer part of the Hinds County jail, giving him a job with the sheriff’s office and allowing Moore to have a gun despite being a convicted felon.
The U.S. Bureau of Prisons’ website on Tuesday still listed Crisler’s release date as Dec. 9, 2026.
Crisler’s wife, Eva Howard Crisler, posted on Facebook celebrating his release.
“You are finally home where you belong. I thank God for bringing you safely home, and I am grateful for the opportunity to begin this new chapter together,” she wrote.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Moore County pays NC family to settle wrongful institutionalization lawsuit
description: A Moore County family has won a settlement from the county over allegations that the social services department would not return custody of children with disabilities to their mother after she received cancer treatment.  Rumina Slazas’ two children were kept in institutions after her 2022 cancer treatment, even though she was able to take care […]
text:
Rumina Slazas and her children sued Moore County. (Photo: Disability Rights NC)A Moore County family has won a settlement from the county over allegations that the social services department would not return custody of children with disabilities to their mother after she received cancer treatment. 
Rumina Slazas’ two children were kept in institutions after her 2022 cancer treatment, even though she was able to take care of them, her 2024 federal lawsuit said. She was in remission for almost a year while the county kept custody of her children. 
The suit went to mediation earlier this year and the county agreed to a settlement totaling $55,000.
Slazas’ son, J.S., who was 16 when the 2024 lawsuit was filed, will receive about $12,633, according to court documents. Her daughter, S.S., who was 15 when the lawsuit was filed, will receive $19,000. Slazas will receive $8,000. Disability Rights North Carolina, which represented the family, receives the rest.
“I did nothing wrong to lose my kids, I just got sick,”  Slazas said in a statement. “This settlement does not undo the trauma my children and I experienced, but I am hopeful it results in better outcomes for other children with significant disabilities in the child welfare system.”   
Moore County officials did not immediately respond to calls and an email for comment. 
According to the lawsuit, S.S. has intellectual and developmental disabilities. She spent nearly nine months at UNC Health and four months in a psychiatric residential treatment facility in South Carolina before she was able to return home.
A family sues Moore County for institutionalizing children after their mother’s cancer diagnosis

J.S. has intellectual and physical disabilities that limit his ability to walk and care for himself. He lived for a while in the county’s social services office before being transferred to an intermediate care facility. J.S. returned home after about 16 months in county custody. 
S.S. and J.S. did not receive the care they needed while institutionalized, resulting in mental and physical decline, the lawsuit said. 
“While no amount of money will ever make the Slazas family whole, this settlement demonstrates that survivors of unlawful institutionalization deserve compensation,” Holly Stiles, Assistant Legal Director for Litigation at DRNC, said in a statement.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: How effective are Iowa recycling programs?
description: The Iowa Department of Natural Resources is working to develop a reporting and data collection system to better understand recycling in the state. In an online stakeholder meeting Tuesday about a study comparing other states’ data collection methods, DNR staff said regular data on recycling streams and collection will help with efforts to improve solid […]
text:
Iowa Department of Natural Resources is working to gather recycling data so it can better understand how much is recycled in the state. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) The Iowa Department of Natural Resources is working to develop a reporting and data collection system to better understand recycling in the state.
In an online stakeholder meeting Tuesday about a study comparing other states’ data collection methods, DNR staff said regular data on recycling streams and collection will help with efforts to improve solid wast management in the state. 
The report and call with Iowa stakeholders was part of DNR’s ongoing Sustainable Materials Management vision initiative to improve solid waste management programs and policies
The initiative started in 2018 and has since produced a landfill material analysis that found more than 70% of waste sent to Iowa landfills could be recovered or diverted to recycling, or compost facilities. 
Another facet of the sustainable materials management plan included a study on food waste management that showed Iowans, on average, throw away 200 pounds of food each year. The initiative also worked to produce a report on Iowa’s recycling facilities based on a voluntary survey. 
Jennifer Wright, the financial and business assistance supervisor with DNR’s Land Quality Bureau, said that since Iowa recycling facilities are not permitted by DNR, there is no method for the department to track recycling activity.
“We need that information because it’s critical for developing and measuring diversion goals, determining processing capacities and our ability to allocate financial support through our grant programs,” Wright said in the stakeholder meeting. 
Wright said that currently, the only way the state can “reasonably calculate that we’re having any success related to recycling” is through a waste characterization analysis, which she said is “cumbersome” and “doesn’t really actually tell us the whole story.”
“Part of the pursuit of this data is one, so that we can actually determine, are we recycling at a reasonable amount,” Wright said. “ …the other part is so that we as DNR … can continue to do grants focused on infrastructure or even improvement of existing infrastructure.” 
What do other states do?
Lisa McDaniel, a project manager with SCS Engineering, a contractor working with DNR on the project, said that whatever data the state collects should be “tied to real decisions” on things like what is being collected, where it is being sent and where there are gaps in service. McDaniel presented findings from the report analyzing other state data collection programs and their strengths.
McDaniel said that while some Iowa facilities report data, it’s a “fragmented” view.
“They’re not collected in a consistent format or reviewed in a way that supports statewide analysis, and that ultimately limits Iowa’s ability to track material flows and recycling performance, guide infrastructure investments, and measure whether policies or programs are having the intended effect,” McDaniel said. 
According to the report, which will is not yet published, 17 states require data reporting from recycling facilities, haulers, processors, or transporters and this data is typically tied to some sort of permit or administrative structure with the state. 
Data collected from these sources, McDaniel said, give a good indication of what types of materials are being recycled, in what quantities and where. 
The other common type of required reporting in states came from municipalities or similar local authorities. McDaniel said this type of reporting, which was required in 14 states, gave a good idea on where and how recycling is available and local gaps that exist, but didn’t always include information on total tonnage recycled, for example. 
Other states have no required data reporting and rely on voluntary information. 
McDaniel presented several potential steps forward for Iowa, including starting with a voluntary reporting program to “test data elements and build a baseline” before looking at policy changes that would lead to statute authority. 
Where can Iowans get their bottle and can deposits back? New interactive site helps

Stakeholders on the call noted that it would be important for them to know any data they reported would be kept confidential, so operators wouldn’t feel they were divulging proprietary information. 
Wright said the department adheres to a confidentiality clause in state code and isn’t “particularly curious” about proprietary information. 
“We’re mostly curious about how much tons are getting recycled in this state,” Wright said. 
The study looked at traditional recyclable materials, like cardboard, glass, paper and cans, but stakeholders said they would also be interested in providing information about materials they frequently received that aren’t recyclable and other less traditional materials they deal with. 
Jeff Phillips, a senior project manager with SCS Engineering, said until the state gets this data, working on Iowa’s Sustainable Materials Management plan is like reading a book “and there’s three chapters missing.” 
“We don’t have the full story even as a baseline to determine exactly what needs to happen holistically across the state of Iowa,” Phillips said. 
The full report will be posted in the coming weeks on the DNR’s Sustainable Materials Management website where the previous reports are also housed.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Meta wants to keep Hyperion data center details protected
description: The Louisiana Public Service Commission will decide Wednesday whether Meta can keep its records on its artificial intelligence data center project in Richland Parish secret from the public.  Environmental and consumer groups have pressed state utility regulators to require Meta provide more information about its massive data center taking shape at its Hyperi[...]
text:
From left, Louisiana Public Service Commissioners Foster Campbell, Eric Skrmetta, Mike Francis, J. P. Coussan, and Davante Lewis hold a meeting in Plaquemine, La., on Aug. 22, 2025. (Photo credit: Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)The Louisiana Public Service Commission will decide Wednesday whether Meta can keep its records on its artificial intelligence data center project in Richland Parish secret from the public. 
Environmental and consumer groups have pressed state utility regulators to require Meta provide more information about its massive data center taking shape at its Hyperion campus in Richland Parish. The facility has contracted with Entergy to meet its electricity needs, starting with three natural gas-powered turbines the utility will build to power the data center. Meta has since announced it intends to expand Hyperion, which will require another seven power-generating units. 
The Alliance for Affordable Energy, the Union of Concern Scientists, the Sierra Club and other organizations want more firm figures from Meta before the Public Service Commission gives a green light for Entergy to build out all that power infrastructure. The groups subpoenaed Meta for information that backs up its prior statements on local investment, job creation and electricity needs. They contend Entergy has never adequately explained how Meta came up with those figures in its applications to the Public Service Commission to construct new turbines for Hyperion. 
The groups also are concerned utility customers might eventually bear the costs of the additional power generation if the data centers back out their agreements at some point in the future.   
“With overall future demand for AI services remaining uncertain, Meta backing out is a possibility that regulators must rigorously take into account,” Paul Arbaje, senior analyst for the Union of Concerned Scientists said in a news release Monday. “Ratepayers didn’t prompt these huge expenses, so at a bare minimum Entergy’s shareholders should have to share this risk, and the LPSC should make that expectation clear at the outset. … If Entergy is making a huge bet that all these costs will be worth it, the company should be betting with its own money, not ratepayer money.”
A PSC administrative law judge ruled last month that Meta needed to provide the records the advocacy groups are seeking. Following the state’s utility regulatory protocol, Meta has appealed the judge’s ruling to the commission.
Meta contends the information being sought amounts to trade secrets which would put the company at a competitive disadvantage if made public. Numerous state and local officials, including Gov. Jeff Landry and Congresswoman Julia Letlow, have signed nondisclosure agreements to conceal their knowledge of the deal.           
The Public Service Commission will decide in December on Entergy’s proposal for seven more power turbines to service Meta.
In a separate item on Wednesday’s agenda, commissioners will consider charging all major utility customers a new monthly fee to finance studies on nuclear energy. 
Chairman Eric Skrmetta, R-Metairie, is asking commissioners to approve a 20-cent monthly fee for customers of the state’s three largest electric utilities — Entergy Louisiana, Cleco and SWEPCO. Ratepayers for Entergy’s New Orleans subsidiary, which its city council regulates, would not see the fee on their bills. 
In March, Skrmetta directed the PSC staff to look into ways to get utility companies to consider adding more nuclear power and new technologies such as small modular reactors and microreactors to their generation portfolios. Money from the fee would give utility companies extra revenue to pay for feasibility studies, potential site assessments, economic modeling and other early-stage work to determine if nuclear power generation is cost-effective in Louisiana. 
President Donald Trump has called on state leaders to promote nuclear energy, and Louisiana was one of a handful recently tapped to be part of a federal initiative to encourage industry investment. Skrmetta has co-chaired Trump’s campaign in Louisiana for the past three elections.
Public Service Commissioner Davante Lewis, D-Baton Rouge, said he’s not opposed to the idea of studying nuclear technologies but thinks it’s a bad time to make Louisiana residents shoulder more costs amid rising energy prices and high economic inflation.
Louisiana has some of the highest poverty rates in the country. If a 20-cent tariff is a small cost for the average ratepayer, then it’s an even smaller cost for a $50 billion utility company and would be nothing for them to pay for it, Lewis said. 
Utilities could even split the cost with their bigger customers such as Meta and Amazon, he added.
The proposed tariff would last for five years with an option to renew it and would generate an estimated $4 million per year, according to PSC records.
Skrmetta, who was recently appointed to a position with the U.S. Department of Energy, did not return calls Tuesday.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico advocates urge feds to move barrels of radioactive waste amid wildfire risk
description: A group of New Mexico advocates unveiled a billboard near Santa Fe on Tuesday that urges the federal Department of Energy to quickly move dozens of barrels full of radioactive waste away from wildfire danger to relative safety underground.
text:
Fire on the Mountain spokesperson James Oyster speaks to reporters Aug. 11, 2026, in front of the group’s new “Bury the Barrels” billboard, which urges the federal Department of Energy to transport roughly 2,500 barrels containing radioactive waste to the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant in Carlsbad. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM) 
A group of New Mexico advocates unveiled a billboard near Santa Fe on Tuesday that urges the federal Department of Energy to quickly move dozens of barrels full of radioactive waste away from wildfire danger to relative safety underground.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The group, known as Fire on the Mountain, said the billboard along Interstate 25 near Cienega is aimed at stopping the Energy Department from fighting a New Mexico Environment Department effort to increase the amount of legacy nuclear waste that is deposited in the federal Waste Isolation Pilot Plant repository in Carlsbad. 
In February, the NMED announced it was seeking to modify its 1999 permit that allows WIPP to operate in the state. The proposed modification would require WIPP to ensure that at least 55% of radioactive waste it deposits at WIPP between 2027 and 2031 comes from Los Alamos National Laboratory.
The department also seeks to require the DOE to inter by July 1, 2028, all of LANL’s above-ground nuclear waste stored at an area known as Disposal Area G, which sits near White Rock, New Mexico.
Area G, among other legacy nuclear waste, contains 2,500 barrels containing radioactive and other chemical waste that is stacked under four tent-like structures. That particular waste is the focus of the new “Bury the Barrels” billboard that a small group of activists gathered underneath Tuesday, as wildfire smoke from the nearby Frijoles Fire cast a pall over the Sangre de Cristo Mountains.
“New Mexicans have a healthy fear of wildfires, but they don’t know that they should fear something else, and that’s wildfire and radiation,” group spokesperson James Oyster said at a news conference under the billboard. “This is a real possibility because the Department of Energy has left Cold War-era nuclear weapons’ waste sitting … right over that way, in drums stacked in fabric tents in a forest known for repeated catastrophic wildfires.”
The group held signs urging the DOE to stop fighting the NMED and sang a version of the Grateful Dead’s “Fire on the Mountain,” with lyrics tweaked the DOE to “bury the barrels.” 
Oyster cited the 2000 Cerro Grande Fire, which burned near Area G and sent smoke plumes throughout the region, as well as other recent wildfires that burned on or near LANL property, as evidence that LANL needs to act swiftly to prevent a wildfire that sends radioactive material through smoke into the lungs of nearby communities. 
The NMED’s move to modify its WIPP permit says that requiring the DOE to reduce the amount of radioactive waste in New Mexico is meant to codify a 2023 settlement agreement between DOE and the state in which the federal government “committed to prioritizing” New Mexico legacy waste. 
Instead, the DOE shipped 992 waste containers from Idaho National Laboratory to WIPP between 2023 and 2025, according to NMED, compared to fewer than 200 waste containers from LANL. 
A spokesperson for the Department of Energy did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment on the billboard or the group’s concerns about wildfire risk to Area G.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: FIU students file federal lawsuit over ICE protest clampdown
description: Just over a year after Florida International University police signed a 287(g) agreement with ICE, an organization formed to contest the move filed suit against the university. The suit stems from a March 13 anti-ICE protest during a public event with FIU President Jeanette Nuñez and retired pro baseballer Alex Rodriguez. Students stood up in […]
text:
View from the FIU campus. (Photo via FIU)Just over a year after Florida International University police signed a 287(g) agreement with ICE, an organization formed to contest the move filed suit against the university.
The suit stems from a March 13 anti-ICE protest during a public event with FIU President Jeanette Nuñez and retired pro baseballer Alex Rodriguez.
Students stood up in the audience, turned around and faced the crowd while donning shirts urging, “ICE OFF FIU.”
“Despite claiming ‘Freedom — of thought and expression’ as a core value in its mission statement, FIU could not let the ICEBreakers’ silent exercise of free expression go unpunished,” the suit filed Tuesday in the federal Southern District of Florida alleges. 
Per the lawsuit, the students left the auditorium on their own, the protest lasted less than five minutes, the students were silent, and the conversation on stage continued throughout.
FIU charged the students with misconduct, saying they violated the school’s “expressive activities” policy.
The university, to “protect health, safety, and welfare and prevent disruption of university activities,” prohibits inside university buildings “protests, parades, marches, picketing, demonstrations, and other similar expressive activities,” per the policy.
The university is requiring the students to produce two-minute videos of themselves reflecting on the regulation and what it means. If not submitted by Sept. 4, they will be barred from registering for classes or receiving diplomas. They have received written reprimands from the university, too.
According to an email exchange between FIU administrators included in the lawsuit, they did not believe the protest disrupted the event.
The students want to continue protesting, but allege this situation has chilled their speech and that they “have suffered and continue to suffer emotional distress and other damages, all to their detriment.”
The students are asking the court to deem the FIU policy unconstitutional and award compensatory and punitive damages.
FIU did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday afternoon. 
287(g)
Last year, Florida law enforcement agencies across the state, including at state universities, signed 287(g) agreements deputizing their officers as ICE agents.
According to an ICE database, no other state universities outside Florida have signed 287(g) agreements.
“Florida’s universities’ eager enlistment is an aberration nationwide,” the suit states. 
FIU police says agreement with ICE is for the best; faculty disagree

FIU Police Department Chief Alexander Casas told faculty last year, in explaining his rationale for participating with federal officers, that he wants his department to have a say in how immigration enforcement goes at the South Florida institution designed to be internationally facing.
Nuñez and Casas held a meeting with faculty who had concerns or questions about the agreement in April 2025.
“Since then, FIU’s enlistment in the federal immigration enforcement regime has sparked intense debate on campus. Through assemblies, town halls, faculty meetings, petitions, and other fora, members of the university community have discussed this issue and expressed their opposition to FIU’s actions,” the lawsuit states. 
ICEBreakers protest during a university event. (Screenshot via lawsuit filing)
According to the suit, ICEBreakers “caries out its mission by educating the university community about FIU’s collaboration with ICE and by galvanizing community members to join in direct actions to protest that collaboration.”
“Despite the lack of disruption the silent demonstration caused, FIU Police investigated the protest, and, ten days later, on March 23, 2026, referred the case to the Office of Student Conduct & Academic Integrity (SCAI) for consideration of further action.”
The students are represented by the ACLU of Florida and Community Justice Project.
“ICE has no place at any university, especially one that calls itself a haven for international students,” Andrew Caro, one of the seven charged students, said in a news release. “Inviting federal enforcement on campus goes against everything this university claims to represent — and instead of listening to students’ real concerns about this, they punished us.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Save the Great Salt Lake, without federalizing it
description: Earlier this year, the Trump administration asked Congress for something unusual: $1 billion to save a lake. The president’s budget request proposes a major federal investment to restore the Great Salt Lake, which it calls “a critical economic and ecological asset” for the nation. It comes after Utah’s legislature passed a resolution calling on Washington […[...]
text:
The northern shores of the Great Salt Lake, at the southern end of Hansel Valley, in Box Elder County, are pictured on Wednesday, May 27, 2026.(Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Earlier this year, the Trump administration asked Congress for something unusual: $1 billion to save a lake. The president’s budget request proposes a major federal investment to restore the Great Salt Lake, which it calls “a critical economic and ecological asset” for the nation. It comes after Utah’s legislature passed a resolution calling on Washington to partner with the state in the lake’s recovery.
The timing is right. After another dry winter, the Great Salt Lake is once again in decline. Utah has spent the past several years building the foundation for recovery. The challenge now is to put this foundation to work at scale.
A new report by the American Conservation Coalition outlines how Congress and the administration can assist. It stresses a simple point: Washington can do plenty, but the best way to help is by supporting Utah’s state-led strategy, not by federalizing it.
The federal government has good reason to partner with the state. More than 2.5 million people live downwind of the lake’s exposed bed, which sends dust laced with arsenic and other heavy metals toward one of the country’s most flourishing regions. The lake generates nearly half the area’s precipitation. It feeds the snowpack that supplies Utah’s farms, cities, and ski resorts. It also produces roughly 40 percent of the world’s brine shrimp eggs, and it hosts more than 10 million migratory birds each year.
Yet no country has ever restored a declining saline lake. The Aral Sea, Iran’s Lake Urmia, and California’s Owens Lake all turned into public-health disasters after upstream users drained the rivers that fed them.
Utah intends to be the exception, and it is trying to do so in a distinctly Utah way: through voluntary market mechanisms and innovation rather than regulatory mandates. After the lake hit a record low in 2022, the state overhauled its water laws, created a commissioner’s office and a water trust to facilitate voluntary water transactions, and committed more than $1 billion in public funds. Private and philanthropic partners have also now pledged $200 million to lake recovery.
The state’s strategy depends on working with farmers, municipalities, industry, and other water users, not against them. Voluntary agricultural leases allow farmers to conserve water, send it downstream, and receive compensation while retaining their underlying water rights. The state is also working with cities and industrial users to reduce consumption and dedicate conserved water to the lake. Together, these efforts are already delivering tens of thousands of additional acre-feet to the Great Salt Lake.
The state has made real progress, but the problem exceeds what Utah can address alone. The Bear River, the lake’s largest tributary, runs through Wyoming and Idaho before reaching Utah, and more than a third of the basin’s irrigated farmland lies outside the state. Federal agencies also manage key lands, including the Bear River Migratory Bird Refuge, where invasive phragmites consume water that could otherwise support the lake.
Washington does not need a new bureaucracy to save the lake. Our report outlines how it can best prioritize its investments in ways that deliver measurable water to the lake, improve the state’s ability to measure water savings, and strengthen Utah’s voluntary approach rather than supplant it.
By those standards, voluntary water conservation should be at the top of the list. Better measurement is also essential, because conservation on paper means little unless the water can be tracked to the lake. Funding should also support invasive-species removal, supply augmentation, and advanced cloud seeding.
Federal investment should flow through the institutions Utah has already built. Federal agencies can provide funding, technical support, and help with interstate coordination and federal land management. But implementation should remain state-led.
Utah has already built an effective strategy for Great Salt Lake recovery. Washington can now help it work at scale. If federal support reinforces the state’s approach instead of replacing it, America could become the first country to save a drying saline lake, the Utah way.

title: Naamans Little League Advances to Semifinal Game in 2026 Little League Mid-Atlantic Regional Tournament
description: Naamans Little League defeated Berlin Little League from Maryland to advance to a semifinal game on Thursday.   Naamans Little League advanced to the semifinal round of the 2026 Little League Baseball Mid-Atlantic Regional Tournament, following their win Monday evening. Naamans scored 12 runs in the elimination game. The game started out as a pitchers’ duel[...]
text:
No. 10 Charles Puit at bat during Naamans Little League’s game against Berlin Little League from Maryland. Photo Courtesy of Little League Baseball and Softball.
Naamans Little League defeated Berlin Little League from Maryland to advance to a semifinal game on Thursday.
 
Naamans Little League advanced to the semifinal round of the 2026 Little League Baseball Mid-Atlantic Regional Tournament, following their win Monday evening. Naamans scored 12 runs in the elimination game.
The game started out as a pitchers’ duel between Delaware starter Jason Pontari and Maryland pitcher Gus VanKlompenburg. Both pitchers threw well and didn’t allow a run through the first three innings of the game. 
Naamans scored the first run of the game in the top of the fourth. Catcher James Grugan scored Robert Heisler — after he started the inning with a lead-off walk — from third base on a two-out single up the middle giving Naamans the first lead of the game.
Berlin captured the lead in the bottom half of the inning on the strength of four hits including a lead-off double by Jonah Isett. Isett scored Maryland’s first run a batter later on first baseman Cooper Smith’s single through the middle. Singles by Jackson Baraby and VanKlompenburg drove in two more runs and, after a fourth run crossed the plate, Naamans trailed 4-1 heading into the fifth inning. 
The Delaware squad responded in a big way with an 11 run top of the fifth. 
Naamans recorded eight hits from seven different batters along with five walks in the frame. The first five runs of Naamans’ rally were scored prior to a weather delay that lasted over an hour. Delaware first baseman Kole Dzwilewski stepped to the plate with the bases loaded and two outs when the game resumed and struck a RBI hit past the third base bag. The hit started a run of two-out success that plated Delaware’s additional six runs.   
Delaware third baseman Taj Amobi scores one of Delaware’s 11 runs in the top of the fifth. Photo Courtesy of Little League Baseball and Softball.
Pontari and Brian Miller recorded the remaining six outs for Delaware, advancing the team to a semifinal game.
Naamans’ semifinal game will be on Thursday at 3:00 p.m. Delaware will take on Capitol Hill Little League from Washington D.C. and the winner will move on to face Pennsylvania in the championship game. Delaware’s game against Washington D.C. will be aired on ESPN.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: County agrees to accept $1.2 million settlement in legal malpractice lawsuit
description: Osceola County has agreed to settle a legal malpractice lawsuit against its attorneys by accepting a payment of $1.22 million. Minutes from the county board’s July 21, 2026, meeting indicate the board held an emergency, closed-door discussion to discuss legal strategy, after which the board unanimously agreed to the $1.22 million settlement amount to be […]
text:
(Photo by simpson33 via iStock / Getty Images Plus)
Osceola County has agreed to settle a legal malpractice lawsuit against its attorneys by accepting a payment of $1.22 million.
Minutes from the county board’s July 21, 2026, meeting indicate the board held an emergency, closed-door discussion to discuss legal strategy, after which the board unanimously agreed to the $1.22 million settlement amount to be paid by the law firm of Dorsey & Whitney.
The board approved the amount subject to the law firm’s approval of the amount, with specific settlement agreement terms to be approved by the county’s legal counsel in the case and by the county attorney.
The settlement stems from a lawsuit concerning an alleged procedural error tied to a proposed 2015 bond issue.
In March of 2015, the City of Harris within Osceola County contacted the county and requested funding assistance for sanitary sewer system and wastewater treatment facilities.
The county agreed to obtain funding to complete the project and also sought to obtain funding to improve a county road known as White Avenue. Attorneys John Danos and Amy Bjork at the Dorsey & Whitney law firm allegedly agreed to prepare all the necessary documentation and proceedings so the county could issue specialized tax increment financing bonds for the project.
On Sept. 21, 2015, Bjork allegedly sent an email to Osceola County that included a proposed resolution setting a date for a public hearing on the creation of an Urban Renewal Area that would be established in connection with the TIF bonds.
Because the area encompassed land in both the county’s and the city’s tax jurisdictions, Iowa law required that a joint agreement be signed and adopted by both the city and the county before final approval of the Urban Renewal Area.
On Sept. 22, 2015, the Osceola County Board of Supervisors adopted the resolution and set the final public hearing date for the formation of the Urban Renewal Area, to be held on Oct. 20, 2015.
The resolution allegedly stated a joint agreement had been presented to the county board and it directed the county auditor to forward that agreement to the City of Harris. In fact, the lawsuit claims, Dorsey never provided Osceola County with any such agreement
On Nov. 3, 2015, the county and city were sued by several taxpayers claiming the new Urban Renewal Area was illegal. The attorney for Osceola County’s insurance carrier allegedly inquired about the lack of the legally required joint agreement, which led to Danos sending county officials an email on Nov. 24, 2015. In that email, Danos allegedly wrote, “Here is the agreement, just have Osceola execute it. The board has already approved it, and it is still timely.” Attached to the email was a copy of an agreement that had never been approved, lawyers for the county later alleged, and the deadline for its approval had already passed.
Danos allegedly followed that email with one that included an “updated” version of the joint agreement indicating it was merely memorializing an August 2015 verbal agreement between the county and the city.
There was no factual basis to support the claim of a prior “verbal agreement,” the county would later assert. “The purpose of Danos’ second joint agreement was an attempt to cover-up Dorsey’s error in failing to send a joint agreement before Oct. 20, 2015,” the lawsuit claimed.
The lawsuit between the county and Dorsey & Whiteney remains active at this point, with no court record indicating the final settlement agreement has been approved by all of the parties.
Calls to the Dorsey & Whitney offices in Des Moines and Minneapolis were not returned Monday and Tuesday.

name: WyoFile
title: Felony intimidation is not Rep. Gary Brown’s only conviction. He pleaded guilty to harassment in 2013.
description:
Police said they collected voicemails where a man they identified as Brown can be heard saying to his ex-girlfriend, “I’m praying that you die soon” and “I promise you I’m going after your daughter.”
The post Felony intimidation is not Rep. Gary Brown’s only conviction. He pleaded guilty to harassment in 2013. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming Rep. Gary Brown pleaded guilty to a harassment charge and received a 14-day jail sentence in 2013, Colorado court records show, almost two decades after he served a prison sentence for felony intimidation of a different ex-girlfriend. 
In the 2013 case, authorities suspected Brown of calling his ex-girlfriend dozens of times, a police report from the time shows. Police said they collected voicemails that Brown left for his ex-girlfriend, which WyoFile later reviewed. On them, a man they identified as Brown can be heard saying, among other things, “I’m praying that you die soon” and “I promise you I’m going after your daughter.”
Brown, who represents Cheyenne’s House District 41, did not respond to questions emailed to him Sunday or voicemails and text messages from WyoFile on Monday.  
In July, WyoFile first reported that Brown had his right to vote and hold public office restored in 2023 in Wyoming following a 1991 felony conviction in a case involving an ex-girlfriend in Larimer County, Colorado. The judge in that case sentenced Brown to four years and six months in prison.
Through public records requests, WyoFile has since obtained additional court filings, police reports and prison records that indicate Brown also has multiple misdemeanor harassment convictions.
Most recently, Brown pleaded guilty in 2013 to a harassment charge after he was accused of calling and texting an ex-girlfriend repeatedly after she ended the relationship. Over the course of two days in February 2013, Brown allegedly called her 40 times, according to a police report. Brown also left her several messages when she did not answer his calls, detailing his intention to hold up her phone line and fill her voicemail so that no one else could call or leave a message, the police report states. 
In the messages, Brown refers to his former girlfriend as Jerry. Because WyoFile was unable to locate the victim for comment, her full name will not appear in this story.
Fort Collins Police collected six voicemails as evidence in the case, and wrote in their report that they were all made by Brown to the victim. WyoFile obtained copies of those recordings through a public records request. 
“Now I’m praying that you die soon in the way you really deserve to,” a man that police identified as Brown can be heard saying in one of them. 
“And you know, I hope with everything in me, Jerry, that you get the hell you deserve when you go to hell,” the man says. “Because obviously there’s no way you’re a Christian.” 


According to Colorado law, a person commits harassment if, with intent to harass, annoy or alarm another person, they make repeated communications at inconvenient hours that invade the privacy of another person and interfere in the use and enjoyment of another’s home or private residence or other private property. Colorado law also provides a domestic violence enhancer which may be applied when a crime is used as a method of coercion, control, punishment, intimidation, or revenge directed against a person with whom the defendant is or has been involved in an intimate relationship.
After pleading guilty on June 3, 2013, to harassment, Brown was sentenced to 14 days in jail, 18 months supervised probation and 36 hours of community service along with fines, fees and court costs, according to a case docket obtained by WyoFile through a records request. 
Brown was also ordered to complete a domestic violence evaluation — the docket shows a domestic violence sentence enhancer applied to his case — and to comply with recommended treatment. In a later document where Brown’s probation officer sought to have his supervised probation changed to unsupervised, the officer indicated he’d completed an “anger management/domestic violence class” on Nov. 5, 2013.
Cheyenne voters elected Brown to the Legislature in 2024. In his first term, Brown served on the House Revenue Committee and the House Corporations, Elections and Political Subdivisions Committee. In 2025 and 2026, he sponsored unsuccessful legislation that would have required local governments to reimburse defendants for costs incurred fighting criminal charges that resulted from the lawful use of self-defense. 
Brown is not a listed member of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, though he does regularly vote alongside the caucus and co-sponsors legislation with its members. He’s now running for a second term and faces opponents in both the primary and general elections. 
‘Everlasting, burning, blistering hellfire for eternity’
The victim contacted the Fort Collins Police Department on Feb. 28, 2013, according to a report filed by Officer Allen Benbow. 
She told the officer that she had broken up with Brown four days prior after dating him for two years, and that Brown had repeatedly called and texted her since she ended the relationship, according to the report. 
“[The victim] said that she had to block all incoming calls and text messages from Brown on her private cell phone, but she’s not able to block numbers on her work number,” Benbow wrote. 
Police reported Jerry showed the officer a series of texts, including one from Brown in which he allegedly wrote, “This isn’t over,” and one from Jerry telling Brown not to contact her, or her family or friends, according to a copy of the document. 
“I don’t need to contact you or them to do what I need to do,” police say Brown wrote in a text, according to the report. He also allegedly sent a message asking Jerry to return several personal items to him within two weeks. 
Jerry showed the officer her call history, according to the report, which alleged that Brown called her 22 times on Feb. 25, 2013. Twenty of those calls “took place between the hours of 0834 and 1211 hours,” the report states. Three days later, Brown allegedly called Jerry 18 times, according to the report, with 16 of those calls taking place between 4:55 a.m. and 6:29 a.m.
The officer listened to six voicemails he said Brown had left Jerry since their relationship ended, according to the police report, and logged an audio recording of the messages as evidence in the case. 
“You need to call me. Need to call me as soon as possible,” a man police identified as Brown said in the first voicemail. “Come on, pick up your phone, Jerry. You need to go ahead and call me as soon as you can. I’m going to keep calling until I fill up your mailbox and your bosses won’t be able to talk to you. I don’t care. If that’s the way you’re going to do that, you’re not going to answer my phone calls, I’ll just fill up your whole mailbox. I can do that. I know how to go about doing that. All I gotta do is keep talking.”


“I just don’t get it,” the man police identified as Brown said in the second message. “I don’t see why you’re doing this, and right now, I got your phone tied up where nobody else can call you. I guess that’d be fine. I’ll just keep anybody from your company from calling you on this phone. That’s what I can do.”
In the third voicemail, police reported that Brown told Jerry he will go after her daughter. 
“OK, Jerry, now you’ve apparently blocked my phone from calling your phone again, so that means that you’re gonna play this stupid game with me,” a man police identified as Brown said. “Well, this is what I’m gonna do. You want to play this game? I’m going after your daughter. I promise you I’m going after your daughter. I’m gonna get her.”


In a fourth voicemail, a man police identified as Brown makes an apparent reference to an apocalyptic interpretation of the Bible that has proliferated in recent decades and includes seven years of suffering that will precede Armageddon. 
“You will be spending seven years through this tribulation period,” he said. “And then you are also going to end up spending eternity in everlasting, burning, blistering hellfire for eternity, Jerry,” 
In a fifth voicemail, a man police identified as Brown talks about the couple’s animals and shared finances. In the final voicemail included in the case, he makes another reference to Jerry dying. 
“The best thing you could do is die quickly for everybody in the world,” he said. 
The victim told police she was concerned for the safety of her daughter and herself, the report states.
When Officer Benbow called Brown on March 1, 2013, Brown allegedly told him “he didn’t remember threatening to get [the victim’s] daughter,” or calling her on the morning of Feb. 28, according to the report. 
The report states Brown agreed to turn himself in to police but failed to do so. A judge signed an arrest warrant on March 7, 2013, though it’s not clear when Brown was taken into custody. As the case proceeded, Brown filed a successful motion for permission to leave the state of Colorado, stating in court documents that he was living in Cheyenne at the time and attending Laramie County Community College. 
Felony conviction
Brown had been in trouble with the law before. Court documents show that in late 1991 he was charged with two felony intimidation counts stemming from alleged harassment of an ex-girlfriend, Patricia Aine, and a friend of hers, Bonnie Scott, in Larimer County, Colorado, where Brown lived at the time. 
Scott told police that an unknown caller, whom she suspected was Brown, had repeatedly called her house and would not hang up, leaving Scott unable to use her phone. When she confronted the caller, “calling him Gary,” a police report states, he “did come on the line and specifically said to her ‘you are going to get it too.’”
Scott told police that she knew Brown through Aine, who had recently broken up with him. In her own report to the police, Aine described several instances of Brown allegedly making threats to her at a local country music venue. Aine told police that on the evening of Oct. 11, 1991, at the Sundance Steak House, Brown made several remarks to her and at one point allegedly “walked past her and had turned towards her and formed a gun with his hand and pointed it at her.” 
A week later, Aine called the sheriff’s office after she arrived home and smelled a gas leak. 
“Our investigation revealed that her residence had been entered through a partially secured sliding patio door and someone had cut the gas line to the furnace,” a police report states. “It was further found that a lighted cigarette had been placed inside a book of matches and left on the victim’s floor, as well as the placing of plugged in curling irons left on the victim’s clothing.” 
Prosecutors initially brought only harassment charges against Brown. Three months into the case, however, Brown was charged with one felony count of criminal attempt to commit first-degree arson and one felony count of second-degree burglary of a dwelling. In 1992, three of the four charges were dropped, according to court filings, when Brown agreed to plead guilty to one felony count of intimidating a witness and victim in relation to Aine. Brown was sentenced to four years and six months in prison. He also received a 129-day pre-sentence credit, according to court records. 



Brown’s Department of Corrections admission form, dated April 3, 1992, indicates that he had three misdemeanor harassment convictions from 1986, 1987 and 1989 on his record at that point. The document does not indicate the county or state where those convictions took place. However, Larimer County court files indicate Brown was charged and convicted of harassment in 1989 for allegedly following his ex-wife to and from her workplace and making obscene gestures toward her. One police report from the case alleges that Brown gestured “as if he had a pistol by extending his index finger and his thumb and then indicating that he was shooting her.” 
About nine months after his sentencing for the 1992 felony conviction, Brown asked a court for an early release from prison.
“At the time of sentencing, Defendant was not committed to change his mental attitudes,” a December 1992 motion for reconsideration states. “Because of his initial therapy in the Department of Corrections, he has gained insight into the source of his problems in interpersonal relationships. He is now committed to change and continue mental health treatment. The mental health treatment can best be pursued in a community setting”
The court denied Brown’s request on Jan. 19, 1993. Colorado Department of Corrections records indicate that Brown was released on April 23, 1995.
The post Felony intimidation is not Rep. Gary Brown’s only conviction. He pleaded guilty to harassment in 2013. appeared first on WyoFile .

name: VTDigger
title: Vermonters deserve honesty about the failure of the data center bill
description:
The bill's failure was about a Senate add-on that turned a strong bill into one Vermont couldn't support.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermonters deserve honesty about the failure of the data center bill.
text:
Dear Editor,
There is no question that the House did indeed do great work on the data center bill, H.727, ensuring strong protections for the environment, communities and ratepayers via joint jurisdiction between Act 250 and the Public Utility Commission.  
The Senate further tightened up the language and improved the House version to help guarantee the law would protect Vermont from a data center’s massive and often devastating impact. Then the Senate Natural Resources and Energy Committee added an “extraction of cash” payment and created a loophole for water pollution. This is where it went wrong.
After the House and Senate committees heard testimony from the Department of Public Service and the Land Use Review Board on these major flaws, they failed to make corrections. The DPS made it clear it could not support the bill with this extortion payment language, and the Land Use Review Board found it unacceptable that its Act 250 process for regulating water discharges was bypassed.  
These were well-defined issues that required resolution. The committees developing H.727 were well aware of them. Two key stakeholders raised legitimate, timely concerns on the Senate version of the bill. Leadership did not address these identified issues in the data center bill, which resulted in a detrimental bill landing on the governor’s desk.  
Understandably, VPIRG and many Vermonters, including Vermonters for a Clean Environment, are upset, but if one wants to point fingers, be honest about the facts and reality of the situation.
Fortunately, Vermont has solid regulations in place via Act 250 and the PUC. In the next legislative session, a bill specific to large-load data centers can be properly developed without last-minute loopholes that compromise Vermont. Vermonters for a Clean Environment will continue to work toward this goal, as we always have.
Annette SmithDanby, Vt.
