title: NU Regents will consider $166M increase in state tax dollars in proposed 2027-29 budget request
description: LINCOLN — A proposed University of Nebraska operating budget request for the 2027-29 budget cycle would increase taxpayer dollars to NU by $91 million compared with NU’s current annual budget. The proposal before the NU Board of Regents this Thursday calls for an additional 4.25% in state appropriations each budget year. NU’s current annual appropriation is[...]
text:
University of Nebraska President Jeffrey Gold, center, meets with senators on the floor of the Nebraska Legislature, including state Sen. Mryon Dorn of Adams. April 2, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — A proposed University of Nebraska operating budget request for the 2027-29 budget cycle would increase taxpayer dollars to NU by $91 million compared with NU’s current annual budget.
The proposal before the NU Board of Regents this Thursday calls for an additional 4.25% in state appropriations each budget year. NU’s current annual appropriation is just over $704 million. Regents will consider an inflation-based request for an additional $29.9 million in the 2027-28 fiscal year and $31.2 million on top of that new baseline in the 2028-29 fiscal year.
The total operations increase for NU, if the request is approved as-is, would be 6.47% more than if lawmakers kept NU’s share of tax dollars for operations flat each year.
The University of Nebraska Board of Regents. Dec. 5, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The budget proposal separately asks for $11.5 million in new funds to support students who ace the ACT, expand research capacity and restore funds for biomedical research.
NU regents will also consider a $55 million request to replace aging software that supports “nearly every aspect of the university’s operations,” according to the meeting materials. State colleges also use the software.
NU President Jeffrey Gold said NU has worked hard to be a “responsible steward” of state resources in recent years while also responding to multiple internal budget reductions. He said NU has always protected its “core mission” of teaching, research and statewide engagement.
“But after years of reductions, we have reached a point where additional cuts will inevitably diminish our ability to serve Nebraskans, strengthen our workforce and fuel the state’s economic growth,” Gold said. “At a time of economic uncertainty, investing in the University of Nebraska is an investment in the people, innovation and opportunities that will shape our state’s future.”
Budget proposal specifics
The proposed operations increase is based on a four-year rolling average of Consumer Price Index data, which the proposal states is a “predictable and objective mechanism.” In June, the regents similarly hiked tuition rates by 4.25% ahead of the upcoming academic year.
University of Nebraska President Jeffrey Gold, left, and interim University of Nebraska-Lincoln Chancellor Kathy Ankerson host a listening session after Ankerson assumed the top UNL administrative role Jan. 12, 2026, and after UNL finalized $27.5 million in cuts under former UNL Chancellor Rodney Bennett in December 2025. Jan. 15, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The proposed non-operations investments are as follows:

$55 million in capital construction funds to replace the Enterprise Resource Planning system, which supports finance, human resources and payroll, procurement, student services and facilities management.
$5 million for biomedical research, which would restore cuts made in spring 2026.
$3 million to support NU’s Presidential Scholars Program, which offers a full-ride scholarship and annual $5,000 stipend to attract and retain prospective students who aced the ACT.
$3 million to expand research capacity and competitiveness in pursuit of rejoining the Association of American Universities.
$500,000 in the 2028-29 budget year and each year after to support operations and maintenance at the new Ag Tech Incubator and Accelerator, which is a companion to the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s National Center for Resilient and Regenerative Precision Agriculture being built at NU’s Nebraska Innovation Campus in Lincoln.

‘Cat’s been out of the bag’
NU’s latest proposal comes as Gov. Jim Pillen, a former NU regent, eyes reelection and as the state faces a nearly $850 million deficit for the 2027-29 budget cycle. Pillen became governor in 2023 and has been more critical of NU’s budget than in his prior role.
For example, NU requested a 3.5% increase for each year of the 2025-27 budget cycle in August 2024. But come January 2025, Pillen suggested a 2% cut in the first fiscal year.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen at a meeting to certify Nebraska’s May primary election. June 8, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Ultimately, lawmakers increased NU’s budget by about 0.6% each year of the 2025-27 cycle.
Pillen told the Nebraska Examiner in a mid-July interview that one of his “greatest frustrations” from his early days as a regent was increasing spending, sometimes upward of 5% every year, no matter whether NU faced inflationary or deflationary pressures.
“The cat’s been out of the bag, and I believe it’s time to rein it back in,” Pillen said in July.
The governor has directed all state agencies to do more with less, and he’s asked his budget director to withhold 5% of legislatively authorized monthly allotments to prepare for more cuts. Lawmakers will have the final say and could choose to release the withheld funds next spring.
NU’s total share of the reductions, if they all go through, would be just shy of $30 million, which NU officials have criticized. Pillen, however, says that “just tells you how severe and how much opportunity there is” to take a deeper look at NU’s budget.
State Sen. Ashlei Spivey of Omaha, left, meets with State Sen. Rob Clements of Elmwood, chair of the Legislature’s Appropriations Committee. March 5, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Pillen said he is asking that NU provide “measurables” to justify any increase, such as whether every faculty member can be held accountable to be a teacher and researcher while working full time. He noted that NU takes a larger per-capita portion of taxpayer dollars than its regional peers and other Big Ten universities but is “critical to Nebraska.”
“The taxpayers are clear on their expectation to reduce government spending, and as the largest operating program in the General Fund budget, the university should be part of the solution,” Pillen told the Examiner on Thursday, when NU released its proposed request.
The Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services and Department of Education receive a greater share of income and sales tax revenue. However, after removing non-operational spending, such as for Medicaid and aid to K-12 schools, NU ranks highest in operational costs.
‘Attitude of priorities’
NU Regent Paul Kenney of Amherst, board chair, told the Examiner it will be interesting to see how the year comes out, especially with Pillen calling for more cuts.
Regent Paul Kenney of Amherst, chair of the NU Board of Regents. April 23, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Kenney noted the request is based on inflation and seeks to keep up with increased costs for salaries, benefits, health insurance and utilities. Asked if he had concerns heading into the next legislative session, he said NU has to understand what’s out there and what’s available.
“Maybe the corn market turns around or the bean market turns around and we have a different picture in six months,” Kenney said.
NU Regent Barbara Weitz of Omaha similarly said NU is helping to shape the next generation of scholars who will determine the well-being of the state and country.
“I think creating an attitude of priorities around educational goals for the state is really important and, clearly, when state revenues are hurt by policies that mean our crop prices go down, it’s a real concern,” Weitz said.
State Sen. Ashlei Spivey of Omaha, a returning member of the Legislature’s budget-writing Appropriations Committee, said she hadn’t reviewed NU’s proposed budget request but has talked to NU leaders. She said NU is an “important and integral asset of Nebraska,” which helps produce the next workforce, attracts and retains talent, and spurs economic development.
“I did not support the cuts previously and will be advocating and championing for the university to be able to be more sustainable and made whole from some of the other decisions that have been made in the previous biennium,” Spivey said.
‘Unlikely to be approved’
The outgoing Appropriations Committee chair, however, had a different view. State Sen. Rob Clements of Elmwood, when told about the proposed 4.25% increase both years, initially laughed and said the Legislature will look at the request, “but it’s very unlikely to be approved.”
University of Nebraska Regent Barbara Weitz of Omaha at a meeting of the University of Nebraska Board of Regents. April 24, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“That’s a real big increase,” said Clements, who will be term-limited in January after 10 years. “All the other state agencies are being asked to reduce their expenses, and so, I guess I would say they’re thinking it doesn’t hurt to ask, but they should not be expecting to get fully funded at that level. That’s a lot of money.”
Weitz said some people have encouraged regents to look at tuition rates. Compared to other Big Ten and regional universities, NU continues to be competitive with tuition rates. However, Weitz said she doesn’t want to see NU using increased student debt as a means to offer those very students the education regents think they deserve.
“The struggle here is all the unknowns, and I think it’s so hard to be a state senator who’s got to balance all the needs across the whole state,” Weitz said. “I get that that’s very difficult, and I know that means setting priorities.”
The regents meeting begins at 9 a.m. Thursday in NU’s Varner Hall in Lincoln.



Other agenda items
In other agenda items Thursday, the NU Board of Regents will consider eliminating multiple degrees that have had declining or low enrollment for multiple years. This includes UNL’s ethnic studies major and insect sciences undergraduate degree. No cost savings are estimated. 
Regents will also consider approving multiple new degrees at the University of Nebraska at Omaha using existing courses and faculty, including a bachelor’s degree in statistics and operations research and a master’s degree in early childhood education.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon addresses DOJ monitoring of polling sites
description: The U.S. Department of Justice announced Tuesday that its Civil Rights Division is monitoring polling sites in in Hennepin and Ramsey counties for the state’s primary election “to ensure transparency, ballot security and compliance with federal law,” according to a press release. The two counties declined to allow the DOJ inside polling precincts, as is […]
text:
Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon speaks Friday, Aug. 9, 2024 before a public accuracy test of voting equipment ahead of the primary election at the elections office at Dakota County Administration Center in Hastings, Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)The U.S. Department of Justice announced Tuesday that its Civil Rights Division is monitoring polling sites in in Hennepin and Ramsey counties for the state’s primary election “to ensure transparency, ballot security and compliance with federal law,” according to a press release.
The two counties declined to allow the DOJ inside polling precincts, as is their right by law, according to Secretary of State Steve Simon, whose office oversees election administration. Instead, DOJ monitors will be required to abide by the same rules as everyone else, restricting access within 100 feet of the polls.
Minnesotans have grown highly skeptical of the federal Department of Justice, given the routine violation of constitutional rights that many suffered during Operation Metro Surge, when the Trump administration sent 3,000 federal immigration agents here. After the killing of Renee Good, for instance, prosecutors in the Office of U.S. Attorney District of Minnesota quit in disgust after DOJ senior leadership instructed them to investigate Good’s wife, rather than her killer, ICE agent Jonathan Ross.
Simon addressed the presence of the DOJ monitors during a Monday press conference, in what appeared to be an effort to calm the waters.
“This has been done the last several election cycles under multiple presidents, including President Biden. And Minnesotans may well have voted at a polling place with a federal observer there and not even noticed,” he said.
The stated reason for the observers, he said, is to make sure the counties are complying with the Voting Rights Act by helping voters in languages other than English and those with disabilities.
He added: “I certainly understand why reports of agents of the federal government at the polls would alarm people, especially here in Minnesota, given what we’ve all gone through over the last several months. So, I want to say we are not taking anything for granted.”
President Donald Trump has repeatedly and falsely claimed to have won Minnesota during his three presidential runs, while also making debunked allegations of widespread voter fraud in mostly Democratic, urban counties around the country.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Nursing home worker keeps license amid theft conviction and pending abuse charge
description: An Iowa nursing home worker charged with dependent adult abuse after being convicted of stealing medications can continue to practice in Iowa, the Iowa Board of Nursing has ruled. The board recently charged registered nurse Rachel Anne Flowers, 43, of Liberty with having a sexual, emotional, social or business relationship with a patient and being […]
text:
Silver Oak Nursing & Rehabilitation Center in Marion, Iowa. (Photo via Google Earth)An Iowa nursing home worker charged with dependent adult abuse after being convicted of stealing medications can continue to practice in Iowa, the Iowa Board of Nursing has ruled.
The board recently charged registered nurse Rachel Anne Flowers, 43, of Liberty with having a sexual, emotional, social or business relationship with a patient and being convicted of an offense that directly relates to the duties and responsibilities of nursing.
The board alleges the disciplinary charges are based in part on a complaint that Flowers had an unprofessional relationship with a patient at some unspecified time in the past and on a 2025 conviction for theft.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
To resolve the case, Flowers and the board recently agreed to a settlement that calls for her nursing license to be placed on probation for two years. Flowers must also complete 60 hours of educational training in patient boundaries and ethics. As part of that same settlement, the board has also lifted a January 2026 order in which Flowers had agreed to refrain from practicing nursing while the board’s investigation of the matter was continuing.
It’s not the first time Flowers has been accused of an unprofessional relationship with a patient.
In 2023, the board ordered Flowers to complete a three-day course on professional boundaries and ethics after alleging that while working at an unspecified care facility from 2019 to 2021, she engaged in a personal relationship with a patient.
Court records show the board’s recent disciplinary case against Flowers is tied to her 2025 conviction for theft of supplies from the Parkview Manor nursing home in Wellman.
According to police reports, on March 28, 2025, the home’s director of nursing, Rebecca Pacha, obtained Flowers’ backpack and found multiple items belonging to the facility. The items, worth an estimated $654, included a Lidocaine patch, a suture kit, an insulin safety syringe, a heartburn medication, a laxative and other medications and medical supplies.
Flowers was later convicted of fifth-degree theft and was awarded a deferred judgment that will expunge the case from court records after the successful completion of probation.
Court records also show that Flowers is currently facing criminal charges related to her 2024 work at different nursing home, the Silver Oak Nursing & Rehabilitation Center in Marion. In that case, prosecutors have charged Flowers with prohibited acts involving prescription drugs, dependent adult abuse, and unlawful possession of a prescription drug.
Prosecutors allege Iowa’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit investigated a series of incidents related to Flowers’ care for a 52-year-old male resident at Silver Oak. The resident allegedly told the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit’s investigator that he and Flowers had kissed multiple times and that she allowed him to touch her bare breasts. Other staff at the facility reported it appeared the man had fallen in love with Flowers and that he believed he was in a relationship with her.
At one point, prosecutors allege, the resident was prescribed Viagra pills, and Flowers was “the only nurse who administered” that particular medication to him. Silver Oak later reported 33 of the man’s Viagra pills were unaccounted for and, according to prosecutors, Flowers was later found to have the “top half of a Viagra pill card” that belonged to the man.
Flowers has pleaded not guilty to the criminal charges in that case. A trial is scheduled for Oct. 12, 2026.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Flowers or her attorney, Shawn Michael Fitzgerald, for comment on Tuesday.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Activists allege Grand Rapids police are working with ICE despite city policy
description: Immigrant rights advocates gathered in the lobby of Grand Rapids City Hall on Tuesday afternoon to state their claim that the Grand Rapids Police Department is coordinating with federal immigration authorities, including ICE, despite city policies against doing so. “The mayor and the chief of police have been repeatedly telling us since January of 2025 […]
text:
Jeff Smith, an organizer with GR Rapid Response to ICE, speaks alongside other anti-ICE advocates to demand the city's police department stop cooperating with ICE agents. Aug. 11, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Immigrant rights advocates gathered in the lobby of Grand Rapids City Hall on Tuesday afternoon to state their claim that the Grand Rapids Police Department is coordinating with federal immigration authorities, including ICE, despite city policies against doing so.
“The mayor and the chief of police have been repeatedly telling us since January of 2025 that GRPD is not cooperating with ICE, and we’re saying that that’s a bold-faced lie because we are seeing it on a regular basis firsthand,” said Jeff Smith, an organizer with GR Rapid Response to ICE. 
A GRPD spokesperson wrote in a statement to the Michigan Advance that the department  “is neither responsible for, nor has the authority to, enforce federal civil immigration laws used to detain or remove undocumented immigrants from the United States” and does not take on the responsibility of performing immigration functions unrelated to investigating and enforcing criminal violations. 
Smith specifically referenced an instance about two weeks ago in which activists with his organization were gathered outside the ICE office in downtown Grand Rapids — they knew ICE had detained someone and were waiting to see what was going to happen to that person. When the building’s garage opened, a van owned by GEO Group — which runs the ICE detention facility in Baldwin, Mich., the biggest in the Midwest — was exiting, seemingly to transport individuals to that facility.
Advocates said that the photo, which shows a photo showing Grand Rapids Police Department officers outside an ICE office in the city as a van transferring detainees leaves the office, demonstrates local police cooperation with ICE. Aug. 11, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
 
“We were blocking their escape because we see what they’re doing as immoral, unjust, and again creates more family separation and trauma,” Smith explained. “Part of our work as rapid response is to try to intervene and disrupt ICE’s ability to abduct people from our community.”
He continued on to say that Grand Rapids police officers were already waiting at the site and prevented the activists from blocking the van, stating that the officers also threatened them with arrest and said they would be forcibly removed from the scene. 
Gema Lowe, an organizer with Movimiento Cosecha GR, holds a photo showing Grand Rapids Police Department officers outside an ICE office in the city as a van transferring detainees leaves the office. Aug. 11, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
“GRPD does respond to incidents where there is an element of public safety or criminal activity (for example, trespassing, illegally blocking roads, etc.) which aligns with our law enforcement responsibilities, regardless of the involved parties,” the GRPD spokesperson said. 
GRPD policies state that “Officers may provide assistance to federal immigration authorities when there is an emergency posing an immediate danger to the public safety or to the federal agents,” as well as that “If a non-emergency request is made by federal immigration authorities the department may provide available support services, such as traffic control or peacekeeping efforts, upon approval of the Chief of Police or a Deputy Chief of Police.”
“This is showing a coordination between ICE, GEO transportation and GRPD. We broadcast everything through our Facebook live, even though GRPD continues to deny coordination with ICE, the evidence is showing the contrary,” Nerida Aviles, an organizer with Movimiento Cosecha GR, said. “City resources should not be used to support ICE’s violence, transit and lawless actions.”
Lauren Coman, an organizer with No Detention Centers Michigan, added that the GRPD’s presence at the scene of incidents such as this, as well as at the Intensive Supervision Appearance Program office in the city — which is home to an “alternative to detention” program run by ICE, where a number of immigration arrests have been made — that they are facilitating the transportation of detainees directly to the North Lake Processing Facility in Baldwin.
Lauren Coman, an organizer with No Detention Centers Michigan, demanded sanctuary city policies in Grand Rapids and an end to Grand Rapids Police Department officers working alongside ICE agents. Aug. 11, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
“ICE will continue to capture our community members and police agencies, just like the GRPD and the Kent County Sheriff’s Office, will continue to normalize this campaign of terror,” Coman continued. “We say no more. Stop the killings. Stop the kidnappings. Enact true sanctuary policies in Grand Rapids and Kent County for your neighbors to shut down North Lake and abolish ICE.”
Aviles, as well as Gema Lowe, another organizer with Movimiento Cosecha GR, also emphasized their dissatisfaction with Mayor David LaGrand’s response. They said LeGrand has been unresponsive to their concerns and requests to meet with him.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Biddeford protest targets Sen. Collins over ICE funding
description: Biddeford resident Monica Davis was helping a friend move on a Monday morning in July when  she saw a girl racing down the road saying, “They’ve just killed someone, ICE just killed someone in the street.” That was how Davis, who lives a few blocks from Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero’s family, found out that he […]
text:
Alessia Gaspar Da Silva, whose husband, Marcos, was taken by ICE in January and still remains in custody, spoke at an Aug. 11 protest outside U.S. Sen. Susan Collins' Biddeford office about the harsh conditions her husband has faced in detention. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/ Maine Morning Star)Biddeford resident Monica Davis was helping a friend move on a Monday morning in July when  she saw a girl racing down the road saying, “They’ve just killed someone, ICE just killed someone in the street.”
That was how Davis, who lives a few blocks from Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero’s family, found out that he had been killed by federal immigration agents.
“I will just never forget that moment of discovering that it had happened right here in the center of town, right next to our home,” she said on Tuesday, holding a sign reading “ICE OUT” at a protest outside U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ Biddeford office.
“Using your voice, it’s a rare chance that we have in this world to be able to speak up for the things that we believe,” Davis added. “So I’m going to be just absolutely blasting my resistance to the ICE and Trump regime at every single opportunity that I get.”
Davis was among more than 150 people who lined Main Street on Tuesday, echoing calls for accountability and criticizing Collins for supporting an additional $70 billion in funding for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in congressional Republicans’ latest budget resolution. 
The group also took time to remember Guerrero and the dozens of others who have died in detention or were shot by immigration agents nationally since President Donald Trump’s enforcement surge began.
Alessia Gaspar Da Silva, whose husband, Marcos, was taken by ICE in January and still remains in custody, spoke about the harsh conditions her husband has faced in detention, including being fed once every 30 hours, denied medical care, and relocated to different states without her knowledge.
“He’s been gone for seven months. It feels like a lifetime,” she said.
Da Silva told the crowd she has repeatedly reached out to Collins’ office. In response, she said she received a newsletter, listing the senator’s accomplishments.
Biddeford resident Monica Davis stands before a mural of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero and his daughter, which was painted by three Maine artists. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/ Maine Morning Star)
“Collins has not done anything,” Da Silva said. “She has no accountability. No transparency. No transparency for the people that are … being terrorized.”
Democratic Maine lawmakers, including Sen. Henry Ingwersen from York County, and Reps. Ellie Sato from Gorham and Marc Malon from Biddeford attended, urging the crowd to vote this November. 
“Susan’s vote to fund ICE with no strings attached was shameful. And we, as voters across this city, across this district, and across Maine, need to make this very clear to her,” Ingwersen said.
“Turn that anger into getting out to the polls, and we can start then to turn this around.”
Mainers from across the state joined Biddeford locals outside Collins’ office. Pam Ericson, a teacher at Lewiston Public Schools and Bath resident, said she attended the protest because of the fear ICE agents have caused in the community where she works.
“Something like that could have happened in Lewiston. The whole community is afraid,” she said. 
“I work with kids who just came to the United States, and they don’t come to school. I have to give them rides, their families won’t go to work,” she added. “It’s very scary.”
Congress to hold field hearing on Biddeford ICE killing
The demonstration, which was organized by the Maine People’s Alliance and Center for Popular Democracy, was held the same day that U.S. Chellie Pingree announced that members of Congress will be holding a field hearing in Biddeford next week on ICE’s use of force in the case.
Pingree, along with U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee, and U.S. Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts will hear from representatives for the Guerrero family, local officials, community advocates, and others who will speak to the state of the investigation and the impact ICE’s operations have had on Maine. 
Biddeford Mayor Liam LaFountain said in a statement Tuesday that he hopes that Republican members of Congress would also participate “because this is an issue that deserves serious attention and oversight from across the political spectrum.”
“Johan’s family and the people of Biddeford deserve a full and independent understanding of what occurred,” LaFountain said. “Federal authority must come with federal accountability, and Congress has an important role to play in providing that oversight when the exercise of federal authority results in the death of a member of our community.” 
Attorney Ben Gideon, who represents the victim’s family, told Maine Public that the family is actively complying with the Maine Attorney General’s investigation but that no federal investigators have reached out.
The hearing, which is open to the public, will take place at 11:00 a.m. on Monday, August 17, at Biddeford High School’s Little Theater.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Mellor declines RI GOP debate with Skoly in CD2 primary
description: Republican 2nd Congressional District candidates Vic Mellor and Dr. Stephen Skoly have separately given TV and radio interviews in recent weeks, but they have yet to appear together on the same stage. And it doesn’t look like they will before the Sept. 9 primary. Mellor declined an invitation to participate in a party-led debate against […]
text:
Republican Vic Mellor is shown at a State House event in support of Second Amendment rights in May 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Republican 2nd Congressional District candidates Vic Mellor and Dr. Stephen Skoly have separately given TV and radio interviews in recent weeks, but they have yet to appear together on the same stage. 
And it doesn’t look like they will before the Sept. 9 primary.
Mellor declined an invitation to participate in a party-led debate against his GOP-endorsed rival, Rhode Island GOP Chair Allyn Meyers confirmed Monday.
Both candidates were invited on Aug. 4 to participate in a debate. Skoly promptly responded, accepting the invitation, but Mellor’s staff held off and promised they would respond soon, Meyers said.
Dr. Stephen Skoly has the endorsement of the Rhode Island Republican Party and the desire to debate his opponent. (Contributed photo)
On Monday, shortly before he received confirmation that Mellor would not participate, Skoly separately issued a public challenge calling for a debate on Aug. 14, or at least before early voting begins Aug. 20.
“Given Mr. Mellor’s decision not to participate, an August 14 debate between the two candidates is no longer feasible,” Meyers wrote via email Monday.
It’s not every election two Rhode Island Republicans run for the same seat, but this year there are two GOP primaries: one in the 2nd Congressional District, and another in the gubernatorial race. The purpose of hosting a debate was straightforward, Meyers said.
“If we are serious about building a professional, independent state party, we must develop our own platforms for Republican candidates to communicate directly with Republican voters rather than relying exclusively on traditional media organizations to frame our primary contests.”
Republicans make up only 16% of the 366,603 registered voters in Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District. Democrats account for 30% while most voters are unaffiliated.
Republicans make up only 16% of the registered voters in Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District with most voters unaffiliated. (Rhode Island Board of Elections)
Mellor’s campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday. Skoly’s campaign also did not respond.
But the Skoly campaign did issue a public statement Monday over social media, and in an email newsletter and a separate letter to the GOP, reiterating the need for a debate. Attached to Skoly’s request was a list of proposed terms, which included a mutually agreed upon moderator chosen by both campaigns, equal speaking time, no advance questions or topics, and no notes, phones or earpieces at the podium. 
Skoly also wanted the event livestreamed in its entirety and available online through primary day on Sept. 9.
“Primary voters deserved the chance to hear both of us answer the same questions, side by side, under the same conditions,” Skoly wrote in a Facebook post Monday evening. “There was a window to do that, and it was not a long one.”
Skoly’s post noted that he asked for an Aug. 14 debate because once “Rhode Islanders begin casting ballots, a debate no longer serves the purpose it was meant to serve.”
“That window has closed,” Skoly wrote. “Not because I withdrew, but because the calendar does not wait and my opponent said No.”
Meyers said the event wouldn’t have been “closed or controlled,” and that it was the RI GOP’s intention “to involve respected and recognizable media professionals while also giving Rhode Island Republicans an opportunity to submit substantive questions for the candidates,” with a focus on the economy, taxes, affordability, public safety, jobs and government accountability.
“With Mr. Mellor declining to participate, consideration of the proposed debate terms is now moot,” Meyers wrote.
The state GOP began planning the debate more than two months ago, said Meyers, who was elected chair earlier this year. In his tenure so far, Meyers said he has tried to have the party show face in a more consistent and professional way via events like conventions, debates and other activities.
“Mr. Mellor has chosen not to participate, and his reasons are his own,” Meyers said. “Following the primary, we hope the Rhode Island Republican Party will have a meaningful role in the general election debates. Our nominee deserves a fair and professional forum to present a Republican vision and address the issues that matter most to Rhode Islanders.”
Mellor — a Marine Corps veteran and now Warwick resident after decades of living in Florida — has described himself to WJAR as a “J6er” who marched on the capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. He does have a busy Saturday ahead, with the scheduling of his second “Rhode Island First” rally at the Cranston Park Theater, with former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani among the announced guests. 
Skoly, an oral and maxillofacial surgeon who lives in East Greenwich and has a practice in Cranston, won the Rhode Island GOP endorsement in June, with the party’s nominating committee recommending him over Mellor, who withdrew from seeking the endorsement. 
At the state GOP convention, Skoly ultimately received the endorsement on a 44-19 vote with the 19 dissenting votes representing no endorsement since Mellor had already withdrawn.
Skoly announced he had received the endorsement of Rhode Island House Minority Whip Gordon Rogers, a Foster Republican, on Sunday. 
In July, the Rhode Island State Fraternal Order of Police endorsed Mello at its 37th Biennial Conference.
Both candidates responded to a questionnaire from Rhode Island Current for the 2026 Primary Voter Guide which was posted Monday.
The victor of the Republican race will go on to face the incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner in the general election.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: AG asks federal court to halt construction of Oklahoma aluminum smelter
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma’s attorney general on Tuesday asked a federal court to block construction in Inola of what would be the largest aluminum smelter in the country.  Attorney General Gentner Drummond, who in June sued to stop construction of the smelter over concerns of foreign ownership and severe pollution in northeastern Oklahoma, filed the […]
text:
Attorney General Gentner Drummond gives a speech for his gubernatorial campaign at the Edmond History Museum on Aug. 19, 2025, in Edmond. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma’s attorney general on Tuesday asked a federal court to block construction in Inola of what would be the largest aluminum smelter in the country. 
Attorney General Gentner Drummond, who in June sued to stop construction of the smelter over concerns of foreign ownership and severe pollution in northeastern Oklahoma, filed the new motion in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Oklahoma to ask a judge to take immediate action while a lawsuit plays out. 
Following intense pushback from residents, the town of Inola issued a moratorium on the smelter project that expires Aug. 28. The proposed smelter is set to be built within miles of Inola schools, homes and farms. 
“The people of Rogers County stand to lose their health, their herds and their livelihoods,” Drummond, also a GOP gubernatorial candidate, said in a statement. “The public interest lies in enforcing Oklahoma’s nuisance and environmental laws, protecting the health of Inola families and preserving the livestock economy and natural resources of the region.”
He said he wants Oklahomans to be able to “fully vet the project” for its environmental impacts, foreign ownership and governance ties. 
Drummond also asked for his original suit to be sent back to Rogers County District Court. A motion from the smelter owners is pending to send the case to federal court. 
The 350 acre aluminum smelter project, a priority of President Donald Trump, has been dubbed Oklahoma Primary Aluminum and has the support of Gov. Kevin Stitt and leaders of the state House and Senate. It is expected to double aluminum production in the U.S. 
While 40% of the project is owned by Century Aluminum Company, which is based in Chicago, the majority is owned by the Dubai-based Emirates Global Aluminum.
Hundreds of millions of public dollars have been directed toward the project, including a $500 million federal grant, a $255 million incentive package from Oklahoma and the creation of a tax-increment-financing district by the City of Inola.
“This motion asks the Court to do one thing: keep the ground at Inola unbroken, as the Town of Inola’s moratorium keeps it today, until the lawfulness of Defendants’ smelter can be adjudicated on the merits,” Drummond’s motion reads. “… When (the moratorium) lapses, nothing will stand between Defendants and groundbreaking except a court order.”
Drummond’s motion on Tuesday also included expert testimony from Dr. Ranajit Sahu, an engineer and environmental consultant. Sahu said the pollution that would be generated by the smelter “pose a wide range of adverse risks of harm,” and ownership is underestimating the pollution that would be generated.

title: Trump taken via catering truck to secret flight amid Iran threats, report says
text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump covertly traveled across Europe in a military plane in July after Iran threatened his life, according to a bombshell report Monday night by The Washington Post that revealed press and White House officials remained on a decoy Air Force One.The extraordinary episode unfolded July 8 after Trump boarded the former Air Force One following the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, after concerns reportedly arose about his safety on a new Air Force One, a retrofitted Boeing 747-8 jet donated to Trump by Qatar.Trump had ordered a fresh wave of military strikes on Iran while attending the NATO summit, breaking a brief period of peace negotiations.According to unnamed officials who spoke to The Washington Post, shortly after Trump waved to cameras as he ascended the older Air Force One, he was secretly taken to the back of a catering truck and shuttled to a nearby smaller Air Force C-32A plane.

 







As the press boards the former Air Force One, this photo clearly shows in the background, to the right, the other aircraft, reported to be the one in which Trump covertly flew from Turkey to the United Kingdom. (White House pool photo)

Upon arriving at the Royal Air Force base in Mildenhall in eastern England, Trump was clandestinely ferried back into the former Air Force One and shortly thereafter descended the stairs in front of cameras. Press corps members who routinely travel with the president, as well as White House officials, remained on the decoy flight from Turkey to eastern England under the impression that Trump was on board, according to officials. The Post granted the officials anonymity because they were not authorized to speak about the incident.The Pentagon referred States Newsroom to the White House, which did not respond for comment.The U.S. Secret Service did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment.The catering truckPhotos taken by the traveling press pool from the tarmac in Turkey show reporters boarding the back of the former Air Force One via stairs on the right side rear of the plane. A catering truck, with its rear container raised to plane level, can be seen toward the front of the jet on the opposite side.Once on the plane, members of the press were instructed by the Secret Service to completely close their window shades, according to a July 8 press pool report and a later press account Tuesday. A pool report is an official dispatch sent to thousands of news organizations to keep journalists and the public informed about the president’s whereabouts and actions.Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that he was flying from Turkey to the United Kingdom on the old powder blue Air Force One “for old time’s sake” and so that U.S. forces stationed in England could tour the newly retrofitted Air Force One bearing a navy blue and deep red design accented by gold stripes.According to official press reports from the night of July 8, the old Air Force One touched down at Mildenhall Air Force Base at 10:16 p.m. local time and Trump descended the stairs at 10:56 p.m. The pool report noted that neither the president or any White House officials had spoken to the press on board while in flight from Turkey.After greeting service members, Trump then ascended the stairs to the new Air Force One and gave a wave to the cameras at 11:01 p.m. local time. The plane was off the ground at 11:14 p.m., according to official July 8 pool reports.‘If I go, you go’Trump spoke to reporters shortly after take-off from the United Kingdom and was peppered with questions about why he did not take the new Air Force One jet after the NATO summit concluded.Trump denied any security concerns and said the new jet was sent early to the U.K., and “the whole base came out and saw the plane,” according to official pool reports.

 







A closer view of the former Air Force One and the catering truck reportedly used to secretly transport President Donald Trump to a military plane in Ankara, Turkey, on July 8, 2026. The truck can be seen to the left, under the plane. (White House pool photo)

When asked why reporters were instructed to keep their window shades shut on the old jet, which they were led to believe the president was also on, Trump said, “Well, yeah, because you’re probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleaze bags that we have to deal with,” he said, referring to Iran, according to the pool reports.Reporters then pressed Trump on whether he was aware of a credible threat on his life from Iran.“Well, I have a threat all the time. I’m number one on their list, before you. But if I go, you go. Right? Perhaps someday you want to change professions,” Trump told reporters aboard the flight according to the pool reports.The New York Times reported on July 8 that Trump had switched planes because of a security threat related to the conflict with Iran. The Trump administration swiftly served subpoenas two days later on the reporters in a sweeping effort to learn the identities of their confidential sources.The administration dropped the subpoenas on July 27 after a federal judge sharply criticized the investigation.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Federal judge denies Southern Poverty Law Center’s motion to dismiss criminal charges
description: A federal court judge Friday denied a motion from the Southern Poverty Law Center to dismiss criminal charges filed by the U.S. Department of Justice over a program that paid informants to gather intelligence on extremist groups. U.S. District Judge Emily Marks wrote that the civil rights nonprofit did not provide the evidence it needed […]
text:
The Southern Poverty Law Center's headquarters in Montgomery, Alabama on February 8, 2023. A federal judge on Friday declined a motion from SPLC to dismiss federal charges brought by the U.S. Department of Justice, writing the SPLC had not shown enough evidence that it was being targeted for opposition to Donald Trump. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)A federal court judge Friday denied a motion from the Southern Poverty Law Center to dismiss criminal charges filed by the U.S. Department of Justice over a program that paid informants to gather intelligence on extremist groups.
U.S. District Judge Emily Marks wrote that the civil rights nonprofit did not provide the evidence it needed to show that the Department of Justice was targeting the SPLC because of its opposition to the actions of President Donald Trump.
“Though President Trump has specifically criticized the SPLC, the organization has not provided evidence that the prosecutors working on this case were in any way motivated by his purported animus,” Marks, nominated to the bench by Trump in 2018, wrote in her order.
The Southern Poverty Law Center said in a statement Tuesday it was “disappointed” in the decision but would “continue to vigorously defend ourselves, our staff and our work.”
“SPLC will continue to fight hate and we will continue to envision and create a safer and more just world,” the statement said. “The actions by the DOJ will not shake our resolve to fight for justice and ensure the promise of the Civil Rights Movement becomes a reality for all.”
A federal grand jury in April approved an 11-count indictment against the SPLC, including wire fraud, making false statements to a federally insured bank and money laundering. The DOJ charged that SPLC’s now-discontinued system of paying informants to gather intelligence within white supremacist groups to disrupt their activities amounted to support for those groups and effectively defrauded donors to the SPLC.
The informant program had been publicly reported since at least 1986, and the fact SPLC was paying some informants had been public knowledge since 1994. Attorneys representing the SPLC filed a request with the court in May to have the case dismissed, alleging that the federal government pursued criminal charges based largely on retaliation by the Trump administration.
SPLC cited statements made by FBI Director Kash Patel, Trump and members of Congress. The SPLC also cited an investigation into its informant program during the first Trump administration. The Biden administration ended the investigation, but it was restarted after Trump returned to the White House.
The organization also cited public statements by Trump and Justice officials, including U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Patel, accusing SPLC of manufacturing “the extremism it purports to oppose.”
Marks wrote that none of the examples proved that the charges filed by the federal government were “the result of such animus.”
“While high-ranking Republican members of Congress criticized the SPLC, the SPLC fails to ‘connect any vindictive animus to those making the challenged charging decisions,’” she wrote.
Marks also said the U.S. Attorney’s Office routinely begins, terminates and restarts investigations, and the fact that the Trump administration started the investigation into the program after it was terminated in the Biden administration does not demonstrate vindictive prosecution.
Trump is also free to criticize the SPLC, but there is not enough evidence that he convinced the federal government to file the charges.
“However, the SPLC fails to establish that President Trump’s statements evince animus on the part of the United States Attorney for the Middle District of Alabama,” Marks said.

text:
Yellowstone National Park sign at the North Entrance; Jim Peaco;
October 1992 (Provided by the National Park Service)Yellowstone National Park is on pace for its third busiest season on record, falling just off record pace during July.
Park officials released the latest monthly and year-to-date statistics showing that 958,706 visited Yellowstone in July, down 2% from last year. It was also 11% fewer visitors than in 2021, the park’s record-breaking year and the busiest July on record.
Through the end of July, 2,635,384 have passed through an entrance station into Yellowstone, compared to 2,668,765 in 2021.
In 2025, Yellowstone saw its second-highest visitation on record with more than 4.7 million visitors. The near-record numbers came despite a 43-day partial government shutdown in October and November, when the park saw a dip in visitation by nearly 8% from previous years.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: AG Dave Sunday sues TikTok for ‘misrepresenting’ suitability for Pennsylvania teenagers
description: Nearly 100 million Americans use TikTok, a popular app for sharing short-form videos, every day, but Pennsylvania joined a growing number of states questioning the platform’s protections for young users.
text:
A woman uses the TikTok app. (Photo by Thicha Satapitanon/Getty Images)Nearly 100 million Americans use TikTok, a popular app for sharing short-form videos, every day, but Pennsylvania joined a growing number of states questioning the platform’s protections for young users.
“Today is an action rooted, very simply, in protecting children,” said state Attorney General Dave Sunday in a Tuesday press conference. “Social media allows us to be closer than ever to celebrities, athletes and musicians that we like. However, as easy as a child can watch (Dwayne) ‘The Rock’ (Johnson) make breakfast or hang out with his kids, they can see someone drinking alcohol or consuming drugs. And that is what is often glorified.”
Sunday alleges that TikTok “misrepresents its app as age appropriate for teens as young as 13,” even though content can include profanity, drinking, drug use and sexually suggestive situations. 
Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday announced a commonwealth lawsuit against TikTok on Aug. 11, 2026, alleging it misrepresented its suitability for young Pennsylvanians. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“To achieve a 13-plus age rating in app stores, TikTok claims mature content is infrequent on their apps. Our investigation reveals that this could not be further from the truth,” said Sunday. “That age rating gives parents the illusion of safety, but actually opens the door to putting content literally in the palm of our kids’ hands whenever they want it.”
This mismatch violates Pennsylvania Consumer Protection Law, he continued. 
Additionally, the app is “intentionally designed … to be addictive to young people,” Sunday said, in a way “that can deteriorate and decay a child’s mental wellness.” 
“They want users to endlessly scroll while they rake in astronomical ad revenue,” he added. “When TikTok is constantly, infinitely in our kids’ viewstreams … we see TikTok as inhibitors of healthy adolescent development.”
According to the lawsuit, filed in the Court of Common Pleas for Allegheny County, “addiction is TikTok’s business model.”
“TikTok employs a number of harmful addictive-by-design features specifically targeted and tailored to exploit, manipulate and capitalize on the developing brains of young users,” the filing read. “Rather than disclosing its platform’s harms and potential harms to young users or their parents, TikTok misleads the public about the ways its platform has harmed — and is continuing to harm — children and teens.”
Sunday pointed to a teenTALK spring campaign that included student roundtable discussions across the state to analyze teenage relationships with social media. He described hearing about concerns with the enormously popular app, which an estimated 20% of American teenagers use “almost constantly.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In-app tools to reduce screen time are ineffective and TikTok knows it, the suit continued. It also shared examples of content it investigated using a test account, with portions of the complaint redacted.
The commonwealth seeks an injunction that would prevent the app from violating consumer protection law — including age restrictions and verification safeguards — alongside civil penalties and fees. 
In a statement to the Capital-Star, a spokesperson for TikTok said, “This lawsuit relies on misleading and inaccurate claims and deliberately ignores the concrete safety measures TikTok has voluntarily implemented to support the well-being of our community. Teen accounts have 50 preset safety, privacy and security settings built-in, and TikTok’s Family Pairing tools give parents direct control over screen time and content filters. We will vigorously defend against these claims.”
 The bigger picture

Pennsylvania joins a list of states with pending cases against the social media platform, which used to be owned by Chinese company ByteDance and was forced to establish the American-majority owned TikTok USDS Joint Venture to comply with federal action. But Sunday’s suit appears to be the first filed since the transition, though he said “the ownership dynamic had nothing to do” with the timing. 
Sunday took office in January 2025, saying he wanted to file lawsuits “that are thoughtful, that we have investigated ourselves (and) that we are in a position to stand by … that’s not something we can do overnight.” 
Congress silenced free speech in TikTok law, platform tells federal court

At least two other states have sued over concerns about inappropriate content geared toward minors: Indiana and Utah. Both Nebraska and New Hampshire individually filed cases against TikTok alleging mental health harms — most of the above cases used state-level consumer protection laws to advance their claims, though none have been resolved.
More than a dozen other states (not including Pennsylvania or the above states), and the District of Columbia filed a coordinated suit in late 2024, claiming the app was addictive for young people. Those cases are still working their way through the legal process.
A release from Sunday’s office pointed to other agency efforts “to protect kids from modern technology that is developed and marketed without adequate consideration of the harm it is causing,” including letters to artificial intelligence companies about harmful chatbots and ongoing litigation against Meta.
He didn’t specifically mention other companies as targets for future action, but said “this is our first legal action like this … you will hear more from us in the near future.”
“The wellness, the mental well-being (and) the safety of our children is an absolute critical component of who we are as a society, and it is a cause that we will always fight for,” said Sunday. “That is exactly why we are doing this.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC environmentalists continue pushing back on Duke Energy rate hike
description: Last week, Duke Energy announced it reached a settlement with the Utilities Commission’s Public Staff.
text:
Environmental advocates called on Duke Energy to lower its rate hike request on August 11, 2026. (Photo: Talton Gibson/NC League of Conservation Voters)Environmental activists and a Democratic state lawmaker are calling on Duke Energy to lower its rate hike request as the North Carolina Utilities Commission reviews its case. 
Evidentiary hearings for Duke Energy Progress’ rate case start this week before the Utilities Commission, which will determine how much the company can raise residential electric rates beginning next year. 
Last week, Duke Energy announced it had reached a settlement with the Utilities Commission’s Public Staff, a department that represents consumers in regulatory cases. They agreed to an average increase of 3.4% each year for the next two years for residential users. A standard residential customer consuming 1,000 kilowatt-hours per month could see an increase of about $9.61 each month starting in 2027. 
The utility originally requested a rate increase of 18% over two years, but lowered its request to 9.5% over two years after months of backlash. 
“We greatly appreciate the diverse partnership represented in these agreements, from Public Staff to businesses and organizations who all came together with us to reach a more cost-effective path forward for our customers,” Duke Energy spokesperson Bill Norton told NC Newsline in an email.
Even though the settlement is well below the utility’s original request, environmental advocates say it’s still too much. 
Dan Crawford, senior director of public affairs at the North Carolina League of Conservation Voters, pointed out Duke Energy shareholders made huge profits in 2025.
“Poor, poor Duke. They’re barely scraping by on $5 billion in profits they made last year, and last week, they announced they’re already on track to make even more this year,” Crawford said sarcastically. “Clearly, they need this increase.”
State leaders have taken action against the proposed rate increases. Last month, Attorney General Jeff Jackson said he wouldn’t support the settlement, believing the rates can still come down. Gov. Josh Stein criticized the increase as well. 
Crawford said he stands with Jackson in asking the Utilities Commission to deny Duke’s request. 
NC AG Jackson rejects Duke Energy’s proposed rate increase

“Cut Duke’s guaranteed profits. Stop raising our bills to pay for it,” Crawford said. “Stand up for the people of North Carolina.”
Prices for consumers have been rising across the board over the past year, according to Terryn Hall, state director for the left-leaning group Climate Power.
Since the Trump Administration passed the “One Big Beautiful Bill” last year, Hall says costs for North Carolina families have gone up by $2,032 per household through June 30 of this year, according to a recent study from Climate Power and the Center for American Progress Action Fund. 
“The reality is North Carolina families cannot afford these rising bills,” Hall said. “We say no to rate hikes. Our bills are just too high across the board.”
Wake County Democratic Rep. Maria Cervania described the rate increase request as “untenable.” 
She said residential customers shouldn’t be responsible for subsidizing the electricity costs for large and profitable corporations building hyperscale data centers. 
Lawmakers passed a budget this year repealing the sales tax exemption on electricity for data centers, but there’s still concern over other costs to upgrade the state’s power infrastructure to accommodate the growth in demand that large data centers will bring.
“We deserve a modern grid capable of supporting our growing economy, but we also deserve electricity that families can afford,” Cervania said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: 2 former Indiana BMV staffers charged with bribery, faking driver’s tests
description: Two former Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles staffers face criminal charges alleging they accepted bribes to submit fraudulent passing scores on written driver’s tests.
text:
The Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles voided more than 300 driver's exam after an alleged bribery scheme. (BMV image)Two former Indiana Bureau of Motor Vehicles staffers face criminal charges alleging they accepted bribes to submit fraudulent passing scores on written driver’s tests.
The two former customer service workers each face one count of Level 5 felony bribery and one count of Level 6 felony official misconduct filed last week by the Marion County prosecutor’s office.
They both worked at the BMV’s Indianapolis Midtown branch on the city’s northeast side, according to the state inspector general’s office.
The charges allege that the two staffers accepted payments and manually entered passing scores for written driver’s tests that customers never actually took, allowing those people to improperly obtain a learner’s permit or license.
Investigators identified more than 300 illegitimate tests entered under those staffers’ BMV log-in credentials between June 2023 and February 2024. 
The inspector general’s office said the scheme was uncovered after workers at another BMV branch “noticed an unusual pattern of customers who had previously failed written tests suddenly obtaining permits or licenses.”
The BMV invalidated all the driver’s licenses and permits linked to the case and required all those involved to pass new exams, the inspector general’s office said.
The former workers face up to six years in prison if convicted of the most-serious charges.
Indiana Inspector General Jared Prentice said their actions “not only betrayed Hoosier trust, but it also created the potential that unqualified and untested drivers were on Indiana’s roads.”

text:
An Avondale resident stands amid the wreckage  of a house heavily damaged Thursday, June 18, 2026, by the storm bands of Tropical Storm Arthur. (Photo courtesy of WVUE-TV Fox 8)Areas of Louisiana that saw physical damage from Tropical Storm Arthur in June have been given more time to apply for assistance from the Small Business Administration, the agency announced Tuesday.
The SBA has also extended the impact period from the storm that passed through June 17 for a full week, allowing business owners to claim any damage that occurred by June 24 when they apply for assistance. The new deadline for applications is Oct. 1.
Physical disaster loans from the SBA are only available to damaged businesses in Avoyelles, Lafourche, Pointe Coupee, St. Landry, St. Tammany and Terrebonne parishes. 
Economic injury disaster loans are available to business owners in Acadia, Assumption, Catahoula, Concordia, Evangeline, Iberville, Jefferson, Lafayette, LaSalle, Orleans, Rapides, St. Bernard, St. Charles, St James, St. John the Baptist, St. Martin, St. Mary, Tangipahoa, Washington, West Baton Rouge and West Feliciana parishes. Hancock and Pearl River counties in Mississippi are also eligible.
The deadline for economic injury disaster loans remains March 30, 2027.
Loan applicants must have a credit history acceptable to the SBA and demonstrate the ability to repay their loans.
Applicants may call the SBA Customer Service Center with questions regarding their application at (800) 659-2955 or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Federal circuit dismisses youth climate lawsuit
description: The federal court system will not give a youth-led constitutional climate lawsuit additional consideration after a panel of the U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals denied a petition to rehear the case before the full circuit.  Lighthiser v. Trump is one of a series of youth-led climate change lawsuits brought by Our Children’s Trust, an […]
text:
Eva Lighthiser, left, and other plaintiffs wait to enter Missoula's federal courthouse on Sept. 16, 2025. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)The federal court system will not give a youth-led constitutional climate lawsuit additional consideration after a panel of the U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals denied a petition to rehear the case before the full circuit. 
Lighthiser v. Trump is one of a series of youth-led climate change lawsuits brought by Our Children’s Trust, an Oregon-based advocacy law firm, which also successfully litigated Held v. Montana in 2023, a landmark climate case that found the Montana Constitution guarantees the right to “a clean and healthful” environment. 
The plaintiffs in the Lighthiser case include young people from Montana, Oregon, Hawaii, California and Florida.
The lawsuit was first argued before a federal judge in Missoula who “reluctantly” dismissed the case.
In June, a three-judge panel of the circuit court also rejected the lawsuit’s arguments that three executive orders President Donald Trump signed early in his second term will accelerate human-caused climate change and harm the youth.
A major sticking point for both the district and federal court judges was that the request by the youth — to roll back the executive orders and prevent any federal agencies from enforcing them — was an “unprecedented” ask and effectively challenged hundreds of existing and anticipated actions. 
Lawyers for the plaintiffs said the court was declining to look at the hard evidence that carbon dioxide emissions from the fossil fuel industry — bolstered in the executive orders — are closely linked to climate change and causing a “children’s health emergency.” 
“In this case, not a single government official even attempted to controvert that climate change is real, that it is rapidly changing our environment in the United States, and that it’s responsible for causing a children’s health emergency,” said Dan Snyder, Director of Public Justice’s Environmental Enforcement Project.
The district court had agreed with the scientific arguments, but not the legal basis of the case, with federal district court Judge Dana Christensen saying the scope of the request from the 22 young people was “an unworkable request.”
“No circuit court in American history has ever said it lacked the power to review an unconstitutional executive order. Until this case,” Julia Olson, Chief Legal Counsel and Co-Executive Director of Our Children’s Trust, said in a statement. “The President cannot lawfully direct a sweeping fossil fuel agenda that endangers children’s lives with no meaningful judicial check.”
Montana, which lost a constitutional challenge from youth plaintiffs — Held v. Montana — in 2024, intervened in the case, with lawyers from the attorney general’s office taking part in both the district and circuit court arguments. 
“The court’s rejection confirms what we’ve said all along, that this case was never about the law, but an attempt to block President Trump’s pro-energy policies and force a liberal climate agenda,” Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen said in a statement. “The court got it right by refusing to rehear a case that was already correctly decided.” 
The challenged orders included Trump Executive Orders 14154, “Unleashing American Energy;” 14156, “Declaring a National Energy Emergency;” and 14261, “Reinvigorating America’s Beautiful Clean Coal Industry.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: GOP lawmakers take symbolic vote to oppose Ky State Fair maneuvers
description: A group of Kentucky lawmakers voted Tuesday to not revoke a contract with a former president of the State Fair Board that had already been voided by the Beshear administration.  Government Contract Review Committee co-chairman Rep. Mark Hart, R-Falmouth, told members the vote would be “basically making a statement.” The committee had deferred review of […]
text:
Kentucky State Fair (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)A group of Kentucky lawmakers voted Tuesday to not revoke a contract with a former president of the State Fair Board that had already been voided by the Beshear administration. 
Government Contract Review Committee co-chairman Rep. Mark Hart, R-Falmouth, told members the vote would be “basically making a statement.” The committee had deferred review of the contract with David Beck, former president and CEO of the Kentucky State Fair, during its meeting last month. 
“The contract’s already been rescinded, so there’s nothing we can do at this point,” Hart added. 
In late June, the Kentucky Supreme Court ruled Gov. Andy Beshear should have appointment power over the State Fair Board. That decision paved the way for Beshear to make new appointments to the board. The board then met days later and ousted Beck from the role and installed Michael Berry as interim president and CEO. 
The committee later voted to not approve Berry’s contract during the meeting. 
Barbara Dickens, the general counsel of the Finance and Administration Cabinet, appeared before the committee Tuesday and said Finance and Administration Secretary Holly M. Johnson was asked to review the validity of Beck’s contract after the Supreme Court ruling and a 2021 law shifting control of the State Fair Board from the governor to the agriculture commissioner was deemed unconstitutional. 
“We reviewed that contract in light of that Supreme Court decision and determined that the board that had voted to renew that contract was not constitutionally constituted, and therefore did not have authority to renew it,” Dickens said.
Sen. Stephen Meredith, R-Leitchfield, asked several questions of Dickens. He also noted that Republican constitutional officers have requested the Supreme Court rehear the case. As of Tuesday morning, the high court had not made a decision to rehear the case. 
“I’m ashamed that the Commonwealth has treated a man who’s dedicated a good portion of his life to serving the Commonwealth has been treated in this manner,” Meredith said. “And if the contract would need to be terminated, I think there should have been for cause. But no one has explained to us why this situation has even arisen, but it is what it is, but it’s just very disappointing.” 
Beshear has previously said Beck “was not willing to work with me, and made that pretty clear” and had “led a charge to prevent any form of accountability from a governor.” 
Rep. Rachel Roarx, D-Louisville, said while voting to revoke Beck’s contract that “the Supreme Court case was very clear, and there is no contract.” 
“For me, this is not about a statement of the quality of work that was done before by the individual or anything like that,” she said. “This is merely the fact that the Supreme Court case is very clear. The constitutionality of the bill that was passed is also unconstitutional.” 
The recent back-and-forth between Beshear and Republican lawmakers over the fair board has become the latest struggle over executive power in Kentucky government. In addition to the ruling on the 2021 law regarding the fair board, the Supreme Court’s decision also ruled a 2022 law giving other executive branch officials appointment power over the Executive Branch Ethics Commission unconstitutional.
The Kentucky State Fair will begin in Louisville on Aug. 20. Ahead of the Fancy Farm Picnic this month, Agriculture Commissioner Jonathan Shell told the Lantern that he believes the event will be “completely fine” as most of the work to prepare had been finished before the changes to the board. 
Shell, who is one of the Republicans who requested the court rehear the case, has a seat on the fair board. He said he’s been reassured “that agriculture will stay a focus and a priority of that facility.” 
“So, now we’re just going to wait and see. We’re going to be involved. We’re going to participate. We’re going to be a great partner for them because that state fair and that venue shouldn’t be about politics or people in those seats,” Shell said. “It should be about the people that are coming in those doors, and we’re going to continue to work to bring the best entertainment, tourism,and agriculture experience possible to the state of Kentucky.”

The even[...]
text:
More than 7 million Americans live with Alzheimer’s across the United States. (Getty Images)The Alzheimer’s Foundation of America is hosting a free educational conference in Bedford on Sept. 16, the organization has announced.
Alzheimer’s experts will be in attendance to teach about the importance of early detection, provide support to caregivers, and discuss the communications challenges the disease brings, according to the event release.
The event will take place at the Bedford Event Center on South River Road from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Those who wish to attend can register online at www.alzfdn.org/tour. For those who can’t attend, the Alzheimer’s Foundation of America also operates a hotline — 866-232-8484 for calling, 646-586-5283 for texting — people can contact if they have questions about Alzheimer’s.
More than 7 million Americans live with Alzheimer’s across the United States, according to the Alzheimer’s Association. There is no known cure, but researchers trying to understand the illness for decades have developed some treatments that can slow the cognitive and functional decline that comes with Alzheimer’s.
“Knowledge is a useful and powerful tool that can help make any situation easier to navigate, especially something as challenging as caring for a loved one with Alzheimer’s disease,” Charles J. Fuschillo Jr., president and CEO of the Alzheimer’s Foundation of America, said in a press release. “Connecting families with useful, practical information and support that can help them now and be better prepared for the future is what this conference is all about. Whether Alzheimer’s is affecting your family, you are a caregiver, or just want to learn more about brain health, we invite you to join us on September 16.”

One thought would […]
text:
Voters cast their ballots at Webster Town Hall in Webster, Minnesota during the primary election Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Ripped from Daily Reformer. Sign up for a free subscription here. 
Turnout. The 2018 DFL primary turnout — about 583,000 in the contested governor’s race; a bit more than 23% of registered voters turned out that year — was the most robust in many years, but the DFL-endorsed progressive candidate still lost. One thought would be that Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan needs a big turnout against Rep. Angie Craig, especially of younger, more progressive voters. On the other hand, maybe the kind of engaged Democrats who turn out in primaries have shifted left and will back Flanagan. As I noted last week, a lot has changed since 2018, including Gen Z entering the electorate; disgust with the Democratic establishment; George Floyd’s murder; and Operation Metro Surge.
Demographics. The median age of Democratic primary voters nationwide is 55 this year (so, half are older). Craig is winning older voters, according to last week’s KSTP poll. Can Flanagan get the yutes out?
CD2 turnout. Unclear to me how turnout affects the race to replace Craig, where Rep. Kaela Berg, Sen. Matt Klein, and DFL-endorsed Matt Little are running. The competitive primary almost certainly helps Craig because those voters know and seem to like her.
Legislative primaries can tell us something. Here’s an MPR rundown of 11 legislative primaries. You can’t make broad conclusions about the state’s politics based on a single legislative primary. Sen. Ron Latz, for instance, seems to be facing some serious local resistance. But if we see a batch of incumbents losing, that might tell us something.
Another Trump Minnesota loss? Despite his claims to the contrary, Donald Trump doesn’t play well here, having lost soundly in the 2016 caucus, and again in three presidential contests. He’s a fancy coastal con man, and most Minnesotans see through it. But GOP primary voters are the exception, and he has a near perfect record in GOP endorsements. Pillow mogul Mike Lindell needs Trump to keep the winning streak alive, while House Speaker Lisa Demuth needs a bigger turnout among normie suburbanites who will go for something more staid than Lindell’s frenetic pyrotechnics.
The fate of progressive prosecutors. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, the former chief public defender, was among a wave of urban progressive prosecutors elected in recent years, but is leaving after a single term. Progressive prosecutors in other jurisdictions were often scapegoated for the pandemic-era spike in crime. Rep. Cedric Frazier won the DFL endorsement and is a former public defender. Anders Folk occupies a more conventional prosecutor lane, having served as acting U.S. attorney.
