title: NC’s Labor Department recovers more than $3.5 million in unpaid wages, setting new record
description: “When you put in the work, you deserve to be paid every single penny that you’ve been promised.” North Carolina Labor Commissioner Luke Farley announced Tuesday that his department recovered a record $3.7 million in unpaid wages for workers in the 2025-26 fiscal year. The recovery helped workers in 89 of North Carolina’s 100 counties […]
text:
North Carolina Labor Commissioner Luke Farley and Kisha Scotton, bureau chief for the Wage and Hour Division, discuss the recovery of $3.7 million in unpaid wages for workers during a August 11, 2026, press conference. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)“When you put in the work, you deserve to be paid every single penny that you’ve been promised.”
North Carolina Labor Commissioner Luke Farley announced Tuesday that his department recovered a record $3.7 million in unpaid wages for workers in the 2025-26 fiscal year.
The recovery helped workers in 89 of North Carolina’s 100 counties and represented a significant increase over the previous fiscal  year, when $2.5 million was recovered.
Farley said the recovered wages are more than numbers on a page – they’re peace of mind for those workers who were owed compensation.
“It represents a worker who can now afford to pay rent or make a mortgage payment. A parent who can cover childcare costs, it’s a family that can buy groceries, pay utility bills, and handle those unexpected expenses that come up in everyday life,” said Farley.
The top industry for wage recoveries this year is retail services, followed by restaurants and bars and the medical sector.
From 2016 to 2022, the recovery rate held steady at about $1.2 million in wages recovered annually.
Kisha Scotton, bureau chief for the Wage and Hour Division, says the Department of Labor has recently been working to strengthen and streamline its operations to better respond to workers and understand employment practices.
“Our investigators examine payroll records, time records, and documentation to verify hours worked, pay rates, and whether workers received all wages due,” Scotton said.
Investigators also review employment classifications to determine whether workers have been properly designated as exempt or non-exempt.
When violations are identified, the division works to calculate how much a worker is owed, and guide employers toward corrective action. Scotton said the overwhelming majority of employers want to do the right thing.
“When mistakes happen, our goal is to achieve compliance through education, communication, and fair enforcement,” said Scotton. “We are committed to creating a level playing field where businesses that follow the law are not disadvantaged by those that do not.”
State law does provide for employers to face fines, but Farley says the goal is really to help individuals get wages they may be owed.
“One of the things that’s changed since I’ve been commissioner is that we are more aggressive about pursuing litigation on behalf of the workers of North Carolina when there’s wage theft,” said Farley.
But not all cases are easily resolved. In March 2026, the North Carolina Justice Center reached a $305,000 settlement on behalf of 99 agricultural workers who came to the United States from Mexico through an H-2A visa program.
In that class action, the farmworkers alleged their Four Oaks employer paid them less than the hourly wage promised in the H-2A job contract, violating state and federal wage and hour laws. These cases often go unreported because agricultural workers fear retaliation or losing their temporary visas.
U.S. House panel weighs labor law amendment to protect workers from wage theft

This year’s recovery of $3.7 million by the NC Department of Labor represents 2,199 complaints that the division was able to substantiate. And that number is expected to grow next year.
The recently passed state budget included additional resources for the Department of Labor. Farley said they are in the process of determining where those funds can be most effective. The Wage & Hour Bureau currently has just eight case analysts and 15 investigators.
North Carolina workers who believe they are the victim of wage theft can call 1-800-NC-LABOR or contact the department through its website: https://www.labor.nc.gov/.

title: Oklahoma grows statewide team of reading coaches as new literacy laws take effect
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — An expanded team of reading coaches will train teachers across Oklahoma as public schools implement new requirements for childhood literacy. The Oklahoma State Department of Education’s HEROES Literacy Instructional Team has grown to 24 reading coaches and six regional supervisors, following recent legislative action. The team, which the stat[...]
text:
A student reads a graphic novel at Hills Elementary in Santa Fe South Charter Schools on Aug. 4 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — An expanded team of reading coaches will train teachers across Oklahoma as public schools implement new requirements for childhood literacy.
The Oklahoma State Department of Education’s HEROES Literacy Instructional Team has grown to 24 reading coaches and six regional supervisors, following recent legislative action. The team, which the state lawmakers converted from a pilot program to a permanent fixture, will work with 120 elementary schools over the coming academic year.
The larger team will visit fewer schools than before, but educators at each served site will get more comprehensive coaching, said Melissa Ahlgrim, the Education Department’s program director of literacy policy and programs.
“It’s 120 schools that will receive more support than just a quick fly-by,” she said. “It’s a slightly reduced number of schools, but it is a more intensive kind of support.”
Last year’s smaller group of 14 coaches visited 150 schools in 2025-26. Team members were assigned 12 to 15 schools each, so they could reach each site only a few times a month, Ahlgrim said. That left time for consulting but not in-depth coaching.
Oklahoma’s updated Strong Readers Act made the HEROES team a permanent program at the Education Department and raised its minimum number of coaches to 20. 
The law instructs the team to serve six geographic regions in the state and to prioritize schools that score the lowest on either annual state English language arts tests or on a statewide reading screener. 
The Legislature also forbade districts from refusing the team’s help or else risk losing Strong Readers Act funds. Previously, the team worked with schools on a voluntary basis.
Each of the 24 coaches will be assigned up to five schools at a time to visit multiple days a week, Ahlgrim said. They’ll join teachers in their classrooms and explain practical ways to improve their teaching methods for reading.
“When a teacher gets into their classroom, because they have so many things going on, it’s really hard to implement something new, and so that’s where coaching comes in,” Ahlgrim said. “It says, ‘Let me walk you through step by step. Let me model this for you. Let me help watch you do it and help guide you along the way.’”
A school must demonstrate sustainable growth in student reading scores for the team to start drawing back its involvement, Ahlgrim said.
School districts will spend the year implementing new legal requirements for small-group instruction, teacher training and progress monitoring of struggling readers. An even bigger change will come in 2027-28, when third graders will be held back a year if they score below a basic reading level on state tests and fail a second literacy assessment.
Lawmakers also required every district to employ or contract with a reading specialist, establishing summer training academies for teachers who wanted to earn this designation. 
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, said these academies are an essential piece of the law because the Education Department “can’t employ enough coaches to go to every school district in the state.” 
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, speaks at John W. Rex Charter Elementary in Oklahoma City during a signing ceremony for Senate Bill 1778 on April 21. Hilbert co-wrote the bill. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Instead, teachers from Oklahoma’s 540 districts could participate in the summer academies to train in the science of reading, earn a $3,000 stipend and return to their schools to help their fellow educators.
“Ultimately, we pass laws as the Legislature, but it’s the teachers, it’s the parents, it’s the principals, it’s the reading specialists who are really the ones implementing this and will make it become a reality,” Hilbert said. “I’m just excited to see what this is going to mean for our kids and our students as the school year starts.”
The HEROES team organized summer literacy workshops, as well, across the state for teacher professional development. The team also offers six- to eight-week online courses during the school year to 150 teachers on best practices for reading instruction, Ahlgrim said.
The Education Department had to quickly add to the team over the summer to comply with the new legislation. 
One hundred candidates applied for the open positions, Ahlgrim said, and all coaches and regional leads were fully staffed by July 4. But, a few recent departures have left three coaching positions open as the school year begins.
A coach’s base salary is $68,200, and each of the six regional leads earns $72,200, she said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Gov. Sherrill targets ‘big tech’ with new law aimed at kids’ social media use
description: The new law limits algorithmic recommendations and data use for minors on social media in a bid to combat social media harms.
text:
A law signed by Gov. Mikie Sherrill Tuesday limits algorithmic recommendations and data use for minors on social media in a bid to combat social media harms. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Social media platforms will face a bevy of new restrictions in New Jersey that limit their use of children’s data, restrict algorithmic content recommendations to minors, and block notifications during school hours, among a range of others.
The new restrictions, which are set to take effect in September 2027, flow from legislation Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed Tuesday and are New Jersey’s bid to regulate tech giants the governor said federal policymakers had largely left to their own devices.
“Big tech isn’t just the big tobacco of our era. They are worse. They designed platforms that highjacked our kids’ attention spans,” Sherrill said at a bill signing ceremony in Jersey City. “The typical American teen spends about 35 hours a week, almost a full-time job, on platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube.”
The restrictions in the New Jersey Kids Code Act would require privacy settings on minors’ social media accounts be set to their strictest mode and would limit platforms’ ability to request minors change those settings.
It would restrict platforms’ use of children’s data to the purposes for which it was collected and bar algorithmic content recommendations unless a minor specifically requests more or less content from a given account or of a specific type.
The restrictions mandate that social media platforms limit the discoverability of children’s accounts, both to adults on their own sites and through search engines.
And the law will bar social media platforms from sending notifications to minors between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. on school days between Labor Day and Memorial Day and block notifications between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. at all times of the year.
Assemblywoman Andrea Katz was a chief sponsor on the bill to restrict how social media platforms deliver content to children. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
“Half of parents say their children’s mental health has suffered over the past year because of social media,” said bill sponsor Assemblywoman Andrea Katz (D-Burlington). “Nearly half of teenagers say they lose sleep every single night because they feel stuck on these platforms.”
The law permits both parents and the New Jersey attorney general to sue over violations. If they’re victorious, courts could award $5,000 per violation or treble damages — an amount equal to three times the harm suffered — whichever is greater, plus attorney fees.
They can also order punitive damages for reckless or knowing violations and injunctions to bar offending conduct.
Lawmakers on Tuesday described a social media landscape that had sold children’s mental health for engagement and shifted threats that once appeared in physical spaces to digital ones.
“When I was a kid, our parents worried about strangers and who’s talking to us at the park or at the mall,” said bill sponsor Sen. Raj Mukherji (D-Hudson). “Today, we have to worry about who’s DMing them, what algorithms are pushing into our kids’ feeds, and what sensitive information is being collected, used, even sold before they’re old enough to understand what they’re giving away.”
Meta, which operates Facebook, Instagram, and other social media platforms, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Other bills Sherrill signed Tuesday order the creation of a social media research center at one of the state’s public four-year universities and direct it to begin studying the efficacy of social media warning labels and disclaimers in curbing social media addiction among children.
The state’s higher education office began accepting proposals for the center Tuesday and aims to open it sometime this fall with a $500,000 appropriation from the state’s budget.

text:
Health system ranks No. 5 in Philadelphia region and earns highest U.S. News rating in 13 procedures and conditions
NEWARK, Del. — ChristianaCare has again been named Delaware’s top hospital by U.S. News & World Report, while also ranking among the five highest-rated hospitals in the Philadelphia metropolitan area.
The health system ranked No. 1 in Delaware and No. 5 in the Philadelphia region in U.S. News’ 2026-27 Best Hospitals rankings released Tuesday. ChristianaCare also earned “High Performing” ratings in 13 adult procedures and conditions, the publication’s highest distinction in those categories.
The recognition continues a run of national rankings and patient-safety awards for one of Delaware’s largest health care providers.
“Awards and rankings like these are really about our people,” said Dr. Kert Anzilotti, ChristianaCare’s chief physician executive and president of its Medical Group. “This recognition reflects the talent, teamwork and commitment of our caregivers, who come to work every day focused on delivering safe, high-quality care and an exceptional experience for our patients and families.”
High marks across major areas of care
ChristianaCare received High Performing ratings for back surgery, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, colon cancer surgery, gynecological cancer surgery, heart bypass surgery, heart failure, hip fracture, hip replacement, knee replacement, leukemia, lymphoma and myeloma, lung cancer surgery, prostate cancer surgery and stroke.
The list includes several areas that involve complex or highly specialized care, including cancer treatment, cardiovascular surgery and stroke services.
U.S. News evaluates thousands of hospitals nationally, examining factors that include patient outcomes, mortality rates, preventable complications and patient experience. ChristianaCare said the latest rankings were based on data drawn from more than 800 million patient-care records.
The High Performing designation is the highest rating U.S. News awards for individual procedures and conditions.
“For nearly four decades, U.S. News has helped families and their medical providers navigate complex healthcare decisions,” said Ben Harder, chief of health analysis and managing editor at U.S. News, according to ChristianaCare’s announcement.
Delaware also scores well for hospital care
ChristianaCare’s ranking comes as Delaware continues to receive relatively strong national marks for health care.
ChristianaCare said the latest U.S. News Best States rankings place Delaware No. 2 nationally for hospital quality, No. 4 for overall health care quality and No. 10 for health care access.
The recognition follows ChristianaCare’s No. 1 Delaware ranking in U.S. News’ 2025-26 Best Hospitals report, when the system received High Performing designations in 14 conditions and procedures.
Other recent recognition
ChristianaCare also has received several other national quality and safety designations.
Christiana Hospital, Wilmington Hospital and Union Hospital received “A” grades in the spring 2026 Leapfrog Hospital Safety Grades, according to ChristianaCare. The organization also has been recognized by Newsweek in areas including maternity care, rehabilitation and overall hospital performance.
ChristianaCare also is Delaware’s only four-time Magnet-designated health care organization, a recognition associated with nursing excellence and patient care.

name: National
title: More college students will have access to abortion medication
description: When college students head back to campus for the fall semester, more of them will have guaranteed access to abortion medication. Colorado recently joined California, Illinois, Massachusetts and New York in requiring public colleges and universities to provide abortion medication to students on campus or arrange to make it available to them through an off-ca[...]
text:
Colorado Democratic state Sen. Katie Wallace speaking on the Senate floor in May. Wallace cosponsored a measure that requires Colorado colleges and universities to make abortion medication available to students. Colorado recently became the fifth state to enact such a law. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)When college students head back to campus for the fall semester, more of them will have guaranteed access to abortion medication.
Colorado recently joined California, Illinois, Massachusetts and New York in requiring public colleges and universities to provide abortion medication to students on campus or arrange to make it available to them through an off-campus provider.
Unlike the other states, Colorado’s new law also applies to private colleges and universities. However, Colorado schools are exempt if offering the medication would be “contrary to the institution’s sincerely held religious beliefs or practices” or if doing so would jeopardize a federal grant. Federal dollars cannot be used to pay for abortions except in limited circumstances.
All five states have enacted laws to expand access to abortion in recent years, both before and after the 2022 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which cleared the way for states to regulate abortion access for the first time in 50 years. Since that decision, more than a dozen states have enacted near-total abortion bans.
“In a post-Dobbs era where patients and providers navigate a frightening national landscape, Colorado has stepped up to safeguard reproductive healthcare,” Colorado Democratic state Rep. Kenny Nguyen, who cosponsored the measure in his state, said in a statement. “While abortion is legal, it’s not always accessible, and this law makes it easier for college students to access abortion medication on campus.”
The new Colorado law states that if an institution has an on-campus pharmacy, it must make abortion medication available to enrolled students. If not, health care providers on campus are required to submit a prescription for abortion pills to a pharmacy off campus.
Anti-abortion groups urge attorney general to halt mailing of abortion pills

California’s law, which has been in effect since 2023, was the first such measure. It requires every student health clinic on a California State University or University of California campus to offer abortion medication, funded by the state.
California is now considering expanding that law to include community colleges. A proposed bill would require community colleges with health centers to offer access to medication abortion beginning in 2029, if the legislature provides funding.
California campus health center directors have cautioned that many community colleges might not have the money, staff or clinical capacity to provide the service. But the bill’s supporters say offering abortion medication on campus would make it much more accessible to lower-income students who might not have sufficient insurance coverage or a car to procure it elsewhere.
“We are closing a critical gap by ensuring that community college students, one of the most diverse and economically vulnerable populations in our state, have the same access to care as their peers at four-year institutions,” said Democratic Assemblymember Catherine Stefani, the lead author of the bill, during a health committee hearing in April.
Massachusetts, which approved its campus abortion accessibility law in 2022, this week took another step to expand abortion access when Democratic Gov. Maura Healey signed legislation making it the 10th state (plus the District of Columbia) to allow abortion at any point in pregnancy. Most abortions occur in the first trimester; beyond the second trimester, abortions are rare and sometimes related to fetal or maternal health issues.
New York enacted its law requiring public college and university access to abortion medication in 2023, and Illinois started enforcing its mandate on public schools last fall, becoming the first state in the Midwest to do so.

text:
Voters cast their ballots at Lyndale Community School in south Minneapolis during the primary election Tuesday, August 11 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)This article will be updated throughout the day with additional voter interviews.
A record number of Minnesotans — more than 240,00, by early Tuesday, according to the secretary of state — have already voted, which could propel Minnesota to a turnout record in a non-presidential year. (In 2018, about 926,000 voters cast ballots, or 22.8% of eligible voters.)
Although he’s not on the ballot, Minnesotans are energized by the second term of President Donald Trump, and especially Operation Metro Surge and other ramifications felt here.
The biggest races on this primary Election Day — when the winners in each party will move on to the November general election — are for U.S. Senate and governor. A hotly contested Democratic-Farmer-Labor primary in Congressional District 2, the state’s most competitive, could help determine control of the U.S. House. Eleven legislators face primary opponents ahead of the November election, when all 201 legislative districts are up for grabs.
Polls close at 8 Tuesday night, and you can still vote even if you’re not registered yet. See here for more information.
The Reformer fanned out across the metro to talk to voters. Here’s some of what they told us so far.
Robbinsdale in the progressive lane
Nicholas Erdos-Thayer, 40, said he prefers candidates who “prioritize people over corporations.” 
Erdos-Thayer voted for Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in her U.S. Senate primary against U.S. Rep. Angie Craig. In another closely contested race, he voted for Rep. Cedrick Frazier, the DFL-endorsed lawmaker running against former acting U.S. Attorney Anders Folk and others in the technically nonpartisan race for Hennepin County Attorney.
Standing next to his bike outside his downtown Robbinsdale polling place, Erdos-Thayer said improving multimodal mobility was a top local priority.
“Generally speaking, we need to do more regarding public transit, bike and pedestrian infrastructure,” said Erdos-Thayer, an at-large member of the Robbinsdale Parks, Recreation, and Forestry Commission who worked on a recent update to the city’s bike and pedestrian plan.
Nick and Allie Heid, both 32, also biked to the polls. They chose Frazier, Flanagan — “enthusiastically,” Nick said — and Rep. Ilhan Omar, whom Allie called “a very strong representative” who’s responsive to constituent needs. 
“We like her stance on ICE … to prosecute the people who have deported our neighbors,” Allie said. 
Both said Sen. Amy Klobuchar — who won the DFL endorsement for governor and is the presumptive nominee — was a reluctant choice.
“(I’m) not thrilled about the governor option; I think she is a little bit too cozy with Republicans,” Allie said.
Nick, an energy auditor with a “non-utility-aligned” sustainability nonprofit, called Klobuchar a “fossil fuel capitalist.” 
He said he prefers candidates serious about addressing climate change. “Are we going to do something,” on climate, he began — “or are we going to keep not doing anything,” Allie finished. Both want candidates committed to police reform, protecting immigrants and repelling attacks on women’s rights and health care, she added. 
Both are optimistic about the November elections; Nick said he hoped for “a nice wave ahead,” propelled by progressives.
“Minnesota has the potential to be a progressive hub — a champion for climate, protecting immigrants, and women’s rights and health,” Allie said.

title: Governor awards $500,000 to task force working on cybersecurity and infrastructure resilience
description: South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden announced Tuesday that he awarded $500,000 from a fund under his control to support the continued work of his Governor’s Resilience and Infrastructure Task Force. The money comes from the Future Fund, which employers support with fees they submit while paying taxes to support unemployment benefits. The governor awards money […]
text:
Gov. Larry Rhoden delivers his State of the State address on Jan. 13, 2026, at the South Dakota Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden announced Tuesday that he awarded $500,000 from a fund under his control to support the continued work of his Governor’s Resilience and Infrastructure Task Force.
The money comes from the Future Fund, which employers support with fees they submit while paying taxes to support unemployment benefits.
The governor awards money from the fund at his discretion, although a state law that took effect July 1 places new restrictions on the fund, including a more detailed description of acceptable uses and a requirement that awards must be recommended by the Governor’s Office of Economic Development. One of the fund’s allowed uses is “development of infrastructure required to support economic development in this state.”
The state employees who ‘live, breathe and bleed cybersecurity’

Rhoden established the Governor’s Resilience and Infrastructure Task Force last year, saying it would “serve as a strategic advisory body to develop policy recommendations, assess risks and vulnerabilities, and support long-term planning and investment in critical infrastructure systems across our state.”
The Future Fund money is going to the state Department of the Military, which supports the task force administratively in collaboration with the Governor’s Office and the state Department of Public Safety. A news release from Rhoden’s office said the money will “equip the task force to build effective communication tools for citizens, gather resources to collect and integrate geographic information system (GIS) data that will enhance statewide infrastructure planning, and work with industry and academic partners to strengthen South Dakota’s resilience efforts.”
The task force’s work includes cybersecurity. Several recent cybersecurity incidents have generated news coverage in South Dakota, including a cyberattack in Pennington County that disrupted some services for weeks, an attempted cyberattack on Rapid City’s wastewater system, and a reported email hacking incident affecting the city of Mitchell.
Rhoden’s other recent Future Fund awards have benefited industrial and business parks in Rapid City and Mitchell, a program helping paraprofessionals become teachers, the addition of a gunsmithing program to to a technical college in Rapid City, and the establishment of a South Dakota Defense Institute seeking to bring more defense industry contracts to the state.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi should set rules before data centers continue growing, Sen. Hillman Frazier says
description: Jackson residents attend a public hearing on data centers at City Hall on Monday, June 23, 2026.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful Mississippians to share their ideas about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.  

Mississippi has an opportunity before it. Across the country, states are competing to attract data centers and the investment they promise.
New jobs, new tax revenue and new technology are all things worth pursuing. But as a state senator, I believe we have another responsibility that is just as important: making sure the people who live here aren’t left asking questions after decisions have already been made.
That conversation is happening today in state Senate District 27 that I represent.
Sen. Hillman Frazier Credit: Courtesy photo
Over the past several months, I have listened to residents concerned about a proposed data center in Jackson. They have attended public meetings, organized their neighbors and asked thoughtful questions about what this project could mean for their community. They are not asking Mississippi to turn away economic opportunity. They are asking for transparency and the assurance that growth will not come at their expense.
Those are reasonable requests. And the Jackson City Council, with the leadership of Councilman Brian Grizzell, did the right thing, listening to residents’ concerns and passing the state’s first data center moratorium. The 183-day pause will allow the council more time to build a plan that puts Jackson residents first.
When a project will place new demands on our electric grid, consume significant amounts of water and reshape a community for decades, the public deserves more than promises. They deserve facts and clear standards. And they deserve to know that the state government has done its homework before asking local communities to shoulder the consequences.
Too often, these projects are presented as an all-or-nothing proposition. Either we welcome them without question or we lose out to another state.
But, I reject that choice.
Mississippi has every reason to welcome innovation. We also have every reason to insist that companies investing here play by clear rules that protect our citizens.
Other states have already begun asking these questions. North Carolina recently repealed sales tax exemptions for electricity used by data centers, Florida recently passed a bill to regulate water usage by data centers, and Texas Governor Greg Abbott is asking lawmakers to repeal data center sales tax exemptions in 2027 and adopt new rules requiring the industry to pay more of its infrastructure costs.
My peers across the country have proposed policies that require greater transparency around energy and water use, protect residential ratepayers from subsidizing private infrastructure and ensure that communities understand the long-term impacts before construction begins. Those are conversations Mississippi should be having, as well.
As state legislators, we should also take a fresh look at the incentives we offer. Taxpayer dollars should encourage investments that provide lasting benefits to Mississippi families, not simply reward companies for choosing a location.
We should be honest about how many permanent jobs these facilities create, what infrastructure they require and who ultimately pays the bill if costs exceed expectations. These should be the requirements, especially when the companies asking for public incentives are owned by billionaires, and yes, even a trillionaire.
Good economic development leaves families and communities stronger long after the ribbon is cut.
That is why I intend to work with residents, colleagues from both parties, local leaders, utility experts and business leaders to develop thoughtful statewide policies before Mississippi sees another wave of data center development. We have an opportunity to learn from the experiences of other states instead of repeating their mistakes.
The people I represent have reminded me of something simple but important – growth works best when the public has confidence in the process. That confidence comes from openness. It comes from planning. And it comes from making sure the voices of local communities carry just as much weight as the promises made in corporate boardrooms.
Mississippi does not have to choose between economic growth and protecting our communities. We can do both.
But first, we have to set the rules.

Bio: Democratic Sen. Hillman Frazier of Jackson has represented state Senate District 27 in Hinds County since 1993. Frazier, a consultant, previously served in the Mississippi House.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico State Ethics Commission announces settlement with group behind Project Jupiter mailers
description: The New Mexico State Ethics Commission on Tuesday announced it had reached a settlement agreement with Elevate New Mexico, the Virginia-based corporation behind pro-Project Jupiter mailers and social media ads.
text:
The New Mexico State Ethics Commission on Aug. 11, 2026, announced a settlement with Elevate New Mexico, the group behind pro-Project Jupiter mailers that promised $360 million in community investments, $50 million in local water system improvements and "thousands of high-paying careers." (Photo courtesy of Neeshia Macanowicz)The New Mexico State Ethics Commission on Tuesday announced it had reached a settlement agreement with Elevate New Mexico, the Virginia-based corporation behind pro-Project Jupiter mailers and social media ads.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The State Ethics Commission sued the group in April – a month after Source NM revealed that an out-of-state company with no publicly listed executives was behind the effort – and accused it of violating the state Lobbyist Regulation Act.
The mailers and social media advertisements encouraged New Mexicans to support the proposal, which has since been withdrawn, to build two natural gas plants to power Project Jupiter, the OpenAI and Oracle data center under construction in Doña Ana County. Developers have since modified the plans to rely on fuel cells rather than on-site gas plants. 
A public hearing on whether to issue an air quality permit for the proposal is scheduled for September.
Under the settlement agreement announced Tuesday, Elevate New Mexico will file paperwork for a lobbying advertising campaign and campaign finance disclosures with the New Mexico Secretary of State, the State Ethics Commission said in a news release.
The State Ethics Commission said that Elevate New Mexico’s filings show it received nearly $3.7 million in contributions, all from Project Jupiter’s developer, Yucca Growth Infrastructure, and reported more than $419,000 in advertising expenses.
“Project Jupiter has attracted widespread public attention because of its potential economic, environmental, and energy impacts for New Mexico,” State Ethics Commission Deputy Director Amelia Bierle said in a statement. “These disclosures reveal the significant financial resources devoted to influencing both the public and, indirectly, the NMED officials considering the permits required for Project Jupiter. By enforcing the Lobbyist Regulation Act, the State Ethics Commission ensures that this information is publicly available, allowing New Mexicans to evaluate advertising campaigns with an understanding of who financed them, the magnitude of the financial resources behind them and how those resources were deployed.”
Elevate New Mexico did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Beau Bayh ad kicks off potentially expensive Indiana secretary of state campaign
description: Television advertising has started in what is poised as an expensive Indiana secretary of state campaign.
text:
An image of Beau Bayh, the Democratic candidate for Indiana secretary of state, from a campaign advertisement. (Screenshot)Television advertising has started in what is poised to be an expensive Indiana secretary of state campaign.
Democrat Beau Bayh’s campaign on Tuesday released what is the race’s first broadcast ad 12 weeks ahead of the Nov. 3 election. 
The 30-second advertisement opens with Bayh target shooting with a rifle while he says he trained as a Marine Corps marksman.
Over images of Bayh in Marines camouflage, he says he’ll work to clean up corruption in the secretary of state’s office and “expose every wasted dollar and no-bid contract.”
The Bayh campaign said it was making “an initial six-figure buy on TV and digital” but did not give any specifics.
Federal Communications Commission filings on Tuesday showed television ad time purchases by the campaign in the Indianapolis and South Bend markets.
Engling campaign says it returned $60K donation from dark money group

Bayh, the son of former Gov. Evan Bayh, ended June with about $2.3 million in his campaign fund, making him the best-financed Democratic candidate in several years as he tries to become the first Democrat to win a statewide office since 2012.
Republican candidate Max Engling had a late start in fundraising as he launched his successful GOP nomination challenge against current Secretary of State Diego Morales in May. 
Engling’s campaign had about $150,000 as of June 30, according to Election Division reports, but significant spending by outside Republican groups is expected on his behalf.
The Engling campaign did not answer a question Tuesday about its advertising plan but knocked Bayh’s ad, saying he “still thinks he’s running against Diego Morales.”
“Democrats and their socialist leadership are so radical that Beau Bayh doesn’t even acknowledge his own party in his campaign ad,” Engling’s campaign said. “Their campaign is behind, which is why they’re getting ads up early.”
Former Republican Indianapolis Mayor Greg Ballard is running as the Lincoln Party candidate and Libertarian Lauri Shillings will also be on the ballot.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Supreme Court seeks swift action in redistricting ballot measure case
description: The Missouri Supreme Court wants a quick resolution in lower courts of a lawsuit that will decide if voters will see a congressional redistricting referendum on the Nov. 3 ballot. In a Monday letter to Cole County Circuit Judge Daniel Green, Chief Justice William Brent Powell noted that state law requires the case to be […]
text:
The chief justice of the Missouri Supreme Court is asking for quick action on ballot measure cases with a September deadline looming. (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent)The Missouri Supreme Court wants a quick resolution in lower courts of a lawsuit that will decide if voters will see a congressional redistricting referendum on the Nov. 3 ballot.
In a Monday letter to Cole County Circuit Judge Daniel Green, Chief Justice William Brent Powell noted that state law requires the case to be moved to the front of the docket “and heard and decided…as quickly as possible.”
Whatever he decides, Powell wrote, the case is likely to be appealed.
“Accordingly, the matter must be handled expeditiously to ensure sufficient time for expedited appellate review to be completed,” Powell wrote. “Your cooperation in ensuring a timely resolution of this matter in both the circuit and appellate courts is appreciated.”
The trial court must act quickly because state law doesn’t allow the courts to add anything to the ballot after Sept. 8.
 Ongoing fight over gerrymandering

The case over whether the referendum will be on the ballot is the last chance for the campaign to overturn the gerrymandered redistricting plan that Republicans pushed through the Legislature last year under pressure from President Donald Trump. Through more than a dozen lawsuits, opponents of the plan have lost or been stymied as they questioned the legality of the map passed to favor Republicans in the 5th Congressional District.
On Aug. 4, Secretary of State Denny Hoskins blocked from the ballot a referendum petition submitted by a political action committee called People Not Politicians that contained more than 300,000 signatures. At the same time, he declared that a proposed constitutional amendment, submitted by initiative petition, will not be on the ballot because it improperly includes more than one subject.
Hoskins declared that the Missouri and federal constitutions do not allow a referendum on a redistricting plan. Hoskins refused to say whether either petition had enough signatures to make the ballot, saying his determination they were unconstitutional made the signature counts irrelevant.
People Not Politicians filed a lawsuit the same day challenging Hoskins’ decision. Respect MO Voters, the political action committee behind the petition that would be Amendment 6 if it makes the ballot, filed a lawsuit on Thursday.
Green late on Monday set the first hearing in the referendum case for Wednesday morning. He will also hold the first hearing on a lawsuit challenging the decision on the initiative.
There will be no decision on Wednesday. The hearings will set a schedule for filing arguments and holding trials.
 Potential long-term effects

There is more at stake in the ultimate outcome of the case over the referendum than whether it will be on the ballot. 
If the court upholds Hoskins, it means Missourians can never again use the referendum process to challenge a redistricting plan.
If the court orders the referendum to be placed on the ballot, it will trigger what could be one of the most expensive ballot measure campaigns in Missouri history. The costliest was in 2024, when more than $50 million was spent for and against sports wagering.
And it would throw the results of the Aug. 4 primary into question. Candidates were nominated in six districts that had their boundaries changed when the gerrymandered map was passed.
The candidates with the most direct interests are in the 5th District. Republican State Sen. Rick Brattin of Harrisonville won the GOP nomination to oppose Democratic U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver of Kansas City.
If the map drawn last year is used, Brattin has the edge, based on Republican success in past elections. If the map used for the 2022 and 2024 elections is used, Cleaver will have the advantage in a district where he has rarely received less than 55% of the vote.
Hoskins, at the news conference announcing his decisions, said that because the Missouri Constitution is silent on the question of whether redistricting plans are subject to a referendum, it is not allowed. He also said the federal Constitution gives power to draw districts to state legislatures and that power cannot be delegated to the people without an explicit allowance in law.
In their court filings, People Not Politicians is asking that the courts order the referendum to be placed on the ballot and block Hoskins from using the new districts in November.
In their filings, People Not Politicians argues that the silence in the constitution means a referendum is legal. 
When Republicans were arguing that they had the power to redistrict at any time, the courts found that because the Constitution does not forbid it, lawmakers had the authority to revise the lines.
Hoskins has not filed a formal response in the case.
The Republican National Committee, the National Republican Congressional Committee and the Missouri Republican State Committee filed to intervene in the case.
They want to participate, their attorney Marc Ellinger wrote, because the referendum’s “passage would undermine political and electoral interests” including diverting resources to a costly ballot measure campaign.
In the answer to the People Not Politicians’ filing, Ellinger said that it is too late to change the districts back to the ones used in 2022 and 2024.
And, he wrote, the issue is one the courts shouldn’t even consider.
“The petition raises nonjusticiable political questions,” Ellinger wrote, “that this Court has no jurisdiction to address.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Trump administration sues CT over in-state tuition for undocumented students
description: The suit challenges CT laws that allow immigrant students lacking permanent legal status to receive in-state tuition, financial assistance.
text:
The U.S. Department of Justice on Monday filed a lawsuit against Connecticut over state laws that provide in-state tuition and financial assistance to immigrant students lacking permanent legal status. 
In its complaint, the DOJ argued that Connecticut’s laws unfairly give benefits such as lower tuition and scholarships to students without legal status while denying the same benefits to U.S. citizens who live outside the state. The DOJ also argued that the laws violate federal statutes and encourage illegal immigration to the U.S.
“This is a simple matter of federal law: colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country.” 
In response to the lawsuit, Connecticut Attorney General William Tong, who voted for the in-state tuition law in 2011 as a state legislator, said he would defend the state’s policies. 
“Note to Trump — stay out of Connecticut,” Tong said in a statement. “Connecticut offers in-state tuition and financial aid to all eligible Connecticut students because all kids deserve the opportunity to learn, to advance, and to achieve their dreams. Donald Trump doesn’t run UConn or any of our state colleges, and we’re not about to let him start.” 
Gov. Lamont also defended the state’s policies, saying in a statement, “kids who grow up in Connecticut and graduate from Connecticut public schools should be able to afford to go to college here, including those who have applied for legal status.”
“We are making Connecticut the land of opportunity and education, and we will not accept his attempts to turn back the clock on progress,” Lamont said.
Connecticut first provided in-state tuition benefits to undocumented students under the 2011 state law, which required them to have attended high school in Connecticut for four years and earned a diploma. The state later reduced the high school attendance requirement to two years in 2015.
In 2018, Connecticut passed another law allowing students without permanent legal status to apply for and receive institutional aid at public colleges and universities.
The lawsuit also challenges other state laws involving financial aid at Connecticut State Community College, Roberta B. Willis need-based grants, and the state’s student loan reimbursement program.
The Trump administration has filed similar lawsuits challenging higher-education benefits in 16 other states.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: AnderBois debuts television ad to stand out in crowded lieutenant governor race
description: With early voting for the Sept. 9 primary set to begin next week, Democratic candidate for lieutenant governor Sue AnderBois on Tuesday announced her campaign’s first television ad, backed by a six-figure broadcast ad buy across Rhode Island.  The 30-second spot titled “Deliver” was filmed in Roger Williams Park in Providence and shows the Ward […]
text:
Sue AnderBois debuted  her first TV ad spot in her campaign for Rhode Island lieutenant governor on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (Screenshot/Friends of Sue AnderBois)With early voting for the Sept. 9 primary set to begin next week, Democratic candidate for lieutenant governor Sue AnderBois on Tuesday announced her campaign’s first television ad, backed by a six-figure broadcast ad buy across Rhode Island. 
The 30-second spot titled “Deliver” was filmed in Roger Williams Park in Providence and shows the Ward 3 Providence City Councilor speaking with a small group of activists and one state lawmaker aligned with progressive causes.
One of five Democrats in the race for Rhode Island’s second highest office, AnderBois introduces voters to her record of championing efforts to lower energy costs, invest in clean energy, build more housing, and make streets and sidewalks safer while framing herself as a candidate who has already shown she can get results.
“I ran for City Council because I knew we could beat corrupt insiders, pass a progressive agenda, and lower your costs. And boy, did I deliver, AnderBois says. “I’m tired of hearing people say it can’t be done. So I’m running for lieutenant governor.”
AnderBois has amassed over 20 endorsements from progressive coalitions and local and state officials including Climate Action Rhode Island, the Providence Streets Coalition, Cranston Forward, and several lawmakers including Rep. Brandon Potter, a Cranston Democrat, who appears in her ad spot.
Her campaign says the ad will begin airing on local television stations next week. Federal law requires broadcast television stations to upload purchase forms indicating how much ads cost and how long they run within one business day of receiving a request from a campaign or super PACs.
Early voting begins Thursday, Aug. 20.
Second quarter campaign finance reports filed with the Rhode Island Board of Elections show AnderBois took in $58,596 in donations in the three months that ended June 30, ending the quarter with $129,932 on hand. 
She was the third-highest fundraiser after Newport City Councilor Xay Khamsyvoravong who raised more than $117,000 and former state Sen. Cindy Coyne who raised $62,883. Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos, who is running for reelection, raised $43,101 while Ross McCurdy raised less than $1,000. 
FCC filings show Khamsyvoravong’s campaign reserved $119,890 for 377 commercials across Rhode Island’s major networks and cable set to begin next week. Coyne’s campaign aired two commercial spots on WNAC on July 31. FCC filings show Coyne’s campaign has reserved $10,770 for 45 spots across WJAR and Coastal ABC between Aug. 13 and 19.
Candidates will have to file two more campaign reports before the Sept. 9 primary: one on Aug. 12, reflecting donations and fundraising from July 1 to Aug. 11; and a second on Sept. 2, reflecting donations and fundraising from Aug. 12 to Sept. 1.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Second state-employed nurse is sanctioned for prison inmate’s death
description: Iowa regulators have sanctioned a second state-employed nurse in the 2025 death of an inmate at the Newton Correctional Facility. In October 2025, the Iowa Board of Nursing charged two Department of Corrections nurses — Penny Lynn Daniels of Newton and David Arterburn of Altoona — with committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s […]
text:
The Newton Correctional Facility in Iowa's Jasper County. (Photo courtesy of the Iowa Department of Corrections.)Iowa regulators have sanctioned a second state-employed nurse in the 2025 death of an inmate at the Newton Correctional Facility.
In October 2025, the Iowa Board of Nursing charged two Department of Corrections nurses — Penny Lynn Daniels of Newton and David Arterburn of Altoona — with committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare; failing to assess or accurately document a patient’s status; and committing an act that causes physical, emotional or financial injury to a patient.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the board, Daniels worked for the state at the Newton Correctional Facility in September 2024 when she failed to provide an inmate with adequate medical care. The board alleges other medical personnel informed Daniels of the inmate’s “worsening symptoms,” which included fever, nausea and vomiting. According to the board, she added electrolyte fluid to his medication order but did not assess his condition and informed others that the inmate had a virus. The inmate died a short time later from a perforated ulcer.
The board resolved the disciplinary case against Daniels with a settlement agreement that called for her license to be suspended for three months. Daniels was also ordered to complete educational training in the area of ethics and maintaining professional boundaries with patients.
Daniels’ license was also placed on probationary status for three years, during which her practice will be subject to monitoring.
More recently, the board agreed to a settlement in the Arterburn case. In that case, the board alleged that Arterburn did not assess or provide medical care to the inmate, even after colleagues made him aware of the inmate’s declining condition. Arterburn, the board added, also did not document any of the calls related to the inmate until after he learned of the inmate’s death.
As part of the settlement, the board has suspended Arterburn’s license for six months and ordered him to complete an unspecified number of hours of educational training on maintaining professional boundaries and ethics. After the suspension is served, Arterburn’s license will be placed on probationary status for three years.
Lawsuit alleges inaction led to death
Court records indicate the two disciplinary cases stem from the September 2025 death of Malga Harun Yanga at the Newton Correctional Facility.
A civil lawsuit filed by Yanga’s estate against Daniels, Arterburn, the State of Iowa and others, alleges Yanga had a week-long history of stomach pain, diarrhea and vomiting blood by the time he twice saw Daniels on Sept. 3, 2024.
By that time, the lawsuit claims, Yanga had “vomited such a large amount of blood, it was all over his hands and the floor of his cell and multiple inmates had to clean it up.”  The lawsuit alleges Daniels was informed that Yanga continued to vomit blood, was unable to speak, had severe abdominal pain, and could not walk — and that Daniels did not perform any additional nursing assessments or request a physician assessment.
About 12:30 a.m. on Sept. 4, 2024, a cellmate of Yanga’s banged on the door and yelled for help from correctional officers, saying Yanga was unresponsive, seizing and making “jerking, twitching” movements. The lawsuit alleges a correctional officer refused the cellmate’s request for medical attention by stating Yanga had already been to the medical clinic and “we’re not taking him again.”
At 5 a.m., Yanga’s cellmate again called out for help, after which corrections officers found Yanga unresponsive. The officers allegedly initiated cardiopulmonary resuscitation before pronouncing Yanga dead about 45 minutes later.
The defendants in the civil case have denied any wrongdoing. The case is scheduled to be tried on May 4, 2027.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Daniels and Arterburn for comment.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Midwest Innocence Project files claim of wrongful conviction in KCK barbershop homicide case
description: Midwest Innocence Project attorneys argue a Kansas City, Kansas, man was unjustly convicted of murder and attempted murder in a 2009 barbershop shooting.
text:
The Midwest Innocence Project is petitioning for a court review of newly compiled evidence suggesting a Kansas City, Kansas, man was unjustifiably convicted of murder in 2009 when framed by corrupt police investigators. In this image, the statue of justice greets visitors to the lobby of a Topeka building where the Kansas Supreme Court convenes. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Appellate attorneys representing Donnell Dobbs say their client had no role in the Kansas City, Kansas, barbershop death of Muryel Josenberger despite a jury conviction for first-degree murder based on testimony from a survivor of the violent melee.
Questions about Dobbs’ guilt lingered after police and prosecutors closed the case. Five years ago, the Community Integrity Unit created by the Wyandotte County District Attorney’s Office concluded that Dobbs was innocent of murder, said Evan Glasner, part of the Midwest Innocence Project’s legal team.
The Midwest Innocence Project says its own inquiry uncovered evidence that former KCK police detective Roger Golubski and others tainted the original investigation to ensnare Dobbs. The organization’s petition seeking to vacate Dobbs’ sentence was filed in Wyandotte County District Court and delivered to District Attorney Mark Dupree.
“Donnell Dobbs is innocent, sentenced to spend decades in prison for a crime he did not commit,” Glasner’s petition says. “Strong evidence implicates an alternate suspect as the perpetrator of the shooting for which Dobbs has spent the last 17 years incarcerated. The single eyewitness in this case provided flawed and unreliable testimony at trial and has since admitted that his testimony was false.”
Dobbs, ordered to serve a life term without possibility of parole for 25 years, claimed he couldn’t have taken part in the slaying because on the day of the 2008 shooting he attended a friend’s funeral and gathered with others at his mother’s residence. No physical evidence tied Dobbs to the crime scene.
Witnesses described the barbershop shooter as a man with braided hair standing about 5-foot-9 and weighing 190 pounds, the Midwest Innocence Project says. Dobbs was a former college football defensive lineman who weighed 260 pounds and wore his hair short. At trial, Dobbs’ defense lawyer didn’t present an opening argument or call witnesses. Dobbs’ alibi wasn’t shared with jurors.
In a twist, the Midwest Innocence Project says relatives of the man killed at the barbershop quickly tracked down an alternate suspect, Keith Wright, who matched the general description of the individual who shot Josenberger. Wright responded to the retaliatory attack by wounding one person in a shootout. Wright surrendered to police, but Dobbs’ current attorneys say no evidence existed KCK police questioned Wright about the barbershop crime.
Dobbs’ appellate attorneys maintain Mario Mitchell, who was shot a dozen times but escaped out a back door of the barbershop, was visited at the hospital by Kansas City, Kansas, police officers. The petition for fresh consideration of the Dobbs case says Mitchell was presented a photo array that included Dobbs and one of his friends, Casey Ellis. In an unrecorded police interview, Mitchell purportedly pointed a finger at Dobbs and Ellis. Both men were arrested the next day. A Wyandotte County jury in 2009 found Dobbs guilty but acquitted Ellis.
In 2013, the Kansas Supreme Court rejected Dobbs’ appeal in the murder case. A three-judge panel of the Kansas Court of Appeals affirmed his conviction in 2018.
The petition filed by the Midwest Innocence Project on Dobbs’ behalf sought an evidentiary hearing, the casting aside of his conviction and scheduling of a new trial.
Glasner’s petition says Golubski, the KCK investigator involved in Dobbs’ case, was implicated in multiple instances of corruption, sexual abuse of Black women and framing of innocent people in Wyandotte County. Golubski died by suicide in 2024 as his federal trial on alleged kidnapping, rape and civil rights violations was to begin.
Golubski was a figure in the wrongful conviction of Lamonte McIntyre in a double homicide in Kansas City, Kansas. McIntyre was released in 2017 after 23 years in prison.
Glasner’s 93-page filing in the Dobbs case drew upon similarities with Golubski’s manipulation of evidence in a campaign to implicate McIntyre. In the McIntyre case, McIntyre’s mother had refused Golubski’s sexual advances. In response, Golubski pressured a woman to falsely identify McIntyre as a killer. Golubski committed suicide before Dobbs’ mother, Davilyn, could testify in federal court that Golubski attempted to coerce sexual favors from her in the years before Donnell Dobbs’ arrest in the barbershop case, the Dobbs petition says.
Documents submitted July 28 on behalf of Dobbs by the Midwest Innocence Project asserted Dobbs’ due process rights were violated because Wyandotte County prosecutors failed to disclose exculpatory evidence that an alternate suspect could have committed the crime. In addition, the petition says Dobbs received ineffective trial counsel and a prosecutor presented evidence at trial that she should have known was false.
“Dobbs makes new and specific factual allegations, supported by records and witness statements, that he is undoubtedly innocent,” Glasner’s petition says. “Not only does Dobbs produce new factual information about his alibi on the day in question, but he also presents new evidence regarding the flawed eyewitness testimony, police misconduct and alternate suspect that demonstrate his actual innocence.”
Since its founding in 2001, the Midwest Innocence Project helped secure the exoneration of 11 wrongfully convicted individuals and the release of eight people.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Poll: Utility costs, the economy and taxes top of mind for voters
description: A majority of Marylanders said they favor raising taxes on wealthy households over other options, including legalizing internet gaming or making changes to the state sales tax, according to a poll released Tuesday.ac
text:
Protesters gathered outside the State House on March 30, 2026 to defend the EmPOWER Maryland program against temporary cuts proposed in the Maryland General Assembly. Utility costs continue to drive the concerns of a majority of a new poll released Tuesday. (File photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)A majority of Marylanders in a new survey said they favor raising taxes on wealthy households over other options including legalizing internet gaming or making changes to the state sales tax. 
The poll commissioned by Blended Public Affairs and Perry Jacobson, a marquee Annapolis lobbying shop, also found that utility costs and data centers are top of mind for Maryland voters. 
Next year, the governor and the General Assembly will face tough choices as they look to close a $3 billion projected structural budget gap. A solution could come with a menu of cuts and tax increases. 
In the poll released Tuesday, 54% said they favored raising taxes on households with $500,000 or more in income. Support for legalized internet gaming — which would require voter approval in a subsequent election — came in at just 36%. Another 27% said they favored tax increases on businesses with 50 or more employees. 
Some of the least favored options included changes to Maryland’s sales tax which currently stands at 6%. 
Increasing the sales tax by a penny would generate $1.2 billion in additional revenue. Such a move is seen as regressive and would hit lower-income households already feeling the economic pinch. 
Advocates, regulators both call for reforms at power grid operator PJM

Just 11% said they favored such an increase. Another 15% said they would a levy on services not currently covered by the sales tax. 
The poll — a text message-to-web interview — surveyed 800 registered Marylanders who were likely to vote in November. It was conducted between July 27 and Aug. 3 and has a margin of error of 3.5 percentage points. 
Of those surveyed in the poll, 3% said they would favor an increase to the state property tax. That tax is earmarked to repay bonds issued annually by the state. 
Marylanders are also increasingly pessimistic about the state of the economy. 
Nearly six in 10 surveyed rated the state economy as “not so good” or poor. Just 2% said it was excellent. Two in five voters rated the economy as “good.” 
Four in 10 said they wanted the next governor to focus on lowering utility costs. Roughly one-third said there should be a focus on “creating jobs and growing the economy.” 
A majority of Marylanders are increasingly concerned about rising energy costs and the accompanying financial pressures, according to the poll. 
Utility costs continue to be top of mind for Maryland residents as 51% of those surveyed said they are “really struggling financially” or “Just getting by.” Another 53% said they worried that utility bills would be so high that they or a family member would not be able to pay them. 
A plurality of voters — 42% — reported difficulties in paying a utility bill in the last year. 
Concerns about utility costs
 are driving public concerns about data centers. Three of every four surveyed said they were concerned or very concerned about the impact of data centers. 
Topping those concerns, 39% of those polled said they worried about increased electric bills. Another 21% said environmental impacts were troublesome.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Andy Lack and Kara Swisher to discuss AI at ‘All In on Mississippi’ summit
description: Media executive Andy Lack and award-winning journalist Kara Swisher will headline a conversation titled "AI and the Search for Truth" during Mississippi Today's second annual "All In on Mississippi Summit" on Oct. 8.
text:
Media executive Andy Lack and award-winning journalist Kara Swisher will headline a conversation titled “AI and the Search for Truth” during Mississippi Today’s second annual “All In on Mississippi Summit” on Oct. 8, the nonprofit newsroom announced Tuesday.
The discussion will explore how artificial intelligence is reshaping journalism, media, business and public trust as technology is rapidly transforming how people consume and evaluate information.
The session is part of Mississippi Today’s 10th anniversary celebration and will bring together leaders from business, government, philanthropy, education and journalism for conversations about the state’s future.
“Artificial intelligence is changing nearly every aspect of life, including how news is produced and distributed and whether people can trust what they read, hear and see,” said Emily Wagster Pettus, editor-in-chief of Mississippi Today. “Andy Lack and Kara Swisher are experts on media innovation and accountability. Their conversation will illuminate one of the most important issues facing journalism and democracy today.”
‘AI and the Search for Truth‘
As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, questions surrounding misinformation, trust, ethics and the future of independent journalism are urgent.
During “AI and the Search for Truth,” Lack and Swisher will examine how AI is transforming the information ecosystem, the opportunities and risks the technology presents, and what journalists, civic leaders and the public must do to preserve trustworthy information.
The conversation will also explore how news organizations are adapting to rapidly evolving technology while remaining committed to accuracy, transparency and public service.
About Andy Lack
Andy Lack is a journalist, television and film producer, and media executive who has received 16 Emmy Awards and four Peabody Awards. During his 15 years leading NBC News as chairman and CEO, he transformed the organization into the world’s most-watched news division. He is executive chairman and founder of Mississippi Today and Deep South Today, the nonprofit network of local investigative newsrooms serving Mississippi, Louisiana and soon to be Arkansas. Lack has also served as CEO of Bloomberg Media Group, chairman and CEO of Sony Music Entertainment, and the first CEO of the Broadcasting Board of Governors overseeing Voice of America and Radio Free Europe. He co-founded MSNBC.
About Kara Swisher
Kara Swisher is one of the world’s foremost technology journalists and commentators. She is the host of “On with Kara Swisher,” co-host of the award-winning “Pivot” podcast, editor-at-large at New York Magazine and a CNN contributor. Swisher co-founded the influential technology publication Recode and has covered Silicon Valley and the technology industry for more than three decades. She is also the author of the New York Times bestselling memoir “Burn Book: A Tech Love Story.”
About the ‘All In on Mississippi’ summit
The “All In on Mississippi” summit is Mississippi Today’s annual gathering focused on innovative solutions, economic opportunity and community impact across the state.
Presented with support from JPMorgan Chase, and with the Foundation for the MidSouth serving as Impact Sponsor, the summit convenes leaders from government, business, education, workforce development, philanthropy and journalism to explore the ideas shaping Mississippi’s future.
Registration
The All In on Mississippi Summit begins at 1 p.m. Oct. 8 at the Two Mississippi Museums in Jackson.
Summit tickets are $25. Additional information, the full agenda and registration are available at: https://summit.mississippitoday.org/
