name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: 1 month after Lindsey Graham’s death, voters go to the polls to choose his replacement
description: COLUMBIA — Voters will choose Tuesday between 10 U.S. Senate candidates competing in a special GOP primary to replace the late Lindsey Graham on the ballot in November. The tight timeline dictated by state law means the contest is being held exactly one month after Graham’s unexpected death at age 71. Officially, the crowded field […]
text:
Polls in South Carolina's special GOP primary for the U.S. Senate are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (File photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Voters will choose Tuesday between 10 U.S. Senate candidates competing in a special GOP primary to replace the late Lindsey Graham on the ballot in November.
The tight timeline dictated by state law means the contest is being held exactly one month after Graham’s unexpected death at age 71.
Officially, the crowded field is competing for the chance to win the next six-year term. But in South Carolina, voters have a history of re-electing their senators as long as they want to stay. And in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the job in 28 years, the Republican primary is typically the main event.
Graham’s win in June marked the third time he bested a crowded field of competitors to win the GOP primary outright. But none of the candidates seeking to replace him is expected to cross the 50% threshold needed to avoid a runoff. The top two vote-getters will face off Aug. 25. Calling a runoff “highly likely,” the state GOP scheduled a debate next week between whoever advances.
It’s not at all clear who those two will be. In many polls leading up to the contest, “undecided” remained the winner.
Graham’s younger sister, Darline Graham, who was appointed to fulfill her brother’s term that ends in January, jumped into the open contest with the encouragement of President Donald Trump. In a rally by telephone Monday night, Trump repeated his “complete and total endorsement” and urged people who called in to “go vote for Sen. Darline Graham.” She’s already been a “fantastic help,” he said, pointing to her votes enabling Todd Blanche to be sworn in Monday as U.S. attorney general.


What to know before voting
Polls close at 7 p.m. If you’re standing in line at 7 p.m., you’ll get to vote.
People who voted in the June 9 Democratic primary are not eligible to vote in this primary.
A runoff, if necessary, is scheduled for Aug. 25.
Click here to find where you vote. Many polling locations have been changed due to school being back in session.
To see our election coverage, click here.


Thanking the president, she called his endorsement “the gold standard in Republican politics.” She also has the support of her brother’s long-time staff, who now work for her.
But Trump’s surprise endorsement of a family member without a political record rankled many of the GOP faithful.
U.S. Rep. Russell Fry, who represents the 7th District, was widely expected to again get Trump’s backing. Fry, a former state legislator representing Horry County, first won the congressional seat anchored by the Grand Strand in 2022 with Trump’s endorsement. Trump’s decision to go with someone else didn’t stop him from jumping into the race. And he still campaigns as a Trump-supported candidate.
Some Republicans have criticized Fry’s decision to run for Senate while also seeking re-election to the U.S. House, potentially leaving the 7th District seat vacant for months during another special election. But Fry, who is endorsed by dozens of former colleagues in the Legislature, contends the ruby red seat will remain in GOP control.
Fry’s critics include U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, who’s running for U.S. Senate after losing his bid for governor in June. So, he’s not otherwise on November ballots. His endorsers include U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace, legislators in the state Freedom Caucus that he helped launch, and former U.S. Sen. Jim DeMint, who in December 2012 announced his resignation in order to lead The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank.
Like Fry, Norman is a former legislator. The Rock Hill developer first won the 5th District seat in a special election in 2017 after Mick Mulvaney resigned to join the first Trump administration.
Former Gov. Mark Sanford, also a former congressman, is running on his familiar message of bringing down bloated spending in Washington and reducing the national deficit he contends will ultimately lead to America’s demise.
On that front and the war in Iran, he’s willing to publicly oppose Trump, he noted on the debate stage. He’s done it before. He was a Trump critic toward the end of his last stint as the 1st District congressman and briefly entered the presidential race in 2019 to challenge Trump’s re-election.
While the notoriously frugal former governor has been preaching against deficit spending for decades, it matters more than ever now, he says, with the deficit quickly approaching $40 trillion and climbing. To make his point, he again brought pigs to the Statehouse last week, recreating a stunt 22 years earlier to protest the state budget.
Others in the field include Upstate businessman Mark Lynch, owner of Jeff Lynch Appliance Center in Greenville, which he says he’s grown from a 3,200-square-foot store in 1985 with five employees when he took over the family business to more than 130,000 square feet of retail space employing 110 people.
Like Darline Graham, Lynch embraces not being a politician.
Lynch, who placed a distant second to Lindsey Graham in the June primary, has turned an attack line into a positive. Acknowledging he was a drug addict in the late ’70s and early ’80s, he talks about how he turned his life around with God’s grace and helps others do the same. He received a state pardon in 1990 for his drug conviction, according to the state’s pardon and parole board. He’s spending millions of his own money — which shows “skin in the game and commitment” — in a quest to turn the nation back to God.
“I’ll bring back biblical principles,” he told the SC Daily Gazette.
Other candidates who didn’t meet polling criteria to get into last week’s debates are Duke Buckner, a Walterboro attorney; Mark McBride, mayor of Myrtle Beach from 1998 through 2005; Glenda Gail Parker, a retired Air Force reservist and Department of Defense budget analyst; and Sam Shepherd, a biomedical engineer and entrepreneur.
The winner of the GOP contest will face Democrat Annie Andrews in November.
This is the first open contest to represent South Carolina in the U.S. Senate in 22 years.
The last Democrat to represent South Carolina in the U.S. Senate was the late Fritz Hollings, who decided not to seek re-election in 2004. He first won the job in 1966 when the vast majority of the state’s politicians were Democrats. And unlike others, he never switched.
Lindsey Graham replaced U.S. Sen. Strom Thurmond when he decided not to seek re-election in 2002.
Thurmond, who switched to the Republican Party in 1964, continues to be the only senator ever to reach age 100 in office. His 47½ years in the U.S. Senate ranks fourth-longest in history. Hollings’ 38 years ranks 13th. Both Thurmond and Hollings were Democratic governors before voters sent them to the Senate.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Can we make sense of today’s politics by reaching into the community?
description: Disagreements about our values and hopes will be hard conversations, but we, as people, cannot walk away from having them.
text:
I graduated from South Windsor High School in 2025. This summer, I returned to work with the school’s paper, The Bobcat Prowl, running a student civic engagement project.In this project, the students have written a series of short, neutral summaries for the August 11th primaries, tailored to the voter who (perhaps like many of us) begins their research the night before, or on the day, they head to the ballot box. This narrowed our coverage to the Democratic primaries for the 1st Congressional District and Governor. We would have covered Republican primaries for these offices, but they were resolved in May. 
Earlier this summer, I asked one of my high school administrators (someone I highly respect and admire) about sharing this opportunity to students through a group of teachers. They responded (with the best intentions) along the lines of: 
“You don’t want to be dealing with politics.” 
And, I agree. Today’s politics feel nasty. By 2022, Pew Research found that around or more than two-thirds of Republicans and Democrats viewed members of the other party as close-minded, dishonest, and immoral. So, of course parents and mentors want to protect their students from politics. Also, what if the very presence of politics sparks conflict? 
I’ll ask another question—perhaps one you have wondered, too—thought it seems unrelated at first. Why have students write summaries, when voters could have asked ChatGPT, instead? 
To me, these questions point to a shared theme. Politics is nasty. Politics should stay away from schools. Politics is perhaps only to be thought of the night before, or on the day of voting—to only be considered quickly, through a possibly 3-minute AI-generated summary. This makes sense in today’s politics.  
But I started this project with the conviction that if we went to residents, and if we accommodated their schedules, that they would share their values and hopes in building a better society. I write this reflection with the belief that we can achieve a better politics. Discussion and disagreements—politics—about our values and hopes will be hard conversations, but we, as people, cannot walk away from having them.  
When these questions first surfaced in my mind, I replayed the steps of our interviewing and drafting process, asking myself if they had been worth our effort and time.  

We mailed our community issues survey to 200 randomly selected voters, of which 7.5% responded. “Cold” mail surveys receive, on average, a 1% to 5% response rate.
Students asked campaign managers, candidates, and other policymakers how each candidate’s ideas, perspectives, and background set them apart from the field. 
Students conversed with community members about their concerns, in a medium most convenient to them (email, text, or call). 
Students tailored their articles to voters, asking themselves: “Would a reader find this valuable? Can I convey this in fewer words?” 

As this project comes to an end, and we post our summaries, I think it’s been worth it. Each of these steps built a little more empathy, curiosity, critical thinking, thoughtfulness, and respect in my students. Keeping politics out of the classroom signals that adults do not think it can change for the better, so they have removed it entirely. I’m not saying politics will be an easy discussion, or that it doesn’t stoke emotions. I’m saying that practicing politics—whether through objective reporting, or respectful, empathetic disagreements—is a discussion of who we are and our dreams for the future. I’m saying that we cannot prepare students for a responsibility we treat as a threat. 
I hope that, as a reader, you find these summaries at least helpful starting points to making an informed vote. We’ve worked to provide the best information we can—not to convince you to support any particular candidate. Read them at The Bobcat Prowl by clicking the links below. If you think we’ve fallen short in any way, please email me at info@south-windsor-voter-summaries.com! 

Bronin, Fortune, Gilchrest, and Larson’s Ideas for Immigration (Emma Hennessey)
Where Larson, Bronin, Glichrest, and Fortune Stand on Healthcare (Deepshikha Paul)
How Ned Lamont and Josh Elliott Plan to Lower Utility Costs (Deepshikha Paul)

Has this project changed anything, though? 
Maybe not noticeably, at first. The Bobcat Prowl plans to continue articles like this into the fall general elections. I hope this idea excites students and teachers at other high schools, and I’d be more than happy to help set up a similar initiative. 
Roger Mao is a rising sophomore at Brown University, majoring in Math-C.S. and International Relations.

name: Nevada Current
title: Nevada problem gambling group cuts ties with national organization over Kalshi deal
description: The Nevada Council on Problem Gambling confirms it intends to formally sever ties this month with the National Council on Problem Gambling over the latter’s partnership with Kalshi, a prediction market that has been banned from taking bets from Nevada gamblers.  The Nevada Gaming Control Board asserts in a lawsuit against Kalshi that state regulators […]
text:
(Photo: Hugh Jackson/Nevada Current)The Nevada Council on Problem Gambling confirms it intends to formally sever ties this month with the National Council on Problem Gambling over the latter’s partnership with Kalshi, a prediction market that has been banned from taking bets from Nevada gamblers. 
The Nevada Gaming Control Board asserts in a lawsuit against Kalshi that state regulators should have jurisdiction over prediction markets. The Nevada Council has submitted amici, or friend of the court briefs in Nevada’s case against Kalshi. 
Some 14 states are in litigation with prediction markets. Others have passed laws prohibiting them. In July, attorneys general from 44 states fired off a letter to the Commodity and Futures Trading Commission, asserting the federal panel lacks authority to regulate sports bets.   
The CFTC, whose five members are appointed by President Donald Trump, claims it has exclusive jurisdiction over the platforms, which accept bets on almost anything from gamblers as young as 18 years old.
Trump and his sons have business ties to several prediction market platforms. 
Trump’s own teleprompter operator is no longer on the job, according to news reports, after the White House learned he was making bets on Kalshi based on inside information gleaned from his position. 
The Current reported in May that the National Council on Problem Gambling formed a new Financial Services and Trading subcategory to accommodate Kalshi, which put up a $2 million two-year investment to “support a strategic initiative focused on trader health and safety,” the National Council announced at the time. 
The Nevada Council raised its concerns “directly with National’s leadership and gave them an opportunity to address them,” Nevada Council Executive Director Trey Delap said in a statement to the Current. “After months of discussion, we’ve concluded that this is not simply a disagreement about one company. It reflects a fundamental difference in how we believe a problem gambling organization should respond to emerging gambling risks.” 
Delap says the uproar over prediction markets “has exposed a larger problem: gambling innovation is moving faster than the public-health infrastructure designed to address it. Our answer isn’t to fight yesterday’s battle. It’s to build what the field needs next.”
The organizations “are no longer mission aligned,” says Delap, who said in May the National Council’s partnership with Kalshi, “announced while significant regulatory and legal questions are being litigated… can create real public confusion,” Delap said. “It risks looking less like neutral harm reduction and more like an endorsement of the platform itself.”
Delap notes other state organizations and regulators have rejected the national group for its embrace of prediction markets, and others are likely to follow suit. 
“Stakeholders including gaming, treatment, regulators, and other state councils are all having serious conversations about withdrawing or redirecting their support,” says Delap. 
The Evergreen Council, a problem gambling organization based in Washington state, wrote that it’s “troubled” by the National Council’s  “willingness to partner with and/or accept an ‘investment’ from an entity disregarding, if not directly threatening, the sovereignty of tribal nations in Washington state and throughout the United States.”
Additionally, last month the Michigan Gaming Control Board announced it’s withdrawing its support from the National Council. 
The National Council did not respond to a request for comment. 
Kalshi, which once attempted to skirt state regulation by deeming its transactions as trades rather than bets, has more recently acknowledged it, with advertisements proclaiming it takes “bets” in all 50 states.
“Our decision is based on the elevated risk of harm to young people,” Delap said. “The activity on the Kalshi platform has the same effect as gambling. ‘Positions’ and ‘trades’ are euphemisms – the effect is the same as gambling, and carries the same risk of harm and suicide consistent with any other form of gambling. This risk is elevated among young people – Kalshi’s primary target.”
Kalshi allows 18 year-olds to gamble, while the National Council supports a minimum age of 21. 
Gambling, once the exclusive province of Nevada, is now America’s favorite pastime, according to Fortune, which reported last month that Americans placed $166 billion in sports bets last year, eclipsing the total revenue generated by the movie, music, book and museum industries in 2025. 
“Affiliation means something. We cannot lend Nevada’s name and credibility to an organization when we no longer believe we’re aligned on a fundamental consumer-protection issue,” says Delap, adding the National Council’s actions “undermine the efforts of problem gambling prevention, treatment, and responsible gambling.”
The Nevada Council was one of 35 state affiliates of the National Council. 
“Words matter in prevention. If we tell young people they’re investing or trading when they’re engaging in behavior that carries gambling risk, we make it harder for them to recognize when that behavior becomes harmful,” says Delap. “A 19-year-old experiencing gambling harm doesn’t care which federal agency regulates the platform. Neither should the public health response.”

title: Trump’s mass deportations cost average NV taxpayer $2,421, report finds
description: Nevada taxpayers paid $2.7 billion on mass deportations in 2025, according to an analysis by the Economic Policy Institute (EPI). Clark County taxpayers accounted for $1.8 billion of that amount, and Washoe County taxpayers accounted for nearly $600,000. Analyzing IRS statistics of income, an Institute for Policy Studies estimate of the costs of the Trump […[...]
text:
(Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)Nevada taxpayers paid $2.7 billion on mass deportations in 2025, according to an analysis by the Economic Policy Institute (EPI).
Clark County taxpayers accounted for $1.8 billion of that amount, and Washoe County taxpayers accounted for nearly $600,000.
Analyzing IRS statistics of income, an Institute for Policy Studies estimate of the costs of the Trump administration’s deportation program in 2025, and other data, EPI estimates that the deportations cost the average taxpayer $2,421. 
That’s money that could have been allocated to other public services and public servants in Nevada, argues EPI, including, SNAP for 1.3 million people, Medicaid for 187,000, medical care for 47,000 veterans, or 10,000 school teachers.
The EPI analysis shows by state how much U.S. taxpayers contributed to mass deportations following the signing of Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025. The 900-page One Big Beautiful Bill Act includes provisions that expand the Department of Homeland Security’s detainment budget and quadruple Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s annual detention budget. 
The administration promised to remove one million immigrants annually, provide Border Patrol and ICE agents with an annual $10,000 bonus over the next four years, expand detention centers to hold 10,000 immigrants, and further expand the border wall. 
While funds for mass deportations increase, cuts to SNAP, Medicaid, and other public assistance programs also occurred under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, leaving thousands locally and millions nationally vulnerable. 
Nationwide, the Trump administration used $268.9 billion in taxes to fund mass deportations, totalling $2,358 per taxpayer. Taxes that could fund 118.2 million SNAP recipients, 1 million firefighters, 9.7 million public housing units, or 6.2 million parents with 12 weeks of paid parental leave. 
In 2025, the Department of Homeland Security reported more than 605,000 deportations and 1.9 million immigrants who voluntarily self-deported. ICE also saw its number of officers and agents double since Trump took office. 
“The Trump administration’s immigration policy is not just inhumane, it is also a huge waste of public resources,” EPI President Heidi Shierholz said in a release. “Every dollar spent on mass deportations is a dollar not spent on critical investments like education, health care, and affordable housing.”

name: Nevada Current
title: They’re making record profits, but oil companies still won’t ‘drill, baby, drill’
description: This story was originally published by Grist. Over the last two weeks, oil companies have announced eye-popping profits from the spring quarter. Exxon Mobil pulled in $14.5 billion. Chevron landed $12 billion, its highest quarterly profit on record. Shell posted $9.8 billion — more than twice its earnings from the same time last year. These […]
text:
The oil industry is foregoing drilling and production growth in favor of tightened belts and bigger payouts to investors. (Getty Images illustration)This story was originally published by Grist.
Over the last two weeks, oil companies have announced eye-popping profits from the spring quarter. Exxon Mobil pulled in $14.5 billion. Chevron landed $12 billion, its highest quarterly profit on record. Shell posted $9.8 billion — more than twice its earnings from the same time last year.
These profits are largely a product of supply constraints brought on by the war in the Middle East. With the Strait of Hormuz effectively blockaded, oil suppliers have rerouted shipments over land and through pipelines. The resulting supply shortages, constrained refining capacity, and higher transportation costs have driven up oil and gasoline prices, delivering windfall profits for producers.
But companies aren’t using those profits to drill lots of new wells or explore untapped oil fields. Instead, they’re pocketing the cash and paying their shareholders, experts say. What was once an industry defined by the “drill, baby, drill” ethos is now defined by another term: “capital discipline.” It’s a phenomenon in which rampant drilling and production growth has given way to tightened belts and bigger payouts to investors.
Oil executives expected a weak financial year in 2026 due to a supply glut, but the closure of the Strait of Hormuz constrained oil production and allowed companies to charge top dollar for use of their refineries outside the Middle East.
“While we didn’t anticipate the current situation, we were prepared for it,” Exxon CEO Darren Woods said in a July call with analysts, according to the Wall Street Journal. “Despite the temporary loss of approximately 10 percent of our upstream production, we delivered exceptional financial results.”
Chevron executives offered a similar assessment. In July, Chief Financial Officer Eimear Bonner told Bloomberg that the company didn’t adjust their production as prices rose. “We did not change any of our plan,” she said.
The Trump administration’s focus on “unleashing” U.S. energy is running headlong into oil companies’ growing commitment to financial discipline. For instance, the administration assured the public that oil majors would leap at oil fields in Venezuela after the country’s leader, Nicolas Maduro, was detained in January. But drilling stayed low throughout the administration’s efforts to pry open public lands for oil development, and corporations have been wary and selective about new opportunities in Venezuela. Similarly, even as the administration has opened up U.S. federal lands for drilling, companies have shown only a lukewarm response. As Americans bleed cash at the gas pump, President Donald Trump has even accused oil companies of “making too much money” from the war, unable to otherwise influence them to significantly ramp up their production.
“Oil and gas companies respond more to financial incentives than they do to political signaling,” said Clark Williams-Derry, an energy finance analyst at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. “They’re going to be looking at their finances first rather than politicians’ demands.”
If the U.S.-Israel war with Iran had occurred in 2012, oil companies might have seen the price spike as a chance to drill more wells. As fracking took off and prices rose during the 2000s, many companies tied their CEO compensation to production growth. Investors poured money into oil companies. But those days of aggressive production eventually ran into price crashes, especially after a Saudi-led coalition of oil-producing countries flooded the market with crude in 2014 and the COVID-19 pandemic sank prices again in 2020.
In the last five years, as investors soured on drill-happy oil companies, they embraced a new, more disciplined approach to capital expenditure. Investors wanted steadier returns. Rather than rewarding aggressive production growth, they pushed companies to focus on lower-cost drilling, restrain spending, and return more cash to shareholders.
“What is perhaps most telling about the corporate response to the turbulent forces impacting the oil and gas sector is just how little changed [in 2026],” Tom Ellacott, senior vice president of corporate research at Wood Mackenzie, said in a July press release. “Capital discipline has proved more durable than either the bears or bulls expected.”
Drilling in the U.S., as measured by the number of oil rigs, has ticked up during the summer, Williams-Derry noted, but only after the president launched a war in Iran that drove up oil prices. As of June, it had only recovered to the rate recorded at the same point last year, according to data from Baker Hughes, an energy technology company.
In this new mode, Williams-Derry said, international oil companies have used wars, notably the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran, to boost their revenues so they can maintain large payments to their Wall Street investors. In times without price spikes, oil majors collectively took out debt as they paid their investors, their revenues unable to support the payments on their own, according to Williams-Derry’s internal analysis of their cash flow statements. In an ironic twist, oil companies have benefited more from constraints on global oil production than from “unleashing” it.
The climate implications of this new ethos are complicated. Already, oil companies’ tight spending has drawn most of them away from renewable energy investments. France’s TotalEnergies is the one supermajor that has charged ahead with its renewables business, though the Trump administration agreed to pay the company more than $900 million to cancel two offshore wind projects off New York and North Carolina. More discipline may also push companies to capture and resell the leaking natural gas from oil fields because maximizing revenue from existing wells has become more attractive than drilling expensive new ones. And this new attitude could keep oil and gasoline prices higher for longer, maintaining the appeal of electric vehicles and renewable energy sources. (Chinese solar panel and EV exports to some countries have spiked during the war.)
At least one analysis firm, Wood Mackenzie, believes disciplined oil companies could fall behind global demand, causing them to lose a share of the global oil market to nationally owned oil companies like Saudi Arabia’s, potentially changing the politics of energy security for Western countries.
Ultimately, however, this phase of “capital discipline” may only be temporary, Williams-Derry said. No oil company wants to be so disciplined that it begins to decline. Eventually, some growth will likely be necessary.
Still, those companies have proven as capable of benefiting from energy shocks to U.S. consumers as they are of relieving them, an important note for political actors hoping to rely on oil companies for energy security.
“At least for now, production of oil is no longer the way executives are getting paid,” Williams-Derry said. “What matters is their ability to generate cash.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: A veteran’s case for more choice and more voice in elections
description: Eight years in the U.S. military taught me that the mission only succeeds when everyone is working toward the same goal, even when we don’t agree on every detail of how to get there. This lesson has stayed with me through every chapter of my life since: as a lawyer representing veterans fighting for the […]
text:
The first day of Maine’s ranked-choice tabulation to determine the winners of three primaries held on June 9, 2026. Officials in the Secretary of State’s office began conducting the count at the Maine Department of Public Safety in Augusta on June 12, 2026. (Photo by Jim Neuger / Maine Morning Star)Eight years in the U.S. military taught me that the mission only succeeds when everyone is working toward the same goal, even when we don’t agree on every detail of how to get there. This lesson has stayed with me through every chapter of my life since: as a lawyer representing veterans fighting for the benefits they earned, as the first woman veteran appointed to a Michigan governor’s cabinet, and as a mother of six.
Now, as Director of Partnerships at Veterans for All Voters, where I work to protect and strengthen our democracy for future generations, it has become clear to me that ranked choice voting is one of the most promising reforms out there to help focus decision-makers and voters on our shared values and mission.
For those unfamiliar, ranked choice voting lets voters rank candidates in order of preference: first choice, second choice, third choice. If no candidate has the support of a majority and your first choice can’t win, your vote automatically counts for your second choice to help elect a winner more broadly supported by voters.
With ranked choice voting, there are no “spoiler” candidates, “wasted” votes, or winners opposed by the majority. It sounds simple because it is. And the effects are profound.
While ranked choice voting is already being used to give more choice and more voice to 17 million U.S. voters in 23 states, Michigan leaders and voters would like to experience it in local elections before deciding whether it might be beneficial for use in elections to higher offices.
Voters in five Michigan cities have already adopted ranked choice voting for local elections, but conflicting language in state law has prevented local use. Rank MI Vote is leading a broad-based coalition of civil rights, voting rights, good government, and pro-democracy groups to pass legislation in the next Michigan Legislature to remedy this and protect the integrity of Home Rule and local control of elections.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This is one of the reasons that Rank MI Vote has shifted its focus from a statewide amendment to incremental progress that will build greater confidence in this change.
I have spent much of my career building bridges — between veterans and the agencies meant to serve them, between state and federal governments, between communities that don’t always trust each other but who need each other. I have also, at various points, considered running for office myself. What has always given me pause is not a lack of conviction, but the way our current system forces candidates to appeal to narrow factions of voters.
To win a primary, you often have to define what you’re against  before you’re ever allowed to define what you’re for and before you can appeal to the broader electorate based on shared values. That process squeezes out exactly the kind of thoughtful and collaborative leaders Michigan needs.
Ranked choice voting changes that calculus. It rewards candidates who can build genuine, broad support rather than candidates who simply survive a narrow primary. It gives people like me, people who don’t fit neatly into an ideological box, who care more about solving problems than scoring points, room to run as who we actually are and still have a real path to winning.
This matters enormously for women and people of color, who have too often been told to wait their turn, tone down their message, or fit themselves into a mold built by someone else. Ranked choice voting opens the door to more candidates like us.
Ranked Choice Voting also gives voters something they deserve and too rarely get: meaningful choice. Under our current system, many voters feel they have to choose the “lesser of two evils” or strategically abandon a candidate they actually like because they’re afraid of “wasting” their vote. Ranked choice voting removes that fear. You can vote your values first and still have a say in the final outcome. That is not a small thing. That is the difference between a democracy that merely processes votes and one that actually listens to people.
This is also deeply personal to me as a veteran. I’m proud to work with Veterans for All Voters, a nonpartisan organization of veterans and military family members advocating for reforms like ranked choice voting. Veterans are thanked for our service constantly: at ballgames, in airports, in political speeches. That gratitude means something, but words are not enough. We didn’t serve a party. We served a country. Many of us signed up precisely because we believed in something larger than any single faction, and many of us came home troubled by a political system that seems increasingly incapable of putting the country first.
Veterans for All Voters is made up of people who understand that the health of our democracy is itself a national security issue, and who are willing to keep serving by fighting for the structural reforms that can heal it.
As a married mother of six, whose husband also served in the Army, we think a lot about what kind of country we are leaving our children. We want them to grow up believing that leadership is earned through building coalitions, not through outlasting your opponents in an ideological arms race. We want them to see women and people of color running for office not as exceptions who beat the odds, but as a normal and expected part of who gets to lead.
Ranked choice voting will not fix everything about our politics. But it is a simple, tested, common-sense reform that gives more choice and more voice to voters and makes our elections more representative, our candidates more accountable to the whole electorate, and our democracy a little more worthy of the sacrifices so many Americans, in and out of uniform, have made for it.
That is why I support it. That is why I hope you will too.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Gluesenkamp Perez hits Braun on abortion as battle begins for WA House seat
description: Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez went on the offensive Tuesday with a campaign ad accusing Republican John Braun of wanting to outlaw abortion in Washington state and the nation. The 30-second spot is an early salvo in what will be a pricey, high-stakes battle between the two-term congresswoman and the veteran state Senate leader […]
text:
Washington state Senate Minority Leader John Braun, left, is on track to square off with U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, right, in Washington's 3rd Congressional District. (Photos courtesy of campaigns)Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez went on the offensive Tuesday with a campaign ad accusing Republican John Braun of wanting to outlaw abortion in Washington state and the nation.
The 30-second spot is an early salvo in what will be a pricey, high-stakes battle between the two-term congresswoman and the veteran state Senate leader for the 3rd Congressional District seat in southwest Washington.
This is the state’s most closely watched federal race and one of a handful of contests nationwide that will decide which party controls the U.S. House. House Speaker Mike Johnson, of Louisiana, campaigned for Braun in the district last week, underscoring the race’s importance.
The commercial targets Braun for voting against legislation concerning emergency care for pregnant women and requiring health plans to cover birth control.
The main jab is a snippet from a video of Braun’s comments to Republicans in Pacific County in March where he voiced support for eventually rolling back the state’s nearly 60-year-old law that made abortion legal.
“Candidly, we are unlikely to change the law in Washington in the near future, but we should be focused … so that someday we get there,” he’s heard saying.
In the ad, an announcer says, “he’ll never stop until abortion is banned nationwide.”
Braun does not support a nationwide ban, his campaign manager said Monday.
Gluesenkamp Perez, of Skamania County, is spending six figures to air the ad on broadcast and cable television along with streaming services and digital platforms over the next two weeks.
The launch comes as ballots continue to be counted in the Aug. 4 primary. Braun is leading Gluesenkamp Perez, who faced a Democrat challenger from the left, Brett Hennrich, who garnered nearly 17%. Hennrich said last week he would not support Gluesenkamp Perez in the general election.
By choosing abortion, Gluesenkamp Perez seeks to peg Braun as a social conservative. She’s also trying to reach independent women voters, for whom abortion rights are an important issue, and Hennrich supporters, by revealing a potential consequence of a Braun victory. 
“While Braun pitches a moderate persona in public, he’s telling supporters behind closed doors that he wants to ban abortion statewide,” said Tim Gowen, Gluesenkamp Perez’s campaign manager.
The congresswoman, he said, is “committed to making sure women — not politicians — have the right to decide for themselves what is right for them and their families.”
Washington’s abortion protections trace back to a citizen initiative in 1970 that was solidified by another ballot measure in 1991.
In the ensuing years, several more laws have been enacted to broaden and strengthen access to reproductive care services, and to protect every individual who seeks it — including those who come from states where abortion is not legal. A U.S. Supreme Court ruling in 2022 overturned the federal constitutional right to an abortion, bringing heightened political attention to the issue in the years since. 
Braun, of Centralia, has been a consistent anti-abortion vote since winning his Senate seat in 2012. As the Senate Republican leader, a post he attained in 2021, he’s repeatedly said enshrining abortion rights in the state constitution — as many Democrats want — is unnecessary.
“The law’s been in place since 1970, passed by the people of the state of Washington, modified by the people of the state of Washington in 1991. I don’t see a path where that changes without a vote of the people,” Braun told The Chronicle in Centralia in 2023. “I think the people have spoken and we’re going to respect the will of the people.”
In the meeting with the Pacific County Republican Party that yielded the recording in the attack ad, Braun was asked specifically what he would do to protect unborn babies, according to a video of the event.
He said he was “super proud” of expanding options for pregnant women to obtain counseling and support if they chose not to have an abortion.
“We have a different situation in our state,” he said, citing the 1970 initiative. “So we have work to do. Candidly, we are unlikely to change the law in Washington in the near future, but we should be focused on winning hearts and minds so that someday we get there.”
On Monday, Max Lavey, Braun’s campaign manager, confirmed the comments in the video reflect his position.
“The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that this is rightly a state issue and not a federal one and it is up to us to convince the voters of our state to change the law,” Lavey said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mexican seasonal employees at Battle Fish farm in Tunica County allege labor abuses
description: The Labor Department sued Battle Fish farm in 2023 for obstruction of a government investigation and retaliatory conduct against farmworkers. Battle Fish denied the allegations. Now, the department is probing conditions at the farm again.
text:
TUNICA – The U.S. Department of Labor is investigating a Mississippi Delta catfish farm where some seasonal workers allege persistent verbal abuse and racism, unpaid wages, substandard living conditions and other violations. 
Employees at Battle Fish North said that, for years, management has relied on threats of violence and denying seasonal work contracts to discourage them from reporting the abuses to authorities. 
The Labor Department also investigated the farm in 2023 for alleged violations of the Fair Labor Standards Act and H-2A regulations and subsequently sued the company and its owners for obstructing the investigation. In the court complaint, which represents one side of a legal argument, the department said the farm concealed noncompliant living quarters and vehicles and threatened to retaliate against workers who agreed to interviews with federal investigators. 
The case ended in a settlement with no findings, and Battle Fish did not “admit or deny” the allegations in the consent judgment. But in a previous memo to the court, the defendants said that they “did not disrupt the DOL’s investigation let alone retaliate against employees who may have participated,” claiming that the “evidence shows the Battle-Magnolia Defendants cooperated in good faith to facilitate the government’s investigation.”
The judge ordered the farm to comply with the Fair Labor Standards Act and improve access to information about the workers’ rights. 
“The contracted employees lose hope because the Labor Department went but they didn’t see changes of any kind,” said an employee who left Battle Fish but remains in contact with former coworkers. 
The employee requested anonymity due to concerns over repercussions for current workers at the farm.
Regarding the 2023 investigation, Andrew Dulaney, an attorney for Battle Fish, told Mississippi Today that “Battle Fish North and Magnolia Processing, Inc have successfully and amicably resolved the employment issues with the Department of Labor in 2023. As the Court’s judgment provided and as we believe all parties understand, there was a misunderstanding on a number of issues. These misunderstandings have been resolved.”
Mississippi Today examined court records and government documents, spoke with government agencies and Battle Fish’s legal representation, and interviewed seven current and former employees who worked at the farm between 2012 and 2026.
The employees are Mexican citizens who have worked in the U.S. seasonally on H-2A visas, which allow agricultural employers to hire workers from outside the U.S. on a temporary basis. Four said they decided to leave rather than continue facing abuse. One said the company wouldn’t rehire him after he spoke with Labor Department investigators about the conditions.
Five spoke to Mississippi Today on the condition of anonymity because they feared retaliation, and two former employees who returned to Mexico – Jacob Vargas Huante and Francisco Chavez Barajas – agreed to their names being published.
“I was a victim, but tomorrow there could be another,” said Vargas.
Former workers told Mississippi Today that the intimidation has come primarily from Houston Battle, one of the owners, and Martín Valencia, an overseer who supervises operations and communicates with workers since Battle does not speak Spanish. 
Neither Battle nor Valencia could be reached for comment after Mississippi Today left multiple voicemails and written messages. 
“During my investigation, multiple Battle Fish employees informed me that Battle and Martín degrade workers by repeatedly threatening to physically harm them, as well as to fire them or have them deported,” read a declaration by Kristina Espinoza, one of 10 investigators who inspected the farm in 2023. According to the court records, an employee told investigators, “I couldn’t tolerate the treatment from the supervisor, Martin Valencia, or the boss at the ranch.… Every day was like that, with insults being hurled at us.”
Former Secretary of Labor Julie Su wrote in a memo to the court that the Labor Department’s investigation had revealed an “extensive and ongoing pattern of threatening and intimidating Battle Fish workers.”
In a motion hearing, primary owner Bill Battle denied having retaliated against workers. 
Labor Department spokesperson Erika Ruthman confirmed that an investigation into the company is open and ongoing, but said she could not give further details to ensure its integrity. Ruthman declined to comment whether the current investigation is routine or in response to a complaint.
Brandon Davis, a lawyer representing Battle Fish, said it would be “inappropriate” to discuss the investigation but that Battle Fish would “continue to work with the federal government as our regulator, as well as with the public and with our various groups of employees.”
A family operation
Farm equipment at Battle Fish in Tunica County, Miss., on Thursday, July 9, 2026. Credit: Claudia Amendoeira/Mississippi Today
Battle Fish sits just outside Tunica in Mississippi’s northern Delta. Hundreds of acres of clustered rectangular ponds punctuate a flat expanse of fields surrounding the two-lane Highway 4.
The family-run catfish farm and an on-site processing plant, Magnolia Inc., are both owned and operated by members of the Battle Family — Houston Battle along with his brother and father. Houston Battle’s grandparents founded the operation in the late 1960s, and today the plant processes around 10 million pounds of fish annually. 
The farm and the processing plant both hire seasonal foreign workers and were defendants in the 2023 court case. Previously, a Labor Department investigation had found that Magnolia Inc. owed over $11,000 in back wages to U.S. employees. 
The Labor Department cleared Battle Fish to hire 14 workers through the H-2A visa program for the 2026 season, from February to November. Hundreds of thousands of people work in the U.S. on H-2A visas annually, the majority from Mexico.
Former Battle Fish employee Jacob Vargas Huante provided a court declaration in the 2023 lawsuit, and he told Mississippi Today that he worked for three employers in the U.S. through the H-2A program without issues before coming to Tunica. “I never had problems, I was never mistreated … only there with Battle Fish.”
However, Noemí Hernández, consul general of Mexico in New Orleans, said the consulate frequently receives reports of violations from Mexican nationals working in Mississippi. “There are cases that are deplorable,” Hernandez said about reports from across the state. “In a few cases employers even turned to violence.”
‘A chilling effect’
When Labor Department investigators arrived at the farm in 2023, they reported that the management’s threatening conduct created a “chilling effect” on workers and made them afraid to speak. Two investigators, Espinoza and Jose Berrios testified that they had to speak to workers at a gas station away from the worksite, and even there some workers hid behind dumpsters and cars and poked their heads out to see who was around.
In his court declaration, Battle said that the Labor Department “apparently even took some of those employees away from the farm to question them at a gas station and behind a dumpster,” but a former employee who spoke to Mississippi Today said that when investigators approached him at the farm, it was he who suggested speaking at a gas station instead. 
“I knew what the situation was,” the former worker said. “I said to him, ‘You want to interview me? You want me to tell you the truth? Let’s go to the gas station where they can’t see me, and we can talk there and I’ll tell you everything that’s going on.’”
“We were forbidden to talk to you … Martín (Valencia) told us that we couldn’t complain, and he said that if we did, he would send us back to Mexico,” an employee told investigators in a written statement. 
During the investigation, Battle Fish management “routinely threatened to fire, deport, or physically harm,” workers who risked talking to investigators, reads a memo from Former Secretary Su to the court. 
In his court declaration, Battle denied retaliating or threatening to retaliate against employees who spoke with Labor Department investigators, adding that “the agents treated me and Battle Fish North in a prejudicial way like we had engaged in wrongdoing.” 
A former employee told Mississippi Today that Houston Battle “yells at us because he thinks he has us in his hands because we don’t want to lose a work visa. It’s difficult to get another one.”
“They do not treat us well here but we have to work. We do make some money here and Mexico is very difficult,” another employee told Labor Department investigators.
Jacob Vargas Huante in his hometown in Michoacan, Mexico, in 2026. He said that the abuse he faced at Battle Fish Farms in Tunica County, Miss., left him “traumatized” and reluctant to seek other employment in the U.S. Credit: Courtesy of Jacob Vargas Huante
According to Vargas, some employees are also concerned about compromising family members’ chances of obtaining visas through Battle Fish because of pressure from the employers. 
“They tell you if you complain or anything, ‘We won’t bring you over, we won’t bring over your family, we’re not going to want your cousin here, your brother,’” Vargas said.
Battle Fish did not respond to requests for comment about not renewing work contracts to employees who reported issues. 
Vargas worked at Battle Fish for around eight years before leaving because of what he described as repeated verbal abuse and death threats from Valencia. Vargas told Mississippi Today that even in his hometown in Michoacán, almost three years after leaving Battle Fish, “there are times I wake up at night because I have nightmares, I think I’m drowning, that they electrocute me, or Martín Valencia kills me.”
Vargas’ work included maintaining electrical wiring around the fish ponds, and he described in his court declaration how Valencia once tried to turn on the electrical current as he worked. Francisco Chavez Barajas worked alongside Vargas and recalled the incident. “We lived all that mistreatment and abuse first hand,” Chavez said. 
Tunica County Justice Court records show Martin Rodriguez filed simple assault charges against Jacob Huante in 2019. Vargas, whose second last name is Huante, said the Martin listed as filing the charges is Valencia. Vargas pleaded not guilty, and the charges were dropped in 2020. He told Mississippi Today that the charges were falsified and Valencia invented the details of an alleged confrontation. Vargas said that when the police arrived at the farm, “I actually wanted them to arrest me so I could file a counterclaim against him, because everything he was doing to me was false.” 
Valencia could not be reached for comment, but in Battle’s court declaration, he said that no employee had reported abusive conduct from Valencia to him. 
In Vargas’ federal labor complaint that preceded the 2023 investigation, he stated that Valencia “bullies” him and other workers, calling him “pendejo” (“dumbass”) and a “fucking liar.” A current employee described Battle as “explosive,” and a former employee remembered Battle’s behavior as “racist” and “arrogant.”
A former employee noted that Valencia was also sometimes “scolded” and “mistreated” by Houston Battle. “Valencia tries to defend Houston more than the people.”
In a written statement from the previous Labor Department investigation, an employee described Battle as intolerant and prone to anger. “If Houston gets angry with a worker, we all pay the consequences,” the statement read.
Investigator Espinoza wrote in a court declaration that when she was preparing to leave the worksite, she overheard a conversation between Battle and his brother. 
“They think I am threatening, they don’t know what threatening is,” she quoted Battle as saying before he went “storming back into the front office.”
Workers also told investigator Jose Berrios about a physical confrontation in which Battle allegedly grabbed a worker, spun him around and started yelling at him. Battle denied having any knowledge of this incident during a September 2023 motion hearing in the Northern District of Mississippi.
Battle’s father, Bill Battle, was also questioned about violent retaliatory practices during the motion hearing. He admitted to having been on probation for breaking the windshield of a vehicle that two employees were driving. A complaint says Vargas sent investigators a TikTok video that showed Bill Battle smashing the windshield “after brandishing his gun at them as they were leaving after going to get their last paychecks.”
Overworked and underpaid
A Labor Department clearance form that authorizes Battle Fish to hire H-2A workers specifies an 11-hour work day from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m., but some workers said upon arrival they found themselves working 12- to 14-hour night shifts without overtime pay.
“Some years, I never rested,” said one former employee. He remembered investigators told him Battle Fish owed him wages for the years of overtime, which he still has not received. “We didn’t get one day to rest.”
“We’re human beings, we’re not machines or animals,” Vargas said.
“The contract doesn’t say I’ll work at night,” said another former employee. “The first year when I arrived they just told me you need to sleep during the day because you’re going to work at night.”
In a declaration to court, Vargas wrote that he worked at least three hours per week over his contracted hours without pay.
Multiple workers said they only received partial reimbursements for travel costs between their hometowns and the farm, expenses that the H-2A program requires employers to cover. In 2022, the Labor Department reported that the processing plant failed to fully reimburse travel expenses to its employees.
Battle Fish denied failing to fully cover travel costs in an email to Mississippi Today.
Davis said he had no knowledge of the night shifts, but he said that “Battle Fish complies with the Fair Labor Standards Act as to all employees.” This federal law requires employers to pay time and a half when employees work more than 40 hours in one week. 
‘Uninhabitable’
The laundry room shared by employees at Battle Fish in Tunica County, Miss., in June 2026. Credit: Anonymous former employee
Federal regulations require employers to provide H-2A employees with housing, reliable transportation between living quarters and the worksite, and access to meals. At Battle Fish, workers stay in small apartments and trailers at two locations, both a few minutes’ drive from the processing plant. 
An investigator testified that, according to her interviews, several workers slept on the floor and lacked access to running water. 
“The stoves do not work, nor does the air conditioning,” reads one employee’s statement to investigators. “The floor and the shower are sinking.”
Some workers told Mississippi Today they lived at the farm in crowded quarters infested with rats and cockroaches, where the flooring was falling to pieces.
Former Secretary Su called one of the facilities “uninhabitable” for workers in a memo to the court.
In another statement, a worker said, “transportation is in very poor condition. It doesn’t have air conditioning, the windows are broken, and the tires are bad.” Former employees told Mississippi Today that unreliable vehicles meant it was hard for them to access grocery stores, and they sometimes had to walk to work through heavy rainfall.
“We were having problems to buy food, it was only one vehicle for everyone and that is not enough and sometimes we can’t go shopping for food,” wrote one employee in a statement.
In his court declaration, Thomas Cooper Battle said that “contrary to the Department of Labor’s assertions, the farm vehicles were in an appropriate state of repair to service Battle Fish North’s on-farm work.” He also said that Magnolia “regularly engages the services of McElhaney Construction to repair and maintain the housing units.”
Battle Fish did not reply to requests for comments on the conditions of employee housing and vehicles. 
Tractors sit parked under an awning at Battle Fish in Tunica County, Miss., on Thursday, July 9, 2026. Credit: Claudia Amendoeira/Mississippi Today
Lives at risk
In a remote corner of the Delta thousands of miles from family support networks, employees said accessing medical care was another recurring challenge. 
The Labor Department requires that H-2A employers have state or employer-provided health insurance insurance for “injury and disease arising out of and in the course of the worker’s employment.” However, six Battle Fish employees who spoke with Mississippi Today recalled incidents where they or their coworkers were severely ill or injured and their boss did not help them access treatment. 
An employee who worked with Battle Fish for one season during the COVID-19 pandemic said that management “abandoned” him when he developed a cough that persisted for days and left him unable to sleep because he felt like he was suffocating. He said that when he asked Battle and Valencia to help him get to a hospital, they got angry and told him he had to keep working. After three days he said he “couldn’t bear it anymore” and ended up paying $100 round trip for a taxi to take him to a hospital in Memphis, and $200 for treatment.
Employees also reported dangerous working conditions. One employee who worked night shifts said he “risked his life” driving tractors without brakes up to the edge of the fish ponds to operate fans that oxygenate the water. “There was the danger that you’d end up in the lake along with everything else.”
“They’ve never been concerned about people’s well being,” said a former employee. Another worker said in a statement to inspectors, “If an accident happens to you, sometimes they don’t take you to the doctor anymore.”
Battle Fish did not reply to requests for comments about specific incidents, but wrote “we value our workers and have a very strong safety record.”
“We are proud to be catfish farmers in the Mississippi Delta and to have the opportunity to provide food for America,” the company stated in an email to Mississippi Today.
‘My life’s worth more than that’
Battle “treats them as if they were slaves, as if they were trash,” said a former employee who is now working in another state, where he says conditions are better. 
Vargas said, “I’d never go back to Battle Fish … not even if they paid me 2 or 3 million dollars. Because my life’s worth more than that.”
For an employee who left this year, government mechanisms for accountability feel slow and ineffective. He said that a lawyer associated with the Mexican consulate told him his case could take years. He risks becoming undocumented if he stays in the U.S. while he waits for a resolution. “I think they want me to give up hope, that I won’t know what to do and I’ll go back to Mexico.”
“The Department of Labor did nothing. The government didn’t do anything to help. The Mexican consulate is supposed to help Mexicans, but they don’t do anything,” he said.
In response to the employees’ statements, a Labor Department spokesperson said that workers who have questions about wages can contact the Wage and Hour Division. Consul General Hernández said the consulate provides guidance to Mexican workers on how to report the issues to U.S. authorities but that the consulate itself does not have the authority to investigate alleged violations.
The employee, who remains in limbo weeks after leaving Battle Fish, said he had been supporting his two children in Mexico with his salary for years, which made leaving a difficult decision. But in the end he renounced his contract mid-season due to the conditions and treatment. “I couldn’t take it anymore,” he said. “I want this to stop here.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Maternity care deserts make up nearly half of Mississippi counties, March of Dimes says
description: Malika Holifield holds her sonogram outside Family Health Center, Inc. in Laurel on Wednesday, June 25, 2026.
text:
Mississippi continues to rank among the states with the fewest resources for pregnant women. According to the latest report from the March of Dimes, nearly half of the counties statewide are considered maternity care deserts without an obstetric clinician or birthing facility. 
These deserts affect close to 107,000 Mississippians and 7,000 births annually, said the report released Tuesday. The March of Dimes is a national nonprofit aimed at improving the health of mothers and babies. 
Across the country, 1 in 3 counties are maternity care deserts. Experts say that’s abysmal. Mississippi’s statistics are worse than the national average, but the report’s authors pointed out those trends are not inevitable. The report concluded maternity care deserts are the result of longstanding underinvestment and policy decisions, including restrictive Medicaid coverage and prohibitive midwifery policies. 
“The U.S. is still one of the most dangerous developed countries in which to give birth,” said Honour McDaniel Hill, director of Infant and Maternal Health Initiatives for March of Dimes. “We still have two women die each day from pregnancy-related causes.”
Those perils are magnified in Mississippi, which consistently has one of the highest rates of maternal mortality and leads the nation in infant mortality. 
Dr. Lakeisha Richardson, one of a few OB-GYNs in the Delta, knows this firsthand. Richardson was born in Indianola and works in Greenville, and she said she has felt called to return home after completing her residency in Jackson. She said other OB-GYNs she knows in the Delta call the place where they practice home.
Richardson said there is a lot of talent to tap into within the state. Efforts to expose Mississippi high school students to healthcare early on and hold spots at the University of Mississippi Medical Center for students who promise to serve rural areas could improve the workforce. But attracting talent from elsewhere to serve some of the nation’s poorest women will require a more holistic approach that includes revitalizing infrastructure in rural parts of the state, she said.
“I think the biggest factor that doctors look at when they’re choosing where to live is where they want to raise their families,” Richardson said. “We all want to serve and come back and help others, but we also have to take into consideration our own children and their education and their culture and experiences, as well.”
To access providers, Richardson said, women often drive more than an hour. Sporadic health insurance statewide frequently translates to patients arriving at pregnancy sicker than those living in places where they are more likely to have insurance. Of the patients she sees, 1 in 5 have a chronic health condition, such as diabetes or hypertension, Richardson said, adding that most of the time, those illnesses have gone untreated for years.
A majority of her patients were uninsured until they became pregnant and qualified for Medicaid. Under Mississippi law, people who aren’t pregnant need to make less than 21% of the federal poverty level, or $6,000 annually for a family of three, to qualify for Medicaid. During pregnancy, those rules change and anyone making under 194% of the federal poverty level, or roughly $54,000 for a family of three, qualifies for the low-cost health insurance. 
If Mississippi were to expand its Medicaid program, as 41 states and the District of Columbia have done, 123,000 uninsured adults could become eligible for the program, by some estimates. Richardson believes many of her patients would see better outcomes as a result. The March of Dimes report also highlights Medicaid expansion as a solution to the maternal-infant health crisis, but Mississippi lawmakers have yet to heed this recommendation.
In 2024, the Mississippi Legislature came historically close to expanding Medicaid but the proposal ultimately died due to partisan politics.
Ninety-five percent of counties in Mississippi have uninsured rates above the national average, according to the March of Dimes. In non-expanded states, 1 in 3 women covered by Medicaid during pregnancy reported being uninsured prior to conception, according to the report. That says a lot about how these states think of women, McDaniel Hill said. 
“A woman’s value does not come from her pregnancy,” McDaniel Hill said. 
Left untreated, hypertension and diabetes can lead to preeclampsia, stillbirth and preterm birth, a condition in which Mississippi leads the nation, as well as long-term health consequences for both the infant and the mother.
For some Mississippi women in maternal care deserts, help may remain tragically out of reach and can result in dying on the side of the road. Midwives could help fill in the gaps – but not in Mississippi. This year, the state was named in a federal lawsuit over how it limits women’s access to nurse midwives. Currently, nurse midwives must pay physicians in order to practice, which advocates say is cost prohibitive for many midwives and irresponsible in a state with a severe shortage of providers. Legislation to change that died in committee this spring.
Richardson said she is proud to reduce poor outcomes and meet the needs of the community that raised her. But it means that she’s almost never off the clock. On average, OB-GYNs in the U.S. deliver a baby once every three days. Richardson said she often delivers multiple babies a day, sometimes as many as five. 
“It can be exhausting,” Richardson said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Federal funding bill could spare Missouri hemp beverages from November ban
description: Hemp-derived THC beverages could stay on Missouri shelves past Nov. 12 — the day the state’s ban on intoxicating hemp products takes effect — if Congress gives final approval to a short-term funding bill and the president signs it. In an overnight vote Saturday, the U.S. Senate approved a measure to fund federal agencies until […]
text:
Hemp-derived THC beverages like these seltzers at Randall's Wine & Spirits can be found at large liquor stores throughout Missouri (Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent).Hemp-derived THC beverages could stay on Missouri shelves past Nov. 12 — the day the state’s ban on intoxicating hemp products takes effect — if Congress gives final approval to a short-term funding bill and the president signs it.
In an overnight vote Saturday, the U.S. Senate approved a measure to fund federal agencies until Dec. 11. It would also delay the federal ban on intoxicating hemp THC products until that date. It now goes back to the U.S. House for final approval before heading to the president’s desk.
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe signed a bill this spring to take all intoxicating hemp products off the shelves starting Nov. 12, largely aligning state law with the federal ban that Congress approved last year.
But the state law carves out one exception: if Congress delays the federal ban, everything except intoxicating beverages is still banned in Missouri as scheduled. 
Jay Patel, president of the Missouri Hemp Trade Association, said there was bipartisan support in the U.S. Senate, with a vote of 61-31, to keep the delay in the funding package and it’s a “good sign” for the intoxicating hemp industry. 
“There’s a lot of support from the White House actually to get some sort of regulation passed that’s meaningful,” Patel said. “Whatever happens on the federal side, it’s not going to fully solve our problems in Missouri.”
The association and a coalition of hemp businesses filed a federal lawsuit last month in an attempt to halt the state hemp ban from going into effect in November.
The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District, claims the bill state lawmakers passed this spring contains “unconstitutionally vague” definitions for hemp and marijuana. 
John Grady, who owns Slaphappy Hemporium with his wife Kara in Rosebud, Mo., said the U.S. Senate’s action shows a strong likelihood that they’ll be able to sell their company’s THC seltzers through December. They’ve already had customers stocking up on their favorite items, such as edibles, that will be banned in Missouri no matter what action the federal government takes. 
“We started off as a beverage producer,” Grady said, “So for us, that is a good thing, but it also hurts the whole other part of our business.”
The Gradys are members of various different organizations that are pushing to use the delay to get comprehensive federal regulations for hemp products in place by Dec. 11.

name: Missouri Independent
title: ‘We are living in reverse’: Fragile HIV funding puts another strain on Kansas City’s safety net
description: Roberto Archuleta was 21 years old in 1991 when he found out he was HIV-positive. At the time, the only medications available to treat the virus were difficult to tolerate and often ineffective. Being diagnosed was commonly a death sentence — something Archuleta, then a hairstylist in Kansas City, witnessed too often. An old snapshot […]
text:
Roberto Archuleta (center), who was diagnosed with HIV in 1991, points to this photo from around that time as an illustration of the damage the virus did. "Everybody in that picture is dead except for me," he said (photo submitted).
Roberto Archuleta was 21 years old in 1991 when he found out he was HIV-positive.
At the time, the only medications available to treat the virus were difficult to tolerate and often ineffective. Being diagnosed was commonly a death sentence — something Archuleta, then a hairstylist in Kansas City, witnessed too often.
An old snapshot of Archuleta with a group of friends reveals the grim truth about what it was like when HIV was the leading cause of death among 25-to-44-year-olds.
“Everybody in that picture is dead except for me,” he said.
Dramatic changes in HIV care and the effectiveness of available medications altered the virus’ trajectory, from 130,400 new infections in 1984 to 38,434 in 2024. 
The COVID pandemic and the lack of HIV testing and outreach it caused led to an uptick in new cases in 2024, including in Kansas City’s 11-county HIV region, which saw a 10% jump to 227 new cases that year. (The city has not released 2025 data.) But the big picture has been one of progress in reducing the number of new HIV diagnoses and suppressing the virus in infected patients.
That will change, public health experts warned, if the Trump administration continues to target funding for HIV care, prevention and research in the U.S. and across the globe.
To Archuleta, who for years served on Kansas City’s HIV Prevention and Care Planning Council, it’s starting to feel like sliding backward.
“It’s like all of the progress and all of the work that we have done throughout the years to get HIV to where it is now is being lost,” said Archuleta, who now lives in California and spearheads the Remember Me Campaign, an effort to increase awareness of the virus. “We’re returning, slowly but surely, back to the days when the work we did didn’t even exist.”
Katie Batza, who chairs the women, gender and sexuality studies department at the University of Kansas, said she’s been hearing much the same sentiment from the activists she interviewed for her new book,“AIDS in the Heartland,” a study of LGBTQ politics in the Midwest during the height of the virus.
“A lot of them are feeling infuriated,” she said. “They’re saying, ‘Now we have all these resources but we’re making them unavailable, and we’re going to have to watch it happen again.”
 Funding cuts and uncertainty

The Trump administration’s 2027 budget request calls for eliminating $1.6 billion in HIV-related spending, a 35% drop from 2026 funding. If Congress adopts the plan, as it declined to do last year when the administration proposed similar cuts, part of the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program — a $2.6 billion grant program that funds healthcare for more than half of those in the United States living with HIV — would go away.
The proposed cuts to Ryan White include AIDS Education and Training Centers to support health providers who treat HIV patients, dental programs, and the Minority AIDS initiative, meant to expand services in minority communities that are more heavily affected by the virus.
The administration has already slashed HIV prevention funding at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Just last month it pulled back millions of dollars in grants going to community organizations and sent the money instead to states.
Andrea Weddle, executive director of the HIV Medicine Association, said all the cuts would have consequences on the health of HIV patients and the larger community.
“We would anticipate a dramatic increase in HIV transmission rates” if the funding goes away, she said, “and much higher healthcare costs.”
Maven Lee, a contractor with BlaqOut, a Kansas City nonprofit working to bring sexual healthcare to the city’s Black LGBTQ community, worries about the potential health consequences that will come with the new HIV funding landscape.
But he also fears the return of bigotry that was once so pervasive around HIV. When education and outreach about the virus don’t happen, progress will be lost, he said. People won’t understand how to protect themselves or they’ll be afraid to disclose their status, for fear of the stigma. Worse yet, he said, they won’t test at all because they don’t want to know.
“There was a time when there was more open conversation where you could educate people,” Lee said. “I don’t think those conversations are happening anymore. … We are living in reverse. We are going back.”
Marvia Jones, Kansas City’s health director, said she is concerned about the gaps emerging in the city’s health safety net, from lost HIV and Ryan White funding to coming changes to Medicaid, which could leave vulnerable people in the city without access to healthcare.
People living with HIV will be impacted, she said, and “when their treatment suffers, we know it makes the city as a whole more vulnerable.”
Jones said the city should be working to plug some of those holes, perhaps with funds from its health levy fund.
“There have been some fairly severe cuts already,” she said, “and it would be great if the health levy were to stand in the gap for folks who are vulnerable.”
The Kansas City Health Commission, which is studying how some funds raised through the health levy will be allocated next year, is expected to take up the issue of HIV funding at its Aug. 31 meeting, a city spokesperson said.
 Waiting to see what happens

Bob Walker, a regional vice president for Vivent Health, said his organization’s St. Louis arm is already absorbing losses in federal funding and he expects to see the same thing in Kansas City, where the organization treats about 600 HIV patients.
As with other organizations providing HIV care, the question has become less whether the cuts will happen and much more when they will happen.
“Unfortunately, I might get an email tomorrow saying (a grant) is going to end in 30, 60 or 90 days, or it’s already ended,” Walker said. “It’s a surprise to everybody and then we have to do a pivot quickly to figure out how we’re going to navigate through that loss of funding.”
Kansas City organizations that provide HIV care have lost some resources already. For example, the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services suspended funding in April to KC Care for a peer navigator program that helped people diagnosed with HIV connect to treatment.
The state, facing budget constraints in its own Ryan White-funded programs, also suspended other HIV-related funding around the state to trim $1.9 million from its budget. Those cuts included a mental health program that served 42 people, an emergency financial assistance program that served 172 people and a dental program in St. Louis that served 1,400 people.
And in June the state limited which drugs it will pay for through its Ryan White AIDS Drug Assistance Program, known as ADAP. Now the program only covers HIV medications, but no drugs for other conditions, such as high blood pressure or mental illness.
ADAP efforts provide free medications to HIV patients who aren’t eligible for Medicaid or other financial assistance, and in many cases the programs purchase health insurance for participants to access drugs. Missouri received nearly $10 million for ADAP in fiscal year 2025.
Like other states, Missouri was dealing with higher costs of drugs and insurance, and it faced major declines in drug company rebates, which have historically subsidized the drug assistance programs.
As more HIV patients transitioned to Medicaid coverage after Missouri expanded eligibility under the Affordable Care Act, it purchased fewer drugs and, therefore, collected fewer rebates. Last year, Missouri pulled in $27 million in drug rebates, compared to $41 million in 2021, said Alicia Jenkins, deputy director of community and public health with the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services.
Jenkins said the rebate decline is the major reason the state’s Ryan White program has had to tighten its belt. The changes were made to ensure the state could afford HIV medication for every participant, she said.
“None of it feels good,” she said, “but in order that we can ensure that we are positioned to cover medication, we did what we needed to do.”
Kansas also reportedly lowered income eligibility requirements for its ADAP efforts, but the state could not be reached to answer questions about the change. In fiscal year 2025, Kansas received $2.6 million in ADAP funding.
Rashaan Gilmore, the founder and CEO of BlaqOut, said the loss of access to non-HIV medications through ADAP is a serious problem for many people living with HIV.
“What does that do to a person who’s trying to manage multiple comorbidities and they can’t get their medication covered?” Gilmore said. “That’s going to mean people making choices about what medications they do pay for, and I think it’s going to lead to people falling out of care because what used to be a one-stop shop is now even more fragmented.”
 A finite amount of money

It’s not just a problem for HIV care providers if funding is cut. As providers work to absorb the higher cost of medication and other medical care, it’s also a problem if federal HIV funding remains flat, which has happened for more than a decade. Meanwhile, enrollment in the program has increased by at least 20% since 2016, according to the Ryan White Medical Providers Coalition.
“Ryan White is a finite amount of money, and the pot doesn’t really change,” said Wil Franklin, CEO of KC Care Clinic. “We have more HIV patients than we’ve ever had — not because there’s a bunch of new cases … but people with HIV are now living longer, healthier lives.”
