Providers used to treat patients until they died. Now they are managing a chronic condition. But the funding hasn’t expanded to meet the growing number of HIV patients or the added expenses of a lifetime of medication.
Missouri’s expansion of Medicaid did offer some relief, Franklin said. HIV patients were able to roll off of Ryan White programs and enroll in Medicaid, which helped stretch the program’s limited funds.
Now, in states like Missouri that adopted Medicaid expansion, six in 10 Medicaid recipients diagnosed with HIV are included in that expansion group.
That’s why a new Medicaid requirement for most people in the expansion group to document 80 hours of work, school or volunteer hours is another big worry in the HIV care community. The new work requirement and more frequent eligibility checks are expected to cause people to lose coverage. People with HIV won’t be automatically eligible for a medical exemption, which means the safety-net program could let some fall through.
At the same time, more people are dropping Affordable Care Act health insurance due to higher costs, which could also leave some HIV patients without health insurance.
“It’s a perfect storm of public health harm for sure,” Gilmore said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri women have fought for abortion rights for decades. They’re still fighting
description: “I was 25 when I started. I can’t believe I still have to fight for women’s reproductive rights at 75,” Marlene Hammerman told me. Marlene notarized hundreds of signature sheets as a volunteer for the 2024 citizen-led ballot initiative that overturned Missouri’s criminal abortion ban. She’s one of the many women I met when I […]
text:
Marlene Hammerman, RHS alum, notarizes petitions collected by Wendy Flusser, chairperson of the National Council of Jewish Women St. Louis’ Jews for Reproductive Access Initiative founded in 1973 (photo by Bridgette Dunlap).“I was 25 when I started. I can’t believe I still have to fight for women’s reproductive rights at 75,” Marlene Hammerman told me.
Marlene notarized hundreds of signature sheets as a volunteer for the 2024 citizen-led ballot initiative that overturned Missouri’s criminal abortion ban.
She’s one of the many women I met when I volunteered for the effort who has been working for access to reproductive healthcare in Missouri since before I was born — some of them since before the U.S. Supreme Court legalized abortion in 1973.
Marlene provided counseling at Missouri’s first abortion clinic, Reproductive Health Services in St. Louis, for 22 years, nearly all of it as a volunteer. She helped prospective patients weigh their options to end their pregnancies, parent or make it through their pregnancies and place their babies for adoption (the clinic had an adoption service on site for a time). 
Marlene calmed women and girls who had been bullied or called murderers when they sought care at anti-abortion facilities posing as abortion clinics. She’d tell patients what to expect during the procedure. For years, she and other counselors would give patients their home phone numbers in case they had questions or needed to talk after their procedures. Marlene estimates she counseled three thousand women.
Rose-Lynn Sokol also worked at Reproductive Health Services. She was there times the FBI came to tell them to check under their cars for bombs, to change their routes driving home, to be careful opening mail. She was there when an Illinois abortion provider serving the St. Louis area and his wife were abducted. She was there when Reproductive Health Services’ other location in St. Louis County was firebombed. 
Rose-Lynn told me this only because I asked, her voice just as-matter-of-fact as she would explain a step in the ballot process to fellow volunteers.
Like most citizen-led ballot initiatives, the 2024 effort to decriminalize abortion was a huge lift. Advocates had to raise millions of dollars, recruit thousands of volunteers, collect hundreds of thousands of signatures and win five lawsuits against elected officials who sought to block the process. 
This is an arduous and inefficient way to make law. And yet, it would have been a disaster to lose it, had Missourians not voted down Amendment 4 last week. 
Amendment 4 would have made it impossible to amend the Missouri Constitution via citizen-led ballot initiatives by raising the bar for passage from a majority of the statewide vote to a majority of the vote in each of our eight congressional districts.
The fact that Amendment 4 was opponents’ answer to Missouri citizens having legalized abortion was not much discussed. So I was frankly grateful to see two abortion opponents say the quiet part out loud to the Kansas City Star, and U.S. Rep. Bob Onder lay out the plan to re-criminalize abortion in a Heartland News op-ed. 
Republican legislators referred a new constitutional amendment to the ballot that will reinstate the abortion ban if Missourians vote for it in November. It will be called Amendment 3. 
The goal of Amendment 4, Onder explained, was to keep the majority of Missourians who support legal abortion access from ever being able to decriminalize abortion in the future should Amendment 3 succeed in reinstating the ban.
That is where Onder’s honesty ended. He went on to repeat talking points from our anti-abortion elected officials that erase or vilify those of us who worked to make abortion legal. 
Onder said “our constitution shouldn’t be for sale.” Attorney General Catharine Hanaway complained of “tyranny of the majority” and living under “mob rule.” Gov. Mike Kehoe lamented “out of state special interests” being able to change our constitution with a “dump truck load of money.” Others railed about the radical left or funding from George Soros (a classic antisemetic dog-whistle).
No one paid me to tromp down dirt paths in the heat or shiver in the wind outside concert venues collecting signatures. Did the campaign also raise money from out of state and hire paid signature gatherers? You bet. Sadly, that’s what it takes. But advocates had to come up with millions of dollars in-state just to get the effort off the ground. 
As the executive director of one of the major donors to the effort, The Fairness Project, explained, they can’t invest if there isn’t a grassroots campaign to invest in.  
Kehoe’s suggestion that there is something illicit about raising money from out of state was particularly disingenuous given that his failed Amendment 5 campaign was powered by a dump truck load of dark money. 
Our elected officials took a similar good-for-the-goose-but-not-the-gander approach to the vote threshold: Amendment 4’s impossibly high standard would have applied to citizen-led amendments, but not those referred to the ballot by legislators.
Missouri’s abortion ban was tyranny of the minority — not that tyranny of the majority would be any better when it comes to whether the state can use the force of criminal law to conscript your body to bring another human being into the world against your will. 
Hanaway’s claim that we are living under “mob rule” because engaged citizens have accomplished what the legislature won’t is false and dehumanizing.  We’re Missourians. We’re women. We’re much better positioned than the state to determine what is best for our lives, families, and health. 
It makes me angry and exhausted that legal recognition of my dignity and bodily autonomy is repeatedly up for a vote since the U.S. Supreme Court decreed that those aren’t fundamental rights after all. 
But I don’t think about that when I’m in the room or on the sidewalk with women who have seen so much worse than me, who have been through so many losses and won so many fragile wins. They just keep doing the work, bringing a joyfulness and sense of solidarity and inspiring many more of us to do it too.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ panel says more terminally ill inmates should be eligible for release
description: Half of the terminally ill inmates deemed eligible for compassionate release died while their cases were still in court.
text:
New Jersey State Prison in Trenton (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)A state panel wants New Jersey to make more inmates eligible under the compassionate release law, saying its requirement of a terminal six-month prognosis often saw applicants dead before they won freedom.
The Criminal Sentencing and Disposition Commission in a recent letter to Gov. Mikie Sherrill and legislative leaders recommended that those with a prognosis of 18 months to live be allowed to seek early release from incarceration, arguing many with six months to live did not survive procedural hurdles in existing law.
“I don’t think that’s the result that anyone wanted,” said Christopher Porrino, a former New Jersey attorney general and the commission’s chair. “We’re just proposing a tweak to try and bring the goal in line with reality and the practice.”
New Jersy’s compassionate release law, enacted in 2019 following a recommendation from the commission, allows inmates with a terminal diagnosis to petition the Superior Court for early release.
Once a prisoner has that diagnosis and a Department of Corrections-issued certificate of eligibility, which is usually available within a day, the victim, their family, and prosecutors are given a chance to respond.
A judge decides whether the person is released, but objections from victims or prosecutors prompt a hearing.
Though the commission said those procedures are sensible, it warned that they can eat into applicants’ remaining time — in many cases, all of it.
Over the last six years, the Department of Corrections issued 46 certificates of eligibility for compassionate release, but 23 of those applicants died before their cases were complete, the commission said.
And that pattern in persisted in 2025, when six of the 14 the department said were eligible for compassionate release died before their cases wended their way through court.
“Like any piece of legislation that’s written in an office, in a conference room, or on a computer, it hasn’t been tested in real life, and that’s what happened here. Now we’ve seen what the numbers look like,” Porrino said.
Allowing applications from prisoners with no more than 18 months to live would better enable humane releases, the commission said, and existing oversight processes around compassionate release would ensure public safety even under expanded eligibility.
Seven states allow compassionate release for inmates with a prognosis of 12 or fewer months to live, four allow it for prognoses of 18 months or less, and two set their limit at 24 months to live. Only Kansas’s one-month limit is stricter than New Jersey’s, the commission said.
“The Commission’s recommendation is a reasonable adjustment to the Compassionate Release Act, and one that gives the process the time it needs to work as intended,” said Attorney General Jen Davenport, whose approval is needed for the commission to issue recommendations.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahomans to decide on adding voter ID requirements to state constitution
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahomans are set to vote later this month on whether to amend the state Constitution to include voter identification requirements and to give lawmakers greater authority over election law.  If State Question 846 is approved by a majority of voters, the Oklahoma Constitution would be amended to require proof of identity for […]
text:
Voters wait in line outside the Oklahoma County Election Board on Oct. 30, 2024 to cast a vote in the Nov. 5 election. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahomans are set to vote later this month on whether to amend the state Constitution to include voter identification requirements and to give lawmakers greater authority over election law. 
If State Question 846 is approved by a majority of voters, the Oklahoma Constitution would be amended to require proof of identity for any method of voting and to allow the Legislature to enact any laws necessary to specify the ID requirements. 
Lawmakers placed the state question on the Aug. 25 ballot by passing Senate Joint Resolution 47 this session. Oklahoma’s current state law, approved by 74% of voters in 2010, already requires identification. 
State law currently requires one of three forms of identification at the polls: 

A photo ID with the voter’s name, photo and a valid expiration date, issued by the U.S. government, the state or a federally recognized tribal government; 
Voter identification card provided by their county election board; or 
A sworn affidavit to prove identity in order to vote with a provisional ballot. 

Cole Allen, a policy analyst for the Oklahoma Policy Institute, said while the state question wouldn’t make any immediate changes, it would grant the Legislature expanded power over state election law in order to comply with the constitutional changes. 
Lawmakers would also need to outline the requirements for voter identification for mail-in voting, which is more complicated since Oklahomans aren’t voting in front of election officials, he said. 
The Oklahoma Constitution currently gives lawmakers the power to determine the how and when elections are held and to pass laws to detect and punish election fraud, Allen said. 
“By expanding the legislative authority, it gives our Legislature and politicians more power over who can vote and how they vote beyond what the Constitution grants them right now,” he said. 
Oklahoma already has very secure elections, and Allen said he’s not sure how the state question would improve election security. Oklahoma’s chief election official recently affirmed the security of the state’s election despite the federal government claiming otherwise. 
Long-term, it’s possible for lawmakers to make the voter identification laws stricter until voters are disenfranchised, whether intentionally or unintentionally, Allen said. 
“But I do think the more likely scenario is that this restricts access to the ballot for people who are legal voters who simply can’t get their hands on or don’t have the time to go to the DMV to get a driver’s license,” he said. “Or can’t afford to get a passport, or don’t know where their birth certificate is.”
Allen said five other states – Arkansas, Mississippi, Missouri, North Carolina and Wisconsin – have a constitutional requirement for voter identification, but the language and requirements vary from state to state. 
Lawmakers in support of the measure have argued the state question will ensure the integrity of Oklahoma elections. 
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, and Senate President Pro Tem Lonnie Paxton, R-Tuttle, were the authors of the legislation that added the state question to the August ballot. 
Neither responded to requests for comment. 
All registered Oklahoma voters are eligible to vote on the state question, regardless of party affiliation.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming corner-crossing pioneer Brad Cape dies at 55
description:
Hunter and leader of “The Missouri Four” fought two court challenges and established rights of public access to public land in six states.
The post Wyoming corner-crossing pioneer Brad Cape dies at 55 appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Bradly Cape, the Missouri hunter who fought and won two legal challenges after corner crossing to hunt elk on public land in Carbon County, died of a heart attack Saturday in his hometown of Steelville, Missouri. He was 55.
Cape, whose name captioned landmark legal cases stemming from a hunt on Elk Mountain in 2021, was found dead on a favorite running trail, his hunting partner John Slowensky said.
Cape, a fence builder, father and hunter, planned elk hunts to Wyoming in 2020 and 2021, intending to reach public land on the wildlife-rich peak by corner crossing. That would involve passing through the airspace above Elk Mountain Ranch property owned by North Carolina pharmaceutical magnate Fred Eshelman.
Corner crossing had lingered in legal limbo until Cape and his companions were charged with trespassing in 2021 and sued by Eshelman in 2022. The Wyoming Chapter of Backcountry Hunters and Anglers supported the hunters’ defense.
A Carbon County jury found “The Missouri Four” not guilty of trespassing. Courts sided with the corner-crossing hunters in Eshelman’s civil trespass suit, Iron Bar Holdings v. Bradly Cape, which worked its way to the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals in Denver.
In 2025, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to consider Eshelman’s appeal, cementing Cape’s name in public access history across Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, Oklahoma and Kansas. The 10th Circuit Court’s decision clarifies the public’s right to access 3 million acres of public land in the six states, according to onX, the digital mapping company that was a key player in the legal drama.
Cape, who knew a bit about property lines from his fence building career, researched his projects and understood “what is right and not right,” Slowensky said. Cape had faith in his convictions.
“We never thought one time that we were doing something wrong,” Cape told WyoFile after the Supreme Court decision.
Show me
Born in 1971, in Rolla, Missouri, Cape graduated from Steelville High School in 1989, according to his obituary at Britton-Bennett Funeral Home. He had two children and worked on the family farm as well as his All-Type Fence business.
His knowledge about fence building and property boundaries led to a corner-crossing breakthrough.
Corner crossing is used to reach public land in the checkerboard pattern of landownership that spans southern Wyoming in a 40-mile wide strip along the Union Pacific Railroad line. Corner crossers step from one public land parcel to another contiguous one where the parcels share a common corner with two pieces of private land.
Corner crossers do not touch private land but necessarily pass through the airspace above the contiguous private property. Many land and ranch owners and some law enforcement officials assert that corner crossing is trespassing.
“We never thought one time that we were doing something wrong.” Brad Cape
The legal cloud over corner crossing deterred access to 2.4 million acres of public land in Wyoming and some 8.3 million acres across the West. By blocking public access, private landowners can treat public land as their own, public-access advocates assert.
At Elk Mountain Ranch, Eshelman’s ranch manager had blocked a common public-land corner with T-posts, no trespassing signs and a wire, chain and lock above the surveyed monument at a common corner of public and private land.
After the hunters corner crossed by swinging around the T-post obstacle in 2020, the ranch manager told them they were trespassing and not to touch the posts — private property — again.
Back in Missouri, Cape and the others built a light stile they used in 2021 to climb over the T-post obstacle. In their defense, attorney Ryan Semerad argued in part that the federal Unlawful Inclosures Act of 1885 prevented checkerboard landowners from obstructing public access to public land. The federal law supersedes Wyoming trespass statutes, courts decided.
Services for Cape are scheduled for Aug. 13 in Steelville. The outdoors, family and faith marked Cape’s life, Slowensky said.
The not guilty verdict in the 2022 misdemeanor criminal trespass trial affirmed Slowensky’s belief in the American system of justice. He remembers standing in the Rawlins courtroom — the only person not seated — as Carbon County Circuit Court Judge Susan Stipe read the verdict.
“It gave us a lot of faith,” he said.
Read about Brad Cape, The Missouri Four and their legal cases through WyoFile’s extensive coverage.

name: WyoFile
title: Lawmakers mull new bill to prevent lawsuits aimed at silencing free speech
description:
Committee will vote on draft bill in October after similar legislation has twice failed to become law. Wyoming is one of just a handful of states without an anti-SLAPP statute.
The post Lawmakers mull new bill to prevent lawsuits aimed at silencing free speech appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming remains one of a handful of states without a law to prevent lawsuits intended to silence free speech. After a measure failed last session, lawmakers are taking another swing at passing a bill to block such “strategic lawsuits against public participation,” known as an anti-SLAPP statute. 
After making several changes to a new anti-SLAPP bill, members of the Joint Judiciary Committee decided Monday to postpone voting on the measure until their next meeting in October. 
“Let’s bring it back at our next meeting in an updated version with the amendments built into it,” Rep. Art Washut, R-Casper, said. “There may be different public comment with the amendments than there was public comment on the draft that we saw today.”
SLAPPs are usually civil complaints brought by the powerful to silence critics through the stress and high costs of lawsuits rather than through legal merits. Anti-SLAPP laws are meant to protect journalists and private citizens who face retaliatory litigation for questioning those in powerful positions. 
Legislation to prevent SLAPP lawsuits in Wyoming died for a second year in a row this past legislative session. House Bill 103, “Wyoming First Amendment Protection Act,” sponsored by Rep. Pepper Ottman, R-Riverton, was meant to provide a way to quickly dismiss frivolous or meritless legal actions. But it had too many holes, lawmakers said — some were concerned about the bill’s applicability to pending cases and to what they saw as its imbalanced approach to attorneys’ fees. 
Plus, lawmakers didn’t like that the bill had been drafted by a Nevada attorney, Marc Randazza. “I’d rather write our own laws than an attorney from Nevada write our laws,” Senate Judiciary Chairperson Sen. Jared Olsen, R-Cheyenne, said in March. 
Lawmakers proposed taking a deeper dive into the issue during the legislative offseason and crafting a different anti-SLAPP bill for the 2027 legislative session. The new bill draft is based on the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act, a model anti-SLAPP law made by the Uniform Law Commission, a nonprofit organization of state-based commissioners who aim to craft laws that offer consistency across states. Roughly half of states with anti-SLAPP laws use that model language. 
“I encourage the committee to adopt this because it is based on the uniform laws, and we do have a little bit more consistency on how that’s applied,” Wyoming Commissioner Scott Meier, speaking on behalf of the Uniform Law Commission, told the committee. 
The most significant proposed changes to the draft bill concerned making the bill “substantive” rather than just “procedural.” Substantive laws are the “what” — they tell courts what people are and aren’t allowed to do. Procedural laws are the “how” — they set the rules for how a court and attorneys can go about deciding, proving or disapproving whether a person violated a substantive law. Substantive state laws can be applied in federal court, while procedural state laws that conflict with federal procedures can’t.
“We’re trying to get to a point where the courts will recognize these types of bills not as procedural only, but as having a substantive component,” Parker Jackson, a staff attorney at the Goldwater Institute, a research and litigation organization, told the committee. 
He noted that states like Ohio and Pennsylvania have added immunity provisions to their anti-SLAPP statutes to protect defendants who face a SLAPP lawsuit over protected expression. “The goal of that is so that the courts will recognize this as substantively protecting constitutional rights, not just providing an expedited procedural mechanism.”
But lawmakers decided not to add an immunity provision to the bill, noting that such provisions have landed some states’ anti-SLAPP laws in court. “This imports a whole concept of immunity [that’s] being litigated in other states right now,” Rep. Ken Chestek, D-Laramie, said. “If that fails, if we include this language, we fail too, maybe, or we’re creating a bigger hill to climb to defend it.” 
The committee opted for a simpler approach, adding the word “substantively” into the bill to describe the rights that the legislation intends to protect from frivolous lawsuits. “I think that is going to go a long way, and maybe all the way, to making this a substantive right,” Chestek said. 
During public comment Monday, speakers encouraged lawmakers to pass an anti-SLAPP bill. Ben Sheffner, an attorney for the Motion Pictures Association, which represents major U.S. motion picture and television producers and distributors, told the Joint Judiciary Committee that the “motion picture industry has a particular interest in this legislation.” Association members “engage every day in constitutionally protected expression,” reporting the news and making films, television shows and documentaries, he said. 
“Sometimes that expression is controversial, and sometimes, people or companies who dislike how they’ve been portrayed respond with meritless defamation, privacy or other lawsuits, with the ultimate goal of censoring such portrayals.” 
Such lawsuits can cost “hundreds of thousands of dollars” to defend, Sheffner continued. “For a filmmaker, a local journalist, or a small production company, that cost alone can be enough to kill a project or chill the next one before it’s even started.”

name: WyoFile
title: Yes, Wyoming voters, your elections are safe and secure
description:
Secretary of State Chuck Gray bashed the state for low election integrity, but that’s no longer his issue, columnist Kerry Drake writes. 
The post Yes, Wyoming voters, your elections are safe and secure appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
I knew Chuck Gray was falling down on the job.
Wyoming’s secretary of state won his office by vowing to make sure we had election integrity.

Opinion

Then last year he began campaigning for a new government job as Wyoming’s U.S. House representative. Sure, he talks a good game about preserving the safety of our elections, and Gray could probably deliver a speech about it in his sleep.
But the old “oomph” in his campaign pitch has been missing, and I’ve brought the receipts to prove it.
I googled Chuck Gray and “insiders,” one of his all-time favorite political targets, and found 11,400 entries.
But his real enemy is the “leftwing media.” A total of 27,200 entries!
“Election integrity?” A paltry 7,200.
Now, I admit you could look at this two ways. During the first three years of his term as secretary of state — and acting governor whenever Gov. Mark Gordon is out of state, which fortunately isn’t too often — perhaps he solved Wyoming’s lack of election integrity.
I’m sure that’s how his congressional campaign would spin it. But that presumes that the state had such a problem to begin with.
It didn’t. All of the 23 county clerks in their state association said Wyoming’s elections are safe and secure, and they should know — they’re the ones at the local level who really supervise them, not Gray.
So, please vote in this primary election Aug. 18, if not before. You only have one ballot, so make it count.
Do you know how many convictions for voter fraud Wyoming has had since 2000? Four, involving three separate cases. By the way, all four phony voters were reportedly Republicans, members of Gray’s own party.
That’s not me, part of the wretched leftwing media, saying it. The Heritage Foundation, the conservative think tank that thinks it’s been running the country for decades, keeps statistics like that.
One of Gray’s predecessors as secretary of state, Ed Buchanan, used to travel throughout Wyoming to give residents the real story: The state’s elections are secure and conducted with integrity. He actively worked to dispel the myths that Gray and other far-right politicians have spread far and wide.
“If people don’t trust their elections, then nothing else matters,” Buchanan said. He knew that public trust in the electoral process is crucial for democracy. 
Buchanan made sure the secretary of state’s website devoted a page to facts about how secure Wyoming’s elections are. Once Gray was in office, that page mysteriously disappeared.
Of course he had other priorities early in his administration, like filling the 12 staff vacancies created by resignations between the time he won the August 2022 GOP primary and his swearing-in ceremony five months later.
They included former Deputy Secretary of State Karen Wheeler and all three members of the Elections Division. Combined, the quartet had 119 years of experience, Cowboy State Daily reported. Overall, more than one-third of the staff quit.
Still, Wyoming’s elections remained safe and secure. The Heritage Foundation even moved Wyoming up on its election integrity scale, giving the Legislature five more points and an “atta boy” for banning ranked-choice voting.
(In reality, that should have lowered Wyoming’s score, because allowing voters to rank candidates generally reduces negative campaigning, increases voter turnout, and makes voters feel they haven’t “wasted” their vote once their first choice is out of the running. That’s just me, a member of the wretched leftwing media, expressing my personal opinion. But I’m right.)
Fortunately, one ban the Legislature didn’t enact was on ballot drop boxes, which are a convenience for voters, especially if they live far from their county clerk’s office and can’t get there during business hours.
Lawmakers rejected many of the bad bills Gray and the Freedom Caucus supported, including junking electronic voting machines and making hand counts mandatory. Gee whiz, Chuck, why don’t we just use the chisel-and-slate system that was good enough for the Flintstones?
But I have to hand it to Gray, who did make some smart choices as campaign season began. First, he asked everyone to vote for him even though he didn’t say what office he was seeking. It gave voters practice imagining his name and poking a hole to the side of it.
Next, to no one’s surprise, he chose an office where he wouldn’t have to face U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman, who was reportedly pondering the gubernatorial contest. Instead, she decided to run for U.S. Sen. Cynthia Lummis’ seat when the senator announced her retirement.
Realizing he couldn’t beat Hageman was a no-brainer for Gray. He dropped out of the U.S. House race in 2022 when Trump picked Hageman to be his candidate, and opted instead for secretary of state. Then Trump endorsed Gray.
But now it’s 2026 and Gray’s plan for this race isn’t rock solid. He could have stayed in the secretary of state’s office, given Wyoming voters’ penchant for reelecting state officeholders. 
Gray, however, felt he deserved to move up. The governor’s race initially looked like an easy way if Hageman didn’t want to come home, but her open U.S. House seat was too good to pass up.
The problem for Gray is that apparently few candidates cowered in fear because he had tossed his ill-fitting cowboy hat into the ring. Of the original 10 who filed for the office, nine remain. Frank Chapman withdrew after loaning his campaign more than $1 million.
But the other members of the Million-Dollar Club — Gray, Reid Rasner and Steve Friess — are considered the favorites, even though supporters of dark-horse candidates always believe they have what it takes to pull ahead. I’m sorry to burst some bubbles, but they don’t.
When Gray released a poll in May claiming a seven-point lead over Rasner and 11 points over Friess, it was probably pretty accurate. He had won a statewide contest and was popular among extremely conservative Republicans who viewed him as a bit of a rebel. They particularly liked how he picks fights with Gordon.
But Friess appears to have the momentum headed into the final week before the Aug. 18 primary. He’s become the contest’s top spender, and I think the idea of an “ABC” campaign — “Anyone But Chuck” —  is likely to make Friess the winner as Gray and Rasner continue to throw dirt at each other. Nothing is sticking on Friess.
It leads to an interesting possibility, though. Gray is one of the fiercest Trump defenders, getting on the “2020 election was rigged” bandwagon before it even left the gate. So, he knows how to play that sour grapes game with the best of them.
But who is he going to blame if he loses, since he’s the supervisor of Wyoming elections? Is he going to throw his own administration under the bus? Of course not.
The insiders and leftwing media rap has become as stale as it gets — I remember him using it during his second legislative race in Casper in 2016 — and I don’t see it holding up now.
So what will be Gray’s fall guy if he loses? Woke wind? Data centers?
My bet is on “illegal immigrants,” who are clearly unable to vote. But somehow during Gray’s last hurrah overseeing Wyoming’s elections, they’re gonna fill up those damn ballot drop boxes.

title: Ongoing Wind River Reservation church protests highlight tension between Indigenous sovereignty, religious freedom
description:
Protests persist as church leaders, who founded Foundations For Nations on the reservation just outside Riverton, continue to hold Sunday services.
The post Ongoing Wind River Reservation church protests highlight tension between Indigenous sovereignty, religious freedom appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
ARAPAHOE—The smell of sweetgrass and sage clung to a shade tent tipped askew on the edge of the barrow ditch, the Northern Arapaho Tribe’s red, white and black flag flipping and clapping in the wind. On that day — July 26 — there were more people outside Foundations For Nations Church than inside it. 
It was the third week of protest over a controversy that sparked national headlines and united tribal leaders on the Wind River Indian Reservation. 
The clash has spurred legal questions focused squarely on tribal sovereignty and religious freedom. While both sides have promised they’re ready to fight in court, Foundations For Nations made the first move Friday with a discrimination complaint filed by a legal nonprofit based in Florida.
After Foundations For Nations Pastor Sarah Lucas condemned Northern Arapaho traditional ways in a sermon during the tribe’s Sundance celebration, diverse voices from across the Wind River Reservation and Native Country have coalesced into a singular message to the church.
Leave. 
“Jesus can stay,” Darci Quiver, a member of the Northern Arapaho Tribe, explained after standing for hours in 100-degree heat outside the reservation church’s gate. “Her and her family?,” Quiver said, referring to Lucas. “They need to pack up and go.” 
The protests have persisted. Church leaders, who founded Foundations For Nations on the reservation just outside Riverton almost a decade ago, have continued to hold Sunday services, punctuated by protests, since. Outside social media posts, at least one appeal for funding from members, and a statement given to CNN, the church has largely remained silent and refused to answer questions about the controversy. 
After the Northern Arapaho Business Council directed the church to leave the reservation in early July, the council announced a new policy requiring outside organizations to consult with tribal leaders to hold recurring “organized activities” on the reservation. The Eastern Shoshone Business Council quickly followed suit. 
A sermon, and a month of backlash
On July 5, just as the Northern Arapaho Sundance was coming to a close, Lucas stood before her congregation and spoke specifically about the tribe’s sacred ceremony. 
“I pray as the people coming out of Sundance today, their last day, they’re going back into community,” she said in a video that quickly went viral. “You have generations, generations, centuries of people doing this offering, going in and being, making vows to change, Father God. And we see no fruit.” 
Lucas ushered several Native people up to share their testimony about how they had rejected their traditional spiritual ways, and urged others to turn away from “demonic activity.” 
Lucas pointed to the Northern Arapaho Tribe’s sacred pipe and its ceremonial and spiritual use, calling it idol worship. “The pipe cannot hear your prayers. It’s just a piece of material, right? And this is a cycle that they’re caught up in, and this is all they’ve ever known,” she said. “And the Lord is saying, ‘Tear down the idols, tear down the altars, the idol worship.’”
The backlash was swift. By that Tuesday, hundreds gathered in protest outside the church. People took to social media to decry Lucas’ statements, generating thousands of posts, comments and videos across multiple platforms. Many demanded the church leave the reservation, but some messages were more ominous; Lucas said she’s received death threats, threats to burn down the church and of physical violence against her. 
Protesters who have set up camp outside the church every Sunday since the July 5 sermon have been clear about their intentions to be peaceful. They’ve alerted law enforcement of their presence at the church and asked that officers keep an eye on things to ensure that no conflicts arise. At a July 19 protest, one protester reported being physically threatened by church security, which prompted the Fremont County Sheriff’s Office to respond to the scene. 
Tribal leaders’ united front
The Friday after the sermon, the Northern Arapaho Business Council met with church leaders and told them they were no longer welcome on the reservation. 
But the church has continued to offer Sunday worship and other programming at the Arapahoe church building, and quickly sent out a message to members asking for funds for an anticipated legal battle. “We are standing firmly on the truth of the Word of God concerning idol worship,” church leaders wrote to members, describing “ongoing death threats and threats to burn our church.” 
Church leaders said they could not be legally removed from property they own on the reservation, adding, “we are in contact with legal counsel and are preparing to pursue this in federal court as soon as possible in order to uphold our Constitutional rights to preach the gospel … We are not stopping.”
On Friday, Florida-based Christian litigation and policy nonprofit Liberty Counsel announced that it had filed a discrimination complaint with the USDA on behalf of the Foundations For Nations church. The complaint argues that the Food Bank of Wyoming unlawfully cut off a partnership that has for years helped stock the shelves of the church’s food pantry in Riverton on the basis of religious, political and racial discrimination. The food pantry is not on the reservation.
Leading up to that complaint, the Northern Arapaho Business Council announced July 20 a new policy requiring outside organizations to “consult” with the tribe before conducting “organized activities” on the reservation, and stated that the church had never received authorization from the tribe to establish the church. The business council requested a meeting with church officials to discuss the new policy. 
“Our responsibility is to protect our people, our culture, and our sovereign authority,” Northern Arapaho Business Council Chairman Keenan Groesbeck said. “This policy is not about preventing anyone from practicing their religion. It is about respecting the sovereign government of the Northern Arapaho Tribe. Any outside organization seeking to conduct organized activities within our jurisdiction should first communicate with the elected leadership of our Nation and work in partnership with the tribe.” 
The Eastern Shoshone Business Council followed suit, issuing a statement outlining its adoption of the same policy. “The Eastern Shoshone Tribe calls on the Foundations For Nations Church and any affiliated representatives to immediately stop all efforts directed at persuading Native children and families to reject traditional practices and to engage in governmental consultation and authorization directly with the Eastern Shoshone Business Council before continuing or expanding any recurring ministry activities, especially where it concerns tribal member children,” the council wrote. 
“The business council further recognizes the historical relationship between many Christian institutions and Native Nations, including the devastating legacy of forced assimilation, boarding schools, and efforts to suppress Indigenous languages, cultures, and spiritual traditions,” the Northern Arapaho Business Council said in its statement. “These historical experiences make it especially important that any outside organization engaging with the Northern Arapaho people do so through respectful government-to-government consultation and with a full understanding of tribal history, culture and sovereignty.” 
For much of U.S. history, Native Americans’ cultural and spiritual practices were suppressed and outlawed, with sacred ceremonies and traditions often practiced in secret to avoid severe penalties. The U.S. Department of the Interior adopted the Code of Indian Offenses in 1883, making it illegal for Native people to practice their faith and traditions; it wasn’t until 1978 that Congress passed the American Indian Religious Freedom Act. While the act protects the spiritual practices of Native tribes, it also reaffirms the rights of all religions, specifically affirming that no tribe, in “exercising powers of self-governance shall make or reinforce any law prohibiting the free exercise of religion” or freedom of speech. 
On July 25, CNN’s Victor Blackwell posed the question to Northern Arapaho Council Chairman Groesbeck: Do you believe you have the authority to tell the church they cannot preach messages condemning traditional ways?
“Yep,” responded Groesbeck. He pointed to a Montana Supreme Court case as providing legal footing for the tribe. 
Just after the July 5 sermon, in a letter to church members and supporters, Foundations For Nations leaders were also gearing up for a legal fight. “We also ask for your earnest prayers,” they wrote. “There is a deep spiritual darkness over this land, but we are confident in the promise that ‘more are for us than against us’ (2 Kings 6:16) … This matter is now moving toward the courts,” they continued, adding that they are preparing to take legal action in federal court. 
Last week, Lucas, who has not responded to multiple requests for comment, offered an emotional statement on her Facebook page on the situation. She said what hurt the most to her wasn’t the “unbelievers” who protest against her, but Christians who have remained silent in her defense. 
“Yet Jesus experienced this too. When He was arrested and facing persecution, His own disciples fled, and Peter even denied knowing Him,” she wrote. “Jesus understands that kind of pain.”
Lucas has also expressed a commitment to continue her mission of bringing people to Jesus at the reservation church. “And I’m not saying this to boast in any kind of way about who I am, but the Lord had said to one of the [Bible study] people, for God so loved the reservation that they sent Sarah,” Lucas said in her July 26 sermon. 
Protests persist
Alice Thomas has spent every Sunday since the sermon outside the church’s fence line, holding up signs, offering protesters food and water, and stressing the need to remain peaceful. Her goal? She wants the church to pack up and go somewhere else. 
“People contact me and ask why [keep protesting], when is it going to stop,” she said. “When they leave. We’re doing this to protect our children and our people.” 
Though protesters consider their message to be one of high stakes for the Northern Arapaho Tribe, Sundays have been filled with laughter and music. “That’s how Natives deal with adversity. We joke about it. We laugh about it,” Thomas said. “Even this — we laugh about it, we joke about it, but it’s something serious to us. It’s something that shouldn’t have happened, especially if she’s the true person that she says she is.”
Quiver, who described herself as a pipe keeper and ceremony woman, said the church has not just offended her tribe, but Indigenous people all across the country. “She was so disrespectful. It hurts my heart for my people, it hurts my heart for our ceremonies, and I just want her to leave,” she said. Like the other protesters, Quiver said her goal was to send the church packing, but added that she hopes they stay away from Indian Country altogether. 
“Every tribe is different. Every tribe has their own traditions, has their own ceremonies,” Quiver said. “But she lumped us all together. She didn’t just disrespect the Arapahos; she disrespected the Shoshones, she disrespected the Lakotas in that — all these tribes that have Sundance, she disrespected them. And it’s not just the Arapahos. She disrespected all Native people.” 
One young protester painted this sign after showing up at a Sunday protest to show support for Northern Arapaho traditional ways and culture. (Sarah Elmquist Squires/The Ranger)
The protests are intergenerational. Zona, who asked to be identified by only her first name, spent her 21st birthday outside, in the heat along the barrow ditch outside the church’s gate, with her protest sign. 
In red on black — the Northern Arapaho Tribe’s colors — it read: “You’re not welcome.”
“Just why? Why say all those things?” Zona said. “When she first said that she was here to help us — so why go against what we believe in?” 
As a young person charged with carrying on the Northern Arapaho traditional ways and culture, Zona said she remembers being a little girl, running off and playing with her friends during sacred tribal events. “But I’ve always loved the Sundance. I’ve always loved just being around my family, and getting to understand my culture a little better,” she said. “And I’ve started going up to the lodge with my mom. I stand there and watch on, listen to the songs. 
“I believe it’s a big part of everybody, to be closer to their own culture, no matter what you are,” Zona offered. “To at least have that be a part of you.”

title: ‘It’s Wyoming’s toad’: Inside a multi-state effort to save a humble species from extinction
description:
North America's most endangered amphibian crawls back outside Laramie with help from a Minnesota zoo.  
The post  ‘It’s Wyoming’s toad’: Inside a multi-state effort to save a humble species from extinction appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The main entrance of Como Park Zoo & Conservatory in St. Paul is busy with strollers and chatty kids on a hot weekday afternoon. Below all that, in a tiny basement room marked “biosecure,” zookeeper Allison Pizel tends to one family in particular.
“This is Meatball,” she said, holding a brown blob of a toad in a gloved hand. Meatball is a survivor, as the only member of Pizel’s breeding program to make it from egg to tadpole to toad in 2025. Meatball also belongs to one of the most endangered amphibian species in North America: the Wyoming toad.
Como is one of seven zoos, plus two other breeding sites, that are working with wildlife professionals to pull the toad from the edge of extinction by building up its population and reintroducing it to its home range.
The species is native to a single valley in the state of Wyoming, called the Laramie Basin. Meatball has never been there; she grew up in the room full of tanks, where she and other toads spend their days eating crickets and mealworms.
The high plains surrounding Laramie, Wyo. are home to the highly endangered Wyoming toad. (Alanna Elder/MPR News)
Each year, Pizel puts some toads in what she describes as a fancy refrigerator for a short hibernation. Then, she pulls them out to breed. She gives them hormones and sets up “an ancient CD player” with their croaks.
This year was much more successful than last. Pizel recently FedExed about 3,000 tadpoles to Wyoming to be reintroduced. She blames last year’s poor numbers on a couple factors: Some toads died in hibernation, and she bred one-year-old males, which are often too young to successfully fertilize eggs.
Pizel also keeps some tadpoles to let them morph into toads in captivity. Some will breed future generations and others will go to Wyoming as adults, with microchips to help track their survival.
She does much of this work alone, and avoids contact with other amphibians, to protect the toads from a deadly skin disease called chytrid fungus. It affects many amphibians, including 20 species in Minnesota, she said, but the Wyoming toad is particularly vulnerable.
The species has suffered not only from disease, but also pesticides and habitat loss. By the mid-1980s, people thought they were gone for good, according to Wendy Estes-Zumpf, herpetological coordinator for the Wyoming Game and Fish Department.
“They were accidentally rediscovered at a private fishing pond out in the Laramie Basin, and that populations seemed to be doing really well,” she said. “But it started crashing in 1989.”
Biologists tried to rescue the species by bringing those toads into captivity and the breeding program was born. Estes-Zumpf says all the Wyoming toads alive today are descended from about ten individuals, a puddle of a gene pool.
“Genetic diversity is what helps species adapt to new threats, diseases,” Estes-Zumpf said. “That’s sort of the biggest issue in trying to help them battle chytrid fungus.”
That’s where Derek Benson comes in. He leads amphibian conservation at the Henry Doorly Zoo and Aquarium in Omaha, Nebraska. He is also in charge of what’s called the studbook for Wyoming toad recovery. Benson tracks births, deaths and breeding pairs across all the sites to try to squeeze as much diversity out of the gene pool as possible. Today, there are about 650 individual toads in captivity, he said.
“Over the last 10 years or so, we have increased that genetic diversity,” Benson said. And each of those years, he said, toads have bred in the wild, another sign of progress.
Despite some wins, the population still can’t sustain itself. It faces major obstacles, including climate conditions. Some of the toads’ habitat in Wyoming is running dry, Estes-Zumpf said, and they need water to live and reproduce.
“We had a drought last year, and a lot of our sites didn’t have sufficient water for tadpoles to metamorphose. This year it’s even worse,” she said. “We’re in an epic drought, and we’re really limited in where we can release tadpoles and toads right now.”
The lives of these toads have always been sort of unlikely, she said, which is part of what she loves about them.
“They’re not agile jumpers like frogs. They just sort of crawl around,” she said. “Somehow these awkward little creatures with grumpy faces; they’ve persisted for this long.”
When glaciers pulled back from what is now the Laramie valley roughly 10,000 years ago, they left behind a different species, the Canadian toad. It evolved into a new, local variety.
Estes-Zumpf says the toad is a special part of Laramie’s natural history. “It is Wyoming’s toad, and we can’t just sit back and let it wink out. What’s so encouraging is that so many people around the country are helping us to make sure that this doesn’t happen.”
Pizel and other zookeepers will travel to Wyoming in early August to meet with partners there and look for toads in the wild. In the longer term, she is looking forward to potentially moving her breeding program to a larger room in Como Zoo’s aquatics building.
There, zoo visitors could also get to know the Wyoming toad, through a window.

title: Immigration searches were conducted on Twin Falls Flock network. A month later, agreements changed.
description: 1:42 p.m., May 3; Indiana State Police entered a Flock automated license plate reader – known as ALPR – network lookup. The reason for the search: “Immigration (civil/administrative).” Quickly, the nationwide system sprung into action; hundreds of ALPR systems searched for a suspect’s license plate. Among the cameras included in the search was Idaho’s Twin [[...]
text:
A Flock Automated License Plate Reader near the Lowe's on Overland Road in Boise,  as captured on Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun)1:42 p.m., May 3; Indiana State Police entered a Flock automated license plate reader – known as ALPR – network lookup. The reason for the search: “Immigration (civil/administrative).”
Quickly, the nationwide system sprung into action; hundreds of ALPR systems searched for a suspect’s license plate. Among the cameras included in the search was Idaho’s Twin Falls Police Department ALPR network.
That’s according to public records obtained by activist group DeFlock Idaho. They show that the Twin Falls Police Department ALPR systems have been searched for immigration-related purposes at least 631 times across March, May and June of 2026.
Nationwide police agencies conducted the searches through Flock’s national network sharing, including lookups from Indiana State Police, Georgia’s Lawrenceville Police, Florida’s Bay County Sheriff’s Office and Florida’s Fish and Wildlife Commission, among others.
In doing so, the searches inadvertently evaded both Idaho Code 49-1432 and self-imposed restrictions by Twin Falls PD prohibiting the use of ALPR cameras for immigration purposes, as outlined in Flock’s Transparency Portal.
Nearly one month after those searches were conducted, however, the Twin Falls Police Department Administrative Services Division Lieutenant Steven Gassert told the Idaho Capital Sun it changed its national network sharing settings to no longer permit outside agencies from searching the system.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



“We want to make sure that we are being respectful of our citizens’ views and opinions on this, while still seeing the importance of technology when it comes to modern policing in our community,” Gassert said in an interview.
With cross-jurisdictional data sharing appearing as a major incentive for police agencies entering into agreements with Flock, communities may need to navigate a complicated patchwork of local, national or agency-specific regulations.
 Local Flock searches limited by Idaho legislation and local agreements

Flock automated license plate readers use AI technologies to automatically scan vehicle license plates for information.
When any vehicle drives past an ALPR camera, the system takes a snapshot of the back, registering its license plate, car make or model, colors and other apparent characteristics.
All eyes on Flock as Idaho navigates surveillance technology across the state

If an alert is tied to that vehicle, such as a wanted person report or car theft, then the system notifies police officers of the suspect traveling past the location.
Officers can also conduct specific searches of the system, accessing the entire network to locate given license plates, and that often includes a national lookup option whereby outside agencies can be searched.
Police departments can opt into the national lookup feature, but the system works by reciprocity: agencies can only access national data by sharing themselves. For some within law enforcement, data-sharing offers a major incentive:
“When (a suspect) leaves our area, we still have the opportunity to follow up and catch them when they end up in another area, so that is a benefit,” said Jessica Clements, Idaho Falls Police Department’s public information officer, said in an interview. “And on the reverse, when someone who has a warrant or who is a danger to the public enters our area, we get notification of that as well.”
Through sharing agreements, police agencies can more easily track suspects across jurisdictions, Clements said.
The web-like national system, however, may invalidate local restrictions for ALPR cameras, as agencies only answer to local or state guidelines for the technology. With the national lookup tool enabled, outside agencies can still conduct searches that local cities might not allow.
“If an officer in Arizona uses a nationwide lookup tool to search for license plate ABC123, all the system does is go out and ask the agencies involved: ‘Hey, do you have anything with license plate ABC123?’” Gassert said. “If our agency had license plate ABC123, then we would provide that information to them.”
The information sharing happens automatically, meaning data identifying suspects would be shared with the requesting agency regardless of manual local input, according to Gassert.
Network audits received by DeFlock Idaho show access information from Twin Falls ALPRs, with information detailing an organization’s name, the date and the reason for the search as listed by officers.
Idaho Code 49-1432 restricts ALPR searches, like those conducted by Flock cameras, to “the investigation of felony, misdemeanor crimes, traffic accidents or to search for missing or endangered persons.”
“I have to follow (these) laws because I am working in the jurisdiction of the state of Idaho,” Gassert said. “Now, if someone in California or Arizona was doing a search, they have to follow the laws of California, Arizona or whatever state they’re working in.”
Immigration searches, especially those labeled “administrative” or “civil,” would not apply.
In addition, the Twin Falls Police Department maintains local policies with the Flock company that should, theoretically, prohibit “immigration enforcement” queries, according to Flock’s Transparency Portal.
“We have a very strong 30-plus year policy outlining that we do not get involved in immigration investigations or immigration situations in our community,” Gassert said. “So we do not allow our officers to utilize that.”
Still, participation in the national system allowed multiple agencies to search Twin Falls data for “immigration,” “civil/administrative” or “I.C.E.”
Gassert said the immigration searches did not result in data pulls from the Twin Falls Police Department, but they occurred nonetheless. Had the ALPR cameras captured any of the suspect license plates, he said the system would have automatically forwarded the information to outside agencies.
Gassert also clarified that Twin Falls PD never granted complete access to the cameras to immigration enforcement agencies.
“We actually, on a weekly basis, receive requests from the FBI and immigration to have access to our Flock system, and we deny it every week,” he said.
The Idaho Attorney General’s Office could not be reached for comment on whether searches of Idaho networks by nationwide agencies could constitute a punishable violation of Idaho Code.
 Policy changes

One month after immigration searches were identified by network audits, the Twin Falls Police Department cancelled its participation in Flock’s national lookup on July 22.
The change means no agency can access Twin Falls data through a national lookup anymore, according to Gassert.
When asked if the shift in department policy came following community concerns, also referenced in an email inquiry about immigration searches sent July 20 by the Idaho Capital Sun, Gassert replied: “Not these (searches) in particular that you’re bringing up. We’re constantly reevaluating this program, and based on some of the conversations and comments that we have about citizens, we go back and look at ways that we can improve.”

title: Federal contract documents show ICE 24-hour call center planned for Adams, Tennessee
description: The Department of Homeland Security has awarded a $63 million contract to an Alaska corporation to operate a national immigration enforcement call center in rural Tennessee, a federal contract database shows. The city of Adams, a Robertson County town of about 600 people near the Kentucky border, is identified in the database as the future […]
text:
Federal contract documents show Adams, Tenn. in Robertson County as the site of a new ICE call center. Pictured:  Five people detained after appearing in Robertson County General Sessions for traffic violations by masked and un-uniformed officers. (Photo John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The Department of Homeland Security has awarded a $63 million contract to an Alaska corporation to operate a national immigration enforcement call center in rural Tennessee, a federal contract database shows.
The city of Adams, a Robertson County town of about 600 people near the Kentucky border, is identified in the database as the future site of the planned call center, intended to function round-the-clock to support local police and sheriffs’ departments across the country that have entered into cooperative agreements with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 
The call center will also help locate unaccompanied migrant children and develop new technologies for ICE, contract documents show. 
The one-year contract, effective Aug. 6, was awarded to Koniag Government Services.The company is a subsidiary of Koniag, a for-profit Alaska Native corporation created for the benefit of 3,400 Alutiiq shareholders, according to its website. 
Local leaders, including Adams City Manager Anna Redfern, told the Lookout Monday they were unaware the town was even being considered. Officials could not immediately identify a potential physical location within the town’s 2.5-square-mile borders and expressed skepticism about the capacity of the city’s existing infrastructure to support a call center.
“I don’t know that little, ole sleepy Adams has got the things that you need to put in a call center,” said Chris Traughber, assessor of property for Robertson County, said of the town that is perhaps best known for he 19th century legend of the “Bell witch” haunting that attracts supernatural enthusiasts and other visitors today.
Traughber said he was unaware of any recent property transactions that could account for an incoming call center. Portions of Adams lie within Montgomery County. The county’s property assessor referred the Lookout to online records, which did not yield any recent transactions by the Koniag company.



Quotation







I don't know that little, ole sleepy Adams has got the things that you need to put in a call center.


– Chris Traughber, Robertson County Property Assessor


Republican State Sen. Kerry Roberts, whose district encompasses Adams, said he had “heard rumors” about the plans but said his office “has had no contact with anyone with the federal government” about the project. 
“They could handle it,” he said of Adams, but cautioned that Internet connectivity and an adequate workforce could pose challenges.
A Koniag spokesperson referred questions about the contract to ICE, including a facility’s precise location, estimated workforce and its physical size. 
“Unfortunately, we are not at liberty to discuss this very recently awarded contract at this time, said Joanie Barr, senior vice president for business operations for Koniag Government Services. 
A spokesperson for ICE did not respond to a request for details about the newly awarded contract. 
Contract documents show the primary function of the call center will be to handle an estimated 6,000-7,000 daily inquiries from law enforcement agencies across the nation that have entered into cooperative agreements with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Call center employees will “analyze data, perform database cross-checks and confirm enforcement actions in the field,” contract documents say. Employees will work round-the-clock eight-hour shifts
The documents, however, show the company will be tasked with a much wider range of duties, including tracking and reporting the locations of unaccompanied immigrant children and identifying “emerging technologies” to increase the effectiveness of local law enforcement’s work with ICE. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
The center will also be tapped to “reduce the non-detained docket” of millions non-citizens living in the U.S. — noncitizens who are going through immigration court proceedings — by providing law enforcement officers and sheriffs with “targeting focus and material.”
The establishment of a national immigrant and enforcement call center represents a significant expansion of the Trump administration’s coordination with local law enforcement departments and sheriff’s offices around the nation as the number of participating agencies 
Administration officials have called the agreements a “force multiplier” to extend the reach of enforcement actions into communities by local police and sheriffs deputized to perform immigration agent duties.  
While the so-called 287(g) cooperative agreements have been in existence since the 1970s, they have dramatically expanded under the second Trump term from fewer than 200 to more than 2,179 in 39, as of August, according to publicly-posted ICE data. 
Lisa Sherman Luna, executive director of the Coalition for Immigrant & Refugee Rights, characterized the plans as “trying to set up shop in middle Tennessee to facilitate this terror on a massive scale.”
Sherman Luna cited an expanded federal presence conducting immigration enforcement as part of the Memphis Safe Task Force and a package of recent Tennessee GOP immigration legislation, crafted in meetings between Republican House Speaker Cameron Sexton and White House advisor Stephen Miller.
“Tennessee is ground zero for this administration’s insidious attempt to embed immigration enforcement in all facets of our everyday life,” she said.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Plaintiffs call for Alabama Supreme Court to reverse Tuberville residency case dismissal
description: Plaintiffs challenging Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville’s candidacy on Monday argued that a lower court erred in dismissing the case. The 45-page brief filed late Monday morning in the Alabama Supreme Court by Barry Ragsdale, one of the plaintiffs’ attorneys, argued that Alabama’s judicial branch has sole jurisdiction to decide if Tuberville[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. and Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville speaking at the Alabama Republican Party's Summer Dinner on July 31, 2026, at the Renaissance Hotel in Montgomery, Alabama. Plaintiffs who argue Tuberville is ineligible for the governor's office asked the Alabama Supreme Court on Monday to reverse a lower court's dismissal of the case. (Photo by Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Plaintiffs challenging Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville’s candidacy on Monday argued that a lower court erred in dismissing the case.
The 45-page brief filed late Monday morning in the Alabama Supreme Court by Barry Ragsdale, one of the plaintiffs’ attorneys, argued that Alabama’s judicial branch has sole jurisdiction to decide if Tuberville meets the state constitution’s residency requirements to run for governor. 
“Contrary to Sen. Tuberville’s assertion that only the Alabama Republican Party and the State Legislature can review the question of his constitutional eligibility for the office of governor, it is the judiciary that has the sole and exclusive function of adjudicating appellants’ quo warranto action,” the brief said. 
The Reflector left a message Monday afternoon seeking comment from Tuberville’s campaign and legal team.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Tuberville has faced questions on his residency for years. The plaintiffs’ complaint echoes many previously reported media findings, like a homestead exemption in Auburn that Tuberville said he has been on since 2018 but was not added to until mid-2024, and a 2023 Florida driver’s license. 
Tuberville has maintained, through eight months of varying election-related contests and years of questions, that he meets the requirements. The constitution requires candidates for governor and lieutenant governor to reside in the state for “seven years next” prior to a general election. 
Plaintiffs also requested oral arguments, but only if the justices have questions that are not answered in briefs filed this month. 
The lawsuit made its way to the Alabama Supreme Court after a Montgomery County judge dismissed the case in July due to a lack of jurisdiction after an hourslong hearing. The judge did not rule on the merits of the case. 
During the hearing, Tuberville’s lawyers asserted that the Alabama Republican Party and the Alabama Legislature have the authority to decide if the U.S. Senator meets the constitutional requirements for governor. The Alabama Republican Party dismissed a primary election challenge against Tuberville in June. 
The case before the supreme court is not challenging Tuberville’s May primary win. 
“Sen. Tuberville is wrong when he asserts that the Legislature can divest the judicial branch of all jurisdiction to hear and decide Constitutional questions such as that presented in this case,” the brief said. “As the Circuit Court held, appellants ‘aver that they do not contest the validity of the Republican primary election, but rather, seek a judicial determination as to whether Sen. Tuberville as a certified nominee meets the constitutional residency requirement to hold the Office of Governor … Those are distinct inquiries.’”
The plaintiffs in the case are seeking relief known as quo warranto, Latin for “by what authority,” challenging Tuberville’s right to hold office. During the lower court hearing, Tuberville’s attorneys argued that quo warranto relief can only be applied to active public office holders. They said in June that quo warranto could not be applied because Alabama’s primary elections are operated by political parties, not the state. 
Ragsdale argued then, and again in Monday’s brief, that it can be applied to “quasi officers” like Tuberville.
“Of course, appellants don’t dispute that a political party has the right to nominate, but that doesn’t mean that the courts must look the other way when a constitutional challenge is mounted against that nominee,” the brief argued. “Political parties have the right to make choices, but those choices have consequences, and there is accountability for those choices.”
Montgomery County Circuit Judge Brooke Reid struggled during the June hearing and her dismissal because there was not a specific Alabama case that allowed a circuit court to declare a gubernatorial nominee ineligible, especially in relation to quo warranto relief. 
In the Monday brief, plaintiffs argued in the brief that just because the quo warranto option has never been used, does not mean it cannot be. 
“Of course, it is also true that the court has encouraged the use of quo warranto to challenge a candidate’s eligibility to hold office and has never ruled it out as the proper remedy in this context.” the brief said. “Indeed, the cases cited above all strongly suggest that, when properly presented with the question, this court would find that quo warranto applied.”
Tuberville’s lawyers will have until Aug. 21 to file their brief. Plaintiffs will have until Aug. 28 to file a response.
