name: Florida Phoenix
title: It’s Fentrice Driskell vs. Michele Rayner in one of the Legislature’s most competitive primaries
description: One of the most interesting state legislative primaries taking place on Aug. 18 is the race for the state Senate District 16 seat in the Tampa Bay area between Democratic state Reps. Fentrice Driskell and Michele Rayner. The district encompasses the downtowns of two of Florida’ biggest cities — Tampa and St. Petersburg — with […]
text:
Democrats Michelle Rayner and Fentrice Driskell are running in an open primary in state Senate District 16. (Photos via Florida House)One of the most interesting state legislative primaries taking place on Aug. 18 is the race for the state Senate District 16 seat in the Tampa Bay area between Democratic state Reps. Fentrice Driskell and Michele Rayner.
The district encompasses the downtowns of two of Florida’ biggest cities — Tampa and St. Petersburg — with the majority of the seat located on the Hillsborough County side of Tampa Bay.
Driskell is term limited after eight years in the Florida House, the last four as Democratic leader. Rayner was eligible to run for one more term after being elected in 2020 but seized the opportunity to serve in the Legislature’s upper chamber with Sen. Darryl Rouson being term-limited out of office.
The district leans strongly Democratic, and because no Republican has entered the race it is an open primary, meaning that Democrats, Republicans, and independents are all eligible to vote. The primary will determine the winner.
For many Democratic voters, it’s not an easy call.
“I would ask voters to vote for me over my opponent because I believe that this district deserves a fighter who will show up and get the job done,” Driskell said in an interview on WMNF-88.5 FM radio in Tampa. “You know, former state Sen. Janet Cruz used to say she’s a workhorse, not a show horse, and I feel a bit similar.”
“Between our records, I feel like there’s no comparison in terms of the impact and the amount of bills that I’ve gotten passed, the appropriations that I’ve brought home to the district,” Driskell added. “The leadership experience that I have leading this caucus and being someone who has led the fight against the extremism wrought by Ron DeSantis and the Trump administration. I’m ready to serve Day One.”
A civil rights attorney, Rayner makes her case by noting her work representing the family of Markeis McGlockton, an unarmed 28-year-old Black man shot and killed in a Clearwater parking lot after a physical dispute over parking in a handicapped space in 2018. The man who killed McGlockton initially went un-arrested by the Pinellas County Sheriff’s Department after the shooter invoked Florida’s “stand your ground” law. He ultimately was convicted of manslaughter and received a 20-year prison sentence.
“I’ve stood up for our community,” she said Friday during her own interview on WMNF. “One of the very few lawyers along with Benjamin Crump who took on the stand your ground law and won, and so the body of work has been very, very clear from day one. So, I don’t shy away from hard fights.”
She added: “People are tired of Democrats that are just the same. People are tired of folks who don’t represent their values. For the last six years, I’ve worked incredibly hard to make sure that I’ve represented the values of people not just in the district, but also the people of the state of Florida as well.”
About those endorsements
Both candidates have received plenty of top-name endorsements, but Rayner released a press released last month attesting that 22 Democratic House members had endorsed her, about two-thirds of the caucus. That’s despite the fact that Driskell has been the caucus’ leader for four years.
Driskell attributes some of that lopsided support for her opponent to the fact that Rayner entered the race seven months before she did, “so a lot of those endorsements are very old.”
“Once I filed, some of those members co-endorsed me and I happened to know that some of those members actually maybe did not endorse my opponent,” Driskell said. “Maybe she might be overstating some of those.”
Rayner fired back, saying, “There’s a reason that there’s not one Black woman in the House or in the Senate Caucus” backs Driskell. “It’s the lack of being able to work with folks. It’s the lack of being able to be principled.”
Driskell insists that as leader of the caucus, she “chose to put the work of our team first, and did not pressure people into choosing a side when I knew we had to spend months working together for the good of Floridians.”
She continued: “While my opponent is free to express her concerns about my leadership style, which I wholeheartedly dispute, she voted for me to lead twice. And only one of us has spent the last four years working non-stop for the good of the caucus as a whole.”
The Phoenix reached out to some of the House Democrats listed by Rayner as having endorsed her. One of them, Rep. Jervonte Edmonds from West Palm Beach, said he was backing Driskell, not Rayner.
“I have respect for Rayner, but I wholeheartedly endorse my leader,” Edmonds told the Phoenix in a text message.
Broward County Rep. Mike Gottlieb said he has co-endorsed both candidates.
“I have respect and admiration for both,” said Orlando Democratic Rep. Anna Eskamani. “Michele Rayner filed first and had my early support in hopes of preventing a primary so the focus would stay on the general.”
The campaign had mostly run civilly until a political committee called People for Honor Project sent out mailers to voters in the district accusing Rayner of having a “real Republican record.”
That’s despite the fact that the left-leaning Rayner has been labeled Ron DeSantis’ “worst nightmare” and has touted being the first “openly Queer Black woman” to serve in the Florida Legislature.
Rayner suspects the motivation for the mailer is that she voted to oppose a bill last session to regulate data centers (SB 484). The measure would require the Florida Public Service Commission to develop tariffs and service requirements for electric utilities “to reasonably ensure that each large load customer bears its own full cost of service and that such cost is not shifted to the general body of ratepayers.”
Critics (including DeSantis) contended the measure had been watered down, however, because the House ultimately removed a provision restricting local governments from entering nondisclosure agreements involved in potential development of data centers.
The People for Honor Project PAC received a $31,500 contribution from Fort Meade LLC, the company seeking to develop a data center in Lake Meade in Polk County. That’s three times the amount ($10,000) Fort Meade LLC contributed to Byron Donalds PAC for governor.
“It’s interesting that this particular data center gave more to this PAC than they gave to Byron Donalds,” Rayner said. “So, you’re more afraid of me coming into the Legislature than you love Byron Donalds.”
Legislative records
When it comes to legislation passed, Driskell is particularly proud of her work on lost, unrecorded, and abandoned Black cemeteries, improving treatment for people with sickle cell disease, and a bill passed a year after the George Floyd uprisings that created minimum standards training for law enforcement.
Perhaps Rayner’s signature piece of legislation was the 2024 measure prohibiting children under 14 from becoming social media account holders and allows 14- and 15-year-olds to become account holders only with parental consent.
Rayner said she “took some heat” from some Republicans and fellow Democrats for her co-sponsorship of the bill, but believes the fact that other states and now other countries have followed suit showed she was on the right track.
Going into the last week of the campaign, Driskell maintained a fundraising lead. In terms of cash on hand, Driskell had around $118,000 combined left in her main campaign account and her two political committees. Rayner had less than $7,000 in cash on hand in her main campaign account and political committee.
Associated Industries of Florida, which labels itself the “The Voice of Florida Business,” has contributed a total of $40,000 to one of Driskell’s PACs. She recently received $2,500 from Meta Platforms Inc., a California tech company that operates Facebook, Instagram, and Threads.
Among some of Rayner’s most notable contributions to her PAC are $5,000 from Equality Florida Action PAC and $10,000 from Coalition for Better Care PC, chaired by Tallahassee lobbyist David Ramba.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A CT prisoner’s gratitude for education
description: We are not students in the true sense of that word and we are not permitted to fully commit or engage in the educational experience.
text:
I’m a lifelong learner but what does that mean?
I went to school in the usual way, suburban public schools K-12, high school graduate, then I was accepted at the University of Connecticut at age 17 (this was an idiosyncrasy of my age, not an indication of any particular dedication to my studies). 
Upon reflection, I realize that I didn’t really appreciate school during my first try at it. I muddled along as a C-average student for most of that time, never finishing college. Then, at the age of 18, my life was interrupted when I came to prison. In spite of this obstacle, I have never given up on learning, though my path certainly diverged from the traditional.
A little over 15years after I graduated high school I made my second attempt in academia. I applied for and was accepted into the lauded Wesleyan University Center for Prison Education (CPE) program. This program gives its incarcerated students the unique opportunity to engage in a premier liberal arts education.  I’ve heard (and I believe it) that this experience is comparable to what “on campus” students experience in both the breadth of knowledge and comprehension gained, as well as the quality and dedication of the faculty who teach here.
This program gives students the opportunity to earn associate’s and bachelor’s degrees equivalent to those earned by any other college student. These opportunities would not be possible without this program and, perhaps more importantly, the people who run this program. This entire endeavor is run on a shoestring budget with only four full-time faculty serving 20-times that many students across two correctional facilities.
Sadly, for these faculty, theirs is the epitome of a thankless job. Not because we (the incarcerated students) are ungrateful, more so because we can’t be. There is this tenuous, anxiety riven dynamic where the Department of Correction makes it abundantly clear that we (the incarcerated students) are “less.” 
We are not students in the true sense of that word and we are not permitted to fully commit or engage in the educational experience because it can be taken from us (for myriad reasons) at any moment. We cannot engage with the faculty who run our program as coequal collaborators — because we are reminded day-in and day-out that we are not equals. We are prohibited from forming connections with these educators, both the professors who teach the individual courses and those crucial faculty members who keep this program actually running. Again, not by their choosing but, rather, because of archaic rules that prevent us from being treated as worthwhile, sincere participants.
And our faculty embody this pain and this heartache in a way that I don’t even want to begin to imagine. They wear their dedication — to us, to the program, to the very ideals of education — every day they come into these prisons. They cope with self-conscious anguish every time they walk out of these prisons, free, and we return to our cells, unfree.
As an adult learner, as a lifelong learner, I want more.  I want more for myself, for the people in my life, and society writ large. I believe in the ability of education to make us better people — more informed, more critically engaged in our world, and, yes, more compassionate. 
A few years ago when I enrolled at Wesleyan, I was dubious as to the value or the purpose of a liberal arts education. It felt impractical. Through the grace of dedicated professors and even more dedicated program faculty, I have come to appreciate the ability to think for myself and to think with purpose. These skills are a direct product of that education.
To the teachers, professors, teacher’s assistants, and the faculty who support all forms of education, a sincere, heartfelt “thank you.”
To those same educators who support us,  the casual students and the lifelong learners, an apology. I apologize on behalf of myself and my peers.  I apologize for every missed opportunity to tell each of you just how much this education means. I apologize for every time you left the classroom feeling drained or dissatisfied. I apologize if I ever made you doubt your choice to educate. This process isn’t easy. This process is doubly difficult when attempted behind prison walls.
Yet, without you, our dedicated educators, our passionate faculty, we would be lost.
Now, after having read this, you may be under the mistaken belief that the educators in your life are immune from this brand of internalized distress because the schools, colleges, and universities in our state are wholly distinct from the unique challenges of a prison educational environment.  
I’ll suggest that you take pause and contemplate what it takes to educate. What are the stressors that these individuals endure — in and out — of the classroom? And how about the plethora of people behind the scenes, making it all work? What does it truly take to educate?
I wouldn’t trade my education for anything. I wouldn’t trade my educators for anyone. I’m just grateful that there are so many who care so much. Thank you.
Ian T. Cooke is incarcerated at the Cheshire Correctional Institution.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s workforce crisis is hiding in plain sight
description: While employers search for workers, thousands of CT young people remain disconnected from the education and career pathways allowing them to contribute.
text:
Connecticut finds itself at a pivotal moment. Employers across industries continue to report difficulty finding and retaining talent, even as policymakers, business leaders, and educators work to strengthen the state’s workforce pipeline. 
At the same time, Connecticut’s population is aging, competition for skilled workers is intensifying, and the long-term economic health of our state depends on our ability to develop the talent already living in our communities.
Yet one of the most promising workforce solutions receives far less attention than it deserves.
While employers search for workers and communities worry about economic opportunity, thousands of young people across Connecticut remain disconnected from the education, employment, and career pathways that would allow them to contribute. Too often, they are viewed through the lens of challenges and deficits rather than potential, despite representing an enormous source of talent and leadership for our state’s future workforce.
That disconnect should concern all of us because the challenge facing Connecticut is not simply a shortage of workers. It is a failure to fully invest in, develop, and connect the talent that already exists. For too many young people, the path from potential to opportunity remains far less accessible than it should be.
For decades, Our Piece of the Pie has worked alongside young people who are navigating significant barriers on their path to success. Through programs such as Hartford Youth Service Corps and other workforce development, education, and youth leadership initiatives, we have seen firsthand what happens when young people are provided with the support, guidance, and opportunities they need to thrive. Many of the young people we serve have experienced poverty, housing instability, academic challenges, or involvement with the justice system. Some have faced obstacles that would test even the most resilient adult. Yet what I have learned throughout my career is that potential is far more evenly distributed than opportunity.
In my experience, most young people are looking for the same things any of us would want: the opportunity to earn a paycheck, develop skills, support themselves and their families, and feel that their effort has a purpose. Almost always, the challenge is not a lack of ambition or motivation. It is a lack of access to the opportunities many people take for granted, whether that is a first job, a trusted mentor, a professional network, or an employer willing to see possibility instead of risk.
When those opportunities are available, the results can be transformative.
Over the past ten years, Hartford Youth Service Corps, one of OPP’s flagship workforce development programs, has served more than 2,700 young people. Participants have completed more than 640,000 hours of paid work experience, earned nearly $10 million in wages, and contributed to more than 2,000 community service projects across our region. Seventy-three percent secured unsubsidized employment, while thousands more gained the skills, credentials, and workplace experience necessary to pursue long-term career pathways.
Those outcomes are important, but the larger lesson may be even more important.
After years of working with young people, employers, educators, and community partners, I have become convinced that Connecticut is not facing a shortage of youth talent. What we continue to face is a shortage of pathways that connect that talent to opportunity. The workforce many employers are searching for is not somewhere else. In many cases, it is already here.

Connecticut is not facing a shortage of youth talent, but a shortage of pathways connecting that talent to opportunity.

Too often, public conversations about young people focus almost exclusively on what is wrong. We talk about crime, chronic absenteeism, disengagement, mental health challenges, and the growing number of young adults disconnected from both education and employment. These issues are real and deserve serious attention. But when they become the dominant narrative, we overlook an equally important reality: young people consistently rise to the expectations we set for them when they are given meaningful opportunities and the support necessary to succeed.
Over the years, I have met countless young people who had been underestimated long before they entered one of our programs. Some had been told they were not college material. Others carried mistakes from their past that followed them into every room. Many had never been given a meaningful opportunity to demonstrate what they were capable of accomplishing. Yet time and again, when those same young people were connected to real work experiences, caring adults, and high expectations, they flourished. Just as importantly, they began to see the leader that already existed within themselves.
I have watched employers experience a similar shift. Initial skepticism often gives way to enthusiasm once they recognize the value these young people bring to the workplace. The employers who take a chance frequently become some of our strongest partners because they discover something our communities cannot afford to overlook: talent often exists where expectations are lowest.
At a time when workforce shortages remain a pressing concern, Connecticut cannot afford to leave that talent on the sidelines.
The strength of our state will ultimately be measured not only by the businesses we attract or the investments we secure, but by whether people believe they have a pathway to participate in that success. Economic growth that excludes large segments of the next generation is neither sustainable nor consistent with the values we claim to share. If we want a stronger economy tomorrow, we must be willing to invest more intentionally in young people today.
That investment takes many forms. It means expanding access to paid work experiences, strengthening career-connected learning opportunities, building deeper partnerships between employers and youth-serving organizations, and ensuring that workforce development and youth development are viewed as inseparable priorities. When we create those connections, everyone benefits.
The stakes extend far beyond filling open positions. At its core, this is about whether young people can envision a future for themselves here in Connecticut and whether employers, educators, community leaders, and policymakers are willing to help create that future. When young people succeed, businesses gain talent, families gain stability, communities gain leaders, and our economy grows stronger.
The young people we serve are not asking for sympathy. They are asking for an opportunity to contribute; To be empowered. They want the chance to build careers, support their families, and play a meaningful role in the future of the communities they call home.
Connecticut does not need to look very far for its next generation of workers, innovators, entrepreneurs, and leaders. They are already here. The question before us is whether we have the vision and commitment to invest in them.
Hector Rivera is President and CEO of Our Piece of the Pie (OPP).

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Rocky Mount leaders vote to continue utility cutoffs despite deaths, calls for resignations
description: Members of the Rocky Mount City Council voted Monday night against a proposal to halt utility cutoffs after a tense meeting at which angry constituents called for their resignations. The decision came after a family of three and their dogs were found dead in their mobile home last week, shortly after their electricity was cut […]
text:
Residential electric meter (Photo: Douglas Rissing/Getty Images)Members of the Rocky Mount City Council voted Monday night against a proposal to halt utility cutoffs after a tense meeting at which angry constituents called for their resignations.
The decision came after a family of three and their dogs were found dead in their mobile home last week, shortly after their electricity was cut off by the city for lack of payment. The family was reportedly using a generator indoors for power, according to relatives.
About 300 other households have also been disconnected, city officials said at the meeting. State lawmakers of both parties said earlier Monday they’re looking into that decision.
NC lawmakers look into Rocky Mount family’s death after city cut off electricity

Rocky Mount resident Dorothy Cook was the first public speaker of many Monday night to criticize the council.
“Enough is enough. Y’all need to stop it. People don’t need to die in order to survive here in Rocky Mount,” Cook said. ”The evil needs to be stopped.”
Robert Lane said the current council gets the “historical high honor of being the worst group ever elected” to run the city. “I want to ask for your resignations, each one of you. None of you are above the other. If there’s any shame, you should have it in the way you handled our business.”
“When you disconnect a human being’s electricity in the middle of a deadly heat wave, you are not engaging in administrative enforcement. You are issuing a sentence,” said Nehemiah Smith. “When did we start trading an algorithm for common sense? Algorithms don’t know what it means to gasp for air in a darkened, sweltering room.”
Unlike in many North Carolina communities, electricity in Rocky Mount is supplied by a city-owned utility. The utility, which already charges higher prices for power than other utilities, has had problems with billing mistakes and delays that have left some city customers owing thousands of dollars, facing disconnection, and unable to contact the utility by phone for help.
The utility delayed shutting off power for several months, but recently resumed disconnections. City councilmen defended that decision Monday night.
“It is hurtful to know that people lost their lives. It is also true that people intentionally did not pay anything on their utilities, and I’m not speaking about this family because I don’t know the circumstance, but I know the buzz,” said Councilman Reuben Blackwell.
“Since October, November, we told everyone weeks before the cutoff occurred what was going to transpire,” Blackwell said. “We didn’t want to do it, but how do you extend services to some and not to all?”
Blackwell said state regulators had forced the city’s hand in resuming disconnections, including the Local Government Commission and state Auditor Dave Boliek, who’ve been critical of the city’s financial management as they oversee its recovery from near-bankruptcy.
“They told us when we have been subsidizing the cost of utilities, that the people need to pay the cost of utilities, so we had to increase the cost of utilities,” Blackwell said. “What utility system in North Carolina will keep your power on for two months, three months, four months, five months without payment?”
Councilmember Andre Knight said he couldn’t agree to a moratorium without a better understanding of what it might cost the city, especially since an earlier moratorium on disconnections had just ended.
“When the auditor came, he told us what we had to do, and the LGC,” Knight said. “You call the state auditor, the treasurer, and the LGC because if they would have come in and taken over. That’s exactly what they would have done.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Community members demand Colorado issue public health order for ICE tuberculosis case
description: Six weeks after local officials issued a public health order concerning a confirmed active case of tuberculosis at an immigration detention center in Aurora, the private company that runs the facility still has not allowed access for health officials to complete a legally-required investigation. The result is a standoff between state and local government and[...]
text:
Andrea Loya, the executive director of Casa de Paz, speaks in front of the Colorado Capitol on Monday. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)Six weeks after local officials issued a public health order concerning a confirmed active case of tuberculosis at an immigration detention center in Aurora, the private company that runs the facility still has not allowed access for health officials to complete a legally-required investigation.
The result is a standoff between state and local government and a company unwilling to cooperate.
On Monday, community advocates once again called for more pressure from the state government, issuing their own “people’s public health order” at the Colorado Capitol, steps from Gov. Jared Polis’ office.
“We are here to demand that the state health department and the governor’s office do everything in their power, including issuing a state public health order, to hold the GEO Group accountable for their wrongdoing,” Maureen Daly, a retired pediatrician, said.
The GEO Group runs the detention facility for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement as a federal contractor.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Advocates, including Daly, worry that state agencies have not pushed harder against GEO’s obstruction out of fear of litigation. GEO is already suing the state over a new law that gives the state increased health and safety inspection authority.
“I don’t think what The GEO Group will do or will not do should have anything to do with this public health decision,” Daly said. “This should be about protecting the health of the people of Colorado.”
The symbolic people’s order, referring to the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, states that the “inaction and lack of urgency from the Governor’s office and CDPHE have lost our trust.”



Quotation







It’s an unprecedented situation to have a federal contractor not respond to a public health order.


– Jill Hunsaker Ryan, executive director of the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment


It demands access to the facility so health officials can complete a proper investigation into the confirmed tuberculosis case and potential spread of the disease. Community members signed an oversized printout of the order in front of the Capitol. An online version also allows people to endorse it. It states that people recently released from the facility have reported people testing positive for tuberculosis through a skin test.
In various statements to reporters, ICE contends that the infected person was “treated, cleared, and removed from the country” and that there are no other cases in the detention center. GEO determined that 61 people were exposed to the original case and placed in a “precautionary cohort,” according to an oversight report last month from Rep. Jason Crow’s office.
State ‘shut out’
Jill Hunsaker Ryan, the executive director of the CDPHE, listened to speakers and spoke with rally attendees on Monday for about 15 minutes.
“I appreciate the advocates,” she said. “I appreciate what they’re doing today and I understand why they’re concerned.”
Ryan said CDPHE used to have a “collegial” relationship with GEO and could enter the facility to inspect and help with disease control. That changed about six months ago, when she said the company began to “shut out” the state.
“We’ve started with the communication route. We used to work together, so we asked our federal partners … to implore them to work with us again. If that doesn’t work, nothing’s off the table,” she said. “It’s an unprecedented situation to have a federal contractor not respond to a public health order.”
CDPHE set a deadline for GEO to comply with Adam County’s public health order by July 17, but that date passed without consequence. Ryan said that a CDPHE-issued public health order would carry the same authority, and she’s unsure it would force compliance. It would, however, have the enforcement weight of the attorney general’s office behind it.
While speaking with Ryan, community members told her the state should start levying fines on GEO, questioned “where the dam breaks” on the issue, and said they will continue putting pressure on the state until there is a CDPHE public health order.
“If we don’t hold the line on this, what is going to make our government act?” said Andrea Loya, the executive director of Casa de Paz, which supports people recently released from the GEO detention center. “If (tuberculosis) isn’t enough, what will be?”
In a statement, Polis spokesperson Ally Sullivan said the governor’s office is “actively monitoring the situation” and has repeatedly requested information from GEO. She did not answer a question about whether the state worries about possible litigation over a second public health order.
“The state is considering next steps including the option of a public health order should it be necessary,” she wrote. “GEO asserts there is not an active case or an outbreak at the facility, and we hope that is true, but we lack critical information to ensure that is the case. The state will continue to evaluate the public health risk and is asking GEO to work with Adams County Health or CDPHE to promptly resolve this matter.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Pilots killed in Utah crash praised for their service as U.S. firefighter death toll rises
description: Two helicopter pilots who died fighting a Utah forest fire were remembered for their dedication in the face of enormous risks.
text:
The Widemouth 2 Fire burns near Fillmore, Utah, in a photo shared by fire officials on Aug. 10, 2026. (Photo courtesy of inter-agency fire officials via InciWeb)Two pilots who died in a helicopter crash while fighting a Utah forest fire were remembered Monday as skilled aviators dedicated to helping attack massive fires from the skies despite the enormous risk.  
Miles Elliott, of Porterville in southern California, and Christopher Andersen, of Stateline, Nevada, perished after their twin-engine helicopter went down Friday near the Widemouth 2 Fire east of Fillmore. The crash ignited a separate fire in rugged terrain that delayed emergency crews from reaching the pilots until Saturday, authorities said. 
More Utah forests are burning than ever before. Here’s why that matters

Porterville Mayor Greg Meister mourned Elliott’s death in a Monday statement, calling him a hero.
“Miles traveled across our nation fighting wildland fires, putting the lives and safety of others before his own,” Meister said. “It was a life of service and selflessness, and ultimately, he gave his life while protecting others.”
An obituary for Andersen, 64, said his death “came while he was doing work that demanded courage without spectacle: flying toward a dangerous fire to protect people he did not know — and who might never have known the risks he accepted on their behalf,” the post reads. 
The tragedy underscored the dangers of a furious wildfire season that has stretched the nation’s firefighting resources, fanned by scorching summer temperatures and dismal snowpack in the West. And it follows earlier deaths of other firefighters this summer, including that of a man operating a dozer Thursday when the Wrights Spring Fire in Oregon suddenly shifted and blocked his escape route. 
Also calling attention to firefighter safety were the deaths of three members of a “helitack” crew trapped in a burnover incident on the Utah-Colorado border in June, while a fourth later died of the burn injuries. A surviving crew member was hospitalized. 
August isn’t letting up. Whipped by strong winds Monday afternoon, the Rocky Canyon Fire in Morgan and Summit counties forced evacuations of the town of Henefer and has torched more than 13,000 acres, with no containment. 
The Sevier sheriff’s office and a coalition of firefighting agencies noted in a statement on Sunday that an “abnormally dry and warm winter has led to an extremely difficult fire season” and said Friday’s tragedy is another reminder of the difficult work that wildland firefighters and their support crews are asked to carry out. 
“Fatalities such as this land heavily on the minds and hearts of our agencies and the wildland fire community as a whole,” they said. 
A line of firefighters check for hotspots and secure the fire line on the Cottonwood Fire near Beaver, Utah, in a photo shared on Saturday, June 28, 2026. (Photo courtesy of U.S. Forest Service)
The two pilots were flying a Sikorsky Skycrane, a helicopter with powerful engines, the Sevier County Sheriff’s Office said Monday. The pair worked for a company that contracts with the U.S. Forest Service called Helicopter Transport Services. 
The circumstances of the crash have not been made public. The National Safety Transportation Board and the Federal Aviation Administration are investigating. 
Both men were recalled Monday as fixtures of their separate aviation communities who introduced aspiring young pilots to flight and were deeply devoted to their families. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Miles was the kind of friend who would do anything for you, without hesitation or expectation,” said Russell Isom, Porterville’s transportation director, in a statement. Isom recalled how his friend could get a burst of inspiration in the middle of the night and get to work using a computer-programmed manufacturing tool to bring it to life. 
“He was always thinking, creating, and excited about what he could do next,” Isom said. Elliott was also a devoted father of one son and was engaged to be married, Porterville officials said Monday.
Andersen’s obituary, posted on social media by his brother Ric Andersen, described him as “a veteran Army aviator and accomplished civilian helicopter pilot whose 40-year career carried him from the NATO frontier to oil fields in Africa and wildfires around the world.” He was also the chief pilot of the helicopter that crashed Friday, according to that remembrance. 
News reports on Monday also noted Andersen’s great pride in his nieces, nephews, and their young children. 
“For those who loved him, there is profound sorrow in the retirement he had prepared for but did not get to enjoy,” his obituary states. “There is also great pride in the life he did live — one defined by service, mastery of his craft, generosity toward those who followed him and an enduring willingness to place himself in harm’s way so that others might be safer.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: We are still fighting to ban Styrofoam in Alaska
description: This year, Gov. Mike Dunleavy vetoed a bipartisan bill that would have eliminated the use of polystyrene, best known as Styrofoam, in Alaska. We are interns at Alaska Community Action on Toxics, a nonprofit focused on the impacts of toxic chemicals and plastics on people’s health, the environment and Indigenous ways of life. We are […]
text:
A torn Styrofoam cup emerges with other trash from a melting pile of snow on April 26, 2026, in a parking lot by Northern Lights Boulevard in Midtown Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)This year, Gov. Mike Dunleavy vetoed a bipartisan bill that would have eliminated the use of polystyrene, best known as Styrofoam, in Alaska. We are interns at Alaska Community Action on Toxics, a nonprofit focused on the impacts of toxic chemicals and plastics on people’s health, the environment and Indigenous ways of life. We are still fighting to end the use of polystyrene — and we are tired of empty promises from politicians like Dunleavy.
We represent young women, scientists and Native peoples. Our voices are often left out of the conversation, yet we have the most at stake. Repeatedly, older generations tell us: “Sorry for the mess we’ve left you.” However, change can only be accomplished through collective and intergenerational action, and we need all ages to help now.
ACAT’s Environmental Health and Justice Program Director Vi Waghiyi from Savoonga always says: “These are burdens we did not create.” Yet they will greatly interfere with our traditions, identities and abilities to live healthy lives. Our Executive Director, Pamela Miller, also published an op-ed in the Anchorage Daily News about how senseless Dunleavy’s veto of House Bill 25 was.
Now, Alaska is falling behind other states: twelve states already passed statewide legislation to eliminate polystyrene. California, Oregon, Washington and Colorado have banned polystyrene packing peanuts, coolers and other food service products. More than 250 U.S. cities and counties already banned or placed restrictions on polystyrene. Even McDonald’s eliminated its polystyrene packaging in 1990.
Rep. Andy Josephson, D-Anchorage and a supporter of the vetoed bill, emphasized the popularity of such measures on the House floor: “Three-quarters of Americans are concerned about plastic foam litter. Over 70% of Americans would support a national ban on foam food ware.” Several local Alaskan businesses submitted letters of support throughout the session, and the bill had bipartisan support, but this support seems to be futile.
Polystyrene contains the chemical styrene, a probable human carcinogen. Styrene has been linked to impaired nervous system function, increased risk of leukemia and lymphoma cancers, vision and hearing loss, and poor memory and concentration. Chemicals from polystyrene can leach into food and beverages, especially when heated. For example, the heat and acidity in hot coffee trigger chemical leaching from polystyrene cups, then these chemicals are absorbed by the fat in milk or cream, which is easily ingested by humans. Multiple studies in the 1980s found styrene in 100% of the human fat tissues they sampled, and polystyrene production and use has only increased since then. Many Alaskans have likely already experienced health harms from this ubiquitous leaching.
Alaskans rely on land and water for livelihood, nourishment and culture. Nationally, roughly 63% of the commercial seafood harvest is from Alaska. But in the ocean, polystyrene breaks down into microplastics from exposure to sunlight, waves and wind. Studies have detected high levels of microplastics in Alaskan waters, harming wildlife, contaminating ecosystems and threatening the population viability of commercial and subsistence fish. Wildlife often mistake floating foam debris for prey, then eat polystyrene or feed it to their young. This fills their bellies with plastic, causing lack of hunger, starvation and permanent injury. 
Further, polystyrene is effectively not biodegradable: it takes hundreds of years to decompose, if it decomposes at all. High wind and wave action breaks foam blocks into tiny beads that are practically impossible to clean up. This foam travels through waterways, causing harm all over the globe. Over 10 years ago, polystyrene and related materials were found in 23 of 28 beaches sampled throughout the Gulf of Alaska; notably, no beaches were free from debris.  
Alternatives to polystyrene include reusable serviceware, recyclable packaging and compostable products. Materials such as paper, cardboard and plant-based plastics are now common substitutes, and these options are more sustainable for food service providers and consumers alike. Some businesses are voluntarily opting out of polystyrene: Green Alaska Solutions provides plant-based, compostable alternatives for restaurants, businesses and events statewide, including rural villages. Their business partners highlight higher customer satisfaction and loyalty, with up to 15% increases in repeat customers after switching to compostable packaging. 
ACAT and its partners will continue to work with policymakers on legislation to eliminate polystyrene in food packaging. Local businesses in Alaska would save money and avoid penalty fees by acting now to adopt alternatives in anticipation of a state or federal ban. The municipalities of Bethel, Cordova and Seward have already successfully enacted bans on polystyrene food containers. 
To avoid polystyrene in your daily life:

Bring an insulated metal mug for coffee instead of drinking from a hot foam cup — disposable lids are often also made of expanded polystyrene or other plastic. 
Bring a metal container to pack hot food leftovers into instead of polystyrene food containers from restaurants. 
Use shredded paper, perforated cardboard, or newspaper to pack items for shipping or moving instead of foam packing peanuts. 
When renovating or building a structure, choose a non-toxic insulation that does not contain polystyrene.

Our faith in public institutions depends on what those institutions do. 
As we watched this carefully considered, bipartisan bill get dismissed without any convincing public justification, we took away a discouraging message. Years of testimony, scientific evidence and legislative work can be set carelessly aside, even when the proposed solution is reasonable and beneficial. 
We do not want cynicism to be the lesson we take from this experience. We remember fishing, swimming and enjoying clear rivers and oceans free from plastic and pollution. We will continue to fight for these reforms so that our children will too.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington state offers expanded assistance for wildfire victims
description: Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson signed an emergency proclamation Monday to temporarily suspend some state laws in order to fast-track the recovery process from wildfires ravaging central and eastern Washington.  The announcement comes as fires have burned over 700,000 acres in Washington this year, destroying more than 871 homes.  “We’re in for the long haul on[...]
text:
Utility crew vehicles are seen in the background in an a neighborhood that burned in the Spokane fires this month. (Photo via InciWeb)Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson signed an emergency proclamation Monday to temporarily suspend some state laws in order to fast-track the recovery process from wildfires ravaging central and eastern Washington. 
The announcement comes as fires have burned over 700,000 acres in Washington this year, destroying more than 871 homes. 
“We’re in for the long haul on this as a state,” Ferguson said during a press conference in Spokane, where fires that began at the start of the month tore through neighborhoods. “We continue to evaluate what we can do to streamline things for folks.”
The services include expanded cash assistance, housing protections and help with recovering personal identification documents.


A full list of available assistance, including for individuals, businesses and healthcare providers, can be found in the governor’s emergency proclamation.


Individuals, businesses and healthcare providers in seven counties will qualify: Chelan, Ferry, Okanogan, Spokane, Stevens, Douglas and Yakima. The proclamation also covers the Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation, the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation and the Spokane Tribe of Indians. 
What the assistance will cover
Several safety net programs have been expanded and expedited for the thousands of Washingtonians grappling with the 21 large wildfires burning through the state. 
Now, regardless of income, people who lost their home and do not have insurance can apply for the state Individual Assistance Program, which can help with home repairs and temporary housing. The proclamation also bars eviction orders in the covered jurisdictions for the next two weeks. 
Before today, the Family Emergency Assistance Program, was reserved for families with children during a disaster. Now, families without children are also eligible. Cash assistance from this program helps cover basic needs and is normally only distributed once a year. The proclamation allows assistance each month if needed, Ferguson said.
Gov. Bob Ferguson speaks at a Monday press conference to announce the expansion of statewide assistance in response to wildfires. (Photo courtesy of governor’s office)
Unemployment benefits have been expedited for people in affected areas. Those who lost their jobs due to wildfire can receive assistance without waiting the standard week or proving that they are looking for another job. Professionals who carry licenses, such as security guards and real estate agents, are also granted extra time to renew if the deadline was missed due to wildfires. 
And those who lost personal documents in a fire, such as birth certificates or driver’s licenses, can start the process of obtaining new documents without charge starting Tuesday. 
Next steps
Ferguson said this year’s fire season will “unfortunately, potentially be our most disastrous fire season of all.”
On Aug. 1, Ferguson declared a statewide wildfire emergency after the National Weather Service warned of especially dangerous fire conditions. He also issued a statewide ban on outdoor burning. That same weekend, the devastating fires erupted in the Spokane area.
By Aug. 4, the federal government approved Ferguson’s request for an emergency declaration, which opened up federal resources to support response efforts.
Ferguson said the state still plans to apply for a major disaster declaration through the Federal Emergency Management Agency. If granted, it would make further federal aid available. 
It’s a “totally different request” than the already-approved emergency declaration and would unlock “significant financial assistance for individuals and for municipalities,” Ferguson said. 
The application is extensive. The governor’s office hopes to submit it by mid-September.

name: Nevada Current
title: Lombardo declares state of emergency for Washoe fires
description: Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo has declared a state of emergency Monday in several areas across Washoe County and the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony as the Bug and Fred Mountain Fires continue to grow. As of Monday evening, the fires have burned more than 16,000 acres, threatening thousands of homes in areas of Washoe County and the […]
text:
More than 6,000 people have been evacuated due to the wildfires from the area, with thousands more in warning zones as the fire continues to grow. (Washoe evacuation perimeter map Monday afternoon)Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo has declared a state of emergency Monday in several areas across Washoe County and the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony as the Bug and Fred Mountain Fires continue to grow.
As of Monday evening, the fires have burned more than 16,000 acres, threatening thousands of homes in areas of Washoe County and the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony.
More than 6,000 people have been evacuated due to the wildfires from the area, with thousands more in warning zones as the fire continues to grow. 
Buildings and infrastructure have also been impacted by the fires, including schools, power lines, natural gas lines, a water treatment facility, a local airport, and telecommunications sites. 
Evacuation zones are still expanding due to the quick growth of the fires, residents in Washoe County can see the most recent evacuation orders on a state website. 
“Thousands of Nevadans have been forced from their homes as these fires continue to threaten communities across Washoe County and the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony,” said Governor Joe Lombardo. “The state is taking every available step to support local responders, protect lives and property, and ensure the resources necessary to confront these fires are where they are needed most.”
The state of emergency will be in place until August 17 unless conditions improve before then, according to Lombardo’s office. 
The state of emergency comes after Washoe County declared their own local emergency, along with the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony declaring a tribal emergency. 
The Reno-Sparks Indian Colony has established an evacuation center for members at the RSIC Reno Gym located at 34 Reservation Road. Those who need assistance evacuating can call 775-842-2902 or 775-895-9835.
Evacuees who are not members of the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony Tribe can go to an evacuation center set up at Evelyn Mount Northeast Community Center at 1301 Valley Rd. in  Reno. 
On Monday, the Federal Emergency Management Agency also authorized the use of federal funds to assist Nevada in combating the Bug Fire in Washoe County.
The state of Nevada submitted the request Aug. 8, after the fires scorched through 3,000 acres, threatening about 1,800 homes in and around Cold Springs and Silver Knolls. At that point, 4,000 people in the area had already been evacuated. 
The Fire Management Assistance Grant provides federal funding for up to 75% of eligible firefighting costs, and is approved through FEMA to assist combating fires that threaten to become major disasters. 
The funding will help firefighters pay for field camps, equipment use, materials, supplies, and mobilization efforts.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Fired Indiana utility regulator sues governor over his removal
description: Fired state regulator Andy Zay filed a lawsuit to regain his seat on the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission before his former colleagues — and a replacement — vote on whether to reconsider a contentious $71 million rate hike for AES Indiana customers.
text:
Then-Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission Chair Andy Zay answers reporter questions during a break in a daylong utility affordability hearing on March 24, 2026, at the IURC's downtown Indianapolis headquarters. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Fired state regulator Andy Zay filed a lawsuit Monday to regain his seat on the powerful Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission before his former colleagues — and a replacement — vote on whether to reconsider a contentious $71 million rate hike for AES Indiana customers.
Zay also described a pattern of the governor’s office infringing on the commission’s statutory duty as an “impartial fact-finding body.”
The lawsuit comes exactly a week after Gov. Mike Braun abruptly dismissed Zay from the IURC, which plays a key role in determining how much Hoosiers pay for electricity, natural gas, water and other utility services.
The State Personnel Department has accused Zay of several “potential violations” of state policy, but he contends the firing is really about his vote to support the rate increase and for control over what happens next.
Zay fired from utility regulator panel weeks after AES hike demotion

“It is clear that Commissioner Zay’s removal as IURC Commissioner was motivated by a desire to alter the composition of the Commission before final action is taken on the Petition for Rehearing in the AES Rate Proceeding,” the complaint, filed in Marion County Superior Court, reads.
Braun has already appointed a successor, former Indianapolis City-County Councilor Joshua Bain, who began serving effective immediately Thursday.
In addition to Braun and Bain, the complaint names Secretary of Energy and Natural Resources Suzanne Jaworowski, State Personnel Department Director Matthew Brown, and Steve Carter, the deputy counsel for appointments at the governor’s office.
A spokesperson for the governor’s office declined to comment.
Goodwill sours
Braun appointed Zay and two others to the IURC in December, describing the trio as “aligned with Governor Braun’s commitment to making energy affordable for families and businesses.”
Zay, a Republican, resigned from an Indiana Senate seat he’d held for nearly a decade in order to join the commission — as chair — in January.
He launched an affordability inquiry in February, questioning the “big five” investor-owned utilities on their rates in March and holding a listening tour for frustrated ratepayers around the state through April.
But his relationship with Braun and the administration soon soured.
Zay joined Commissioners David Veleta and David Ziegner on June 17 in a 3-1 vote to approve the increase. Commissioner Bob Deig voted in opposition, while a fifth member, Anthony Swinger, recused himself.
Zay’s complaint alleges that Jaworowski called him on June 15, two days before the decision to tell him, “You know affordability is a big deal to this governor” — as well as the day of, to “conve(y) Governor Braun’s disappointment with the outcome.”
Other representatives of the governor’s office told Zay he had “let the governor down” and that they’d “told (him) not to do this” in a meeting he attended later on June 17, according to the complaint.
Story continues below. 
Verified Complaint For Declarato
 
Zay was called into another meeting on June 18 — this time featuring Braun, Chief of Staff Joshua Kelley, Jaworowski and Utility Consumer Counselor Abby Gray, whose office represents ratepayers in IURC matters.
“During that meeting, after discussion concerning utility rates and the AES Rate Proceeding decision, Governor Braun asked Gray, ‘How are we going to fix this?'” Zay’s complaint alleges.
He excused himself from the meeting, believing discussions had crossed into banned “ex parte” communications — seeking to sway a decision-maker in a case without the other parties to the case present.
Zay reported seeking guidance on June 22 from the Office of Inspector General about his ex parte communications and impartiality concerns.
That day, according to the complaint, Jaworowski asked Zay to change the agenda for an upcoming IURC meeting and provide her with an unreleased affordability report. He declined, according to the complaint.
Demotion bleeds into firing
Zay’s complaint alleges that later on June 22, Jaworowski asked him to resign from the IURC, at the governor’s request. When Zay refused, Braun demoted him and elevated Swinger to the chairmanship.
In July, Gray petitioned the IURC to reconsider the AES Indiana increase or rehear the case, in accordance with Braun’s wishes.
Last Monday — days before the IURC was scheduled to vote on the petition — Zay was fired. The vote was called off.
In his complaint, Zay recounts how Brown and Carter came to his office and attempted to interview him. When he declined to participate without a lawyer present, they “told Commissioner Zay that he could resign or he would be fired.”
Zay declined. They handed him a letter, already signed by Braun, immediately removing him from the commission.
The letter fired regulator Andy Zay received when he refused to resign, according to his legal complaint. (Screenshot from lawsuit)
Commissioners are appointed to four-year terms and can only be dismissed “for cause” under Indiana law.
The lawsuit asserts Zay wasn’t provided with any reasons for his firing or given a chance to respond to any allegations before he was forced to collect his personal belongings from his office and was escorted from the building.
“Zay was discharged from employment with the State of Indiana today, August 3, 2026, for non-adherence to state policies and laws related to his role as Commissioner at the IURC,” SPD spokesman Kirollos Barsoum said in an email to the Capital Chronicle the night of his dismissal.
More specifically, Barsoum said he was dismissed for “multiple potential violations of state policy; including failing to file a required financial disclosure after his removal as Chair, improperly awarding payments and personal gifts to employees, and directing staff to alter a public meeting agenda without consulting the new Chair.”
Asked why alleged violations were framed as “potential,” Barsoum only said his previous statements “provid(e) the factual basis for the discharge,” adding, “No additional information is available regarding this matter.”

Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



In his complaint, Zay responded that he didn’t have to file an additional financial disclosure after his demotion and that payments to employees were made with approval from SPD and Jaworowski.
Records obtained by the Capital Chronicle show that the IURC’s 64 employees each received $900 bonuses on May 9. A spokesperson for the commission didn’t respond to a request for comment on the justification for the bonuses, while SPD didn’t respond to questions on its approval of the bonuses or for spot bonus guidance directed to agencies.
Zay also reported that he used his own money to give IURC staff $8 Starbucks gift cards on their birthdays.
Additionally, while he didn’t direct any staffers to put any particular item on an agenda — and that it was staff alone who put the AES Indiana petition on last week’s meeting schedule — Zay said he wasn’t aware of any policy requiring the chair’s approval to put anything on an agenda.
Lawsuit’s goals
Zay alleged the real reason for his firing was political, pointing to the governor’s comments to reporters in the days after.
“Nothing else to announce there other than I was disappointed that he didn’t take on affordability and holding utilities accountable,” Braun said last week.
Asked what led to the firing, and if he asked Zay to resign beforehand, he replied, “No, it was from the very beginning, when it was clear I was looking for folks (who are) ratepayer-conscious, and the first thing out of the gate was granting a big increase — and that was not part of the interview. … If you don’t have staff, people working with you in the same mindset, it’s better to find somebody that does.”
Zay wants his seat on the IURC back immediately. He also asked the court to stop Bain from taking over the spot or exercising any commissioner powers until the lawsuit is settled.
“Each matter heard, considered, voted upon, or decided by the Commission during Commissioner Zay’s exclusion constitutes an exercise of governmental authority in which Commissioner Zay is prevented from performing the duties of his position,” his complaint reads.
It asserts that, even if Zay wins the lawsuit, no amount of money in damages will make up for the decisions he’ll be excluded from if he’s left off the IURC while the lawsuit is pending.
“If the IURC acts upon the Petition for Rehearing while Commissioner Zay remains excluded and Bain occupies his seat, the Petition will be considered and voted upon by a Commission whose composition was unlawfully altered by Governor Braun,” the complaint reads.

name: VTDigger
title: A traffic stop, a deportation and a test of Vermont’s Fair and Impartial Policing Policy
description:
Records show a sheriff’s deputy used his personal phone to summon federal agents — then offered to buy them Subway.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A traffic stop, a deportation and a test of Vermont’s Fair and Impartial Policing Policy.
text:
A protest by Migrant Justice at the Chittenden County Sheriff’s Department in South Burlington in December 2019. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

A Chittenden County sheriff’s deputy is under investigation for violating Vermont’s Fair and Impartial Policing Policy by calling U.S. Border Patrol to a Franklin County traffic stop that ended in an area farmworker being deported.
The internal investigation could test the limits Vermont places on cooperation between local police and federal immigration authorities. State policing policy generally bars officers from sharing someone’s location or vehicle information with federal immigration authorities unless there is a safety risk and state or local officers cannot provide urgent assistance.
“We have fought hard to create Vermont’s Fair and Impartial Policing Policy and have celebrated its implementation in this state,” Cristian Santos of Migrant Justice, an immigrant rights group, said. “We will not allow this to be swept under the rug: we demand justice for Alex and for an end to police collaboration with deportation agencies.”
Genri “Alex” Jimenez, 22, had worked on Franklin County dairy farms for about two years before he was detained during the July 19 traffic stop by sheriff’s deputy Sgt. Scott Costella, according to Migrant Justice. Jimenez spent nearly three weeks in federal immigration detention in Vermont, New Hampshire and Louisiana before being deported to Mexico, Migrant Justice confirmed on Monday.
The sheriff’s office “is conducting an internal review into the matter to determine if the actions taken during the reported incident were consistent with the agency’s Fair and Impartial Policing Policy,” Sheriff Dan Gamelin said in a complaint filed with the Vermont Criminal Justice Council.
Gamelin referred his deputy to the council’s Professional Regulation Subcommittee after Migrant Justice obtained records of the encounter and questioned whether Costella’s actions complied with the policy. 
“A man who was living and working in this state has been separated from his partner and his family. That is serious, and I am not going to talk around it,” Gamelin said in a press release from the Sheriff’s Office. “We turned over what we had, and we did not hold back the uncomfortable parts. That is what accountability looks like at the front end, before anyone knows how the story ends.”
A message left for Costella’s attorney on Monday, asking for comment, was not immediately returned. 
Migrant Justice alleges Costella summoned Border Patrol without first seeking state or local backup, and without identifying a specific threat that would qualify for the policy’s safety exception.
“It appears that there’s an effort on behalf of the department to justify these actions and square them within what is permitted under the policy,” Lambek said. “But, that falls apart very quickly once you look at what actually happened, and by any objective measure, there is no articulated risk of physical injury to Sergeant Costella that would justify his information sharing with Border Patrol.”
Records obtained by Migrant Justice and shared with news organizations show that Costella’s explanation for calling Border Patrol changed after the county’s internal legal review. Costella’s initial account cited the remote location, the impending tow of the vehicle and his uncertainty about its occupants. 
The final version described Border Patrol as “officer safety backup” and added that Costella was “unsure how they would react,” apparently referring to the occupants of the stopped vehicle.
“I had requested a USBP agent for officer safety backup as I was out with two individuals, on a back country road, knowing that the vehicle was subsequently getting towed and unsure of how they would react, and I still do not know the history or circumstances involving the occupants of the vehicle,” Costella wrote in a statement to Migrant Justice.
‘Need one of you’
On July 19, Costella stopped a Chevrolet Spark on Potato Hill Road in Berkshire after noticing it did not have a front license plate. Anthony Cruz-Morales, who had recently purchased the vehicle, was driving. Jimenez was in the passenger seat.
According to Costella’s statement, state police dispatch had informed him that the vehicle registration had expired. Costella also said he confirmed by phone that the vehicle was not registered.
During the stop, Costella retrieved his personal cellphone and texted a group of Border Patrol agents, according to records obtained by Migrant Justice. “Potato hill rd on stop,” he wrote, followed by, “Need one of you.”
Dashcam footage allegedly shows Scott Costella, a member of the Chittenden County Sheriff’s Office, at the detention of Genri “Alex” Jimenez. Screenshot
Two Border Patrol agents arrived about 15 minutes later. As they detained Jimenez, Costella assisted them in holding and handcuffing him, according to Migrant Justice’s review of body camera and dash camera footage. Costella then turned off his body camera for several minutes while speaking with the Border Patrol agents. After Jimenez was taken away, Costella texted the agents and offered to get lunch for them at Subway.
In his statement, Costella denied that his actions were based on the race or gender of Jimenez and Cruz-Morales.
“Until walking up to the vehicle on the passenger side for the initial approach, I was not aware of how many individuals were in the vehicle, male or female, or what race they were,” Costella said.
This is not the first time a deputy in the Chittenden County Sheriff’s Office has faced allegations of violating the state’s policing policy.  
In 2023, the Chittenden County Sheriff’s Office paid a $25,000 settlement to an immigrant farmworker, after another deputy called Border Patrol during a 2019 traffic stop that resulted in his deportation.
The Criminal Justice Council can investigate alleged professional misconduct by Vermont law enforcement officers. Gamelin’s complaint asks the council to review whether Costella’s actions amounted to a violation of agency policy. The sheriff’s office is conducting its own review, and neither investigation has reached a conclusion.
The policing policy was put in place, Lambek said, to place a “firm barrier” between local police and federal deportation agencies.
“Simply put, Vermont police should not be in the business of deportations,” Lambek said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC lawmakers look into Rocky Mount family’s death after city cut off electricity
description: North Carolina state lawmakers are asking Rocky Mount officials for answers after a family of three was found dead in their mobile home not long after their electricity was cut off due to an unpaid bill. The family was reportedly using a generator in the home, according to relatives. Assistant city manager C J. Jordan […]
text:
Electric utility meter (Photo: Getty Images)North Carolina state lawmakers are asking Rocky Mount officials for answers after a family of three was found dead in their mobile home not long after their electricity was cut off due to an unpaid bill. The family was reportedly using a generator in the home, according to relatives.
Assistant city manager C J. Jordan told Newsline Monday the investigation is still ongoing and the state medical examiner has not yet released an official cause of death for Kenny, Tracey and Mahala Swann. The three were found dead on Aug. 3.
Relatives told local news outlets that the Swanns offered the city utility a partial payment to try to avoid having their power cut off, but city policy requires full payment or a plan to pay the entire balance within three months to prevent disconnection, so the city refused the family’s offer.



Quotation







Don't forget to add quote


– N.C. Sen. Natalie Murdock, D-Durham


Sen. Natalie Murdock said hearing about the tragedy “honestly gave me chills.”
Murdock, D-Durham, and Sen. DeAndrea Salvador, D-Mecklenburg, filed a bill earlier this year that would ban utility companies from shutting off power for nonpayment during periods of high heat.
“I would hope that we would dream of a world where no one dies simply because they’re behind on their energy bill,” Murdock said. “That’s just not acceptable.”
Senate Bill 1027 was never given a hearing by Republican legislative leaders, and no Republicans signed onto the measure.
Unlike in many North Carolina communities, electricity in Rocky Mount is supplied by a city-owned utility. The utility, which handles water, gas and trash as well as power, already charges higher prices than other utility service providers. It has had problems with billing mistakes and delays that have left some city customers owing thousands of dollars, facing disconnection, and unable to contact the utility by phone for help.
The utility delayed shutting off power for several months, but recently resumed disconnections.
A federal program known as LIHEAP — the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program — is available to help low-income people pay their utility bills. But Murdock said the program is cumbersome for people to navigate, and its funding has been reduced under the Trump administration. She said the Swanns’ case illustrates the growing need for help.
“When you simply do not have the money when it is extremely cold or extremely hot, and you have these cut-offs, it could literally cost people their lives,” Murdock said. “Now you have three human beings who are no longer with us.”
Rep. Allen Chesser, R-Nash, represents part of Rocky Mount. He declined to be interviewed for this story, but said in a statement he’s been in contact with city leaders about the deaths.
“The investigation is ongoing so I will resist the urge to speculate before it is complete,” Chesser said, adding that his prayers are with the Swann family.
Chesser said Rocky Mount’s city manager and mayor have told him they are “in the process of reviewing how residents actually experience the utility billing process — not just what the written policy provides, but whether a customer in trouble can reach a person, understand their options, and get on an arrangement in time for it to matter.”
“They’re evaluating their procedures against best practices to build in more flexibility where it’s needed, and my office will be following up to check on the progress,” Chesser wrote.
Sweating that next electric bill? NC Senate Democrats say these bills could help.

Murdock said she doesn’t understand why the family’s attempt to make a partial payment wasn’t enough to forestall disconnection.
“We know that there are folks that are operating in good faith. They simply don’t have it,” Murdock said. “They’re making decisions between buying groceries, paying for their medication, paying for increased healthcare, or skipping debt because they know they have a power bill that they can’t afford.”
“When you get to where bills are $1,000 plus in arrears, you’ve got to work with folks because it will take them a long time to dig themselves out of that hole,” she added.
In the meantime, Murdock said she plans to follow up with the city and utilities to look for solutions to the larger problem of rising energy bills in a state that experiences hotter summers every year.
“I will be going directly to the utility, following up with these co-ops to see what can be done, and that includes Duke Energy, I will be asking them what else can we do to assist low-income ratepayers that just simply cannot afford to keep up,” Murdock said. “We just can’t leave them hanging.”

text:
The Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing oversees nursing homes and licensing boards in the state of Iowa. (Photo via Getty Images; logo courtesy of the State of Iowa) An Iowa nursing home administrator has been fined by state regulators for failing to report a 2019 criminal conviction to licensing authorities.
The Iowa Board of Nursing Home Administrators recently charged administrator Brian Douglas Reindl with failure to notify the board within 30 days of a criminal conviction. According to the board, Reindl was working in both Iowa and Minnesota care facilities when the offense occurred seven years ago.
The board has not disclosed the nature of the criminal offense, other than to say that on Oct. 11, 2019, it resulted in a conviction for an unspecified misdemeanor offense in Minnesota.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Minnesota state records indicate that on July 2, 2019, sheriff’s deputies responded to a complaint at Pioneer Memorial Care Center in Erskine, Minnesota.  Reindl, the facility’s administrator at the time, had allegedly entered the office of the director of nursing while she was on break and refused to leave after being asked to do so.
The director of nursing alleged that when she attempted to leave the office, Reindl used his body to hold the door shut and only allowed her to leave after she indicated she was going to call the police. She alleged that she then entered the office of a third employee, locked the door, and called board members for the facility.
Reindl was charged with one count of misdemeanor harassment and one count of misdemeanor assault in the fifth degree, and a no-contact order was issued in the case.
According to the Minnesota Board of Nursing Home Administrators, Reindl’s employment at the home ended the next day, and he later pleaded guilty to a charge of assault causing fear and was placed on probation for one year. Several months later, in 2020, the Minnesota board issued an order of corrective action against Reindl, requiring him to complete six hours of educational training on professional conduct.
The Iowa Board of Nursing Home Administrators recently agreed to settle its case against Reindl with a $500 civil penalty and a requirement that he complete three hours of educational training on ethics.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Reindl for comment.

name: WyoFile
title: Weiser Knoll Fire explodes on South Pass, quickly becoming Wyoming’s largest wildfire of 2026
description:
The fast-moving blaze prompted evacuations and chewed through dozens of square miles of sagebrush-steppe and pinyon juniper in its first 24 hours.
The post Weiser Knoll Fire explodes on South Pass, quickly becoming Wyoming’s largest wildfire of 2026 appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A wind-driven blaze tore downslope across the Wind River Range foothills Sunday and Monday, quickly chewing up enough acreage to become Wyoming’s largest wildfire of the year.
The Weiser Knoll Fire ignited on Sunday afternoon due to a mechanical fire on a trailer being towed, Fremont County Fire Protection Chief Ron Wempen told County 10 News. Within hours, the blaze was throwing up a smoke column and quickly burning through sagebrush and grasslands on South Pass — and it didn’t let up once darkness fell. 
“It burned fairly active all night,” said Jerod DeLay, Wyoming’s fire management officer. “There was some pretty extreme fire behavior yesterday, with the dry fuels and the wind and low humidity.” 
The Weiser Knoll Fire started Aug. 9, 2026, southeast of Lander and by Monday afternoon had grown to more than 13,000 acres. (InciWeb)
Trying to keep the fire west of Twin Creek Road, wildland fire crews conducted controlled fire operations and “for the most part were successful,” DeLay said. 
As of midafternoon Monday, the fire perimeter also remained confined to an area east of Wyoming Highway 28 and south of U.S. Highway 287, according to Fremont County Emergency Management Coordinator Milan Vinich.
Nevertheless, the Weiser Knoll Fire’s estimated acreage grew dramatically over its first 24 hours and reached 13,350 acres with no official containment by 3 p.m. on Monday. Winds gusted to 41 mph in nearby Lander that afternoon, and a Red Flag warning — which means there are “critical fire conditions” — remains in effect until 9 p.m. Tuesday, increasing the likelihood for growth. 
A Fremont County evacuation order remains in place for the Twin Creek drainage and portions of South Pass.

A helicopter drops water on the Weiser Knoll Fire.  (Sequeil Lozier/U.S. Wildland Fire Service)

The new U.S. Wildland Fire Service is taking the lead on the fast-growing wildfire, trying to extinguish it with a “type 3” incident management team. An estimated 85 personnel committed to the 21-square-mile blaze and a handful of aircraft have also assisted, including multiple helicopters and large and small fixed-wing air tankers. 
Wyoming State Forestry also dispatched its new Lander-based wildland firefighting team to help combat the Weiser Knoll Fire. The team was diverted from the 443-acre Bare Fire in the Wyoming Range, DeLay said. 
In the hours after the conflagration began, engines from all over Fremont County swarmed on South Pass to try to tamp down the fast-moving front of flames. 
“You had Jeffrey City, Lander, Hudson and Fremont County battalions 1, 4, 5, 12, 3, 9, and 10 on it,” Vinich told WyoFile. “BLM, U.S. Forest Service and BIA engines were also involved.” 
Wyoming so far in 2026 has mostly dodged the massive wildfires that have plagued other parts of the intermountain West. Neighboring Utah has already broken its state record for wooded and forested acres burned, the gargantuan 550,0000-acre Big Grass Fire is burning along the Oregon-Idaho state line and year-to-date acreage burned across the country is more than 50% above average and the most in at least a decade, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.
Wyoming has had an active year, too. But the Weiser Knoll Fire is the largest incident of the year, surpassing Sheridan County’s Lumin Fire, which was extinguished in late July.
“We’ve been pretty successful this year,” DeLay said. “Most of the fires have been one, two or three day events, so we’ve been pretty fortunate that way.”
