A news release Monday said the action followed restrictions put in place by Lake County and the Confederated Salish and Kootenai […]
text:
Campfire illustration (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan).Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks said Stage 1 fire restrictions are in place on land it manages in Lake County.
Those places include state parks, fishing access sites, wildlife management areas and other areas.
A news release Monday said the action followed restrictions put in place by Lake County and the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes.
“Under Stage 1 fire restrictions, campfires are generally prohibited unless an exemption is in place,” the news release said.
The news release outlined the following details:

FWP sites in Lake County are exempt because campfires are only allowed in steel fire grates provided at those locations.
Outside of those fire rings, campfires are not allowed at those sites.
Smoking is limited to enclosed vehicles or buildings, developed recreation sites, or areas at least 3 feet in diameter that are cleared of all flammable materials.
Cooking is permitted on liquid petroleum gas or propane stoves that can be turned off.

FWP has already implemented Stage 1 restrictions in Big Horn, Phillips, Wheatland, Roosevelt and Richland counties.
Additional updates on closures and restrictions can be found here. The agency said more information about wildfire prevention is available here.
It said restrictions will be in place at FWP sites until further notice.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Much of New Mexico’s tribal, pueblo land ripe for geothermal power, energy leader tells lawmakers
description: The majority of New Mexico’s tribe, nation and pueblo land could be ripe for exploring geothermal energy, an energy expert told a panel of state lawmakers Monday.
text:
Located in Lordsburg, Lightning Dock is the only utility scale geothermal power plant in New Mexico. (BLM New Mexico via Flickr)The majority of New Mexico’s tribe, nation and pueblo land could be ripe for exploring geothermal energy, an energy expert told a panel of state lawmakers Monday.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rebecca “Puck” Stair, the New Mexico Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Department’s Energy Conservation and Management Division director, spoke before the interim Indian Affairs Committee in Shiprock about the potential for the state’s Indigenous populations to harness the heat beneath the ground as a form of energy.
The state’s largest electric provider, PNM, has already tapped into a southern New Mexico geothermal plant that uses the heat beneath the earth’s crust to create steam, turn turbines and generate electricity.
Stair’s presentation to the committee focused on the advantages of geothermal energy — such as its renewable nature and its relatively low water demand — and said tribal leaders could consider investing in the technology not just to generate electricity, but potentially to sell excess energy or to strengthen New Mexico’s outdated power grid.
“If you’re using geothermal, the heat beneath our feet to generate electricity, that’s wonderful,” Stair told lawmakers. “It could offer electricity revenues to tribes…it’s clean energy, and that’s in alignment with a lot of tribal values.”
State leaders have increasingly eyed geothermal energy alongside renewables such as wind and solar as deadlines approach to comply with the landmark Energy Transition Act’s renewable energy goals. The ETA, which Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham signed in 2019, requires that utilities use 50% renewable energy by 2030, 80% by 2040 and 100% by 2045.
A 2025 report from Project InnerSpace, New Mexico Tech and the New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources found that “a significant amount of Tribal land sits on top of some of the best subsurface heat.” In addition to generating jobs and revenue on Native lands, the technology could also help Indigenous communities achieve “enhanced energy sovereignty,” the report said.
One state lawmaker at Monday’s hearing spoke along similar lines.
Rep. Patricia Roybal Caballero (D-Albuquerque) said she would like to see leaders in New Mexico’s 23 tribes, nations and pueblos work together and collectively benefit from the technology.
“I am proposing — and have proposed — that they come together and pool their resources and create their own geothermal development group,” Roybal Caballero, a member of the Piro Manso Tiwa Indian Tribe, Pueblo of San Juan de Guadalupe, said. “It’s natural heat coming from our natural earth, and it belongs to us.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC candidates for US Senate clash over diversity programs in final days of campaign sprint
description: WEST COLUMBIA — As candidates sprint to make their pitches to voters ahead of the special Senate election Tuesday, questions over what qualifies as diversity, equity and inclusion have emerged as a central issue. Ten candidates are running to replace U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham as the Republican nominee on the November ballot following the longtime […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham makes her case to voters at a Lizard's Thicket in West Columbia, S.C., on Monday, Aug. 10, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)WEST COLUMBIA — As candidates sprint to make their pitches to voters ahead of the special Senate election Tuesday, questions over what qualifies as diversity, equity and inclusion have emerged as a central issue.
Ten candidates are running to replace U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham as the Republican nominee on the November ballot following the longtime senator’s unexpected death last month.
Usually, candidates have months, sometimes years, to fundraise and make their cases to voters. For this election cycle, they had weeks.


What to know before voting
Polls open at 7 a.m. and close at 7 p.m. If you’re standing in line at 7 p.m., you’ll get to vote.
People who voted in the June 9 Democratic primary are not eligible to vote in this primary.
A runoff, if necessary, will take place Aug. 25.
If you’re unsure about your polling location, click here.
To see what your ballot will look like before you go, click here.
To see our election coverage, click here.


Candidates include Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, who was sworn into the seat days after his death. She’s running for a full term with President Donald Trump’s endorsement, which is coveted in a state that has voted overwhelmingly for Trump every time he’s run.
Graham, who has never run for public office, is up against candidates with much more political experience, including U.S. Reps. Ralph Norman and Russell Fry, as well as former Gov. Mark Sanford, who spent a cumulative dozen years in Congress.
Also on the ballot is Danny Ford II, son of Clemson’s first football national championship coach, who ran unsuccessfully for commissioner of agriculture earlier this year.
The state Republican Party initially decertified Ford for violating a new party rule that requires candidates vote in two of the last three GOP primaries. Ford sued, arguing the rule violated the state constitution.
After a Richland County judge ordered the State Election Commission to put Ford back on the ballot, the GOP party appealed to the state Supreme Court. The state’s highest court allowed Ford to stay on the ballot.
The decision was because of logistical confusion, since early voting had already begun, not because justices agreed with the lower court, the order emphasized. The case is expected to continue regardless of whether Ford makes it to the runoff.
Nearly 62,000 people cast their ballots during three days of early voting last week, and another 745 had voted absentee as of Monday, according to the State Election Commission.
Final jabs
Tensions ignited between Graham and Fry, who was widely expected to receive the president’s endorsement, in the final days of campaigning. Fry accused Graham of supporting diversity, equity and inclusion efforts during her time as executive director of the Commission for the Blind, which Graham said were actually programs meant to help blind people.
Fry’s campaign pointed to an annual report from 2020 that said the agency made changes “to develop a culture of diversity and inclusion.” Last year’s report makes no mention of similar initiatives.
But Fry’s campaign used the issue to question whether Graham was actually as supportive of conservative priorities as she’s telling voters.
“Bless her heart — Darline Graham is playing political chameleon, changing her colors and pandering to whatever audience is in the room,” Fry’s campaign spokeswoman, Kayla Lott, said in a news release.
The commission was helping find blind people jobs, not hiring employees just because of their race, gender or sexuality, which is often the concern among opponents of diversity, equity and inclusion programs, Graham said during a campaign stop Monday.
“We helped blind people find jobs, go to work, so that they didn’t have to rely on the government, saving taxpayer dollars,” Graham told about two dozen people at a Lizard’s Thicket. “How do you attack me for supporting transgender (people) for that?”
Fellow Republicans Trey Gowdy, a former Upstate congressman, and U.S. Sen. Tim Scott jumped to Graham’s defense as well, sparking a GOP vs. GOP debate over what DEI — diversity, equity and inclusion — actually means.
US Sen. Lindsey Graham remembered by his ‘beloved’ South Carolina: ‘He was us’

Gowdy and Scott, who were among speakers at her brother’s funeral, suggested helping people with disabilities enter the workforce doesn’t raise the same concerns as initiatives to balance race and gender in a university or company.
“If you are actually supporting blind folks in your job, I would not conflate that with DEI, personally,” Scott said on his Sunday Night in America show on Fox News.
Graham has also faced criticism for her lack of political experience.
The other frontrunners stress she’s unproven beyond the votes she’s taken in the last few weeks and bills she’s signed onto that her brother co-sponsored.
“I’ve got a record people can look up, no guessing needed,” Norman, a former legislator first elected to Congress in 2016, said in a statement. “I walk the walk.”
Norman, a member of the U.S. House’s hardline Freedom Caucus, has positioned his campaign as the most conservative in the field.
While taking a job at the Trump-endorsed candidate, Fry touts he’s the one who’s voted to pass legislation supporting Trump’s agenda.
“I didn’t inherit a record. I earned it,” Fry said during the state GOP debate last week. Like Norman, Fry is also a former state House representative. He was first elected to Congress in 2022 with Trump’s backing.
Graham said Monday her lack of previous political experience is a positive, saying “people want a fresh change.”
She has led the Commission for the Blind, an agency with 110 direct employees, for seven years.
“I bring experience to the table,” Graham said. “I’m just not a politician.”
Hilda Barnwell, a retired respiratory therapist who came to Graham’s stop at Lizard’s Thicket in West Columbia on Monday morning, said she sees the senator’s lack of political experience as a reason to support her.
“I think it’s time for a change, to maybe not send someone to Washington that’s a career politician,” Barnwell said.
The 78-year-old Columbia resident long supported Lindsey Graham, she said. He wrote her grandson a letter of support for West Point, the nation’s military academy, and they stayed in touch after that.
But Barnwell hopes his sister’s priorities might stick closer to home. Graham, who traveled the world, had just returned from a visit to war-torn Ukraine when he died.
Darline Graham has said she would concentrate more on pocketbook issues. She used to urge her brother to talk more about “what matters to the average person,” such as the cost of healthcare, gas and groceries, she told Sean Hannity during a Fox News interview.
Her opponents have said the same. Asked during a debate last week how they’d chiefly differ from the late senator, all four Republicans on stage — Fry, Norman, Sanford and Upstate businessman Mark Lynch — said they’d focus more on spending and affordability here at home rather than foreign policy. Graham was in Washington during that debate.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Cassidy abandons yet another principled stance with backing of Blanche
description: There was a near total lack of passion when Sen. Bill Cassidy delivered a floor speech Friday at the U.S. Capitol to declare he would support the nomination of Todd Blanche as U.S. attorney.  “I’ll be criticized for this vote. What’s new?” Cassidy deadpanned as began his conclusion, having seldom looked up from his written […]
text:
Louisiana Republican U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy talks with reporters in the Dirksen Senate office building on Wednesday, Dec. 3, 2025. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)There was a near total lack of passion when Sen. Bill Cassidy delivered a floor speech Friday at the U.S. Capitol to declare he would support the nomination of Todd Blanche as U.S. attorney. 
“I’ll be criticized for this vote. What’s new?” Cassidy deadpanned as began his conclusion, having seldom looked up from his written comments on the lectern during his six-minute-plus address. 
It wasn’t until his final sentence that the outgoing Republican’s stoic façade broke.
“But the people of Louisiana can be assured I worked hard to make the right decision” Cassidy said as his lips quavered, with clipped pauses every few words, before leaving the Senate floor. 
The moment capped a routine that’s become characteristic of Cassidy’s tenure in Congress while President Donald Trump has occupied the White House: Take a principled stance against executive power, follow it with capitulation, then provide a confounding explanation as to why you did what you did.
This pattern has changed little since Cassidy suffered a crushing re-election defeat in May, failing to advance from the Republican primary. That outcome was all but assured in 2021 after the senator from Baton Rouge boldly voted to convict Trump in his impeachment trial for the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. 
Even with that writing on the wall, Cassidy’s campaign did its utmost to paint the incumbent as a loyal subject kneeling at the throne of Trump. Voters weren’t swayed. U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow, with the president’s endorsement, and state Treasurer John Fleming, running a largely self-financed effort, advanced to the runoff, where Letlow prevailed.   
Just days after his primary loss, Cassidy joined three other Republicans to provide the deciding vote in support of a resolution to limit Trump’s powers to engage in war with Iran. He had voted against the measure seven times previously.
Some thought this signaled a new, defiant Bill Cassidy, intent on providing more resistance against Trump’s unchecked powers. But before and since the May vote on the Iran war, Cassidy has fallen in line with much of the president’s agenda. 
The die was cast with Cassidy’s committee vote in January 2025 to clear the way for Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to become the nation’s top public health official. The senator, who’s a physician, backed Trump’s nominee despite railing against RFK Jr.’s anti-vaccine views and his affinity for conspiracy-theory medical advice.
More recently, Cassidy gave his nod to Sean Kaufman as assistant U.S. health secretary in charge of preparedness and response. The senator previously had concerns about confirming Kaufman over his past statements that called vaccine safety into question, including the repeatedly disproven link between vaccines and autism.
“Mr. Kaufman has said some pretty stupid things and irresponsible things regarding immunization. He has owned up to that in his conversations with me,” Cassidy said after advancing Kaufman’s nomination July 30.
Once again, a seemingly firm Cassidy stance crumbled under pressure no one would think still exists given his lame-duck status.
As for his vote to confirm Blanche, Cassidy offered what could be considered valid reasoning. He said he had spoken personally with two of Louisiana’s federal prosecutors — Trump appointees David Courcelle and Kurt Wall — and former Trump AG Bill Burr. All told him Blanche has brought stability to the U.S. Department of Justice during his time as its interim leader, according to the senator. 
But Cassidy totally muffled the already-muted trumpet he blew for Blanche in his milquetoast speech with his closing declaration: “I’ll be criticized for this vote. What’s new?”
It’s not that Cassidy isn’t capable of a passionate argument for a cause he backs. Just two days before the Blanche vote, he delivered an energetic, impassioned appeal for support from the floor for his bill to ensure Social Security’s solvency, complete with the clever visual aids he’s turned to in the past.
In contrast, Cassidy could barely muster a pulse to deliver his speech in support of Blanche. It was not so much of an endorsement for the attorney general as it was an acknowledgement from the senator that he would once again disappoint anyone clinging to the slim hope he might dare once more to stand up to Trump.
As recently as last month, Cassidy had been critical of Blanche for furthering the president’s plans to create a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund and possibly shielding the Trump family from any tax-law repercussions should they run afoul of the Internal Revenue Service. The inviolability of the U.S. Constitution was at stake if you were to believe some of the senator’s prior remarks.  
Is Cassidy being criticized for his vote for Blanche? Yes, but that was inevitable regardless of his choice.
Is it new? No, but not because he has turned into Louisiana’s favorite political scapegoat.
It’s because few people believe Cassidy will adhere to any firm stance he’s taken. Absent a spine, he’ll be hard-pressed to find that posture in the five months he has left in office.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: State’s expenses for Rushmore fireworks were greater than economic impact, Tourism Department says
description: The fireworks display last month at Mount Rushmore cost the state of South Dakota $450,000 more than the event generated in economic impact, according to the state Department of Tourism. The state spent $2.8 million to plan and produce the July 3 celebration, which generated $2.35 million of economic impact, the department said in a […]
text:
Fireworks explode above Mount Rushmore National Memorial in South Dakota on July 3, 2026, after a speech by President Donald Trump to mark the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)The fireworks display last month at Mount Rushmore cost the state of South Dakota $450,000 more than the event generated in economic impact, according to the state Department of Tourism.
The state spent $2.8 million to plan and produce the July 3 celebration, which generated $2.35 million of economic impact, the department said in a Monday press release. The department attributed the economic analysis to the research firm Tourism Economics.
Broadcast and digital media coverage generated nearly $51 million in additional “publicity value” from 53.7 billion “audience impressions,” according to the department, although the publicity value was not included as part of the economic impact. The department said the publicity included 107,000 views of the event’s video livestream.
Trump uses Mount Rushmore speech to allege ‘mortal threat’ from communism

South Dakota Tourism Secretary James Hagen celebrated the numbers.
“It’s an investment that strengthened our tourism economy while reinforcing South Dakota’s place as one of America’s most iconic destinations,” Hagen said in the press release.
The costs included $700,000 for pyrotechnics and lighting effects, according to a public contract between the department and California-based Pyro Spectaculars. The department said other costs included media production, shuttle bus contracts and cost recovery payments to the National Park Service. The Park Service manages Mount Rushmore as a national memorial.
South Dakota Searchlight sent questions to the department about whether the costs reported in the press release included expenses incurred by other public entities such as the city of Keystone, Pennington County and the U.S. Forest Service. The department said it would it work on responses and supply them later.
The $2.35 million economic impact estimate includes visitor spending, hotel room rentals and sales tax revenue, the department said in the press release. There were 4,800 tickets for the event, and the department said attendees came from 40 states.
The event, officially known as South Dakota’s Freedom 250 Mount Rushmore Fireworks Celebration, featured a keynote speech from President Donald Trump — which he used to allege a “mortal threat” to the nation from communism — and a fireworks display above the carved faces of Mount Rushmore in South Dakota’s Black Hills.
This year’s event and past fireworks displays at the national memorial have drawn criticism for the wildfire threat to the surrounding national forest posed by stray sparks from fireworks, and for litter and pollutants from fireworks packaging and chemicals. There was no organized protest against the fireworks this year, but a group of Native Americans advocating for the return of the Black Hills to Lakota tribes protested the prior event in 2020.

name: VTDigger
title: Family farms like ours need a farm bill that respects states
description:
A provision buried in the farm bill would strip states of the power to set their own livestock standards.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Family farms like ours need a farm bill that respects states.
text:
Dear Editor,
Long Wind Farm began in 1984 with a team of oxen and a simple goal: produce exceptional food while caring for the land. More than 40 years later, we’re still growing crops in Vermont soil and providing New England with fresh food year-round. Our success has come from earning the trust of our customers. Rather than overriding state protections, federal policy should support standards that promote responsible farming.
That’s why we’re concerned about efforts to include the Save Our Bacon Act in the next farm bill.

READ MORE

Despite its name, this proposal goes well beyond bacon. It would override certain state standards for livestock products sold across state lines, taking decisions away from states and local communities. That’s the wrong direction for American agriculture.
The farm bill should strengthen family farms, support rural communities, expand market opportunities and protect livestock from serious disease threats, not strip states of their ability to address local agricultural priorities. This is especially true now that screwworm has become such a threat. 
Last year, Sens. Peter Welch and Bernie Sanders joined many other senators in signing a letter urging the Senate not to pass laws like the Save Our Bacon Act. We thank them for their leadership on this important issue. And we hope they’ll continue fighting for responsible Vermont farmers by opposing attempts to include the Save Our Bacon Act in the farm bill or any other legislative package. 
Dave Chapman 
East Thetford, Vt.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Anti-uranium advocates wrest control of public hearing on proposed mine near Navajo Nation
description: A recent hearing meant to inform the public about a new uranium mine proposal near Church Rock instead exposed wounds around the legacy of mining’s impacts on Navajo communities, as well as fresh concerns about whether technology that promises to safely extract the mineral is as clean as the industry claims.
text:
Anti-uranium advocate Jenn Nez, holding microphone, addresses NuFuels, Inc. vice president Josh Leftwich on Aug. 6, 2026, after he agreed to hand her the microphone midway during his presentation regarding the company’s efforts to extract uranium near Church Rock, N.M. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)GALLUP — A recent hearing meant to inform the public about a new uranium mine proposal near Church Rock instead exposed wounds around the legacy of mining’s impacts on Navajo communities, as well as fresh concerns about whether technology that promises to safely extract the mineral is as clean as the industry claims. 
Laramide Resources, a Canadian mining company, and its subsidiary NuFuels, Inc., held a public hearing Thursday at a casino near Gallup as it seeks a permit from the New Mexico Environment Department to discharge. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But Navajo anti-mining advocates, as well as those who still remember the cascading consequences  from the 1979 Church Rock mine spill, shouted out repeatedly during the company’s presentation. They expressed frustration that NuFuels would pursue a uranium mine in an area still contending with the biggest uranium spill in the nation’s history, as well as numerous other public health and environmental harms from decades of uranium mining.
About half way through company Vice President Josh Leftwich’s presentation, advocate Jenn Nez slowly got to her feet and walked toward Leftwich, ultimately convincing him to hand her his microphone. 
Through tears, Nez described cancer and other health issues she said uranium contamination caused in her family. Leftwich did not get the microphone back for most of the rest of the 90-minute meeting, as a line of fellow opponents gathered alongside Nez and waited for their chance to speak. 
“Thank you for giving us this opportunity, because we took it from you,” Teracita Keyanna, vice president of the Red Water Pond Road Community Association Executive Committee, told Leftwich. “This is my community. This is my family. That’s my home you’re talking about.”
Leftwich’s presentation centered on a proposed uranium project called Church Rock Section 8, which the company hopes to build on a 175-acre site of private land surrounded by the Navajo Nation, which bans uranium mining. Before Leftwich was interrupted, he detailed how the company sought to use a mining method known as in situ recovery to access roughly 10 million pounds of uranium contained in sandstone formations in the underground aquifer. 
In situ recovery entails the injection of lixiviant — a chemical solution composed of water, oxygen and either carbon dioxide or sodium bicarbonate — to dissolve the uranium underground. From there, pumps extract the uranium liquid into recovery wells, where the uranium is separated. The leftover water is then discharged back into the aquifer. 
“It’s a closed-loop system,” Leftwich said. “There won’t be any other discharges. The water just circulates through the formation to extract the uranium.”
Bertha Nez, a Navajo elder who grew up in the Red Water Pond community, listens Aug. 6, 2026, as presenters from NuFuels, Inc. describe their proposal to extract uranium from the Church Rock area. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)
The company’s permit application notes that, when fully operational, it will seek to discharge roughly 4,000 gallons of leftover water a minute back into the aquifer, which provides drinking water to the Crownpoint community. That would be the equivalent of about nine Olympic-size swimming pools’ worth of water a day. 
The company cannot begin mining until the NMED rules on the permit application, which officials said will take at least a year.
Still, Leftwich’s presentation extolled the virtues of in situ recovery as a low-emissions means of extracting uranium without risking the lives of workers underground.
By the #s: More mining claims filed in New Mexico in last 4 years than previous century

The company would also employ monitoring wells to ensure the water quality meets federal and state standards, and the company is in preliminary stages of a research project with Los Alamos National Laboratories that aims to restore the groundwater supply with “approaches tailored to the geology of the Churchrock deposit.”
However, state officials are dubious about the company’s promises to restore the groundwater to its pre-mining condition. Earlier Thursday, the New Mexico Department of Justice weighed in on the company’s pending license renewal application to the federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission with a 39-page rebuttal of numerous claims the company has made regarding its operation and in situ recovery more broadly. 
The NMDOJ’s “petition to intervene” argues that in situ recovery has never been proven to restore groundwater supplies to their pre-mining states and that no technology yet exists to do so. It cites NuFuels’ own statements in an unrelated filing before the NRC in 2023, in which the company states that, “to date, no ISR site has restored all groundwater constituents of concern to pre-operational concentrations” and that uranium levels “tend to gradually rebound” in aquifers after the treatment.
Therefore, the NMDOJ wrote, the company has acknowledged “that the technology needed to ensure compliance with the governing restoration standard does not yet exist and that developing it is the object of ongoing research.” 
Advocates who wrested the microphone from Leftwich on Thursday also raised concerns about what they said is untested technology, with one woman shouting that the NuFuels was making “Guinea pigs” out of the communities downstream of the mine site. 
Leftwich told Source NM after the hearing that he was surprised the New Mexico Department of Justice would weigh in on what he sees as a “pretty small issue” regarding a single mine in the Church Rock area, “compared to big issues, like across the state.” 
As for the hearing itself, he said he was content to let people “speak their minds” about the issue, but also that legacy uranium issues and “misinformation” are preventing a productive community debate. The hearing also marked the beginning of a 60-day public comment period. 
“This is the first of hopefully multiple meetings that we can get more in-depth,” he said. “I really wish we could have good meetings.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas governor to appoint temporary Supreme Court justice to fill in for Webb
description: Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders will appoint a temporary special justice to fill in for Barbara Webb, who has been recovering from a fall at her home, the governor’s office said Monday.  In a letter dated Monday, Chief Justice Baker requested that the Republican governor appoint a temporary special justice “until such time that Justice […]
text:
The Arkansas Justice Building on the state Capitol grounds in Little Rock on Jan. 14, 2025. The building houses the state Supreme Court, the Court of Appeals and the Administrative Office of the Courts. (Photo by Sonny Albarado/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders will appoint a temporary special justice to fill in for Barbara Webb, who has been recovering from a fall at her home, the governor’s office said Monday. 
In a letter dated Monday, Chief Justice Baker requested that the Republican governor appoint a temporary special justice “until such time that Justice Webb notifies the Supreme Court that she is ready and able to resume her duties.”
Supreme Court Justice Barbara Webb (Photo courtesy of the Arkansas Supreme Court)
“Governor Sanders is grateful for Justice Webb’s years of service and is praying for her swift recovery and return to the bench,” Sanders’ spokesperson Sam Dubke said in an email. “In the interim, the Governor will appoint a temporary special justice who displays Justice Webb’s same judicial temperament and dedication to the letter of the law.”
Webb’s absence from the court became public in May when Baker sent a letter to Sanders notifying her that Webb was “temporarily unable to serve” while the court heard two constitutional challenges, two criminal appeals and a civil appeal. Webb’s husband, Doyle, last month said she was recovering from a head injury sustained during a fall.
Sanders appointed Cory Cox as a special justice to replace Webb for the two constitutional challenges, in which lower courts ruled that Sanders violated the state constitution in her scheduling of special elections to fill two vacant legislative seats. The high court dismissed the cases as moot because the special elections had already occurred.
Instead of appointing a special justice separately for each case, Baker asked Sanders to appoint someone whose service would expire when Webb returns. 
Arkansas’ constitution gives Sanders 30 days from Baker’s letter to appoint a special justice, unless that timeframe is extended by Baker. If Sanders fails to appoint someone within 30 days or the extended period granted by the chief justice, Lt. Gov. Leslie Rutledge would commission a special justice, according to the letter. 
Arkansas’ high court is technically nonpartisan, but Republican-linked justices hold a 5-2 majority that includes Webb.
Doyle Webb didn’t immediately return a request for comment Monday afternoon. He is a former state senator and Arkansas Public Service Commission chairman. He also served as chairman of the Republican Party of Arkansas.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Ex-NBA guard Monta Ellis is named Alcorn State men’s basketball general manager
description: Indiana Pacers guard Monta Ellis (11) plays during the second half of an NBA basketball game in Indianapolis, Sunday, March 26, 2017.
text:
LORMAN — Alcorn State has hired former longtime NBA guard Monta Ellis as general manager of the men’s basketball program.
Ellis is a native of Jackson, and Alcorn State’s main campus is in Lorman. Ellis was drafted by the Golden State Warriors in 2005 out of Lanier High School in Jackson, where he won two state championships. Alcorn State described Ellis as “One proud Mississippi son” in its announcement Friday.
“Monta Ellis brings a championship pedigree and a wealth of basketball knowledge to our program, and we’re thrilled to welcome him to the Alcorn State family,” athletic director E. D’Wayne Robinson said in a statement.
“His experience at the highest level of the game, combined with his passion for developing young talent, makes him the perfect addition to our basketball leadership.”
Alcorn State finished 9-23 overall and 7-11 in the Southwestern Athletic Conference under first-year head coach Jake Morton last season.
Ellis averaged 17.8 points in his 12-year NBA career with Golden State, Milwaukee, Dallas and Indiana. He was voted the league’s most improved player after averaging 16.5 points in the 2006-07 season with the Warriors. He completed his career with Indiana in the 2016-17 season.
Ellis, 40, now begins a new career in college sports.
“It’s official, Braves fans. I’m now the new general manager at Alcorn State University,” Ellis said in Alcorn State’s announcement posted on X. “I can’t wait to work alongside with the coaches, the staff, the alumni, and the passionate fans at Alcorn State. Let’s go Braves!”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Signing new abortion law, Healey cites stories of ‘anguish and heartache’
authors: Ella Adams | State House News Service
description: Gov. Maura Healey on Monday signed legislation removing restrictions on abortions after 24 weeks of gestation, a change that supporters say will help more patients stay in-state to receive care.
text:
AFTER LAWMAKERS FAST-TRACKED the bill, Gov. Maura Healey on Monday signed legislation removing restrictions on abortions after 24 weeks of gestation, a change that supporters say will help more patients stay in-state to receive care.
The law (H 5595) eliminates the existing four-pronged framework enabling abortions for pregnancies at or beyond 24 weeks in life-threatening situations for the patient or fetus, instead writing a new law that states “an abortion may be performed by a physician based upon the professional judgment of the physician.” 
“We’ve heard so many stories — stories that are filled with a lot of pain and anguish and heartache and a lot of trauma. We heard stories about the worst moments of a person’s life, of a couple’s life,” Healey said, surrounded by lawmakers, advocates and physicians at a press conference she hosted in her ceremonial office. “We’re signing this law today so that new patients, people we won’t know or won’t meet, will be able to get the care that they need in Massachusetts.”  
The bill was filed at the start of the two-year session by Rep. Christine Barber, who is running this fall for an open Senate seat. It began to take off on July 22 when it was released from the House Ways and Means Committee and was pushed through both branches in a flurry of late-July legislating. The new law will go into effect in 90 days, Healey’s office confirmed.
“We know that protecting abortion access and reproductive health care has been under fire,” Healey said, noting the US Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022 and adding, “Today, one in three women in America live in a state with an abortion ban.” 
The House on July 22 voted 119-33 to pass the bill, with all Republicans who voted casting their votes against it. Democrats who rejected the bill included Reps. Brian Ashe, Lisa Field, Michael Finn, Dennis Gallagher, Russell Holmes, Christopher Markey, Francisco Paulino, Alan Silvia and Jeffrey Turco. Rep. Susannah Whipps, the chamber’s only Independent member, voted yes. 
The Senate on July 31 passed the bill with a 15-4 standing vote. 
According to Judiciary Committee Chair Rep. Mike Day, it’s the fourth time in 16 years that lawmakers revisited the issue “in an effort to get it right, to get government out of the way of a health issue, and to lessen the trauma inflicted on pregnant women, who are suddenly confronted with unbelievably tragic news about their pregnancies more than six months into their term.”
“We hear that some medical professionals are still uncomfortable with the specific language restrictions that they say continues to interfere with their professional medical judgment, and that some patients continue to have to leave the commonwealth or stay and endure unnecessary trauma because a treating physician is afraid that they will somehow run afoul of the law based on those restrictions,” Day, who was at the bill signing Monday, said on the House floor before the late July vote. “We’re also still hearing of patients who, after receiving this news, are ultimately unable to receive necessary medical care because they don’t have the means to afford to leave Massachusetts for it.”
Kate Dineen and her husband Alex Lawton recalled the journey they took to Washington, DC in 2021, when Dineen was 33 weeks pregnant and learned her baby had suffered a stroke in utero. 
“He would either die or survive for some period of time with a spectrum of devastating outcomes. And so upon learning of the prognosis, I asked, ‘What are my options?’ And I will never forget the response. ‘You may still be able to explore termination if you’re able to travel,'” Dineen said. “Travel where? We were standing in our kitchen in Boston, just less than a mile from some of the best hospitals in the country.”
The diagnosis didn’t qualify for an exception, Dineen said, and their doctor’s “highly capable hands were tied by Massachusetts state law.” 
The Massachusetts Health and Hospital Association, Beth Israel Lahey Health, Mass General Brigham, Tufts Medicine and UMass Memorial Health in mid-July sent a letter of support to House Speaker Ron Mariano, writing that the state’s existing statutory framework “does not adequately meet the needs of all patients.” 
According to Department of Public Health Data, there were 99 abortions done at 24 weeks or later in 2024, compared to 84 in 2023. There was a sharp increase in the total number of abortions in Massachusetts in 2024 compared to those done in 2023, which public health officials have said was due to out-of-state patients accessing care through telehealth.
“The reality is that medicine does not always fit into clearly defined legal categories,” Worcester Sen. Robyn Kennedy said on the Senate floor on July 31. “Physicians need the ability to use their medical judgment and advise their patients when facing complex and rapidly changing medical circumstances.”
Public Health Committee Chair Rep. Marjorie Decker said last month that the legislation “does not tell a patient what decision to make. It does not force anyone to have an abortion. It does not take decision-making away from the patients.”
The Massachusetts Family Institute on August 3 urged people, “Tell the governor to veto radical late-term abortion!” The institute called the bill “a dangerous attempt to remove virtually all remaining protections in the Commonwealth for unborn babies.” 
Massachusetts Family Action sent out an email on August 7, writing that the Legislature “passed one of the most extreme abortion bills in the country — allowing abortion at any point in pregnancy, for any reason, outside the safeguards of a hospital.” The group plans a webinar Tuesday on “what’s really in this bill — and how you can help elect leaders who will protect life.”
“Abortion is on the ballot this November in Massachusetts and around the country,” Healey said Monday when asked what role she thinks abortion politics play in campaigning this year. “My opponents are anti-abortion. One of my opponents, Mike Minogue, is proudly anti-abortion.”
Minogue in May said during an appearance that he’s Catholic and “pro-life,” adding that “as governor, I know what the law is, and I’m going to uphold the law.” GOP gubernatorial candidate Brian Shortsleeve called himself a “pro-choice Republican” on GBH’s “Boston Public Radio” in May, and suggested Minogue isn’t electable across the state due to his stance on the issue. 
According to Reproductive Equity Now, abortion care after 24 weeks represents less than 1 percent of terminations in the United States. The group’s interim executive director Claire Teylouni has also said that the provision within the law that would remove the requirement that abortions beyond 24 weeks occur in a hospital is meant to expand abortion care in other settings as hospitals deal with federal funding concerns.  
“Massachusetts is affirming again that abortion is essential health care, and that politicians should never stand between a patient and their doctor. The significance of this law goes far beyond our state borders,” Teylouni said Monday. 
ACLU of Massachusetts executive director Carol Rose applauded the law Monday in a statement, and said that it ensures “pregnant patients in Massachusetts will no longer have to travel far from their home state to access the care they need.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Northwest CT, Hartford suburbs had most early voting
description: Nearly 55,000 CT voters cast ballots early and 12,410 cast absentee ballots for Tuesday's primaries, including about 7.8% of Democrats.
text:
Nearly 55,000 Connecticut voters cast their ballots early and another 12,410 cast absentee ballots for Tuesday’s primaries — including 61,846 of nearly 790,000 active Democrats, or about 7.8%.
Fewer towns have GOP primaries to vote in, but 5,351 Republicans cast early or absentee ballots for their General Assembly or Congressional primaries.
Bloomfield had the highest percentage of early voters, followed by West Hartford.
Towns in the northwest and suburbs of Hartford also saw returns above average.
House District 50, which covers a clump of towns from Mansfield to Woodstock, saw an increased percentage of active Republicans and Democrats early voting, which might be a bellwether for higher turnout overall.
This is the first Connecticut gubernatorial primary to offer the option of early voting.
The last gubernatorial primary, when Bridgeport Mayor Joe Ganim challenged Ned Lamont in 2018, saw 212,543 total ballots cast.

name: National
title: Anti-abortion groups urge attorney general to halt mailing of abortion pills
description: A group of leading anti-abortion organizations sent a letter to newly confirmed U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche urging him to review the U.S. Department of Justice’s authority to use  a 150-year-old anti-obscenity law to prevent people from obtaining abortion medication or other related materials through the mail. Advancing American Freedom, a conservativ[...]
text:
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche appears at his confirmation hearing in front of the Senate Judiciary Committee on Capitol Hill last month. A group of leading anti-abortion organizations sent a letter to Blanche urging him to consider using a 150-year-old anti-obscenity law to prevent people from obtaining abortion medication or other related materials through the mail. (Photo by Eric Lee/Getty Images)A group of leading anti-abortion organizations sent a letter to newly confirmed U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche urging him to review the U.S. Department of Justice’s authority to use  a 150-year-old anti-obscenity law to prevent people from obtaining abortion medication or other related materials through the mail.
Advancing American Freedom, a conservative advocacy group founded by former Republican Vice President Mike Pence, authored the Aug. 7 letter. It is co-signed by four major anti-abortion organizations, including Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, Americans United for Life and Students for Life of America. The nearly 30 other signees include the North Carolina House of Representatives, the Oklahoma Council of Public Affairs and The Conservative Caucus.
The Comstock Act, enacted in 1873, made it illegal to send “obscene material” by mail, which included any “article or thing designed, adapted or intended for producing abortion.” The Comstock Act is considered a “zombie law,” meaning it hasn’t been repealed, but has not been enforced in many decades. In 2022, during the Biden administration, the U.S. Department of Justice issued legal guidance stating that Comstock did not prohibit the mail of certain abortion drugs when the sender does not intend for the recipient to use them unlawfully.
“Not only does this language appear nowhere in the Comstock Act but, as a practical matter, a sender’s subjective intent and a recipient’s intended use are unknowable, making the Comstock Act a dead letter,” the letter to Blanche said.
The groups thanked Blanche for pledging to evaluate the 2022 opinion and said they look forward to the result of his review.
In a conference call hosted by the White House Faith Office on July 30, Blanche told thousands of religious leaders that he was committed to advancing policies that would outlaw abortion in every state.
Unpacking the fight over telehealth access to abortion medication

In 2022, the U.S. Supreme Court’s Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health decision cleared the way for states to regulate abortion access for the first time in 50 years, prompting more than a dozen states to enact near-total abortion bans. In the wake of that ruling, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2023 changed its rules on mifepristone, one of two drugs typically used to terminate a pregnancy before 10 weeks and to treat miscarriages.
Mifepristone halts the pregnancy, while a second drug, misoprostol, physically clears the uterus.
The new FDA rules allowed mifepristone to be dispensed without a visit to an in-person provider, which made it easier for people in states with bans to obtain the medication from online sources and receive the pills in the mail.
According to the Society of Family Planning’s #WeCount report, 27% of all abortions in the first six months of 2025 were obtained through telehealth, adding up to more than 162,000 cases.
Anti-abortion groups and Republican state attorneys general have sued the FDA trying to reverse the 2023 rules or establish legal authority to enforce Comstock. A Texas judge in 2023 ruled that Comstock was enforceable, but the U.S. Supreme Court eventually overturned that ruling.
If the challenges to FDA rules around mifepristone are successful, abortion-rights advocates have said they would continue prescribing misoprostol, which is effective on its own.
GOP states try new ways to target abortion pills and telehealth

But enforcement of Comstock would apply to any equipment needed to perform abortions. Abortion-rights legal advocacy organization Center for Reproductive Rights said that could make supplies difficult or illegal to obtain for any type of obstetrical care, including miscarriages and pregnancy complications.
Gavin Oxley, spokesperson for Americans United for Life, told Stateline by email that the restrictions should extend to those categories and not just mifepristone.
“Any drug or instrument mailed with the intention of abortion falls under the law’s authority, proactively protecting women from new or adapted abortion methods, including misoprostol-only abortions,” Oxley said. “Righting the politicized Biden-era OLC opinion denying the strict application of Comstock must be an immediate priority for General Blanche.”
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.

name: VTDigger
title: Londonderry community convenes in the wake of local ICE raid
description:
Several people were detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Londonderry last week.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Londonderry community convenes in the wake of local ICE raid.
text:
Morrow and Bliss speaking to attendees. Photo by Ryan Pacheco/Bennington Banner 

This story by Ryan Pacheco was first published in the Bennington Banner on Aug. 8, 2026.
LONDONDERRY — Concerned citizens and community members packed a meeting room at Neighborhood Connections in Londonderry on Saturday, Aug. 8 to discuss recent immigration enforcement operations that resulted in five Ecuadorian individuals being detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement a day prior. The community conversation was hosted by Neighborhood Connections, and organized in the immediate aftermath of the detention by concerned state legislators and immigrant justice advocates.
Community members had the chance to hear from, and ask questions to Rep. Chris Morrow, D-Weston, and Migrant Justice member Will Lambek. The conversation was guided and moderated by Jon Bliss.
The dialogue opened with a synopsis of recent events, intended to deter false information and rumor mills from blooming in the aftermath of the ICE raid. Five Ecuadorian immigrants were arrested by ICE during a traffic stop near Taylor Farm. Despite proximity to the farm and rumors that had begun to circulate, Taylor Farm was confirmed to not be the employer of the detained individuals. Vermont News & Media was able to independently verify that Taylor Farm has no connection to the five individuals detained by ICE.
The detained individuals had been allowed to enter the country while awaiting the results of their pending asylum cases, and are being held at an ICE contracted detention facility in Plymouth County, Massachusetts. According to Lambek, detaining migrants regardless of permission to enter the U.S. has become commonplace.
“They came to the Southern Border, were allowed entry with a pending asylum application, and are all currently in court proceedings. This is a common practice right now where, despite people having been allowed to come into the country with asylum claims, (ICE and Customs and Border Patrol) are detaining them anyway, even without any change in their circumstances,” said Lambek.
Migrant Justice has established contact with some of the detained individuals’ families, and is working on contacting the rest. According to Lambek, all five have had money deposited into their commissary accounts to facilitate making phone calls to family members and support systems.
Migrant Justice encouraged attendees and the community-at-large to sign up for their ‘Rapid Response Network’, a volunteer initiative that provides community members with the tools and training to safely and legally respond to the presence of ICE in their community. Attendees were passed a sign-up sheet, as well as pamphlets describing their “ALERTA” approach to reporting ICE interactions.

Morrow and Lambek speaking to attendees. Photo by Ryan Pacheco/Bennington Banner 

ALERTA is an acronym, standing for activity, location, equipment, request aid, time and date, and appearance. The ALERTA approach encourages concerned citizens to report ICE by making reports to Migrant Justice’s emergency hotline that includes details such as what is happening (A), where it is happening (L), what tools the officers are using (E), what are the requested action steps (R), when it happened (T) and what the officers looked like (A).
Migrant Justice directed concerned citizens to view a selection of resources, including guides to constitutional rights and instructions for navigating ICE encounters, which are available on their website. Spanish language translations are available, according to Lambek.
During the question-and-answer portion of the meeting, a community member raised a question about involved agencies. While Vermont News & Media can confirm that the Vermont State Police had no involvement in the Aug. 7 incident, video footage obtained by a concerned citizen showed ICE agents, many of which were wearing masks, wearing tactical vests with identifiers such as “ERO” and “POLICE.” ERO is a common ICE acronym, standing for “Enforcement and Removal Operations.” Loose regulations on ICE duty attire have been criticized in recent years.
According to Morrow, Vermont has made attempts to limit ICE practices that have been described as non-transparent.
“Here are some things we tried to do last session, since this has been an on-going issue. We had a bill through the legal committee to outlaw masks, and mandate badge-wearing in Vermont for any public safety or law enforcement official. While that was happening, the Second Circuit Court of Appeals in California had said it was unconstitutional for a similar law in a different state. There was a big debate about whether or not we should go forward and do it anyway in the Legislature, and see what happens in the Ninth Circuit around here. I was in favor of that, but the bill did not pass,” said Morrow.
“What we did manage to pass was a bill that just applies to state law enforcement. That is useful, but not really helpful here. We did manage to pass Act 150, which was signed into law in June, that prohibits civil arrests in designated sensitive locations, and ensures public access to essential services without fear of detention,” added Morrow.
Morrow said that Act 150 applies to immigration arrests, but not to criminal arrests.
The community conversation has drawn criticism from supporters of the Trump Administration’s immigration enforcement efforts, who have taken to social media to publicly decry Neighborhood Connections’ willingness to host the conversation. According to Executive Director Thom Simmons, the backlash has been disappointing, but ultimately un-deterring to the organization’s primary function: helping people.
“We work with people. It does not matter what problems people bring to us, whether it is addiction, being un-housed, emotional-mental, or cognitive health status, or immigration status. We work with people who are in our local area. We are not aware who (the five detained individuals) are, we have not worked with them. We are aware that they may have family in the area who may be in need of food, counseling or transportation. We are more aware of community members who are living in fear, and have cancelled important things like doctors appointments out of fear. We want to be here for them to provide counseling, and whatever support they need,” said Simmons.
“On social media, people have made up this narrative that we are helping people be illegal. We are not. We are helping people indiscriminately, the way we have for 17 years,” added Simmons.
Community member Robert Montuoro attended the meeting and said that he cannot imagine his community without the positive impact of the local immigrant community members.
“I moved to Vermont 25 years ago. I own a lot of restaurants, and that was always my dream. Over the years, these people have become some of my closest friends. I would not be able to survive without them, and not be able to live my dream if it were not for the people that came to this country to live their dream,” said Montuoro.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Court: Minneapolis schools can keep providing layoff protection to teachers of color
description: A federal judge has dismissed a U.S. Department of Justice lawsuit targeting a Minneapolis Public Schools policy that shields teachers of color from seniority-based layoffs. In his ruling Monday, U.S. District Judge Patrick Schiltz wrote that the policy — adopted in 2022 to help end a 14-day Minneapolis Federation of Teachers strike — does raise […]
text:
(Photo by Will Jacott/Minnesota Reformer)A federal judge has dismissed a U.S. Department of Justice lawsuit targeting a Minneapolis Public Schools policy that shields teachers of color from seniority-based layoffs.
In his ruling Monday, U.S. District Judge Patrick Schiltz wrote that the policy — adopted in 2022 to help end a 14-day Minneapolis Federation of Teachers strike — does raise concerns about the “legality of the racial discrimination in which MPS is forced to engage.” The lawsuit cannot proceed, however, without the teachers union — which was left off the list of defendants when the Trump administration sued the district in December. 
The policy ended typical last-in, first-out rules for teachers from underrepresented backgrounds in an effort to improve recruitment and retention in one of the state’s most diverse districts. It was adopted by MPS as part of a collective bargaining agreement, making the union a necessary party to the federal government’s lawsuit. The problem for the Trump administration: DOJ can only bring cases alleging discrimination against government entities. Labor unions, like the MFT, are private. 
Schiltz said proceeding without the union would leave MPS in an “untenable position” as it chooses to violate either a federal injunction or its own collective bargaining agreement with the teachers unions. 
“MPS and the union sit on opposite sides of the bargaining table, and the court cannot simply trust that one party to a (collective bargaining agreement) will safeguard the interests of the other party,” Schiltz wrote. 
The teachers union pushed for layoff protections in 2022 because teachers of color tend to be younger and disproportionately affected by last-in, first-out downsizing. Around 20% of Minneapolis teachers are people of color, compared to two-thirds of their students. The policy requires the district to skip over staff members from “underrepresented populations” during seniority-based layoffs or involuntary reassignments. Laid-off teachers from underrepresented groups must also be the first to be reinstated if called back. 
The policy doesn’t explicitly mention race to help withstand legal challenges.
Minneapolis Public Schools praised Schiltz’s order in a statement to the Reformer.
“Minneapolis Public Schools is pleased the Court granted our motion to dismiss this case. We remain committed to working with our labor partners to ensure collective bargaining agreements are in the best interest of our students and employees.”
Marcia Howard, president of the teachers union, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
The Trump administration alleged the MPS policy was discriminatory after the school district defended the same policy in another lawsuit by a local resident. Deborah Clapp, with the backing of conservative legal foundation Judicial Watch, argued that she was harmed as a taxpayer for funding a discriminatory policy. (A judge tossed the case in January of 2025.)
Schiltz said teachers who wish to challenge the policy can file a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which can pursue cases against private entities.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana governor deploys National Guard to support Washington fire response
description: A five-soldier Montana National Guard team will deploy Tuesday to help support fire response in Washington after Gov. Greg Gianforte responded to a request. The state of Washington is experiencing significant wildfire conditions in many parts of the state, including active fires in Spokane that have burned more than 10,000 acres. The Washington State Standar[...]
text:
Airmen assigned to the 219th Red Horse Squadron connect sling load rigging to an MEP-806 power generator before it is lifted by a CH-47 Chinook helicopter assigned to the 1st Battalion, 189th Aviation Regiment (General Support Aviation) during a joint field training exercise at Fort Harrison, Montana, June 26, 2026. (U.S. Air National Guard photo by Senior Master Sgt. Devin Doskey)A five-soldier Montana National Guard team will deploy Tuesday to help support fire response in Washington after Gov. Greg Gianforte responded to a request.
The state of Washington is experiencing significant wildfire conditions in many parts of the state, including active fires in Spokane that have burned more than 10,000 acres. The Washington State Standard reports that around 700 homes and other buildings in the city burned, with more than 65,000 individuals told to evacuate.
According to Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, resources from more than 20 states and 100 jurisdictions are aiding the effort to fight the Spokane fires.
Brig. Gen. Trent Gibson, Adjutant General of Montana, said in a statement that helping neighbors is what Montanans do.
“Montanans understand the devastating impact wildfires can have on communities, and we’re proud to support our neighbors in Washington during this critical time,” Gibson said. “Whether here at home or across state lines, we’ll continue to do our part to help communities recover and overcome challenges together.”
According to the governor’s office, the initial Montana National Guard support includes one Montana Army National Guard CH-47 Chinook Heavy-lift helicopter, its crew, and one maintainer, for a total of five soldiers. The CH-47 provides critical heavy-lift capability to support wildfire suppression operations, including the movement of personnel and equipment.
The request for support from the Montana National Guard was sent through the Emergency Management Assistance Compact through which Montana can provide mutual assistance to member states.
By issuing an executive order, Gianforte can mobilize state resources including additional personnel, aircraft and capabilities in coordination with Washington while maintaining the ability to respond to emergencies within Montana.
Within Montana there has been moderate fire activity, and the governor said the state has adequate resources to manage existing incidents. According to the state’s wildfire dashboard, there are currently 26 active fires and nearly 90,000 acres have burned across the state this year.
“Deploying these resources will not compromise our ability to respond to any current fire activity in Montana, and the Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation remains ready to continue executing an aggressive initial attack on all fire starts,” Gianforte said in a statement.

House Finance Chairman Vernon Criss, R-Wood, filed paperwork Aug. 10, 2026 in the West Virginia Secretary of State’s Office to run as a write-in candidate in the 12th district. (Photo by Amelia Ferrell Knisely/West Virginia Watch)Del. Vernon Criss, R-Wood, has filed to run as a write-in candidate in the upcoming November election to hold onto his House of Delegates seat.
Criss, the House Finance chair, lost his reelection bid in May to Charles Hartzog, a 23-year-old Walmart employee heavily backed by Gov. Patrick Morrisey. 
The governor and Criss have openly clashed over state budget matters. The dispute prompted Morrisey to travel to Wood County and campaign against Criss last spring ahead of the May primary election.
The Republican primary was closed this year to independent voters, prompting Criss to file as a write-in candidate with the Secretary of State’s Office on Monday afternoon. He believes the closed primary impacted his race results in Wood County.
“Approximately 40% of the vote in my district were independents, and they did not have the chance to vote in this primary, and because of the repercussions of that, people (are) finally waking up and determined that they didn’t have the opportunity to vote,” said Criss, who represents the 12th district in the House. “The only way they can have an opportunity to vote is to be … on the ballot through a write-in process.”
Criss, who was seeking a sixth consecutive term in the House, also cited low voter turnout in the May election as an issue in his race. Hartzog received 688 votes in the closed primary compared to 422 for Criss. The vast majority of registered voters didn’t participate in the election, he said, or couldn’t vote on the GOP ticket due to the closed primary. 
“That’s less than 4% of the citizens in that district that gave (Hartzog) the opportunity to be the Republican nominee,” Criss said. 
West Virginia permits individuals to file as an official write-in candidate by submitting paperwork with the proper filing officer no later than the 49th day before the election.
Only official write-in candidates will have their votes tallied; persons who simply have their name written on a ballot are not eligible to win any election, according to the Secretary of State’s office. The write-in deadline for candidates is Sept. 15.
Official write-in candidates’ names will be posted at the entrance of each polling place and will be provided at the poll worker table inside the polling place upon request by a voter.
Morrisey’s spring political attacks on Criss centred on the Hope Scholarship and educational freedom – key issues for the governor. The House Finance Committee, under leadership of Criss, considered a bill this year to put guardrails  — like banning the use of funds at out-of-state schools – on the $300 million education voucher program. The cost of the program skyrocketed this year due the Hope Scholarship opening up to all West Virginia students for the first time. 
While lawmakers didn’t end up making any change to parents’ use of the voucher program, the proposed changes resulted in Americans for Prosperity’s West Virginia chapter strongly opposing Criss. AFP-WV has deep ties to Morrisey.
“It was amazing the fact that the governor personally and several of his people provided some even door-to-door operations, along with coordinating staff from AFP … to go out and spend nearly $100,000 to have against me in this process,” Criss said. “It’s up to us to determine how the monies are to be spent for the state of West Virginia …  I think simply that he just was doing whatever he could to make sure that I wasn’t going to return.”
Criss said he wants to continue work on the state’s finances and touts a record of cutting taxes for residents. He plans to campaign this fall. 
“We we have done some amazing things as far as the other structure of our tax system is concerned, and I think that the people, especially in Wood County, recognize that and they see the value in having somebody like myself in the Legislature to look out for the betterment of Wood County, and I think they need to have an opportunity to do that again,” he said. 
Nov. 3 is Election Day. Voter registration deadline is Oct. 13.

name: VTDigger
title: DOJ sues Vermont, other states to stop in-state tuition for undocumented students
description:
The Department of Justice filed lawsuits against New York, Connecticut and Vermont in the latest effort to claw back protections and benefits for undocumented students.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  DOJ sues Vermont, other states to stop in-state tuition for undocumented students.
text:
Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a news conference at the Department of Justice, Wednesday, August 5, 2026 in Washington. (AP Photo/Rod Lamkey, Jr.)
This story was produced in partnership with NOTUS, a publication from the nonprofit, nonpartisan Allbritton Journalism Institute. VTDigger has partnered with NOTUS to cover federal actions affecting Vermont.
The U.S. Department of Justice filed lawsuits against Vermont, Connecticut and New York on Monday for allowing undocumented students to receive in-state tuition — and vowed to keep pushing to end the practice nationwide.
Seventeen states have already faced legal challenges over state laws that give undocumented immigrants access to financial assistance programs.
The DOJ argues that the state programs in question unconstitutionally discriminate against students with U.S. citizenship — although New York, Connecticut and Vermont all offer in-state tuition reductions to all students who meet certain state residency requirements.
“Our efforts will not cease until President Trump’s promise is fulfilled: illegal aliens will not receive benefits denied to our Nation’s own citizens,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in a statement.
The Trump administration prevailed in some of its prior lawsuits, and multiple states have halted their tuition policies, including Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska and Illinois.
Some of the lawsuits led to the end of programs started by decades-old state laws, like the Texas Dream Act, which passed with bipartisan support in 2001.
Woodward said the Justice Department has “now sued every state in the Second Circuit that seeks to thwart Congress’s clear prohibition by placing alien over citizen.”
The university systems for New York, Connecticut and Vermont did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the new legal challenges from the Trump administration.
Approximately 2.4% of all students enrolled in U.S. colleges and universities are undocumented, according to an October report from the Higher Ed Immigration Portal. Nearly 28% of those undocumented students are estimated to have or be eligible for Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, a program that provides temporary work permits and protection from deportation for individuals who came to the U.S. as children.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  DOJ sues Vermont, other states to stop in-state tuition for undocumented students.

name: Delaware
title: Beatles’ Complete Musical Journey Starts Tonight in Wilmington
description: The Rock Orchestra’s six-night “All Together Now” festival offers families a rare chance to share 217 Beatles songs — and generations of musical history — together WILMINGTON, Del. — Beatles fans have six nights beginning tonight to experience something far different from a traditional tribute concert — and perhaps introduce a child or grandchild to the musi[...]
text:
The Rock Orchestra’s six-night “All Together Now” festival offers families a rare chance to share 217 Beatles songs — and generations of musical history — together
WILMINGTON, Del. — Beatles fans have six nights beginning tonight to experience something far different from a traditional tribute concert — and perhaps introduce a child or grandchild to the music that changed popular culture.
The Rock Orchestra opens its ninth annual “All Together Now” festival Monday night at Delaware Theatre Company, launching a six-night musical journey through all 217 officially released Beatles songs in chronological order. Performances begin at 8 p.m. each night through Saturday, Aug. 15.
For longtime Beatles fans, the festival is an opportunity to hear familiar favorites alongside songs rarely performed live. For younger listeners, it offers something more: a chance to discover the Beatles the way their parents and grandparents did — as a band whose sound changed dramatically in just a few remarkable years.
That makes the festival an unusual opportunity for families to share some musical history.
Parents and grandparents who remember the Beatles can bring younger generations to hear why songs recorded more than half a century ago continue to influence the music they hear today. Instead of simply playing an old record or streaming a playlist, families can experience the music together in a live theater, performed by musicians recreating the increasingly complex arrangements that defined the Beatles’ career.
Six nights tell one musical story
“All Together Now” does not simply assemble the Beatles’ biggest hits.
Each evening picks up where the previous night ended, presenting albums, singles and deeper cuts in the order in which they were originally released. The format allows audiences to hear the transformation from the youthful rock-and-roll energy of the band’s earliest recordings to the increasingly ambitious studio experimentation of its later years.
Tonight’s opening performance features “Please Please Me” and “With The Beatles.”
Tuesday moves to “A Hard Day’s Night” and “Beatles For Sale,” followed Wednesday by “Help!” and “Rubber Soul.” Thursday features “Revolver,” “Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band” and “Magical Mystery Tour.”
Friday brings “Yellow Submarine” and “The Beatles,” commonly known as the White Album, before the festival concludes Saturday with “Abbey Road” and “Let It Be.”
That progression is central to the experience.
“The Beatles didn’t stand still for a single album,” said Joe Trainor, co-founder and musical director of The Rock Orchestra. “When you experience every song in release order, you hear them grow from a great rock-and-roll band into fearless musical innovators.”
More than a Beatles tribute show
Recreating those recordings requires considerably more than four musicians with guitars and drums.
Over the festival’s nine-year history, more than 112 musicians playing nearly 30 instruments have participated. A seven-piece core rock band is joined throughout the production by strings, brass, woodwinds and instruments including harp, sitar, tabla, mandolin, French horn and clarinet.
The result is designed to recreate not just the songs but the expanding musical imagination behind them.
Founded in 2017 by Trainor and Matt Urban, The Rock Orchestra has produced concerts celebrating artists including Bruce Springsteen, Elton John, Fleetwood Mac, Queen, Genesis, Chicago, Tom Petty, Peter Gabriel, Eagles and R.E.M. But “All Together Now” has become its signature summer event.
“It’s become a tradition for the musicians on stage and for the audiences who come back every summer,” Urban said.
Make it a family night
For people who grew up with the Beatles, the week offers six chances to revisit music tied to their own memories.
But taking a son, daughter or grandchild could make the experience even more memorable.
Young people may already recognize more Beatles music than they realize. “All Together Now” gives older generations an opportunity to put those songs into context — and then watch younger listeners discover for themselves how dramatically the band evolved.
With the festival beginning tonight and ending Saturday, the opportunity lasts only six nights.
Whether attending one favorite era or following the entire 217-song journey, this may be the kind of summer experience worth turning into a family tradition.
TO GO

What: All Together Now: The Complete Beatles Festival
When: Monday, Aug. 10, through Saturday, Aug. 15
Time: 8 p.m. nightly
Where: Delaware Theatre Company, 200 Water St., Wilmington
Tonight: “Please Please Me” and “With The Beatles”
 Single-night tickets, festival passes and VIP packages are available through Delaware Theatre Company.
Why go: Hear all 217 officially released Beatles songs performed chronologically — and consider bringing your children or grandchildren for a night of music that connects generations.
