name: Missouri Independent
title: Maybe Missourians are smarter than Jefferson City gives them credit for
description: Missouri Republicans have been making the case for years that our state constitution is getting hijacked by out-of-state interests. Gov. Mike Kehoe said it plainly in a video backing Amendment 4, the proposal that would have made it virtually impossible for voters to amend the Missouri Constitution. “Our constitution,” he said, “shouldn’t be the victim […]
text:
(Getty Images).Missouri Republicans have been making the case for years that our state constitution is getting hijacked by out-of-state interests. Gov. Mike Kehoe said it plainly in a video backing Amendment 4, the proposal that would have made it virtually impossible for voters to amend the Missouri Constitution.
“Our constitution,” he said, “shouldn’t be the victim of out-of-state special interests who spend millions to deceive voters and pass out-of-touch policies.”
To hear him tell it, cash pours into our politics to bankroll initiative petition campaigns, buying signatures and TV time. Missourians — decent people with jobs and kids and no particular interest in reading a 30-page, proposed constitutional amendment — get talked into things.
And before you know it, voters have expanded Medicaid, legalized marijuana or guaranteed abortion rights over the objections of the Republican supermajority they sent to Jefferson City.
The implicit message: Missourians keep getting duped.
But it’s hard to square that with Tuesday’s primary election results.
A political action committee called Missouri Promise raised $23 million to boost a GOP-backed tax overhaul on the ballot as Amendment 5. It did so through a fountain of cash flowing through a pipeline of nonprofits — two with Missouri addresses, one of them a Jefferson City post office box, and others at private mailboxes in Ohio, Virginia and Maryland.
It flooded the airwaves with ads, promising to take on data centers, put more money in taxpayers’ pockets and, down the home stretch, give the middle finger to the commies.
It lost by 67 percentage points statewide and was defeated in every county.
Historic defeats for Missouri GOP priorities raise questions about what comes next

On the same ballot was Amendment 1, renewing the one-tenth-cent sales tax that pays for state parks and soil and water conservation.
Supporters of Amendment 1 had been nervous about Amendment 5. Their fear was pretty understandable: Spend weeks telling voters that one amendment could lead to higher sales taxes and maybe they start seeing the words “sales tax” everywhere and vote no on both.
They didn’t.
Amendment 1 received about 82% of the vote. So on the same trip to the polls, Missouri voters gave one sales tax amendment 82% support and another 16%.
Then there’s Amendment 4.
Its supporters wanted citizen-led constitutional amendments to win not just statewide, but in every congressional district, citing the complaint over wealthy interests spending millions to manipulate voters.
Voters don’t seem to have a problem with the system. Amendment 4 couldn’t muster 20% of the vote.
That’s what I think Jefferson City sometimes misses about the initiative petition process. Republicans tend to study the amendments voters have approved and conclude something has gone wrong with the process.
Democrats have their own version of this. They see that same list, decide Missouri is a secretly progressive state waiting on the right candidate, and then watch voters hand Republicans another supermajority.
Both parties keep concluding the electorate must have meant something other than what it said. Whatever you think of Medicaid expansion, marijuana, minimum wage or abortion rights, voters had opportunities to hear arguments, watch millions get spent and make choices.
Sometimes they said yes.
Tuesday they said no. Loudly.
None of this makes Missouri voters uniquely wise. They’ve made decisions they’ll regret. So have legislators. So have governors. That’s democracy’s rather inconvenient feature: Nobody gets a monopoly on good judgment.
That doesn’t mean money doesn’t matter. Of course it does. Nobody spends $20 million on political advertising because political advertising doesn’t work.
But Tuesday was a useful reminder of the difference between voters being persuaded and voters being stupid.
Missourians may keep making choices Jefferson City wishes they wouldn’t.
That doesn’t mean they don’t know what they’re doing.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri is No. 3 in the number of cyclosporiasis cases in the nation
description: Missouri has officially been added to the list of states linked to the shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms that caused cyclosporiasis. Five other states — Arkansas, Iowa, Nebraska, New Hampshire and North Carolina — are also new to the list. They join Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia. Boone[...]
text:
Vegetables and lettuces at a grocery store in Michigan. Michigan health officials say lettuces and salad greens are emerging as a likely source in the nationwide cyclosporiasis outbreak, which has sickened hundreds of people across 31 states (Jon King/Michigan Advance).Missouri has officially been added to the list of states linked to the shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms that caused cyclosporiasis.
Five other states — Arkansas, Iowa, Nebraska, New Hampshire and North Carolina — are also new to the list. They join Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia.
Boone County counted 97 cases by Thursday, said Austin Krohn, spokesperson for the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department.
As of Sunday, the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services reported 1,095 cases — nearly double the number of cases it reported last week.
The Food and Drug Administration and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention determined that 568 of the Missouri cases are directly tied to lettuce from Taylor Farms, likely infected by contaminated water in the fields in Mexico. Missouri now ranks No. 3 in the country for the highest number of cases linked to the outbreak, after Michigan and Ohio.
The lettuce was widely distributed to Taco Bell outlets, Walmart stores and various food service locations in 29 states. Taco Bell has removed the affected lettuce from its supply chain and restaurants nationwide.
“We can expect to continue to see the number of confirmed cases rise, despite the recall, due to the fact that it can take as long as six weeks for CDC and state officials to determine if a sick person is part of this outbreak,” the FDA reported this week on its website.
Nationwide, 6,358 cases are directly tied to the outbreak, and another 10,468 may not be connected. Additionally, more than 12,000 cases are awaiting laboratory testing or require further investigation.
Taylor Nelson, an infectious disease specialist with MU Health Care, said Thursday that 96 cases had been reported in the UM Hospital System, with one hospitalization.
“Everything has been able to be managed on an outpatient basis, and there probably are more cases that are pretty mild that haven’t been identified,” Nelson said. “It can be a fairly prolonged illness, but oftentimes, it’s not a fatal or severe illness.”
Cyclosporiasis is not a new infection, he said. There are small, produce-related outbreaks every summer.
“It’s not like this is completely out of the norm to see things like this, but it’s definitely the biggest outbreak that we’ve seen,” Nelson said.
This outbreak is likely much larger than previous ones because of the number of people who eat at Taco Bell, and because the lettuce was distributed across the nation, Nelson said.
The first two deaths due to cyclosporiasis were reported recently in Michigan, where the majority of the cases have been tracked.
According to Michigan Health and Human Services, “Both individuals had significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration.”
Dehydration due to diarrhea and vomiting is a major concern for health care professionals.
Generally, the infection is highly treatable by antibiotics, but people with weakened immune systems, the elderly and children might have more severe symptoms and require longer treatment, Nelson said.
Ensuring people are hydrated is a high priority for medical personnel, Nelson said. If someone can’t stay hydrated through oral intake of fluids, that may be a reason for hospitalization.
According to the CDC and the FDA, the investigation into cyclosporiasis cases will continue.
“I would be hopeful, now we’re several weeks out from the recall, that we would start to see a decline,” Nelson said.
This story originally appeared in the Columbia Missourian. It can be republished in print or online.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Governor signs law to expand microtransit to seniors, disabled residents statewide
description: A bill signed by Gov. Mikie Sherrill seeks to expand access to microtransit for seniors and disabled residents statewide.
text:
A bill signed by Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Friday seeks to expand access to microtransit for seniors and disabled residents statewide. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)More state aid would be available for county programs that provide seniors and residents with disabilities with on-demand microtransit programs under legislation signed by Gov. Mikie Sherrill.
New Jersey lawmakers voted unanimously in late June to pass a bill that expands NJ Transit’s existing accessibility program to include microtransit options, vehicles people can hail from their phone to take them to work, school, or doctors’ appointments, or to connect with existing public transportation.
“For too many seniors and residents with disabilities, the biggest barrier isn’t whether transportation exists — it’s whether they can actually access it when they need it. This law gives counties another tool to bridge that gap,” bill sponsor Assemblyman Kenyatta Stewart (D-Passaic) told the New Jersey Monitor.
The law, signed by Sherrill on Friday, allows counties to seek funding from the state’s senior citizen and disabled resident transportation assistance program to pay for their microtransit options. The state budget has about $56 million for that fund this year.
Passaic County now runs a microtransit program that offers $1.90 rides through a service called Via that operates in Passaic and Clifton. Trenton residents can take GoTrenton for $2; it’s also available for free to maternal health workers and women who are pregnant or recently gave birth under a partnership with the New Jersey Maternal and Infant Health Innovation Authority. NJ Transit has the MicroLink pilot program that serves a half-dozen towns in Bergen and Monmouth counties.
New Jersey is home to some 1.7 million seniors, roughly 18% of the state’s population, and more than 25,000 people with disabilities receive services from the state.
“Every New Jerseyan deserves the opportunity to remain independent and connected, and this legislation helps move us closer to that goal,” Stewart said.
The law does not specify what counties must include in their plans, but it defines “on-demand microtransit” as a shared motor-vehicle service that allows a rider to select pick-up and drop-off locations by phone or mobile app, with transportation provided at a time of their choice or as “as soon as possible” after the rider logs on.
It also requires that programs funded through the program and operated by the county, even via a subcontractor, to pay drivers as regular employees as opposed to independent contractors.

name: Michigan Advance
title: If it’s socialism, show us
description: Michigan voters have barely finished choosing their candidates for November, and already one of the oldest labels in American politics is getting another workout. Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in this week’s Democratic primary for U.S. Senate offers a timely example. El-Sayed is unapologetically progressive, and voters should scrutinize his proposals, challenge t[...]
text:
Campaign signs supporting President Donald Trump sit in the front yard of a home on November 01, 2020 in Kenosha, Wisconsin. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)Michigan voters have barely finished choosing their candidates for November, and already one of the oldest labels in American politics is getting another workout.
Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in this week’s Democratic primary for U.S. Senate offers a timely example. El-Sayed is unapologetically progressive, and voters should scrutinize his proposals, challenge their costs and consequences, and decide whether they want them enacted.
But they should evaluate the policies he actually proposes, not an economic system attached to them because the label is politically useful.
Most of what is being called socialism in American politics today isn’t socialism.
Socialism encompasses many traditions, but its fundamental distinction from capitalism concerns who owns and controls the economy’s productive assets. Under capitalism, the bulk of businesses and other means of production are privately owned and controlled. Under socialism, the bulk are under some form of social, collective, worker or democratic control.
Communism goes further, ultimately envisioning common ownership of the means of production and a classless society.
Compare that with what is routinely labeled “socialist” today: higher taxes on wealthy Americans, expanded health coverage, stronger labor protections, environmental regulation, public investment and a larger social safety net.
U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks during a rally in Ferndale, Mich., on July 25, 2026. U.S. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Van Hollen and U.S. Rep. Pramila Jayapal also spoke at the event. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
Those policies may be wise or foolish, affordable or too expensive, effective or ineffective. But they do not abolish private property, eliminate private businesses, transfer the American economy to collective ownership or end capitalism.
That distinction is the entire point.
Calling something “socialist” or “communist” carries political power because of what those words cause many Americans to imagine: the Soviet Union, Cuba, Maoist China, Venezuela, state control, economic failure, political repression and the loss of freedom.
That history is authentic. But raising a tax rate or expanding health coverage within a capitalist economy is not the Soviet Union.
Branding it as such creates an emotional association before voters examine what is actually being proposed. Call a healthcare proposal socialist, and perhaps you don’t have to explain why it will fail. Call a Democrat a communist, and perhaps you don’t have to engage with what that person actually believes.
It’s lazy politicking. The label does the work the argument should have done.
And it assumes remarkably little of the American voter. Repeat the label often enough and perhaps we stop asking what a proposal actually does.
The more frightening the label, the more evidence we should demand.
What specifically makes a proposal socialist? Does it move substantial portions of the economy from private to social or collective control? Or does it leave America’s capitalist economy intact while changing a tax rate, regulation or government program?
If someone calls a Democrat a communist, ask what belief or proposal makes that description accurate. If there is an answer, examine it. If there isn’t, perhaps the label wasn’t intended to inform you, but to provoke you.
But this is about more than political vocabulary. Democracy depends not only on laws and institutions, but on honesty, trust and good faith. Deliberately misrepresenting an opponent’s position undermines those norms. So does treating policies as somehow illegitimate simply because voters choose something we oppose.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Democracy does not promise us the policies we want. It gives citizens the power to choose among competing ideas. If Americans vote for higher taxes, expanded public programs or greater regulation, that does not make the system socialist.
It means the system worked.
We are free to believe voters made the wrong choice. But the democratic response is to make a better argument and persuade them to choose differently, not attach a frightening ideological label to a legitimate democratic choice.
If a policy costs too much, show us the numbers. If it will hurt Michigan businesses or families, explain how. If a regulation will eliminate jobs, provide the evidence. If a program will create waste, make the case.
Those are arguments. “Socialism” and “communism” are not.
When political leaders repeatedly substitute those words for a substantive case against what their opponents actually propose, voters should consider another possibility, that perhaps the label is necessary because the argument isn’t strong enough without it.
America has always debated the boundary between private markets and public responsibility. We built public schools and universities, Social Security and Medicare, highways and libraries while maintaining an overwhelmingly private, market-based economy.
We can and should argue about where that boundary belongs. But we can’t genuinely have that argument if every movement of the boundary becomes “socialism” and every political opponent becomes a “communist.”
So the next time “socialist” or “communist” appears in a political speech, advertisement or social media post, look past the label. Ask what it actually means, whether it accurately describes the policy and what evidence supports the claim. Then ask the question that matters most: Why does the speaker need me to fear the label instead of persuading me to oppose the idea?
Michigan voters don’t need politicians to tell us what to fear. We need them to make their case. If an idea is bad, defeat it with facts. If a policy is misguided, expose its flaws. If an argument is strong, make it.
Words still mean things. We should insist that our politics does, too.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Legal Marijuana NOW candidate says he never planned to leave Senate race
description: Legal Marijuana NOW U.S. Senate candidate Mike Marvin told the Examiner he doesn’t plan to hold any campaign events.
text:
Signs in the bowels of the Nebraska State Capitol advocate for legalization of marijuana. (Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Legal Marijuana NOW U.S. Senate candidate Mike Marvin told the Examiner that he never planned to leave the race. 
Marvin said that, as of “right now,” he doesn’t plan to hold any campaign events before the November election. Marvin is currently running alongside nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn and incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts.
U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., center, faces nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn, left, and Legal Marijuana NOW nominee Mike Marvin in Nebraska’s Senate race this fall. (Candidate photos courtesy of respective campaigns | U.S. Capitol photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
Legal Marijuana NOW Party officials said they have never had an interaction with their Senate nominee. While the national and local media has focused on former Democratic nominee Cindy Burbank and her efforts to get on and off the ballot, Legal Marijuana NOW, which officially became a party in 2021, has also been part of the twists and turns of this year’s Nebraska Senate race, as well as the 2024 race between Osborn and Republican U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer.
“He never contacted any of the members of our executive committee. As chairman of the party, I have never met or talked to him,” Legal Marijuana NOW Party Chair Ed Williams said. 
Williams said he was vice chair of the party since its inception. Asked by the Examiner whether the party planned to replace Marvin if he dropped out, Williams said that, to the best of his knowledge, no one wanted to replace him. 
Marvin was one of the candidates accused of being a “plant” for Osborn. On his website, Marvin said he would “work with other candidates to make sure” to have a “united front against Pete Ricketts.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Former Democratic nominee Burbank paid Marvin’s $1,740 candidate filing fee earlier this year. She dropped out of the race one day after the secretary of state verified Osborn’s signatures to be on the fall ballot.  
Marvin has denied being a plant for Osborn. 
The Senate race between Osborn and Pete Ricketts will differ from Osborn’s bid in 2024 against Fischer because that was a true “head-to-head” race. Legal Marijuana NOW party leaders at the time chose not to run a candidate because supporters of Osborn and Kerry Eddy, the former 2024 nominee who stepped aside for Osborn, threatened to sue. 
Nebraska Democrats decided not to go forward with a write-in candidate in 2024 after Osborn flirted with seeking Democratic and third-party support until it was too late for the Democrats to run a candidate of their own, which led to some hurt feelings among some of his potential supporters on the left. 
Osborn’s campaign had no comment on how Marvin’s staying on the ballot would affect the race. 
‘Unlikely to be enough to make a difference’
Dona-Gene Barton, a political science professor at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln who studies political behavior, said she thinks Legal Marijuana NOW’s presence in the race is “unlikely to be enough to make a difference in the final election result, as has been the case in past statewide elections.” 
While Ricketts and Osborn are considered the leading candidates, there will likely be two new political parties as efforts by two groups met the petition signature threshold, though it’s unclear which races will get candidates from the new parties. There is also a lawsuit trying to force state Democrats to find a replacement for Burbank. 
Rick Beard, Legal Marijuana NOW’s gubernatorial candidate, said party members don’t know Marvin as “he doesn’t contact us, he won’t do a town hall with LMN candidates, we don’t endorse him, and he doesn’t endorse me, as he supports Lynne Walz.” 
Beard also pointed out that Omaha Tribe Attorney General John Cartier is the treasurer for Marvin, the sponsor of the new “America First Party” and “Osborn’s lawyer.” 
“Figure that out,” Beard said. 
Cartier wrote a letter to Legal Marijuana NOW leaders in 2024, arguing that the party had flubbed its handling of a convention that year to weigh replacing Eddy. Cartier, currently registered nonpartisan, is listed as treasurer for the Marvin campaign, according to the Federal Election Commission. Cartier also received $500 from Osborn’s campaign for legal fees in November 2024, according to the FEC. 
A comment on an Examiner Facebook post about Marvin staying in the Senate race, which appears to have been written by Marion Beard, Rick’s wife and the vice chair of the party, reads, “No one in the legal marijuana NOW party knows Mike Marvin. He has never contacted us and we do NOT endorse him.” 
The general election is Nov 3.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma offers property tax breaks to businesses. Now lawmakers want to change the rules
description: Imagine ordering the most expensive cut of steak at a restaurant and telling the waitress that you’ll pay. But when she brings the bill, you balk over the price and attempt to negotiate it. It sounds completely ridiculous doesn’t it? Yet that’s exactly what lawmakers are attempting to do with State Question 844, and they […]
text:
A person counts money. (Getty Images)Imagine ordering the most expensive cut of steak at a restaurant and telling the waitress that you’ll pay. But when she brings the bill, you balk over the price and attempt to negotiate it.
It sounds completely ridiculous doesn’t it? Yet that’s exactly what lawmakers are attempting to do with State Question 844, and they want voters to give them permission to do it later this month.
For 40 years now, legislators have been utilizing a state program that offers a tax break to manufacturers willing to come to Oklahoma. In exchange for opening up shop, qualifying manufacturers earn a five-year property tax exemption, meaning they don’t have to pay a key tax that counties, schools, libraries, health departments and other local entities rely on to operate.
In 1985, voters decided that it’s fine for lawmakers to offer this exemption as a way to draw new businesses and jobs, but they prudently included a constitutional requirement that ensures the Legislature covers the missed money for the local entities that would otherwise benefit from the taxes generated by these big businesses. 
Reminder: The state doesn’t receive revenue from property taxes. Only local and county governments do.
For years, lawmakers faithfully paid the tab. But now that more businesses are utilizing this credit and property valuations are increasing, lawmakers no longer want to have to pay the piper.
So they want to change the rules, and they want the public to help.
They’re asking Oklahomans on Aug. 25 to vote on a state question that would grant the Legislature the power to calculate how much — or how little — schools and counties should be reimbursed for lost revenue. They plan to do so in such a way that no one county receives reimbursements that would be “a detriment to other counties in the state.” 
Don’t forget, our lawmakers also set the parameters of who qualifies. Local governments don’t have any say in that, though they will certainly feel the pain if the Legislature starts mucking around with their reimbursement calculations.
Legislators contend that the $88.6 million the state had to pay in reimbursements last year is too much. Of that, about 73% supplemented public school losses.
They’re also bellyaching that this program disproportionately benefited a few counties. 
For instance, about 40% of reimbursements are currently being allocated to Mayes County, which boasts Pryor’s booming MidAmerica Industrial Park in northeast Oklahoma. 
Imagine that. The reimbursement is disproportionately affecting a location that our state’s economic development officials have been actively recruiting businesses to. It wasn’t many years ago that our lawmakers were involved in an unsuccessful quest to lure a massive Panasonic battery plant to the same county that they’re now complaining about. 
I remember a legislative study a few years ago that featured lawmakers befuddled that the price tag for this program had soared amid a rise in qualifying projects, which at the time included wind farms and some oil and gas infrastructure. 
In short, this has been an ongoing issue for years.
Republican House Speaker Kyle Hilbert told Oklahoma Voice that the Legislature doesn’t intend to change any existing reimbursement rates. Lawmakers only want to intervene in new deals.
Hilbert said lawmakers want to have input if a manufacturer’s property value assessment is too high. The state is on the hook for paying the tab regardless of what the property is assessed at and has no ability to contest it, he said.
There are plenty of other options to solve this than legislators going nuclear and inserting themselves in a property assessment process that they have no expertise in.
Why don’t lawmakers give themselves the power to contest these valuations?
Why not pass legislation requiring that counties hire a previously agreed upon independent assessor, who specializes in these valuations — on the state’s dime — as a stopgap to the county’s work to ensure these developments are properly valued?
Or why not insist the tax program be eliminated entirely if it’s too expensive? Legislators have disqualified wind farms and data centers and plan to phase out solar farms. We have plenty of other needs in this state that could use that money.
Legislators don’t want to get rid of it because it’s a handy tool for economic development leaders to dangle in front of prospective businesses.
The other problem is Hilbert and pretty much every other current lawmaker isn’t going to be in office 10 years from now due to term limits. There’s nothing to stop future legislators from reneging on his pledge, particularly if budget times get tough like they always seem to. 
And if we lift the guardrails, there’s nothing to stop lawmakers from expanding this program to even more industries when they have even less skin in the game.
If legislators like what’s on the menu, then that’s fine. If not, they have the power to change it.
But if we’re going to change this, it should be for the betterment of all and not the detriment of local governments whose communities have been able to capitalize on our state leaders’ push to diversify our economy.
Like ships on an ocean, we all rise and fall together. Our already cash-strapped schools and counties shouldn’t be left footing the bill for this program.

name: WyoFile
title: Sorry, governor. Opposing data centers doesn’t make us sheep.
description:
Industry has a habit of promising Wyomingites the moon, and the data center boom is no different. How many times must we learn this hard lesson, asks guest columnist Heather Madrid.
The post Sorry, governor. Opposing data centers doesn’t make us sheep. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
While arguing against data center moratoriums, Gov. Mark Gordon recently told Wyomingites to “lead, follow, or get out of the way.” He attributed the quote to Gen. George Patton, his great-uncle. The core of the full quote is simple: We herd sheep, drive cattle and lead people. The quote fails to capture that Wyoming citizens are sovereign. We are not livestock and we are not soldiers serving at the command of the governor. 

Opinion

Asking questions about the unprecedented data center build-out in Wyoming and its’ impact on our grid, the long-term and cumulative strain on our regional resources, tax incentives, and the “business park” siting loophole does not make us fearful sheep. It means we are civically responsible American citizens participating in democracy and exercising our constitutional rights.
For decades, Wyoming has eagerly hosted massive booms. We were told to unquestioningly open our doors to industries such as oil, gas and coal and were promised prosperity if we would just get out of the way. How quickly we forget the impact on the host communities who were left to deal with the fallout when the market shifted and those companies packed up. Imagine where those communities could be now had they demanded long-term protection and permanent community benefits. Imagine what Wyoming would look like today if our leaders had the foresight to demand more for our people instead of letting industry dictate the terms. How many times must we learn this hard lesson?
Now, we are being asked to repeat history with artificial intelligence and data centers. Our local governments have been captured by corporate America. Rather than protecting the communities that elected them, they are signing nondisclosure agreements, fast-tracking data centers through the “business park” loophole and changing local zoning regulations to minimize the public’s voice. Permitting data centers in business parks allows these power-hungry, resource-consumptive, industrial complexes to bypass the Industrial Siting Act process, where cumulative impacts on our communities and environment would be studied rather than assessed in isolation, with no studies on the impact to our hospitals, housing and job markets. What happened to government of the people, by the people and for the people? Our public offices are not meant to serve as a taxpayer-funded concierge service for the wealthiest companies in the history of the world.
If these multibillion-dollar corporations wanted to be good neighbors, they would offer actions instead of words while running us over at city council meetings. Instead, they target local nonprofits and specific businesses, handing out scraps to further their interests. This is not neighborly. This is a strategic corporate investment in return for financial dependence, silence and compliance to ensure no one speaks up at public hearings. A good neighbor doesn’t tell us what we need. A good neighbor sits down with the residents whose lives are being upended and asks them what they need. The people who live here should be benefiting from their intrusive presence, not just a local government that counts the increasing property tax revenue while its citizens are sidelined.
We can meet modern challenges head-on. But the Wyoming way does not have to mean blindly following, like sheep, without a plan. We need leadership that will protect the citizens who will still be living, working and raising families here long after the corporate executives have moved back to Silicon Valley.
James Madison, a Founding Father and architect of our democracy, warned about this present danger over two centuries ago by stating that “the power of all corporations ought to be limited … the growing wealth acquired by them never fails to be a source of abuses.”
Do not tell us to get out of the way. Invite us to sit at the table that we the people bought and paid for.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming must choose its future
description:
With the primary election around the corner, columnist Khale Lenhart shares his take on what qualities make a good candidate.
The post Wyoming must choose its future appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
In 1964, Ronald Reagan gave a speech that would launch his political career. It was titled “A Time for Choosing” and was given on behalf of then-presidential candidate Barry Goldwater. In the speech, Reagan decried big government and the erosion of freedoms in the face of top-down decisions. He framed the choice facing the American people as one not just between personalities, but between a path that preserved the ideals of the American founding and one that led to decline. Although his candidate was unsuccessful that year, this speech launched Reagan’s own political career and led to the rise of the conservative movement that would define American politics for the next 50 years.

Opinion

Wyoming is facing our own time to choose. Although the motivating issues are different than in Reagan’s 1960s, we are at an inflection point as we choose what type of state we are going to be. Do we continue down the path of decline, letting our infrastructure crumble and opportunity slip away based on shortsightedness? Or do we choose a more vibrant future, based on our state’s needs and strengths?  
I hope that my fellow citizens will take this decision seriously. Elections have consequences, and the people we elevate into public office matter. The change in tone and direction of the last several years of Wyoming state government is a direct result of the choices voters made, wittingly or not. As we make these choices, we should all be reminded of what types of questions are important in deciding our political future.
With that in mind, I believe the most important questions we should be asking are not just about specific policies — although those are important — but about how the candidates see the world around them.  The first thing I look for in a candidate is a long-term vision. Sacrificing future well-being for instant convenience is the path to ruin, and we have seen too much of that in recent years. Too many of our elected officials are focused on tearing down so that they can reap temporary benefits instead of building a state that will succeed after their short time in office is done.
Second, we must find candidates who have good judgment. Specific policy proposals will tell you how a candidate will act on one or two issues, but elected officials are faced with hundreds or thousands of decisions. It is impossible to anticipate every topic a candidate will have to decide on, so we must trust their ability to exercise their own judgment. Those who have exhibited an inability to make good decisions, whether it be in office, in their public actions or in their personal life, should not be trusted to make decisions on behalf of the rest of us.  
This goes hand in hand with the need for independent thought. Our elected officials must be beholden to the voters of Wyoming, not to outside groups or influences. Critical thought and independence are how we make good laws. Tribalism and lockstep voting deprive us of the best part of an elected body — the diversity of views and fresh ideas that come from a group of different people. If our officials, and especially our legislators, depend on others to tell them how to vote, we are all worse for it.
We also must vote for candidates who are committed to actually solving problems, not just parroting ideology. There is nothing conservative about undercutting effective government. Conservatism isn’t anarchy, and it benefits no one to deprive those who perform legitimate, necessary government functions of the means to do so effectively. Our state and local governments are not infested with the same bloat and inefficiencies we see at the federal level. We are a frontier state with limited resources and low taxes. Our neighbors in government service already do more with less. We need candidates who can discern reality from talking points and are willing to speak honestly about what we need to have a functioning state. This means that the panderers and the ideologues are ill-suited to actually govern.  
Lastly, we need officials of good character and capability. Elected office is based on trust, both in the person and their work. Bad characters are not going to change just because they have been elevated in office. Similarly, those who simply lack the skill set to lead or communicate effectively are not going to magically develop those skills simply by winning an election. Instead, it is up to us to decide whether our officials are really the best we can do. Voting is the way we all can have a say in our government. With the primary elections looming, we must all recognize that now is our time to choose. What future do we want?

title: These paramedics do more than emergency calls. Idaho wants more of them. This grant could help.
description: Dave Walls remembers winning an argument with Medicaid.  At first, the state-run public assistance program wouldn’t cover an in-home caregiving service for a patient that he was helping out. But after he pointed out coverage guidelines on the state’s website, Walls said the state’s tune changed. “That feels almost as good as a code save,” […]
text:
Dave Walls is a community paramedic at Ada County Paramedics, one of few EMS agencies that adopted a program to embed paramedics to help patients manage chronic health conditions. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)Dave Walls remembers winning an argument with Medicaid. 
At first, the state-run public assistance program wouldn’t cover an in-home caregiving service for a patient that he was helping out. But after he pointed out coverage guidelines on the state’s website, Walls said the state’s tune changed.
“That feels almost as good as a code save,” referring to when emergency responders save someone from a heart attack, said Walls, who has worked for almost three years as a community paramedic in Ada County, Idaho’s most populated county.
It wasn’t a typical call for paramedics, who usually deal with emergency medical situations. But it’s part of the norm for community paramedics, a specialized type of paramedic or EMT that helps people manage chronic conditions in the hopes of preventing future hospitalizations — and even bigger bills. 
And as Idaho seeks to tap into millions of dollars in federal grant funding through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act dedicated to rural health care access, Wayne Denny, the leader of Idaho’s Bureau Emergency Medical Services, or EMS, wants to use some of it to expand community health EMS providers into rural communities across Idaho. And he hopes it can be a critical infusion to Idaho’s EMS system, which is experiencing a shortage amid funding struggles. Some also see promise in expanding community paramedics in a largely rural state that has long had a doctors’ shortage. 
“This very possibly will kind of serve as that seed money that we were going to need to start getting the system built out. Because we really think that if if we can get this foundation created and demonstrate that the model that we’re suggesting has value and that it will end up saving money in the end,” Denny said in an interview, adding that the investment could allow EMS agencies to demonstrate that the model works to help ease the process of getting coverage from health insurers. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 What are community health EMS providers? 

Across the U.S., more than a third of emergency department visits are not urgent, according to a 2013 study that’s been cited by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. 
That’s where community EMS providers step in.
They are EMTs trained to handle chronic health conditions and non-urgent health conditions. They often visit patients who frequently call for ambulances or patients recently discharged from the hospital, and they may even do house calls to draw labs for somebody who lives far away from clinics. And they might do a laundry list of other things: like connect patients with resources for how to navigate the health care system or programs, such as medical transportation, and even share resources for a new diagnosis, like dementia, or how to make their homes more accessible by walkers. 
In Idaho, a public transit program can take you to the doctor. If it has enough funding.

In the Magic Valley, an area of southcentral Idaho, James Rhom has seen the impact of community health workers. He said the hospital has less demand for the emergency department, freeing up beds, and fewer patients recently discharged from the hospital need to be readmitted.
Rhom manages the EMS team at Magic Valley Paramedics.
He said the shift to community health EMS from traditional EMS was “an eye opening experience.”
“As a paramedic, I knew … there’s something more going on here, right? You’d go out and … someone’s sick, and then there’s an emergency or a minor injury or illness or something, and you’re like, ‘There’s something here that I’m missing that I just can’t piece apart about how they got to where they are today,’” Rhom said.
But in community health EMS work, he said there’s more opportunity to understand what’s driving health outcomes.
“When you sit down with a patient, you can really go back and sit down with them, and they may have been calling 911 six, eight, 10 times over the last couple months,” Rhom said. 
The Magic Valley program, founded in 2019, covers Twin Falls, Jerome and Gooding counties. 
An Ada County community paramedic holds up a pamphlet explaining what home visits from community paramedics look like. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
In Ada County, the community health paramedic program has been up and running for more than a decade. Mark Babson signed up early.
“I always have thought that EMS — paramedics and EMTs — have been underutilized in that larger health care system delivery model because of that connection to community,” he said in an interview.
Then he helped get Walls on board. 
In 2012, Babson frequented the Starbucks that Walls managed. Hearing Babson’s stories as a paramedic, and the agency’s goals of innovating the EMS system, helped convince Walls to go back to school and become a paramedic.
Today, Walls’ calls look different than a typical paramedic. He isn’t showing up in an ambulance; he drives a GMC Yukon branded for Ada County Paramedics. And he doesn’t have a partner.
Dave Walls, an Ada County community paramedic, sorts through pamphlets he gives to patients on calls. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
“We’re very much more of a nondescript, just a guy with a bag that’s walking in,” Walls said. “… Sometimes we get to spend time that a normal EMS provider wouldn’t have, and sometimes it might be time that a specialist or a primary care physician may not have either.”
“Sometimes it can be as simple as, ‘I just don’t know how to get to my doctor’s appointments anymore,’ or ‘I’m going to lose my home because I’m on … limited income and I don’t know who to reach out to to find support for my power bill,’ or ‘I’m on oxygen, and they’re going to turn my power off. What do I do?’” he said.
And he acknowledges that community paramedics fill a niche.
“The days of the doctor coming to your door are fewer and far between,” Walls said. 
 The pitch to fund more community health EMS providers

Right now, only a handful of EMS agencies in Idaho are doing community health EMS work — such as in Ada County and the Magic Valley, said Denny, who leads the state’s EMS Bureau. But he hopes to place at least one community health EMS provider in every Idaho county that lacks one.

CONTACT US



Denny is still waiting to iron out details about his proposal to expand community EMTs – like how much money he’ll need. But he previewed the idea last month to a panel of state lawmakers tasked with overseeing how the state spends the rural health funds.
He told lawmakers that the EMS Bureau, which is now part of the Idaho Military Division, hopes to tap into the rural health funds to bolster Idaho’s 911 system — by modernizing the state’s communications center, and shift local dispatchers toward next-generation 911, a more sophisticated system. And he hopes to bolster the EMS workforce, by expanding community health EMS providers, non-clinical community health workers that he said serve as patient navigators, and placing at least one-paid EMS provider in each of Idaho’s 44 counties. 
That’s in hopes of chipping away at the state’s EMS shortage, which is a largely volunteer workforce and isn’t required to be funded by the state, Idaho Public Television reported. 
And he touted the promise of community health work. 
“We’ve already demonstrated, in some of the work that we’ve done over the years, is that if you pay us $10 to do prevention, we’ll save you $100 on the ER,” Denny told members of the Legislature’s Rural Health Transformation Committee. 
But Idaho is on a clock to spend the money. The funds must be doled out by Oct. 30, or the federal government will claw them back.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: OPINION: Belief, popularity differ from the truth
description: From the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, to the 2020 election, columnist George Ayoub explores Americans' relationship with the truth.
text:
Construction work at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on May 5, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)When historians finish chronicling the politics and cultural issues of this age, librarians and booksellers may have to file those annals among other works of fiction. That’s because the conundrum of our time has become our tenuous relationship with the truth.
There’s more. Considering our wont to let slide all manner of “truthiness,” whether we care enough about the dysfunction remains an open question.
Unless you’ve been vacationing on a distant planet without wifi, you know politics is awash in duplicity. Some in power seem either unable or uninterested in getting to the truth. When things, like a vote, don’t go their way, they too often claim conspiracy, offer head-scratching explanations or simply deflect. They even muse that it’s the work of the devil … or the previous administration. Blaming communists is now all the rage, too.
Let’s start in the nation’s Capital because the fun-filled Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool fiasco has become the metaphor for fabrication that keeps on giving. Even with its watery wackiness, the pool problems are only a single instance of one’s ability to weave a tangled web. The reality is that current political lies come in a variety of flavors and force, each with its own dissembling design: whoppers, whites, bunk, bamboozle, bald-faced, fibs, myths, con, cap, cock and bull, dodge, ruse, jive, smoke blowing — with and without mirrors — and the ever present prevarication. Artificial intelligence has even contributed to the disinformation through slop and hallucinations.
Deceit does have limits. As “AlgaeGate” has shown, trafficking in whole-cloth lies along the internet superhighway, in coffee klatches or under the auspices of ChatGPT pales when making the same subterfuge hold up in a court of law. Some people — judges, to be exact — demand verifiable evidence. You remember the facts, don’t you?
The Department of Justice is dropping cases against a handful of reflecting pool “vandals” as the charges against them evaporate and the truth becomes clear. Nevertheless, the president and others in his orbit continue — without proof — to blame vandals rather than what was apparent early on: science and shoddy work.
Nebraskans know exactly how modern mendacity has real-world consequences.
Remember the abundance of conspiracy theories questioning the fidelity of the 2020 presidential election making the rounds for several months after the votes were in? They fueled an attack on the nation’s Capitol to undo the voters’ decision and essentially overthrow the government. After nearly 156 million votes were cast and counted, no discernable proof was ever found that would have changed the election’s outcome. Still, the conspiracy theories persisted (and still do). They came to be known collectively as “The Big Lie.”
Undaunted and apparently unconvinced of the 2020 election’s veracity, a Nebraska group launched a petition drive to ask voters if they should be required to show a photo ID when they cast their ballots. Granted, there was no evidence that voter fraud was even a thing in Nebraska. Nevertheless, the measure passed easily, we solved a problem that didn’t exist, and we became one of 19 states to enact a voter suppression law after the 2020 election and the advent of “The Big Lie.”
No one is arguing with the efficacy of showing a photo ID to vote in Nebraska. But if one eligible voter is disenfranchised because of the lack of photo ID, that’s one too many.
Department of Justice efforts to obtain state voter rolls are based on the same faulty premise: Our elections from registration to the voting booth to the counting process are defective. This also ignores the constitutional imperative that voting is the purview of the states, not the federal government.
As of this writing, the department is 0-21 in court cases where states have refused to turn over their voters’ information. Nebraska sent along its voters’ details to the Department of Justice early on. To where and to what effect, no one seems to know.
Meanwhile, we edge closer to a political tipping point where opponents for office, parties at odds or debaters at the dinner table share very few truths … or none at all. When we run out of common truths, hopes for cooperation and community are dimmed.
Logicians and psychologists might counsel that we’ve driven into the neighborhood bordering confirmation bias: Seeking information that confirms what we already believe and rejecting information that does not.
If it were only as easy as turning around. Meanwhile, just because something aligns with my worldview or my party, my favorite podcaster or my political hero says it’s true, doesn’t make it so.

title: Idaho public housing authorities approach proposed work requirements with caution
description: Only one of Idaho’s public housing authorities has signed on to a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development coalition to consider adding work requirements to its subsidized housing programs. Other authority leaders say they remain skeptical about the benefits of a work requirement.  Feds encourage public housing authorities to impose work rules, time[...]
text:
Many of Idaho's public housing authorities are still weighing the benefits of a proposed work requirement. (Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun)Only one of Idaho’s public housing authorities has signed on to a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development coalition to consider adding work requirements to its subsidized housing programs. Other authority leaders say they remain skeptical about the benefits of a work requirement. 
Feds encourage public housing authorities to impose work rules, time limits

The Work and Dignity Coalition was announced by HUD earlier this year in tandem with a proposed rule to allow independent housing authorities to enforce “work requirements, time limits, and supportive service frameworks for able-bodied, non-elderly adults receiving assistance.”
“Housing assistance was never meant to trap work-able individuals on government support their entire lives,” U.S. Secretary of Housing and Urban Development Scott Turner said in a press release. “Rather it should be a temporary foundation to launch into a life of self-sufficiency. Getting a paycheck is empowering, getting a welfare check is not.”
The proposed rule and the coalition signal a change in HUD’s approach to public housing assistance, focusing on proving self sufficiency.
 How would HUD’s proposal affect Idahoans?

While the leadership of many of Idaho’s housing authorities align with these goals, slashed operating budgets, increased administrative burden, and concerns around efficacy leave them circumspect about joining the coalition.
Sunny Shaw leads four different Idaho housing authorities, overseeing the work of Twin Falls, American Falls, Jerome and Buhl. Many of the programs she manages, which overwhelmingly serve disabled and elderly populations, would not see changes from a work requirement rule, she said. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“There’s 196 households that we serve in Twin Falls. 82% of those are elderly disabled, so that eliminates them. I have 34 households that are able-bodied by definition, and 83% of those are working. So it’s such a minor amount,” Shaw said. “I don’t generally see a population who is just choosing to be able-bodied and not working.”
One Idaho housing authority, however, sees opportunities to combat fraud in the system. In Pocatello, Housing Alliance and Community Partnerships joined the Work and Dignity Coalition this May. 
With a work requirement as part of the system, Executive Director Jared Magnum said, the government could have a better understanding of enrollees’ income. 
“If someone’s working under the table or they’re doing something on the side, it’s just unreported — that happens a lot,” Magnum said. “With the work requirements, it has to be a W-2 job, something the government’s going to be able to track.”
Magnum also praised the coalition’s consideration of time limits on housing vouchers, which provide government assistance to pay for housing in the private market.
“Someone could be on the voucher for 20 years, or 30 years, or 40 years, as long as they otherwise qualify,” Magnum said. “If you were doing two-year vouchers, you would probably be able to help a lot more people, because the only time that a new voucher is going to come available is if someone passes away or they lose the voucher. ”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Other Idaho housing authority officials are still weighing their options

The Southwestern Idaho Cooperative Housing Authority and Boise City/Ada County Housing Authorities have not made final decisions on joining the work and dignity coalition. 
Elisa Velasco, executive director of Southwestern Idaho Cooperative Housing Authority, expressed concern about extra work her staff might have to take on, without extra funding, should a work requirement be instated. 
Idaho leads the nation in housing growth. The data shows it’s still not enough.

“They’re only funding us at 86% of what we’re entitled to right now. So we’re not being paid anymore to do this,” Velasco said.
“So many of the targets set by this program are laudable and worthwhile, there remain some concerns,” said Deanna Watson, executive director at Boise City/Ada County Housing Authorities. “Too often employment does not pay a living wage, does not include benefits or paid time off so the loss and risks of losing assistance in a trade for precarious working conditions.”
Idaho’s largest housing authority, the Idaho Housing and Finance Association, has not joined the coalition. 
“Idaho Housing won’t make a decision about what, if anything, changes until the final rule is published,” IHFA spokesperson Jason Lantz said. 
In Pocatello, Magnum remains optimistic about the possibility of improving the public housing system. 
“It’s a monster to try to tackle something that big, and I applaud HUD for at least trying to do something,” he said.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: A voter guide to Alabama’s special primary elections
description: Voters in Alabama’s 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th Congressional Districts will go to the polls Tuesday to vote in the state’s special primary election. Following a special session held by the Alabama Legislature, Gov. Kay Ivey called for a special primary election in those districts after a U.S. Supreme Court order allowed the state to […]
text:
A sign saying "Vote Here" is seen at the Dean Road Recreation Center in Auburn, Alabama, on May 19, 2026. Voters in Alabama's 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th Congressional Districts will vote in special primaries on Tuesday. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector) 


 Key Points

Voters in Alabama will choose Republican and Democratic nominees in the Aug. 11 special primary election for the state’s 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th congressional districts.
There is no runoff election meaning the candidate with the most votes will be the nominee on the ballot in the November general election. 
Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Tuesday.




Voters in Alabama’s 1st, 2nd, 6th and 7th Congressional Districts will go to the polls Tuesday to vote in the state’s special primary election.
Following a special session held by the Alabama Legislature, Gov. Kay Ivey called for a special primary election in those districts after a U.S. Supreme Court order allowed the state to use a 2023 Legislature-approved map instead of a court ordered one. The 2023 map, previously struck down for being racially discriminatory, had led to two Black representatives being elected at the same time, first in Alabama’s history.
Democratic candidates have been largely decided in every race except for 6th Congressional District.
Sample ballots for counties having an election can be found on the Alabama Secretary of State’s website. Alabama has open primaries meaning voters will be allowed to pull either a Republican or Democratic ballot at their polling location.
There will be no runoff in the election, meaning the candidate who gets the most votes on Tuesday will be the nominee.
Alabama’s 1st Congressional District
Voters who pull a Republican ballot in south Alabama centered around Mobile will choose between Jerry Carl, John Mills and Austin Sidwell. The redrawn district covers all of Mobile, Baldwin and Escambia counties and part of Covington County.
The seat is currently held by U.S. Rep. Barry Moore, R-Enterprise, who is the Republican nominee for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who is running for governor.
Carl was elected to serve as U.S. Rep. for Alabama’s 1st Congressional District in 2020 and he lost re-election to Moore in 2024 according to election results. He said last month he wants to preserve an underwater petrified forest by turning it into a national park to prevent companies from harvesting the timber and said voters should choose him because of his experience in Congress.
Three Republican candidates in AL-01 face fears of low turnout in August special primary

Mills said last month he was running in the special election because he didn’t like any of the candidates running to replace Moore. If elected, Mills said he would ensure election integrity, border security and “stop reckless spending.”
Sidwell told the Reflector last month he wants to control government spending and address issues with Social Security.
The winner of the election will face Democratic nominee Clyde Jones in November. No other Democratic candidate qualified for the race.
Campaign finances: According to Federal Elections Commission filings through July 22, Carl has raised $1.2 million and spent $865,000; Sidwell has raised $199,000 and spent $194,000; Mills has raised $18,000 and spent $15,000.
Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District
Voters in Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, centered on the Wiregrass in southeastern Alabama, will choose between Republican candidates Hampton Harris, Christian Horn, Rhett Marques, David Matthews, Joshua McKee and James Richardson. The district covers the southeastern part of the state including Geneva, Houston, Montgomery and Macon counties and a portion of Covington County.
Horn said in a recent interview that his top priority is affordability.
“People want to be able to have policies that are going to be able to give them an opportunity to save money at home, to be able for seniors to be able to not have to make the choice between food and their pharmaceuticals,” he said.
Marques, a state representative, has touted his endorsement from President Donald Trump, mentioning it six times during a Republican Republican candidate forum in Eufaula last week. Marques said afterward that he wanted to run to “help President Trump pass his agenda and help the state move forward.”
One week before primary, AL-02 GOP candidates pitch platforms at Barbour County forum

According to his website, Marques wants to strengthen rural areas through investments in broadband and infrastructure to support healthcare, economic opportunity and education.
Richardson said during the forum his top priority is addressing veterans’ healthcare. Richardson served in the Marine Corps and lost his father, a veteran, to suicide after he was unable to get mental health resources at the VA hospital.
Harris said he wants to focus on restricting acess to abortions and said he would not raise taxes for Alabamians. Harris previously criticized Marques for his vote to increase the gas tax through the Rebuild Alabama Act of 2019. Prior to the vote, the gas tax had not been raised in the state since 1992, and the Business Council of Alabama and other organizations supported the measure to provide improvements to Alabama’s infrastructure. The bill passed by comfortable margins, with Democratic and Republican support. 
McKee said during the forum’s spur of the moment question and answer segment that he wanted to invest in communities to keep them sustainable.
Matthews, a former Trump appointee in the U.S. Department of Agriculture, said in an interview after the forum people should vote for him because he knows how D.C. policy works.
“Very rarely do people have the opportunity to elect somebody who understands how the executive branch works at a granular level,” he said. “I’ve dealt with infrastructure problems, and I’ve dealt with healthcare and housing and economic and business development, and I understand an aspect of governance that most people never get exposed to because usually people get elected into the legislative branch, and the way that they learn about the executive branch is through a superficial means.”
The winner of the primary will face U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, in the November general election. No other Democratic candidate qualified for the election.
2nd Congressional District: Marques has raised $1.3 million and spent $1.1 million; McKee has raised $521,000 and spent nearly $525,000; Harris has raised $246,000 and spent $82,000; Matthews has raised 48,000 and spent $36,000 and Richardson has raised $7,700 and spent $7,600. Horn has not reported any filings as of Friday afternoon.
Alabama’s 6th Congressional District
The 6th Congressional District in the southern Birmingham suburbs and central Alabama is the only district where both parties have contested primaries. The seat is solidly Republican. 
Republican voters will choose between U.S. Rep. Gary Palmer, R-Hoover, and challenger Case Dixon. Democratic voters will choose between Jacob Bouma-Sims, Ashtyn Kennedy, Maurice Mercer and Keith Pilkington.
Palmer, the 12-year incumbent for the district, said on his campaign website that he believes in religious freedom and supports repealing the Affordable Care Act in favor of a healthcare program that will “free-market, patient-centered solutions that increase competition, expand choice, and put individuals back in control of their health care decisions.”
Dixon, Palmer’s only GOP challenger and a first-time candidate, told the Reflector last month he wants to reduce the cost of living and address affordability.
Longtime U.S. Rep. Gary Palmer faces first-time candidate in August special primary

Pilkington initially qualified for the 6th Congressional District seat in January as the only Democratic candidate on the ballot. He said last month he qualified for the special election because of persisting issues with affordability and immigration. Pilkington said he would focus on creating affordable housing options.
Ashtyn Kennedy, a social media content creator, said she wanted to create a data center moratorium in Alabama and would support a federal data center moratorium bill sponsored by U.S. Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York, and Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont.
Mercer, a former Pelham City Councilman Maurice, said in a recent interview he wants to stop the current war in Iran.
“Whether that is working to see both sides peacefully stop the war, or just pulling the USA out. We have our sons and daughters over there, and right now, I think the American people still don’t know 100% why,” he said.
Bouma-Sims wants to address issues with Alabama Power by making an federal alternative program through a plan he calls the “Cahaba River Corporation.”
“It’s not a takeover of Alabama Power, it’s not abolishing Alabama Power with the swipe of a pen, it’s an alternative,” he said to the Reflector last month.
Four Democrats vie for central Alabama congressional seat in special primary election

Dixon and Mercer accused Palmer of breaking his term limit campaign promise. According to a 2023 report from Al.com, when Palmer initially ran for office, he pledged to only serve 10 years but changed his mind when he decided to seek reelection in 2024, saying God told him to run for another term.
The winners will move on to the November general election. 
Campaign finances: Dixon has raised $25,200 and spent $25,000; Palmer has raised $1 million and spent $946,000; Kennedy has raised nearly $10,000 and spent $9,300 and Mercer has raised $6,500 and spent $4,700. Pilkington and Bouma-Sims had not reported any filings as of Friday afternoon.
Alabama’s 7th Congressional District
Two Republican candidates, Ammie Akin and David Perry, are running to represent west Alabama in the 7th Congressional District.
Akin told the Reflector last month that she wanted to address crime and affordability in the district and create educational opportunities.
Two Republicans vie for 7th congressional district nomination in special August primary

“You can’t create opportunity without education. This is why I love education, because education opens the door for everything,” she said. 
Perry also said he wants to prioritize public safety in the district. According to a report from the Tuscaloosa Police Department, violent crime decreased from 2024 to 2025. 
The winner of the election will face Democratic nominee and current U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham, in November. No other Democratic candidate qualified for the election.
Campaign finances: Akin has raised $151,000 and spent $35,000. Perry had not reported any filings as of Friday afternoon.
When do polls open?
Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Tuesday.
Where do I find my polling place?
The Alabama Secretary of State’s website allows you to check voter registration and the location of your polling place. You can find it here.
What do I need to vote?
Voters must present a valid photo ID before voting. Valid forms of ID include: 

Alabama driver’s license (not expired or expired less than 60 days)
Alabama Law Enforcement Agency digital driver’s license
Alabama Non-Driver ID (not expired or expired less than 60 days)
Alabama Photo Voter ID card
State-issued ID (Alabama or any other state)
Federal-issued ID
U.S. Passport
Employee ID from the federal government; state of Alabama; county; municipality, board or other entity of Alabama
Student or employee ID from a public or private post-secondary educational institution in Alabama or other states (including colleges, universities, postgraduate technical and professional schools)
Digital student or employee ID from a public or private post-secondary educational institution in Alabama or other states (including colleges, universities, postgraduate technical and professional schools)
Military ID
Tribal ID

What happens after Tuesday?
Each nominee will face their counterpart in the general election on Nov. 3. Independent candidates have until election day to qualify.
When will we know the results?
When polling locations close at 7 p.m., local election offices will begin counting ballots and reporting results to their county probate offices. The Alabama Secretary of State’s office will post results as they become available Tuesday night.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Local governments in Colorado enact moratoriums on data center development
description: Amid a nationwide race to develop large data centers to drive the artificial intelligence boom, some local Colorado governments hit pause by enacting moratoriums to research what local regulations make sense. Public criticism concerns the environmental and health effects of data centers, especially hyperscale sites that provide massive computing power for co[...]
text:
Construction on a data center expansion at the QTS site in Aurora, Colorado is pictured on Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Amid a nationwide race to develop large data centers to drive the artificial intelligence boom, some local Colorado governments hit pause by enacting moratoriums to research what local regulations make sense.
Public criticism concerns the environmental and health effects of data centers, especially hyperscale sites that provide massive computing power for companies like Google and Amazon, and inaction from the state government.
“The pushback against data centers is only growing right now,” state Sen. Cathy Kipp, a Fort Collins Democrat who sponsored a data center regulatory bill this year, said.
“There is a place for data science in the world because we do so much online and we do so much with electronics and data,” she said. “But people are failing to recognize the environmental concerns and … how the whole massive expansion of the hyperscale (centers) seems to be being built in a financially unsustainable way. I don’t know if we can solve the problem before the bubble bursts.”
Data centers can range from a single room in a company’s office to millions of square feet. They house servers and data storage infrastructure and have been used for decades to keep websites online, process digital payments and enable streaming, among many other uses. Recently, data centers increasingly are built to train and run AI and cloud storage, a workload that requires a bigger footprint and significantly more energy and water. One federally-funded study found that data centers accounted for 4.4% of the country’s energy usage in 2023 and could triple by 2028. The seemingly-unchecked proliferation is causing concern across the country.

A recent Gallup poll found that about 70% of Americans oppose data center construction in their town. Respondents were concerned about centers’ energy and water use, which they fear could lead to higher utility bills. They also cited worries about diesel exhaust from generators and noise pollution, as the humming of cooling systems, generators and fans at some data centers can sometimes be heard for hundreds of feet.
Supporters and those in the data center industry contend that development creates short-term construction jobs and property tax revenue, and can set a city up as a technological hub.
The Colorado Legislature considered two bills during its regular session this year on data center regulations but did not pass either one. One would have required so-called large load data centers — with a peak electricity need greater than 30 megawatts — to seek renewable energy for its power consumption, as Colorado pursues its clean energy and environmental goals. A competing bill backed by industry would have offered sales tax exemptions for data centers, and also had a more permissive renewable energy component. Both bills died in the final days of session after negotiations for a compromise bill failed.
One hyperscale data center
New York is the only state to enact a broad data center moratorium. Tax incentives are much more common, with 38 states offering some kind of benefit to attract data center construction.
The sponsors of the Colorado bill that would have required renewable energy sources, Kipp and Democratic Rep. Kyle Brown, plan to bring data center legislation forward in 2027, but they aren’t yet sure what the provisions will be.
“I certainly respect each and every community to be able to determine what they think is best on this particular issue,” Brown said of Colorado cities enacting moratoriums. “I think what it also highlights is the need for some kind of floor from the state, right? Moratoriums only exist for a finite period of time, and then what do we do afterward?”
About a week after the legislative session wrapped up, Denver City Council voted unanimously, with strong community support, on a one-year moratorium on new data center development. Leaders said it was an opportunity to figure out what new regulations and zoning policies make sense for the city eventually to adopt.
“We aren’t the only council in the country that’s addressing this, but we are early among councils that are looking at what this means for communities across the country,” Council member Diana Romero Campbell said during a May 18 meeting. “I’m also grateful that we are not waiting for the state to decide what happens in Denver. We need to be able to decide how and what we want our community to look like.”



Quotation







This moratorium will allow us to think of equitable regulations that put our communities first.


– Serena Gonzales-Gutierrez, member of Denver City Council 


The ordinance created a working group to study variables like noise levels, air pollution, energy use and zoning. It did not stop any current data center operations or permitted construction, including the controversial new CoreSite multi-tenant project in the Globeville Elyria-Swansea neighborhood. About 50 data centers operate in Denver, Council member Serena Gonzales-Gutierrez said during the May 18 meeting. There are about 60 in the whole state.
“This moratorium will allow us to think of equitable regulations that put our communities first,” she said. “We are hopeful that our future regulations will preserve our water and energy resources, address climate concerns and protect our neighbors from any potential consequences that arise from the construction and use of data centers.”
A day later, Jefferson County extended its moratorium until March. County commissioners noted that “data center” does not have a clear definition in county zoning policy, and the closest definition is from almost 50 years ago. Like Denver, the county sees a moratorium as a way to allow time to develop and debate regulations.
“We know that there’s a lot of interest and demand right now, but I am glad we are taking the time to fully consider some of the significant impacts to both our public and private infrastructure, looking at what those demands would be on our electrical power, on our water supply, on our telecommunications networks and even on our transportation systems,” Commissioner Rachel Zenzinger said during that May 19 meeting.
Larimer County decided to extend its existing data center moratorium to February, and Boulder County enacted a six-month moratorium at the beginning of June. In July, Broomfield passed an 18-month moratorium on data centers that use 10 megawatts of power or more. Woodland Park and Monument, two cities in conservative counties, also voted for 18-month and six-month pauses, respectively.
“There’s a lot of information out there and there’s a lot of different definitions of data centers. We need to be thoughtful in how we do this so we don’t create an ordinance that limits businesses like the city or Walmart or Safeway from having a server room,” Woodland Park Council member Catharine Nakai said during a July 16 meeting.
In Longmont, the City Council specifically targeted hyperscale data centers, voting in June to cap data center energy usage at 5% of the region’s grid, or 100 megawatts. Hyperscale data centers are the enormous campuses typically used by tech giants to deliver AI and cloud services on a large scale. They have an enormous power draw. QTS, the largest data center operator in the world, has a hyperscale location in Aurora south of the Denver International Airport. It is the only hyperscale site in Colorado.
And in Lochbuie, a small town on the border of Adams and Weld counties near Brighton, leaders passed a moratorium that at five years is the longest in the state.
“Why not set a precedent across the state of Colorado that this is not something we’ll rush into, that we want to be thoughtful, that we want to give all of our residents time to let their voices be heard?” Mayor Jamie Jeffery said during a July 21 meeting.
Role in Colorado’s growing economy
Other areas of Colorado are allowing data centers, but with varying levels of regulation. In April, Weld County updated its zoning code to allow data centers with a power draw of less than 50 megawatts in industrial areas in unincorporated parts of the county. County commissioners a special review process that requires a public hearing. Windsor is also weighing code changes but the City Council has not voted on a proposal yet.
And in Colorado Springs, a data center for a California-based AI company is set for a final vote from the City Council after a tumultuous journey through preliminary approval and an appeal from opponents.
In a statement, Dan Diorio, the vice president of state policy for the Data Center Coalition, said the industry “plays a significant role in enabling Colorado’s growing 21st-century economy” by paying taxes and supporting “stable, high-paying careers.”
“Rather than enacting moratoriums which will discourage investment and send a signal to the industry that the locality is closed for business, the community and its local leaders should work with the industry and all stakeholders to establish reasonable regulatory frameworks that meet the needs of the area without deterring the industry and the benefits it can bring,” he said. “The data center industry will continue to work with Colorado residents, communities, and policymakers to support the responsible development of this critical infrastructure and ensure Colorado remains competitive in the modern economy.”
