name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The abandoned — CT’s talented and gifted students
description: Nearly three quarters of CT's 202 districts served no gifted and talented students in the 2025-26 school year.
text:
It’s not every day that you meet a student who can name all the countries in the world based on their flags. Have you ever met someone called “Brain” whose real name is Brian? What about the 5-year-old who can play advanced piano compositions and complete complex mathematical equations two grades above peers?
 What happens to Talented and Gifted Students (TAG)? They are the forgotten, underserved population. Some students come cloaked as twice exceptional or may be so bored in class that they have behavioral challenges.  
Connecticut is not protecting our geniuses; they are abandoned.
Why this matters
As a parent of a talented and gifted student, I’ve seen the devastating effects of districts failing to identify and serve these students. Likewise, I’ve witnessed bright, misunderstood individuals throw away their talents because systems didn’t support them. Personally, I’ve never been formally identified as talented and gifted, but I’ve been recognized for my creative talents, and I have one gift that is immeasurable: my intuition. Gifts aren’t always measurable, and don’t fit neatly into test scores. Also, I’ve empathized with Asian parents who experienced hate for their talented and gifted students.
There’s no oversight.
Let’s start with the Connecticut State Department of Education (CSDE). Districts are required to submit talented and gifted data to EdSight. In reality, the state doesn’t check the statistics. It’s up to the district to provide accurate data, with final sign-off from the Superintendent.
In EdSight , there are 202 districts; 31% identified zero talented and gifted students, and 73% served zero students in the 2025-2026 school year. Such is the case in Enfield which has a gifted and talented program and serves no students. Sadly, Connecticut identified 3% talented and gifted students and served 1.8%, which is 70% behind the national average. The U.S. Department of Education’s Office of Civil Rights estimates that 6% of public school students are enrolled in gifted and talented programs. 

Credit: CSDE

As a program manager in the Connecticut State Department of Education Performance Office, managing EdSight statistics, I would see this as a red flag if districts are legally required to identify talented and gifted students. Is it possible that all these districts have no such students, or is it more likely that they aren’t providing the correct data?
There’s no accountability and funding.
There’s no federal funding for gifted and talented programs; they are excluded from the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) . Therefore, districts aren’t required to serve students even if they have a program.
 Federal policies like   No Child Left Behind   often focus more on bringing struggling students up to grade level, rather than investing in students who are excelling. As a result, districts are pooling financial resources into children with disabilities because they are required to serve them, leaving the forgotten. 
The term “equity” fits its context.
Equity is meeting students where they are. Critics argue that talented and gifted programs under-identify minority students.
Recently, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani proposed phasing out gifted and talented programs to reduce racial disparities. There Black and Hispanic students make up 66% of the population and represent 21% of talented and gifted participants, but this is hardly a reason to kill the pathway entirely.
Asian Americans are classified as a racial minority group too. Nationally, Asian students are twice as likely to be identified. Caucasian and Asian kids represent two thirds of the gifted and talented population.
So, if you want to talk about equity, let’s look at our high-needs Connecticut students. The majority of districts served zero high-needs talented and gifted students. This includes twice-exceptional learners with a disability.
 Also, the   Washington Post   warned, “Politicians tread on dangerous ground when their pursuit of equity comes at the cost of children’s opportunities.” 
If gifted and talented students need a more advanced curriculum, they deserve to receive that at their level. Likewise, if a student with high needs requires a little extra support, then they should receive it. That’s what equity actually means. Similarly, Psychology Today argued that “Equity shouldn’t mean holding bright minds back. Equity means giving every child the support they need to reach as high as they can.” 
Identifying and serving the talented and gifted: the path forward.
Districts need to move away from the “identify, not-serve” model. They must have a highly visible and accessible process for identifying and serving gifted students, using multiple measures to determine who should receive services.
Del Siegle, Director of the National Center for Research on Gifted Education at the University of Connecticut, stated:  “We need to do a better job of identifying kids for these services, and then we need to do a better job providing these services.” 
More importantly, we should build systems that help kids nurture their gifts and talents, even those that are not measurable.  Connecticut is not protecting our geniuses; they are abandoned.
Danielle Brown lives in Enfield.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Ned Lamont finds places to speak Sunday; less so for Josh Elliott
description: Gov. Ned Lamont and his challenger Rep. Josh Elliott spent the last Sunday before the Democratic primary making appeals to urban voters.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont spent the last Sunday before the Democratic primary making  appeals to Black and urban voters from two church pulpits and get-out-the-vote rallies in Hartford, Meriden, New Britain and New Haven — all providing speaking opportunities reflecting the advantages of incumbency.
His challenger, Rep. Josh Elliott, campaigned in Bridgeport and at Ecuadorian flag-raising events in Stamford and Danbury. It was not to be a day for Elliott to deliver any speeches. His last event did put him amid 16,000 people, but it was a Nate Bargatze comedy show in Hartford.  
Elliott was in the audience, not on stage.
Sunday was the last day of early voting, and Elliott’s challenge of Lamont for the Democratic nomination is the only statewide contest in either party. More than 50,000 Democrats already have cast their votes through absentee ballots and early voting in advance of Tuesday’s primary.

Gov. Ned Lamont listens to a speaker during a Get Out The Vote Rally in New Britain on Sunday, August 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Lamont is the beneficiary of the contacts amassed over nearly eight years as governor, as well the political infrastructure that comes with being endorsed at the state party convention. He and his wife, Annie, began the day at First Cathedral, a Black megachurch in the Hartford suburb of Bloomfield.
It was not the governor’s first visit, nor the first time he used the church as an important conduit to the Black community. Lamont chose a clinic there in February 2021 to get vaccinated against COVID-19, sharing the stage then with the church’s trusted pastor, Archbishop Leroy Bailey Jr., who vouched for the vaccine.
Bailey, now semi-retired at age 80 as pastor emeritus, welcomed the Lamonts into the office suite he shares with his son, the current senior pastor, the Rev. Michael David Bailey. The archbishop would escort the governor and first lady to their seats with him in the front row of the sanctuary.

Gov. Ned Lamont greeting congregants at Rehobeth Church of God in Bloomfield on Sunday. Credit: mark pazniokas / ctmirror

His message at First Cathedral and then at the nearby Rehobeth Church of God, where the congregation is dominated with immigrants and descendants of immigrants from the West Indies, focused less on the primary than on what Lamont called the unsettled state politics created by the Trump administration.
At Rehobeth, where he witnessed two christenings before Bishop Jonathan Ramsey invited him to speak, Lamont congratulated the two families.
“Two things in life that get you through: God and family,” Lamont said.
The congregation applauded.
“Really proud to have my wife Annie here, the first lady. Wouldn’t be anywhere without her,” he said, pausing for more applause. “I’ll just say that there’s some storm clouds out there. I know everybody’s anxiety, but we’re here in this amazing Rehobeth Church, because we know that with God, all things are possible. With God, all things are possible.”
“Now I want to say one last thing. There’s one thing that really particularly hurts me coming out of the White House. There’s a certain sense that we’re not all God’s children. We seem to be saying we don’t all belong. I want you to know here in Connecticut, in my heart, we all belong.”

Gov. Ned Lamont speaks with New Britain resident Adrienne Benjamin about the Profound Autism Alliance during a Get Out The Vote Rally in New Britain on Sunday, August 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal and Hartford Mayor Arunan Arulampalam delivered testimonials on behalf of Lamont at the rally in Hartford’s North End. U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes of the 5th District did the same in New Britain. 
Last weekend, Lamont emphasized expressions of support from 10 members of the General Assembly’s Black and Puerto Rican Caucus. One of them, Rep. Toni Walker of New Haven, was featured in an attack ad.
Elliott said there was no special strategy in attending two Ecuadorian events on Sunday.
“That’s what was happening today,” he said.
He skipped a plan to work the crowd at a street festival in New Haven outside City Hall, the early voting polling place. He said he had campaigned at a Puerto Rican festival in the city earlier in the weekend. He was running late, and he and his girlfriend, Jenn Lepore, had tickets for Bargatze at PeoplesBank Arena in Hartford.

Josh Elliott arrives with his girlfriend, Jenn Lepore, for a comedy show in Hartford on Sunday. Credit: mark pazniokas / ctmirror.org

He agreed to meet a reporter on his way to the venue to talk about his day and the decision to take in a comedy show. 
“The work’s important, being seen, talking to people,” Elliott said. But he added, “I’m not changing the result by how much I do on a Sunday before the election.”
Once he qualified for his $3.75 million public financing grant, his ads went on the air, and he could increase staffing.
“We have a full team. We hit about 4,000 doors yesterday,” he said. “I think we probably hit about 5,000 today.”
The Bargatze tickets were purchased months ago. Is he a fan of the comedian who generally stays away from politics?
“I’m a fan of comedy.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Libertarians to nominate new candidates Wednesday
description: The Libertarian Party of Iowa will nominate new candidates to run for Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District and as lieutenant governor at a meeting Wednesday, party leaders said Sunday. Originally, the replacement candidates were meant to be nominated at the Sunday LPIA State Central Committee meeting, but party officials moved the nominating date to comply with[...]
text:
Jules Cutler, the lieutenant governor candidate for the Iowa Libertarian Party, spoke at a State Objection Panel meeting June 15, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Libertarian Party of Iowa will nominate new candidates to run for Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District and as lieutenant governor at a meeting Wednesday, party leaders said Sunday.
Originally, the replacement candidates were meant to be nominated at the Sunday LPIA State Central Committee meeting, but party officials moved the nominating date to comply with state law. The state Libertarian Party plans to name new candidates who can appear on the ballot in the contests for governor and for the 3rd Congressional District.
The original Libertarian candidates in these races were removed from the ballot by the State Objections Panel in June. In the 3rd District, Marco Battaglia was removed by the panel because they said the name he used as a candidate was too different from his legal name, Mark T. Anderson, which could cause voter confusion.
The panel also ruled the Libertarian ticket of Nicholas Gluba for governor and Jules Cutler for lieutenant governor did not qualify for the general election ballot. The state panel found Cutler had not submitted an affidavit of candidacy for lieutenant governor by the June 2 deadline, though Cutler and her attorney argued she was told by an employee at the secretary of state’s office that she did not need to submit this paperwork.
Both decisions were challenged by the Libertarian candidates in court. In late July, a Polk County District Court judge released a ruling upholding the decision to keep these candidates off the ballot. Both Gluba and Battaglia told reporters they planned to appeal the ruling. But on Tuesday, the Iowa Libertarian Party announced Battaglia had ended his campaign because of a medical emergency. Speakers at the Sunday meeting said Cutler similarly moved to end her campaign, allowing for the nomination of a new gubernatorial running mate for Gluba.
Iowa Libertarian Party Chair Stephanie Berlin said Sunday these two updates mean the party must choose new candidates to appear on the ballot.
“Unfortunately, Marco had a medical emergency, so he is completely withdrawn,” Berlin said. “So we will not be moving forward with the appeals in his case at this time, hence, the need for the nomination and voting for replacement Libertarian candidates. Jules is not able to continue either after the court cases.”
The party meeting was originally scheduled to include nominating votes for new Libertarian candidates to enter these races — a process that must be completed by Aug. 14 under Iowa law. Berlin said the schedule for nominating candidates changed because the committee had to first change its non-party political organization (NPPO) “vacancy protocol” — new language specifying how substitute candidates are chosen — before it could officially nominate new candidates.
The LPIA committee approved the new language, but Berlin said Libertarians need to file the new revised protocol with the secretary of state before nominations can happen — paperwork she said she plans to submit at 8 a.m. Monday.
After the planned nominating votes Wednesday at 8 p.m., Cutler said the chosen replacement candidates will go with her and the LPIA secretary to file affidavits of candidacy, minutes of the vote and signatures with the Iowa secretary of state.
“It’s fairly straightforward, so there’s no more, I guess, need to have a lawsuit — at least at this point,” Berlin said. “… Now, obviously, if there is an objection to this process, we will have to go through that process. But there are no more lawsuits specifically related to Battaglia or Cutler.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: In final days, Dems seeking 1st District seat take message to voters
description: John Larson, Luke Bronin, Jillian Gilchrest and Ruth Fortune focused on union rallies and door-knocking in their pitches to Democratic voters.
text:
In a campaign that’s been waged aggressively on the airwaves and through mail in recent weeks, the four Democratic candidates running for the 1st Congressional District nomination spent the final days of their primary campaigns knocking on doors and meeting voters face-to-face in blistering heat.
U.S. Rep. John Larson, who has been in office since 1999, faces three Democratic challengers who are calling for generational change. It’s the first time in 28 years that Democratic voters in the district will vote in a contested primary that features a sitting lawmaker.
Tuesday’s primary will test whether voters in the Hartford-based district want experience and seniority in Congress or a fresh face that’ll bring a new approach as incumbent lawmakers stare down challenges in primaries across the country.
In the waning days of the campaign, Larson and former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin leaned into messaging around labor, holding dueling rallies with their union supporters on Sunday. Support from unions and debate over labor records has been a recurring theme of the campaign and primarily an attack line from the congressman.
All four candidates, including West Hartford state Rep. Jillian Gilchrest and Hartford Board of Education member Ruth Fortune, fanned out across the 1st Congressional District Sunday to make their final pitches to voters on the last day of in-person early voting before Tuesday’s high-stakes primary.
Gilchrest and Fortune spent the majority of their weekends door-knocking throughout the district. The union allies of Larson and Bronin lent a hand to the campaigns in broader canvassing efforts on Sunday.

Former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, Democratic candidate for the 1st Congressional District, speaks during a rally with members of Carpenters Local 326 and the Uniformed Professional Firefighters Association in Manchester on Sunday, August 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Larson, 78, started Sunday with several dozen labor allies at a union rally before supporters embarked on a large canvass of the congressman’s native East Hartford. He’s had support from dozens of unions and the Working Families Party.
He also got backup from the president of Social Security Works PAC, which has endorsed his campaign. Social Security has been Larson’s signature issue for years, and he says there’s even more urgency with estimates showing the trust fund’s insolvency  in the early 2030s.
Larson proposes his legislation “Social Security 2100 Act”  every session to boost benefits across the board and have high earners contribute more through payroll taxes, but it has stalled in Congress regardless of the party in control — something his opponents have noted.
If Larson wins a 15th term and Democrats take back the House in the fall, he’ll regain the gavel of the House Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security.

Jon “Bowzer” Bauman  speaks during a labor rally for U.S. Rep. John B. Larson with local members of the building trades in East Hartford on Sunday, August 9, 2026.  Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Jon “Bowzer” Bauman, the president of Social Security Works PAC and the lead singer of the rock band Sha Na Na, leaned into his musical career as he propped up Larson, at one point saying the congressman will hopefully be flexing his muscles Tuesday night — a nod to his signature pose from his days in the band.
“You know I love the music in the ’50s and the ’60s. That does not mean that I actually want to return to the ’50s or the early ’60s before Medicare and Social Security, when most American seniors lived below the poverty line,” Bauman said. “And I know that labor knows how important it is to send John Larson back to Congress.”
Larson spent most of his rally speech focused on President Donald Trump.
“This isn’t only about this race. This is about the future for the country. But for the three opponents that I’m running against, I can put them to the side,” Larson said. “Because my focus is Donald Trump. It remains Donald Trump because Donald Trump is no friend of labor.”

U.S. Rep. John B. Larson speaks during a labor rally with local members of the building trades in East Hartford on Sunday, August 9, 2026.  Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Instead, allies like Joe Toner, the former director of the Hartford Building Trades Council and current director of the State Building Trades Council, did the bulk of criticizing Bronin and his tenure as mayor. Toner has argued that Bronin at the time prioritized developers over project-labor agreements in Hartford.
“We understand that folks in America are being attacked,” Toner said. “But there’s a couple of ways to fight back. You could fight back with a 30-second sound bite on social media, or you could actually do what you’ve been doing for the last 28 years in Congress.”
As Larson’s opponents take aim at his decades-long career in Congress, Toner sought to flip the script on questions around age and seniority that have been percolating in other Democratic congressional races. Toner argued that Bronin’s freshman status wouldn’t position him to take on Trump: “He’s going to be in the broom closet for the first two years, trying to get his name tag spelled correctly.”
Voters “know me, they respect me, they respect the job we’ve done. I’ve always run, not only on my record, in the past, going back to the time when I was a board of education member now to the United States Congress,” Larson said. “Ironically, my three opponents and Trump have the same thing in mind — they want to get rid of me.”
A few hours later, Bronin, 47, held his own rally in Manchester that included a slate of speakers from Carpenters Local 326, which has endorsed his campaign. He’s also been endorsed by the Uniformed Professional Firefighters Association of Connecticut.

Former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, candidate for the 1st Congressional District, speaks during a rally with members of Carpenters Local 326 and the Uniformed Professional Firefighters Association in Manchester on Sunday, August 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

The speakers commended his two terms as Hartford mayor, saying he left the city in “good hands” with the current mayor and made sure Dunkin’ ballpark was “done correctly” and that schools were built under project-labor agreements.
Referencing the flurry of mailers arriving at voters’ homes from the campaigns and super PACs supporting Larson’s and Bronin’s campaigns, Marc Okun, regional manager for Carpenters Local 326, sought to paint a different picture. He spoke about Bronin wanting to write letters to express his gratitude to workers building a school during the pandemic. Okun said Bronin had just won his second term as mayor.
“What people do when nobody is watching and they’re not running for an office, they’re not running for a position, they’re doing it because they’re a good person and they actually care,” said Okun, who said he hears from Larson every two years for a check but hasn’t met with him much in the past 15 years.
Bronin, who won the party’s endorsement at the May nominating convention, made his own reference to the ads in the race that have come from both campaigns as well as the super PACs supporting them. But he largely kept the focus on his vision for “rebuilding a party that needs to be rebuilt.”
“The carpenters are used to heat, and after about a month of b-s attacks against me, I’m used to heat too,” Bronin said with a smile, to laughter and applause, but quickly pivoted.

Miguel Fuentes, a council representative with the Carpenters Union Local 326 speaks during a rally for former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, Democratic candidate for the 1st Congressional District, with members of Carpenters Local 326 and the Uniformed Professional Firefighters Association in Manchester on Sunday, August 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

“I believe in my core that you don’t have to be against somebody to be for something new. We don’t need to tear a fellow Democrat down to say that we as a party can do better,” he continued. “We don’t need to tell lies about each other. We can just lay out a different kind of vision for what we are going to be as a country.”
Miguel Fuentes, council representative with the Carpenters Local 326, said he spoke with all of the candidates but said Bronin’s campaign was the one that “had the right idea about how we move forward.”
Fuentes said his union has supported Larson for decades, but he’s “fallen short.” Similar to Bronin and some of the other Democratic candidates, they’ve been critical of Larson’s laser-like focus on Social Security.
“We’re not a monolith. We’re not a single-issue constituency,” Fuentes said. “You can’t just be a single-issue representative. You’ve got to be able to command the information on all of those issues and address those concerns one at a time to get things done.”
Before the union rally, Bronin crossed paths with Gov. Ned Lamont — who faces his own primary on Tuesday from a progressive challenger — at worship services at the First Cathedral, a Black megachurch in Bloomfield that was built under the leadership of Archbishop Leroy Bailey Jr., who is 80 and has taken emeritus status.
“I respect the person I’m running against. I do,” Bronin said in an address to the congregation, his only overt reference to his primary challenge to Larson. “But to everything, there is a season.”
He paused, waiting for the applause that quickly came. He suggested that the archbishop set an example to be admired.
Gilchrest and Fortune didn’t have big or splashy events but continued to fill their days with canvassing and smaller stops throughout the 1st District.

Democratic candidate Jillian Gilchrest knocks on doors in Wethersfield in the final weekend before Tuesday’s Democratic primary for Congress. Credit: Lisa Hagen / CT Mirror

Gilchrest, 44, made her way to Wethersfield in the late morning for a solo canvass of the neighborhood. Even with a week of early voting winding down on Sunday, a few Democratic voters who came to the door said they haven’t voted yet but plan to.
Canvassing has been a major piece of her campaign strategy, like it was when she unseated a 12-term incumbent in 2018 for her West Hartford seat. She goes door to door to make the same pitch: Get billionaires out of politics, restore the Democratic Party and send a social worker to Congress.
In the final months of the congressional campaign, she said the debates and forum have given her more visibility, and voters are more aware of the fact that four candidates are running, not just Larson and Bronin.
As she knocked on one door in Wethersfield, Gilchrest realized it had a no-solicitation sign and quickly left a campaign flyer on the door before moving on. While walking away, a woman walked to the door and recognized who she was. She wished her good luck and said through the screen, “I know people voting for you.”

Democratic candidate Jillian Gilchrest leaves a campaign flyer on the door of a voter’s home in Wethersfield. Credit: Lisa Hagen / CT Mirror

Others say they recognize her from TV. A household with split political affiliations was critical of the Democratic Party. They said Larson had been in office too long and seemed lukewarm on Bronin. He appeared open to voting for Gilchrest.
Gilchrest believes Tuesday night’s results will be a true test of whether money or grassroots wins out. And regardless of the outcome, she thinks it sends a message about the current state of the Democratic Party.
“I think it says that there’s an overall frustration with how our federal government is not working right now. And voters are sick and tired of politicians saying one thing and then not taking action,” Gilchrest said while walking between homes in Wethersfield. “So I think that this primary really illustrated that voters want people who have new ideas, and who want to push for actual change, because this country is not functioning right now. People cannot afford to live their basic lives, and it shouldn’t be this hard.”
After canvassing and visiting churches on Sunday, Fortune, 38, stopped by Blue Back Square in West Hartford to watch her husband’s band play. Interrupting the music for a few minutes, Fortune took the stage to address a smattering of listeners, some who came to see her and others who were in the town’s center with their families.

Democratic candidate Ruth Fortune addresses a small crowd at Blue Back Square in West Hartford. She took the stage in the middle of her husband’s band’s set. Credit: Lisa Hagen / CT Mirror

She spoke about her family’s journey moving from Haiti when she was 12 and the logistical feat of getting through the state’s restrictive ballot access laws, getting her name on the primary ballot after she collected thousands of signatures via a petition to qualify. She said her work as an estate attorney also informed her views, saying she watched some people struggle to reach financial stability while others “amass insane amounts of wealth.” 
“I think it shows you we are at a bit of a breaking point in our democracy where things are so broken that we feel like we need to do things differently,” Fortune said after addressing the crowd. “And even for Congressman Larson, I would hope to goodness that he sees that he could have served differently and effectively based on the way we have pushed him as the challengers to his campaign.”
“I think if nothing else, I hope he saw that, that there’s things he could have done differently,” she said, not just on votes but on a different legislative approach.
Sunday’s concert had small foot traffic, but it was one of many things she had on her docket for the day before she resumed more door knocking. Two people came up to her to compliment her campaign but weren’t Connecticut voters. But she approached a group of 1st District residents who hadn’t voted yet and others who were new to the area. She informed them how they still have time to register as Democrats by Monday.
One of the people in the crowd was Lisa Sanchez Gonzalez, a 59-year-old Democratic voter from Berlin. She met Fortune at a Democratic Town Committee meeting months ago and has stayed connected with her since.
But she’s deeply torn between voting for her or Gilchrest. As someone who voted for Larson in the past, she said both the congressman and Bronin “are just not for me,” both on policy and style. She’s tired of the “bickering” and the campaign ads and mutes them every time she’s watching TV.
She said going to make a “booth decision” on Tuesday between the two women, whom she said she resonates with for different reasons. She cited Gilchrest’s experience in the state legislature and someone she knows very well. (She noted the Gilchrest campaign sign that’s on her front lawn.)

Ruth Fortune, 1st Congressional District Democratic candidate, greets her husband David Reynolds after they cast their ballots during the first day of early voting for the state primary election at Hartford City Hall on Monday, August 3, 2026.  Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

On Fortune, Sanchez Gonzalez, whose family are Cuban immigrants, said she feels a kinship with Fortune, who came to the U.S. from Haiti as a young immigrant and was undocumented for a decade.
“[Gilchrest] represents me as a woman, as a woman of a certain age,” Sanchez Gonzalez said. “And then there’s Ruth, who represents me as a woman, as an immigrant family woman. And I know that they will both fight really hard, and I know this about the both of them.”
Sanchez Gonzalez sung Fortune’s praises as they parted ways Sunday afternoon, explaining to the candidate herself how torn she remains on her choice. Fortune said to vote her conscience.
